item.title: [SCMP] Race for UN top job enters final stage: choice may ‘make or break’ organisation
item.description:
It is financially strapped, structurally flawed, infamously bureaucratic, reputationally damaged and riven with infighting.

So why would anyone want to take on the role of the next secretary general of the United Nations?

“I really think there should be some sort of psychiatric test for wanting this position,” said Richard Gowan, global issues and institutions director at the International Crisis Group (ICG). “The stakes are exceptionally high, and there is a strong sense around the UN that the next secretary general may make or break the organisation.”
item.content:encoded:
It is financially strapped, structurally flawed, infamously bureaucratic, reputationally damaged and riven with infighting.

So why would anyone want to take on the role of the next secretary general of the United Nations?

“I really think there should be some sort of psychiatric test for wanting this position,” said Richard Gowan, global issues and institutions director at the International Crisis Group (ICG). “The stakes are exceptionally high, and there is a strong sense around the UN that the next secretary general may make or break the organisation.”

The official start of the race to become the 10th UN chief in the organisation’s eight-decade history is under way, at an existential time for an organisation framed by noble ideals but dragged down by bickering and human failings.

While in theory the choice is made by its 193 member states, the real power is with the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (P5). The archaic several-month process that officially kicked off late last month includes secret ballots on coloured paper, with the largest voices going to major donors Beijing and Washington.

Once the P5 reaches a consensus, the others generally go along with it, and the new secretary general is usually in place for the five-year term by year’s end.

As member states assess which candidate will best protect their interests, the gossip-infused UN obsesses over every twist, which candidate is ahead, whether late entries will emerge, and what clues can be gleaned from the vague Chinese utterances and blunt American declarations.

“It’s everyone’s favourite parlour game around the UN,” said Elizabeth Cousens, president and chief executive of the UN Foundation, a civic group. “Every secretary general election is unpredictable, but this one comes at a particularly unpredictable time geopolitically.”

Shaping the selection is a concerning dilemma. Even as the Iran war rages, artificial intelligence upends societies and humanitarian crises intensify, UN peacekeeping has faltered and aid funding is drying up.

That ideally demands a strong, visionary leader capable of guiding the unwieldy global community through painful restructuring. But getting Washington and Beijing, along with Moscow, Paris and London, to agree – each with its red lines, parochial interests and rivalries – suggests a minimally objectionable candidate will prevail. Hardly the recipe for success.

“They’re all grey mouses of the system,” said one UN insider. “A lot of secretary generals have come in, made promises, moved a few deckchairs and lost their political capital.”

The hope, analysts say, is that a non-offensive winner finds their backbone once in office, as happened with past heads Dag Hammarskjold and U Thant.

Current Secretary General Antonio Guterres, who promised a “surge in diplomacy for peace” during his selection, has emerged as a cautious leader largely focused on humanitarian relief.

Critics also say he failed to seriously tackle cost-cutting, including expensive private school stipends and business-class travel.

While he is credited with forging a Russia-Ukraine Black Sea grain initiative in 2022, it was more in response to conflict than resolving the conflict itself, admittedly not an easy task.

One indication of the daunting challenges is the number of candidates, just seven compared to 13 at this stage in 2016, including some not supported by their home country. One withdrew after just two weeks; another just joined.

By UN convention, it “should” be a woman and the “turn” of someone from Latin America and the Caribbean, although these are not rules.

China has held its cards close, other than signalling support for women and Global South candidates.

“To sum up, commitment to the UN Charter, outstanding competency, integrity, impartiality, and the initiative to take responsibility,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in New York in May, outlining the characteristics needed for China’s preference.

What does Beijing seek?

Analysts say Beijing wants a candidate who will support more Chinese in top UN jobs, including China’s growing UN peacekeeping role, and back further integration of its Belt and Road Initiative, as well as its global security, development and civilisation initiatives into the UN architecture.

“The Chinese don’t want the UN interfering in their business, but the UN has been really meek on most things in the Asia-Pacific for quite a while,” Gowan said.

“They certainly don’t want anyone who presses them on their human rights record. That’s a given.”

The administration of US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, is looking for someone who is compliant with its unilateral approach to foreign policy, can improve the UN’s poor record on conflict resolution and can champion its aggressive financial reform agenda.

Washington’s US$4 billion arrears for core and peacekeeping operations, nearly half that budget, have sparked the UN’s crisis.

“Similar to China, the US has very entrenched interests on the world stage and doesn’t want the next secretary general to present themselves as someone who’s standing in the way,” said Daniel Forti, ICG’s UN affairs director.

“The Trump administration sees it as a ‘my way or the highway’ approach.”

US partiality is further fuelled by China hawks, Maga lawmakers and US social interest groups.

“The secretary general sets a tone,” Stefano Gennarini, vice-president with the conservative Centre for Family and Human Rights advocacy group, testified in Congress. “It’s fundamentally important that UN officials do not interfere in internal political debates about abortion or other controversial social policies.”

US-China interests overlap, however, in favouring serious structural transformation, even if Beijing talks in upbeat generalities and lets the US espouse brutal reform. Given the US’ responsibility for 22 per cent of the general budget and China’s for 20 per cent, every candidate has at least nodded to restructuring in their platforms.

“Many countries, including China, were thinking along the same lines anyway – that these reforms are way, way, way overdue,” said Dan Negrea, US ambassador to the UN Economic and Social Council.

Another change from past leadership transitions is that the Trump administration cares less than its predecessors did, giving China more opportunities in soft power.

“The US burned so many bridges, and China has taken over so completely and cleverly,” said Marc Limon, executive director, Universal Rights Group. “They’re not at loggerheads, but I don’t think they’re working together partly because the US is just useless. They think they can shout and everyone will do what they want.”

But both seem keen to avoid the selection process dragging on, given the Iran war, the energy crisis, economic problems and other pressing issues.

This contrasts with 1996, when the US vetoed the re-election of Egypt’s Boutros Boutros-Ghali against China’s wishes, ultimately resulting in Ghana’s Kofi Annan. And in 1981, after the Washington-supported Nazi-tainted Kurt Waldheim stood for an unprecedented third term, Beijing balked. That led to 16 contentious rounds of voting before Peru’s Javier Perez de Cuellar was picked as a compromise candidate.

Seven candidates in running

This year’s seven declared candidates include Michelle Bachelet, Chile’s former president and a former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights; Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, secretary general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development; and Rafael Mariano Grossi, a long-time Argentinian diplomat who heads the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The others are Macky Sall, Senegal’s former president; Maria Fernanda Espinosa Garces, Ecuador’s former defence and foreign minister and the UN’s former General Assembly head; Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana’s former foreign minister; and late entrant Olara Otunnu, Uganda’s former UN undersecretary general.

Five are from the Latin American and Caribbean region; four are women, and each has varied expertise, whether in human rights, global development, security and financial reform or small-state diplomacy.

Washington is generally seen as favouring Grossi given his ties to far-right Argentina. Some expect China to oppose Bachelet; others argue that Beijing appreciated her handling of Xinjiang as human rights head.

Betting app Kalshi gives Grynspan a 49 per cent chance of winning, compared to 42 per cent for Grossi and 8 per cent for Bachelet.

Trump’s long record as a showman has also spurred speculation that he could try and force through a preferred candidate using US funding leverage or pre-empt the process by announcing a winner at the G20 summit in Miami in mid-December to grab the credit and limelight.

Trump already floated Swiss football administrator Gianni Infantino for the job after he gave the attention-grabbing president a “Fifa peace prize”.

Expect stereotypes and sniping as race heats up

Amid the manoeuvring has come catty UN backbiting. That female candidates will not be respected handling security portfolios. That “woke” candidates will not survive Trump’s onslaught. That certain ages or religions are not ideal. That candidates who remain in their UN jobs while campaigning should be excluded.

The next leader will confront huge challenges. The UN has some 40,000 active tasks, reports, panels and working groups, many involving crises long since over, across 400 intergovernmental bodies, requiring some 27,000 meetings a year. UN initiatives are easy to launch but difficult to kill.

They also must grapple with two of the P5 – the United States and Russia – violating the UN Charter prohibiting use of force against another state, as Washington embraces “America first” policies.

And they will also face a World War II-era P5 that is badly out of step with the current geopolitical landscape, as India, Japan, Brazil, Nigeria and others clamour to join.

Under the selection process, candidates for the US$227,000 annual position are nominated to the Security Council and General Assembly, followed by interviews, town halls, visits to major capitals and several informal “straw polls” to gauge the preferences of Security Council members.

The first of these was held on July 30 and showed Grynspan as the early front-runner, followed by Rodrigue Birkett – with Grossi in third place.

“It’s supposed to be confidential, but they never are,” Gowan said. “It’s often out before the diplomats get back to their mission to write them up.”

These continue until one candidate gets nine of the 15 Security Council votes without a P5 veto, at which point the General Assembly can, in theory, reject them, although it never has.

The next winner of this poisoned chalice faces daunting odds and will need huge amounts of tact, wisdom, muscle and luck, analysts say.

“If they don’t use this crisis to make changes, then the UN will collapse,” Limon said.

“Like the League of Nations, people want to do good. But a lot of people earn ridiculous wages, golden handcuffs, and they don’t want to change.”

.

item.title: [SCMP] Myanmar touts economic potential but is it pie in the sky with it still at war?
item.description:
Rina left Myanmar shortly after the 2021 coup as military violence escalated against pro-democracy protesters like herself and the economy of her country, once a Southeast Asian frontier that had flickered with promise, ground to a virtual halt.

Now in Bangkok, the 21-year-old has found work in a cafe, a regular, albeit low-salaried income, the minimum required by the millions of her age group forced to survive outside a domestic economy in ruins, where civil war has killed an estimated 100,000 people in five years.

But her thoughts on who is to blame for the destruction of her country remain unchanged: Min Aung Hlaing, the junta chief who became civilian president this year after elections in the parts of the country the military controls.
item.content:encoded:
Rina left Myanmar shortly after the 2021 coup as military violence escalated against pro-democracy protesters like herself and the economy of her country, once a Southeast Asian frontier that had flickered with promise, ground to a virtual halt.

Now in Bangkok, the 21-year-old has found work in a cafe, a regular, albeit low-salaried income, the minimum required by the millions of her age group forced to survive outside a domestic economy in ruins, where civil war has killed an estimated 100,000 people in five years.

But her thoughts on who is to blame for the destruction of her country remain unchanged: Min Aung Hlaing, the junta chief who became civilian president this year after elections in the parts of the country the military controls.

He is currently in the Thai capital basking in the welcome of an official visit to Thailand, following trips to China and India that have offered a diplomatic ladder out from isolation since the coup.

In Bangkok, the welcome included a red carpet, honour guard, gala dinner and a chance to offer business leaders a vision of his civil-war-torn nation as a future regional infrastructure and investment hub – rather than the regional basket case his coup created.

“Min Aung Hlaing is the reason we are living here outside our country. The day he is gone – and the military is defeated – we will go back and we will build our country again,” she told This Week in Asia, giving her nickname to avoid any recriminations.

“But we will have to wait. Who knows how long? Maybe it will be 3, 5 or 10 years?’’

The realisation that the former army chief – wanted for war crimes at The Hague and sanctioned from the UK to the US – is firmly at the helm of an albeit fractured country, has also shaped Thailand’s diplomatic outreach.

Thailand has embarked on what it calls a “calibrated re-engagement’’ with Myanmar, a position it says is inevitable given the long shared border and interests that involve close cooperation, no matter who is in charge in Naypyidaw.

“We have issues every day and need to cooperate … so bilaterally we need to talk, we need to cooperate particularly on issues of border security: the border itself, how to work together to suppress the transnational crimes, scams, drugs,’’ Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told reporters on Thursday evening, adding that air and cross-boundary water pollution were the most pressing issues, referencing toxic run-off that has hit river communities along the Mekong and its tributaries in northwestern Thailand.

While emphasising that Thailand wants to keep Myanmar pegged to outcomes of a five-point consensus – an Asean bloc peace deal to end violence against civilians and ensure aid gets to the millions of displaced since the coup – Sihasak said there were also economic reasons to extend a hand to Myanmar’s government.

“It’s not just the immediate opportunities,” he told reporters. “Many of the private sector are looking long-term. If Myanmar returns to peace and stability there will be a lot of opportunities, whether in trade and investment.”

While Myanmar’s economy has shown signs of life this year after years of sky-high inflation and negative growth partly caused by a devastating earthquake, experts say it is far from recovering its previous footing which began with political and economic reforms in 2011 – a period of growth abruptly ended by the coup.

“The projects Min Aung Hlaing is pushing with neighbours centre on infrastructure construction, gas development, and energy,” said Htwe Htwe Thein, an associate professor of international business at Curtin University in Australia.

Min Aung Hlaing’s economic plans pivot on highways, railways, dams and power projects, she added, to remodel the war-shattered but strategically important country – pinned between India, China and Thailand – as a manufacturing hub in the heart of Asia’s supply chains.

But “serious obstacles’’ stand in the way of that bright vision, Htwe Htwe Thein added, in a country where the United Nations say 16 million people – nearly a third of the population – need humanitarian relief and foreign investment has collapsed as the war has deepened.

“For one, how do you build infrastructure corridors through active war zones? No serious investor is going to commit capital to projects running through contested territory the government doesn’t fully control,” she said.

“Layer sanctions and the banking restrictions that follow on top of that, and any financing tied to Myanmar comes under heavy scrutiny at every step.”

That leaves economic drivers of jade and gems, tin, copper and rare earths operated by military cronies and shadowy tycoons rather than creating a wider economic base as the likely outcome, she added.

“Real investment has narrowed to resource extraction carried out with little proper due diligence, and also murky financial flows. None of that is capital that builds a manufacturing base or delivers broad-based development.

“It’s extraction and survival financing, not growth.’’

While the economic picture uneven at best, Thailand’s renewal of relations has come under scrutiny.

The militaries of Myanmar and Thailand share good relations that have stretched back decades, said Paul Chambers, an analyst of Thai politics at University of Oklahoma in the US, adding that Myanmar’s “abominable human rights record’’ has rarely been the deciding factor in their diplomacy.

Myanmar’s diplomatic reintegration in its Asian neighbourhood owes more to military gains of the last 18 months, he said, that were secured in part with Chinese and Russian military aid that has pulled back the patchwork of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic armed groups that at one point threatened to overwhelm the military.

Still, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is yet to fully readmit Myanmar to its main summits until the five-point consensus is firmly back on track.

Instead, Myanmar’s tip-toe back into the diplomatic fold represented by this week’s Bangkok trip – after Beijing and New Delhi – represents the national interests of its neighbouring countries, according to Richard Horsey, Crisis Group’s senior Asia adviser.

“China, India, and Thailand are taking on real reputational risk by doing so, and the rest of the world is watching,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ subtitle-less ‘Spider-Man’ screening shows deaf inclusion is just lip service
item.description:
The release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day in the Philippines was supposed to be a shared cinematic moment for fans who had waited months for the latest instalment in the superhero franchise.

But for some deaf viewers, the experience was defined less by the action on screen than by what was missing: subtitles or captions that would allow them to follow the dialogue.

That frustration, captured in a viral Facebook post, has pointed to a wider accessibility gap in the country, where advocates say deaf audiences are still too often excluded from cinemas, entertainment and public information.
item.content:encoded:
The release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day in the Philippines was supposed to be a shared cinematic moment for fans who had waited months for the latest instalment in the superhero franchise.

But for some deaf viewers, the experience was defined less by the action on screen than by what was missing: subtitles or captions that would allow them to follow the dialogue.

That frustration, captured in a viral Facebook post, has pointed to a wider accessibility gap in the country, where advocates say deaf audiences are still too often excluded from cinemas, entertainment and public information.

In the post, a user named Cherry Ann described watching the film with her deaf friend and urged local movie distributors to consider adding subtitles to films.

“My friend is deaf, and we were so excited to watch the new Spider-Man movie … We thought that subtitles were going to be provided,” she wrote in the post, which was shared more than 11,000 times.

“It was painful to see that I could understand what was happening, while she was just staring at the screen, trying to figure out what was happening. Imagine sitting there for almost two hours when you cannot understand the dialogue and you don’t know why people are laughing or reacting inside the cinema,” she wrote.

“This isn’t a huge request, we are just asking for accessibility. Everyone deserves to enjoy movies, not just those who can hear.”

The scenario described in the viral post was not an isolated case.

“I saw my deaf friends who were excited to watch Spider-Man, but the movie had no subtitles. They were unhappy and found it difficult to understand the dialogue and important parts of the story,” said Chindee Cruz, a content creator and part-time deaf special education teacher. “They were very disappointed because they had been so excited to watch the movie, but without subtitles, they could not fully enjoy or understand it.”

Exclusion zone

Inaccessible screenings can also mean exclusion from shared social experiences, according to Hennie Parrocha, a graphic designer and Filipino Sign Language (FSL) advocate.

“I remember watching a movie with my family without subtitles. I could understand the characters’ facial expressions, actions and emotions but I couldn’t understand what they were saying or follow the story. I ended up having to ask my family what was happening,” Parrocha said. “If a movie doesn’t have subtitles, I usually choose not to watch it in theatres because I know I won’t fully understand or enjoy it.”

Deaf advocate Ahira Lotivio said many films were still produced without accessibility features such as FSL interpretation, captions or subtitles.

“For deaf audiences, this creates barriers because they may miss important dialogue, sound effects and emotional details that hearing audiences can easily access,” Lotivio said. “The situation highlights that accessibility should not be treated as an extra service but as a basic right for equal participation.”

The lack of accessible screenings is not new, according to advocates.

Deaf people were eager to understand what was happening in society “and wanted to enjoy the same entertainment that hearing people could access without barriers”, said Angelita Capanang, a Philippine Association of the Deaf board member.

The FSL interpreter for nearly 30 years recalled accompanying a deaf friend to watch the musical film Les Miserables in the 1990s, when media accessibility was an even greater concern. Because the film did not have subtitles or closed captions, her friend asked her to interpret the dialogue.

“It was extremely difficult because the theatre was dark and flashlights were not allowed inside. I did my best but naturally, much of the dialogue and music could not be conveyed effectively,” Capanang said.

Philippine Federation of the Deaf president Mariah Agbay called for a removal of such barriers and accessibility to be “systematically integrated” into public services, entertainment, education, and other sectors.

Limited implementation

Several laws have been adopted in the Philippines to support the inclusion of the deaf community in mainstream society.

The Filipino Sign Language Act was passed in 2018, declaring FSL the national sign language and requiring the use of interpreters in news and public affairs programmes as well as emergency announcements.

The Philippines also signed the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2007 and ratified it in 2008, while the 2016 Closed Captioning Act required television networks to provide closed captions for news and public affairs programmes.

But advocates said those measures remained limited in scope and implementation.

For one, Capanang said, the laws do not require movie producers and cinemas to provide closed captions or sign language interpretation.

Even when provided, not all captions are accurate or of high quality, according to Lotivio. “Some captions may be incomplete, delayed or unavailable. Stronger monitoring, enforcement and expansion of accessibility policies are needed to ensure deaf people can fully access media content,” she said.

Such gaps showed that the inclusion of persons with disabilities was often treated as a compliance issue rather than a human rights concern, Agbay said. “Policies may exist on paper, but they are not always supported by adequate funding, trained personnel, accessible communication, or meaningful consultation with persons with disabilities and their representative organisations.”

Advocates say accessibility should go beyond captions – because captions alone do not meet the needs of every deaf person.

“For many members of the deaf community, FSL is their first language, while written Filipino or English is their second. Providing both high-quality captions and FSL accessibility gives deaf people meaningful choices and ensures that information is presented in the language they understand best,” Agbay said.

Capanang said some deaf people had limited written vocabulary because they had not had the opportunity to attend school, making sign language their primary means of communication. She called for greater support to encourage cinemas and distributors to expand accessibility options, as well as stricter enforcement of accessibility laws.

The government, film industry and deaf organisations needed to collaborate to ensure no one is left behind, Agbay said. “By working together, [they] can create a media environment where everyone has equal access to information, culture and entertainment.”

item.title: [SCMP] Thai teen kills at least 5 in school, after shooting grandparents at home
item.description:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.
item.content:encoded:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.

Police said 23 people were wounded in the incident.

The boy appeared to have shot his grandparents first before attending school as normal, said Royal Thai Police spokesman Police Lieutenant General Trairong Phiwphan. After class had started, the boy began shooting from inside his classroom, before walking out and continuing to shoot.

Trairong said the boy fired more than 20 shots and over 30 rounds were found on him after he shot himself.

Several family members of the alleged shooter told police the boy usually kept to himself and was a good student. They said they were unaware of any troubles he faced at home or school.

Harrowing video footage shared on social media, apparently filmed by a pupil during the shooting, shows children in blue uniforms cowering under wooden desks, as five shots ring out while the school’s automatic public address system announces the time is 10am. One pupil reaches an arm out to comfort another who is crying as the shots are fired in what appears to be a methodical manner.

“It’s really awful, this shouldn’t have happened,” Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters.

“I’m not just sad about the people who died, I’m sad that something like this could happen in our country at all. This is exactly what I’ve been saying – the reason the government doesn’t allow people to carry guns, doesn’t allow ownership, doesn’t allow licence renewals, is because of exactly this kind of thing.”

Anutin confirmed reports that the shooter was 14 years old and killed himself, according to Associated Press. He said the boy, who lived with his grandparents, had shown signs of stress related to school.

The gun, described by police as small and compact, was legally registered to the boy’s grandfather, Anutin said.

The prime minister on Friday also vowed to introduce a new firearms control law.

Anutin, who previously tightened gun ‌laws when he was interior minister, will now propose a law to restrict the carrying of firearms by the public.

“The new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns,” he told reporters on Friday, but did not provide any specifics for the envisaged legislation, including whether it will tighten gun ownership requirements.

Images shared by police showed what appeared to be the gunman’s weapon, a semi-automatic pistol with multiple rounds packed in a pouch, as questions emerged over his mental health and the motive behind the attack. Several pupils suggested the shooter had been bullied.

“Our school doesn’t check out bags when entering school,” Kittipat Choolert, 16, told This Week in Asia. “He fired several shots, I was two buildings away from him and I heard the gunshots, the entire school heard it and we were in shock.”

Emergency worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, 47, described arriving during the shooting and his team treating students with injuries to the back, ‌chest and arms. They found a teacher dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room a female teacher with chest and arm wounds.

Kiatikhun said he was called to treat the teenage shooter after hearing a final shot. “We rushed up ‌and found ‌that the perpetrator had shot himself in the right side of the head and collapsed. When we got up there, we checked his pulse, he still had one, so we started CPR.”

The school said it suspended all classes next week and staff had been instructed to work from home during that time.

It is the latest shooting to stun a nation where millions of firearms are in circulation, many unlicensed and unregistered and where shootings are commonplace, but mass killings involving children are rare.

Last weekend, Anutin was at the scene of the killing of five people in Chonburi, including Russian siblings, one shot by an alleged robber.

In February, a teacher ‌died and a ‌student was injured in southern Thailand’s Hat Yai district after a gunman opened fire at a school.

In 2023, a shooting by a 14-year-old boy killed two – a Chinese and a Myanmar citizen – at Siam Paragon, one of Thailand’s most famous downtown malls.

It was a tragedy that spurred calls for stricter gun controls, yet killings have continued, with regular police raids unearthing large caches of heavy weapons and pistols.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia, second only to Pakistan but far surpassing its Southeast Asian neighbours.

Data collected in 2017 by the groups Small Arms Survey and GunPolicy.org in their last extensive international study found civilian gun ownership in Thailand was about 15.1 guns per 100 people, compared with fewer than one per 100 in neighbouring Malaysia.

Thailand had 3.49 deaths by firearms per 100,000 people, according to 2023 statistics published by World Population Review.

“I think we need to learn why we still haven’t learned from everything that’s happened,” Krisanaphong Poothakool, a leading criminologist and adviser to the Royal Thai Police on police reform, told Channel One News.

“Why do firearms in Thailand seem so easy to access? The fact that children and youth have access to guns and gun sets is really not something normal in Thai society.”

In the worst episode of its kind in living memory, Panya Khamrab, a 34-year-old former policeman with a history of drug abuse, massacred 37 people – 24 of them children – in a shooting and stabbing rampage at a day care centre in the northeastern province of Nong Bua Lam Phu in 2022.

Additional reporting by Associated Press and Reuters

item.title: [SCMP] Trump signs new orders targeting birthright citizenship and ‘birth tourism’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday seeking to narrow birthright citizenship and intensify a crackdown on “birth tourism”, making a new attempt to restrict automatic citizenship after his original policy was rejected by the Supreme Court.

Trump announced the measures unexpectedly during a White House event, describing the Supreme Court’s June 30 ruling as “very unfortunate” and arguing that wealthy foreigners had built businesses around securing US citizenship for their children.

“They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen,” Trump said.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday seeking to narrow birthright citizenship and intensify a crackdown on “birth tourism”, making a new attempt to restrict automatic citizenship after his original policy was rejected by the Supreme Court.

Trump announced the measures unexpectedly during a White House event, describing the Supreme Court’s June 30 ruling as “very unfortunate” and arguing that wealthy foreigners had built businesses around securing US citizenship for their children.

“They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen,” Trump said.

The measures are likely to renew a politically and legally contentious debate that has increasingly focused on China, with Trump and Republican lawmakers repeatedly alleging that wealthy Chinese nationals and commercial operators have exploited US citizenship laws.

The first order directs federal agencies not to recognise the US citizenship of certain US-born children when neither parent is an American citizen.

It applies when either parent is classified as an “alien enemy”, a category the order defines to include members of designated foreign terrorist organisations and individuals designated as global terrorists.

It also covers children whose parents include foreign government employees, a category encompassing ambassadors, foreign embassy or consular staff, people employed by foreign governments in an official capacity and some employees of international organisations.

The order additionally seeks to deny citizenship when either parent paid to arrange for a mother to be present in the United States or one of its territories to give birth, including through a commercial surrogacy arrangement.

It also covers children born in US territories or territorial waters where citizenship is not already conferred by federal law.

The order describes these categories as “non-exhaustive”, leaving open the possibility that the administration could attempt to identify others. It directs relevant federal agencies to issue implementation guidance within 30 days.

The second order directs the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security to take action against “birth tourism”, which it defines as entering the US on a non-immigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth – or helping another foreign national do so.

Measures authorised by the order may include denying or revoking visas, permanently barring people from entering the country, removing those found to have engaged in the practice, and taking action against individuals or organisations facilitating it in the US or overseas.

The order allows the secretaries of state and homeland security to grant exemptions on humanitarian or national-interest grounds.

The measures test the scope of the 14th Amendment, which provides that all people born or naturalised in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are US citizens.

“The practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned,” said Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff for policy and widely considered the chief architect of Trump’s hardline immigration agenda.

Miller said people would no longer be allowed to obtain US visas for what he described as the fraudulent purpose of giving birth in the country.

US rules already allow consular officials to deny tourist visas when they believe a person’s primary purpose for travelling is to give birth in the United States so that the child will acquire citizenship.

The new orders go further by applying to entry on any non-immigrant visa, authorising permanent exclusion and removal, and targeting people and organisations accused of facilitating such travel.

Giving birth while visiting the country is not itself a crime. Previous prosecutions involving alleged birth-tourism schemes have generally relied on charges including visa fraud, conspiracy and money laundering.

Together, the orders appear to expand the crackdown by attempting to deny citizenship in certain cases and expanding enforcement against companies and individuals accused of arranging such travel.

Trump’s original executive order, signed on his first day back in office in January 2025, directed federal agencies to deny citizenship documents to children born in the US when their mothers were undocumented or temporarily present and their fathers were neither citizens nor permanent residents.

On June 30, the Supreme Court rejected that policy in a 6-3 ruling, holding that children born in the US to parents who were unlawfully or temporarily present were citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment.

Trump said on Thursday that the administration was now “ending it in a different way”.

White House staff secretary Will Scharf said the administration was confident the narrower measures would withstand judicial scrutiny.

“There’s absolutely nothing in here that runs afoul of any of the Supreme Court’s opinions on the subject,” Scharf said, adding that the White House would release a detailed fact sheet.

Trump claimed that “hundreds of thousands” of people had taken advantage of birth tourism, but did not provide evidence supporting the figure.

Estimates vary widely, in part because the federal government does not maintain a data set measuring how many women enter the country primarily to give birth.

Trump has repeatedly singled out China in his arguments against birthright citizenship, although he did not name the country during Thursday’s announcement.

After the Supreme Court ruling, he sarcastically congratulated Chinese President Xi Jinping and China for what he called their “massive Birthright Citizenship WIN”.

In March, Trump argued that the constitutional guarantee was “not about rich people from China, and the rest of the World, who want their children … to ridiculously become citizens of the United States of America”.

Republican-led congressional committees have also scrutinised companies accused of helping foreign clients give birth in the US.

The House Oversight Committee said earlier this year that expectant mothers travelling for that purpose came predominantly from China and Russia, raising what it described as national security and election integrity concerns.

The Justice Department has meanwhile instructed federal prosecutors to prioritise investigations into alleged birth-tourism schemes.

Cases cited by the department include those involving Chinese operators who charged clients tens of thousands of dollars to travel to the US and give birth.

Available statistics, however, suggest births to non-US residents from China represent a small fraction of total US births.

The National Centre for Health Statistics recorded 113 births to non-US residents from China in 2023, out of around 3.7 million births nationwide. The data do not indicate why the women travelled to the US or whether they misrepresented their intentions.

item.title: [SCMP] US presses China over alleged scam bosses despite growing police cooperation
item.description:
US President Donald Trump has personally pressed Chinese President Xi Jinping over transnational criminal organisations involved in Southeast Asia’s sprawling online scam industry, a senior State Department official said on Thursday.

Michael DeSombre, assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that Washington was raising concerns about both fentanyl trafficking and scam centres “at the highest levels” with Beijing.

“President Trump has raised transnational criminal organisations with President Xi,” DeSombre said during a hearing on Washington’s response to global scam operations.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has personally pressed Chinese President Xi Jinping over transnational criminal organisations involved in Southeast Asia’s sprawling online scam industry, a senior State Department official said on Thursday.

Michael DeSombre, assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that Washington was raising concerns about both fentanyl trafficking and scam centres “at the highest levels” with Beijing.

“President Trump has raised transnational criminal organisations with President Xi,” DeSombre said during a hearing on Washington’s response to global scam operations.

He said the US had urged Beijing to demonstrate that it was not helping alleged Chinese crime bosses evade international accountability.

“We’ve encouraged China to demonstrate that it is not abetting these crimes by allowing Chinese crime bosses to be held accountable internationally,” DeSombre said.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

DeSombre's comments come as the Federal Bureau of Investigation has expanded cooperation with Chinese authorities on cyberfraud and other transnational crimes, including through exchanges of law-enforcement personnel and joint operations.

The unusual partnership has created a delicate balance for Washington: US officials are seeking Beijing’s help dismantling criminal networks while questioning whether China is doing enough to hold their leaders accountable for crimes committed against Americans.

Pressure on Beijing

Although major scam compounds are concentrated in Southeast Asian countries including Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, US officials and international investigators have linked many of the operations to Chinese transnational criminal groups.

The compounds frequently rely on trafficked workers who are lured with fraudulent job offers and then forced under threats of violence to conduct online scams.

Senator Jim Risch, the Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the compounds had become a multibillion-dollar criminal industry involving human trafficking, money laundering, drugs and arms.

“As these scam centres evolve to use AI and other technologies to stay ahead of law enforcement, it is more important than ever that we mount an effective response,” Risch said.

Fraudsters increasingly use artificial intelligence to create realistic voices, messages and online identities, allowing them to impersonate relatives, employers and government officials. Such technology has been deployed in romance scams, fraudulent job offers, investment schemes and sextortion.

Americans reported losing more than US$12.5 billion to fraud in 2024, according to the Federal Trade Commission, although authorities say the actual total is likely considerably higher because many victims do not report their losses.

DeSombre said a preliminary US estimate placed reported American losses to Southeast Asia-based scam groups alone at US$12.5 billion in 2025. The State Department expected its final estimate to be “significantly higher”, according to his written testimony.

Lawmakers questioned whether Beijing was concentrating its enforcement efforts on operations targeting Chinese citizens while doing less to stop the victimisation of Americans and other foreigners.

“What about the idea that China is selectively enforcing the law on these scam operators that are targeting Chinese citizens, but not really worrying about Americans or other foreigners?” asked Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican from Nebraska.

DeSombre said Washington was urging governments in the region not to return suspected criminal leaders to China before they could be held accountable elsewhere for alleged crimes against foreign victims.

A prominent example is Chen Zhi, the founder and chairman of Cambodia-based Prince Holding Group. Cambodia extradited Chen to China in January after arresting him at Beijing’s request.

US prosecutors have separately charged Chen with wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracies, alleging that he directed forced-labour scam compounds in Cambodia. He has not faced those charges in a US court.

The US Justice Department also filed a civil action seeking the forfeiture of roughly 127,000 bitcoin linked to the alleged operation and valued at about US$15 billion when the action was announced. The department described it as the largest forfeiture action in its history.

China has conducted its own sweeping crackdown on online fraud, working with Southeast Asian governments on raids and the repatriation of suspects.

Analysts say Beijing’s campaign sharply reduced scams targeting Chinese citizens but also accelerated a shift by many syndicates towards American and other foreign victims.

One common form of investment fraud is known as “pig butchering”, derived from the Chinese term shazhupan . Scammers cultivate a victim’s trust over an extended period before persuading the person to transfer money into fraudulent investments.

Expanding cooperation

Despite Washington’s criticism, cooperation between Chinese and American law enforcement agencies has grown substantially over the past year.

FBI Director Kash Patel recently told Reuters that the bureau and China’s Ministry of Public Security had established working groups covering cyberfraud, fentanyl, crimes against children and fugitives.

The cooperation has included reciprocal visits by officials, intelligence sharing and joint operations. Patel said Chinese officers had visited FBI facilities in the United States, while American agents had travelled to China to work on cases, according to reports.

Patel visited Beijing in July and met Chinese Public Security Minister Wang Xiaohong, with both sides pledging to deepen what Chinese state media described as “practical cooperation” against transnational crime.

The closer relationship has nevertheless prompted concerns among former US law-enforcement officials about the counter-intelligence risks of allowing Chinese security personnel inside FBI facilities and sharing investigative information with them. Patel has said the exchanges are narrowly limited and that foreign visitors are vetted.

Trump signed an executive order in March directing federal agencies to develop a plan to disrupt cybercrime, fraud and predatory financial schemes targeting Americans.

The administration has also formed a 13-country Counter-Scams Contact Group to coordinate law enforcement, asset seizures, sanctions and information sharing. China is not among the countries listed as members of the group.

Congress is considering the bipartisan Scam Compound Accountability and Mobilisation Act, introduced by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat from New Hampshire.

The legislation would establish a government strategy against overseas scam compounds and human trafficking, authorise sanctions against people and entities supporting the networks, and improve help for victims.

“The good news is that the United States has begun responding to this threat,” Shaheen said. “If these criminal organisations operate across borders, our response has to operate across borders.”

item.title: [SCMP] US sanctions Cuba’s military representative in Beijing over China procurement
item.description:
The United States sanctioned Cuba’s senior military representative in Beijing on Thursday, accusing him of helping procure military-related equipment from China for the island’s armed forces.

Waldo Perez Cortes, Cuba’s military, naval and air attache in Beijing, was among six Cuban nationals and five entities added to the US Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list.

The US State Department said Perez Cortes was an official of Cuba’s Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces, known as MINFAR, who had been “involved in the procurement of military-related equipment from China to Cuba”.
item.content:encoded:
The United States sanctioned Cuba’s senior military representative in Beijing on Thursday, accusing him of helping procure military-related equipment from China for the island’s armed forces.

Waldo Perez Cortes, Cuba’s military, naval and air attache in Beijing, was among six Cuban nationals and five entities added to the US Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list.

The US State Department said Perez Cortes was an official of Cuba’s Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces, known as MINFAR, who had been “involved in the procurement of military-related equipment from China to Cuba”.

It did not identify the equipment, Chinese suppliers or transactions allegedly involved.

Cuban state news agency Prensa Latina has identified Perez Cortes as a senior colonel serving as Cuba’s military, naval and air attache in Beijing.

Perez Cortes has appeared publicly alongside senior officers from China’s People’s Liberation Army and spoken about Beijing’s support for Cuba’s defence capabilities.

At a reception in Beijing in November 2025, he said Cuba received help from several friendly countries, including China, as it worked to strengthen its defensive capacity, according to Prensa Latina.

Lieutenant General Wu Aimin and military, naval and air attaches accredited to China attended the event, the Cuban news agency reported.

The US State Department declined to make further comments beyond the official statement of the announcement. The South China Morning Post has also contacted the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment on the allegations and sanctions.

The sanctions package also targeted several Cuban officials and state enterprises accused of obtaining military equipment from China and Russia.

Among them was Heriberto Sanchez Alleyne, director general of the state-owned importer Tecnoimport. The State Department accused Sanchez of procuring military-related equipment and services from China and Russia.

Tecnoimport, a subsidiary of Cuba’s military-controlled Grupo de Administracion Empresarial SA, or GAESA, imported military equipment on behalf of MINFAR, according to the department. Washington alleged that the company had acquired military-related equipment from China and Russia.

Another sanctioned company, Duna SA, was accused of importing military-related equipment from the two countries.

Also sanctioned was Monica Milian Gomez, whom the State Department identified as Cuba’s military attache to Russia. The department accused her of involvement in transferring military-related equipment from Russia to Cuba.

Jose Antonio Remon Rodriguez, head of MINFAR’s Foreign Relations Directorate, was accused of involvement in transferring military-related equipment from China and Russia to Cuba.

Oscar Enrique Biosca Gallego, head of MINFAR’s Economic Directorate, allegedly participated in efforts to procure military-related equipment from both countries.

The other newly sanctioned officials included Roberto Jesus Viciana Mousset, director general of Cuba’s Military Industries Union, and Sanchez.

Actions taken under Trump order that broadened US sanctions powers

Defence Minister Alvaro Lopez Miera and Roberto Legra Sotolongo, chief of the general staff and first deputy minister of MINFAR, were also designated under the new Cuba-related sanctions authority. Both were already sanctioned under a separate US human-rights programme.

The State Department accused Lopez Miera of advancing Cuba’s foreign military cooperation and Legra of attempting to procure weapons systems from Russia.

The entities targeted included Cuba’s Military Industries Union, known by its Spanish initials UIM, and four companies involved in military equipment, technical products and trade: Tecnoimport, Tecnotex, Duna SA and the Yuri Gagarin Military Industrial Enterprise.

The State Department described UIM as a military holding company responsible for producing and repairing weapons and equipment for Cuba’s armed forces. It accused the company of working with Russian defence entities to modernise Russian-origin weapons systems.

The Yuri Gagarin enterprise was accused of maintaining and repairing Cuba’s Russian-made military aircraft, while Tecnotex allegedly took part in efforts to refurbish the country’s Russian-origin helicopter fleet.

The action was taken under an executive order signed by US President Donald Trump in May that broadened Washington’s authority to sanction foreign individuals and organisations associated with key sectors of Cuba’s economy or the Cuban government.

Perez Cortes and five other MINFAR officials were designated under a provision covering leaders and officials of the Cuban government or newly blocked entities.

Four of the companies were designated for operating in Cuba’s defence sector, while Tecnotex was targeted for acting on behalf of the Cuban government.

US accuses Cuba of being staging ground for China, Russia, Iran plans

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio accused Cuba of serving as a staging ground from which China, Russia and Iran could conduct operations against the United States.

“Today, the Trump administration is taking further action to protect our national security by sanctioning entities and individuals who facilitate Havana’s military relationships and the shipments of arms to the Cuban regime,” Rubio said.

Any property belonging to those designated that is in the United States or under the control of US persons must be frozen and reported to Treasury. American individuals and companies are generally prohibited from conducting transactions involving them.

Foreign individuals and financial institutions may also risk US sanctions if they transact with the designated parties or operate in specified sectors of Cuba’s economy, according to the State Department.

The sanctions come amid heightened scrutiny in Washington of Cuba’s security relationships with China and Russia.

A State Department report released last month alleged that three of 18 foreign-linked intelligence facilities in Cuba were operated by China, while other sites had connections to Russia. Beijing and Havana have repeatedly rejected US allegations about Chinese intelligence activity on the island.

The Trump administration has intensified economic pressure on Cuba this year, targeting senior officials, military-controlled businesses, banks, mining companies, energy suppliers and other state enterprises.

Washington says the campaign is intended to deny resources to Cuba’s political and military leadership. Havana has denounced the measures as economic coercion that worsens shortages and harms ordinary Cubans.

Beijing has repeatedly opposed Washington’s pressure campaign against Havana. China’s foreign ministry said last week that the US should stop its threats of force, unilateral sanctions and blockade against Cuba, adding that China would continue supporting the country in defending its sovereignty and opposing external interference.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond call centres? Philippines reopens Manila for outsourcing edge
item.description:
The Philippines is reopening Metro Manila to new outsourcing hubs as it tries to defend its place in the global services market and win more complex work from multinational companies.

Officials, industry executives and property analysts say the move could help the country compete for higher-value offshore functions – from software engineering and finance to healthcare documentation, data work and AI-related services – by making more modern, incentive-eligible office space available in the capital.

But the decision has also revived a concern raised when new IT parks in the capital were restricted seven years ago: whether allowing more investment back into Manila could weaken the push to build outsourcing hubs in provincial cities such as Cebu, Davao and Clark.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines is reopening Metro Manila to new outsourcing hubs as it tries to defend its place in the global services market and win more complex work from multinational companies.

Officials, industry executives and property analysts say the move could help the country compete for higher-value offshore functions – from software engineering and finance to healthcare documentation, data work and AI-related services – by making more modern, incentive-eligible office space available in the capital.

But the decision has also revived a concern raised when new IT parks in the capital were restricted seven years ago: whether allowing more investment back into Manila could weaken the push to build outsourcing hubs in provincial cities such as Cebu, Davao and Clark.

On July 23, President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr issued Administrative Order No. 45 (AO 45) allowing the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (Peza) to accept and evaluate applications for new information technology parks and centres in the National Capital Region.

Peza oversees special economic zones where eligible companies can apply for incentives, making its accreditation an important factor for outsourcing firms and multinational service hubs choosing where to locate.

The order partially lifts a 2019 moratorium which aimed to steer more economic activity into the provinces.

Tereso Panga, Peza’s director general, told This Week in Asia the reopening of Manila would not divert provincial investment.

“Instead, a larger Metro Manila investment pipeline can serve as a gateway for second and succeeding expansions into Central Luzon, Calabarzon [an agglomeration of Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal and Quezon provinces on Luzon island] and other emerging growth centres”, he said.

According to Panga, Peza has observed that global companies commonly establish their first Philippine operations in locations with deep talent pools, mature infrastructure and established business ecosystems.

Those initial Metro Manila investments could later lead to expansion in other parts of the country, he said, citing the growth of information technology and business process management (IT-BPM) activity in Cebu, Iloilo and Davao.

The Philippines’ IT-BPM industry includes outsourced services for global companies ranging from customer support and back-office work to software engineering, data and AI-related services, healthcare documentation and financial analysis.

“The Peza board is directed to formulate and issue the guidelines necessary to effectively implement the policy and ensure that the thrust to accelerate countryside development continues,” Panga said.

This Week in Asia has reached out to IT-BPM associations in Davao and Cebu for comment.

Panga said Marcos’ order resolved a long-standing policy constraint and would help Peza respond to the changing requirements of the IT-BPM industry, while opening opportunities for property developers.

The IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines, which represents the sector nationally, welcomed the order as a “timely and pragmatic policy” that would strengthen the country’s competitiveness for new investment.

“In today’s highly competitive investment environment, speed and flexibility matter,” said Jack Madrid, the association’s president and chief executive.

“Administrative Order No. 45 gives investors greater confidence that the Philippines can respond to evolving business requirements while preserving our long-term commitment to countryside development.”

Panga said Peza saw growing demand from markets including Australia and Japan for outsourced business services, digital operations, engineering and other knowledge-based activities beyond the country’s traditional IT-BPM base.

Five projects in Metro Manila have already received Peza board approval and are awaiting presidential proclamations that will formally designate their sites as special economic zones.

They are Altaire and The Yuchengco Centre in Makati City, One Trium Tower in Muntinlupa City, ARCA South 1 in Taguig City and Parqal in Paranaque City.

Sites designated as special economic zones allow eligible tenant companies to apply for Peza registration and tax incentives, though developers that build or operate the facilities will not receive fiscal benefits.

The authority said the five projects could be proclaimed within the year if they met all requirements, but did not disclose their planned office space, investment values, prospective tenants or projected employment.

This Week in Asia has asked Ayala Land, which is developing ARCA South 1, for comments.

Property consultancy Colliers said Marcos’ order could help resolve a widening supply mismatch in Metro Manila’s office market, noting that companies requiring at least 5,000 square metres faced a more limited range of suitable registered offices.

Peza said last month that 44 per cent of available accredited office space was considered ageing.

Kevin Jara, a director in Colliers Philippines’ Office Services division, said older Peza buildings “may face greater pressure to reprice, upgrade or reposition” as companies increasingly prioritised sustainability and operating efficiency.

He cited Quezon City, Mandaluyong and the Bay Area, which offered more Peza-compliant choices for global capability centres (GCC) and IT-BPM companies, as the most likely beneficiaries of AO 45.

A GCC is an overseas hub that handles functions such as technology, finance and customer support for a multinational company.

Quezon City has about 317,700 square metres of Peza-proclaimed office stock, according to Colliers’ second-quarter data. Mandaluyong has roughly 276,000 square metres of proclaimed and potential supply, while the Bay Area could add about 242,000 square metres of potential space.

Jara said those districts could provide scalable alternatives for companies constrained by limited Peza-accredited options in Fort Bonifacio and Makati’s central business district.

“AO 45’s largest impact will likely be felt in districts where the pipeline can translate more quickly into broader tenant choice and more competitive leasing alternatives,” he said.

Kath Taburada, research manager at Colliers Philippines, said the order could also upgrade the quality of Metro Manila’s office market.

Since the 2019 moratorium, the capital added about 4.3 million square metres of office supply, but only around 40 per cent was Peza-proclaimed, she said.

“AO 45 is not simply adding more space; it is helping unlock newer office stock that was previously unable to fully serve Peza-registered occupiers.”

The supply would serve both third-party outsourcing firms and GCCs, Taburada said, but the stronger strategic opportunity lay with the latter because they typically needed larger offices, stronger infrastructure, skilled talent and room for long-term growth.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong aims to be a global tech hub, but can it hold on to its young talent?
item.description:
At just 18, Hong Kong tech enthusiasts Rexan Wong Chak-chi and Ken Mochizuki are both rushing to deliver their business ideas.

However, their choices of launch pad could not be further apart. While Wong is eyeing Silicon Valley in the United States for better support, Mochizuki is keen to stay in the city and contribute to the local community.

Their contrasting approaches highlight Hong Kong’s advantages and challenges as it strives to become a global innovation and talent hub under China’s strategic blueprint, with artificial intelligence (AI) and research transformation listed among the priorities of the city’s first five-year plan, to be released by the government later this year.
item.content:encoded:
At just 18, Hong Kong tech enthusiasts Rexan Wong Chak-chi and Ken Mochizuki are both rushing to deliver their business ideas.

However, their choices of launch pad could not be further apart. While Wong is eyeing Silicon Valley in the United States for better support, Mochizuki is keen to stay in the city and contribute to the local community.

Their contrasting approaches highlight Hong Kong’s advantages and challenges as it strives to become a global innovation and talent hub under China’s strategic blueprint, with artificial intelligence (AI) and research transformation listed among the priorities of the city’s first five-year plan, to be released by the government later this year.

While the city boasts cutting-edge university research, critics have warned that an increasingly risk-averse culture and a lack of early-stage support may push young tech talent towards overseas ecosystems.

California dreaming

Wong developed an interest in AI when he was 15 after joining a class on building mobile applications.

He later connected with many leading tech entrepreneurs through X, formerly known as Twitter, and built an AI-powered app called Text Behind Image in 2024. He said the app allowed its 500,000 users to design images with text behind featured objects.

Despite launching his first product in Hong Kong, Wong is looking to San Francisco and nearby Silicon Valley as the future launch pad for his AI business, believing the US tech hub can offer him better support.

“The main reason was really the access to support for early-stage founders. In Hong Kong, I think there is really a lack of support,” said Wong, a computer science undergraduate at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“In San Francisco, there are a lot of incubators that help young founders go from zero to one.”

In January, he joined a two-month incubation programme with Founders Inc, a major San Francisco-based start-up community, making connections and receiving guidance from those with experience.

The “beauty” of the programme was having founders at different stages under the same roof, allowing them to discuss problems they faced, he said.

Intending to run an AI-powered market analytics company in the future, Wong is busy reaching out to tech start-ups in San Francisco and observing their operations.

Wong also pointed to the United States’ early adoption of advanced AI tools, such as models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, as an advantage, while most Hongkongers used AI “at a very basic level” and some tools were not even available in the city.

“So it is really a lack of talent density, a lack of support and a lack of accessibility to these tools and knowledge on how to use frontier technology that holds Hong Kong back, which is why I picked San Francisco over Hong Kong,” he said.

Silicon Valley has been ranked the top start-up ecosystem in the world, while Hong Kong has come 29th, according to this year’s Global Startup Ecosystem Report, released by consultancy firm Startup Genome.

On a scale of one to 10, Hong Kong scored only two to four for its start-up performance, funding, talent, market reach and the degree to which it encourages AI start-ups. In contrast, Silicon Valley received full marks for each of these indicators.

Hong Kong only scored one for its research and development capacity, compared with Silicon Valley’s score of five.

Other Asian markets, such as Singapore and Seoul, and some major mainland Chinese cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Hangzhou, also outperformed Hong Kong.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said Beijing’s strength lay in its strong research capabilities, supported by top universities and close collaboration among the industrial, education and research sectors.

South Korea excelled because major enterprises devoted resources to research in key sectors such as semiconductors and biotechnology, while Singapore had outperformed Hong Kong because of its high density of venture capital firms and incubators – all of which Hong Kong could learn from, Shui added.

“If we cannot have our own major [tech] companies now, we should think about how to attract some of the largest institutions from other places to operate in Hong Kong,” he said.

According to the government’s investment arm, InvestHK, Hong Kong was home to 5,221 start-ups as of 2025, with 186 of them focusing on core or applied AI.

The San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley, has nearly 200,000 funded start-ups, with 80 per cent of funding going into AI, according to start-up data tracking platform dealroom.co.

‘A-Eye’ funding

But as Mochizuki sees it, Hong Kong’s young tech entrepreneurs are blessed with abundant support, and the only problem is that they are not told about available resources, so more publicity was needed.

Mochizuki, who is studying electrical engineering at City University (CityU), learned coding on his own in 2022, when he was still in secondary school and the Covid-19 pandemic forced pupils to study at home.

Within two years, he built “A-Eye”, an AI shopping assistant designed to help visually impaired people identify products and compare prices.

The project recently received HK$200,000 (US$25,500) in funding from CityU and the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) through the university’s HK Tech 300 project.

CityU’s law school also offered free legal consultation under the programme, he added.

“My goal is to stay in Hong Kong and try to use my skills to contribute to this place and serve people,” Mochizuki said.

“Although other countries like the US or the United Kingdom may have better resources or a better culture for start-ups, the competition is much [fiercer] than in Hong Kong.”

Apart from university-based projects, Hong Kong authorities have made multiple start-up programmes available through the government-backed HKSTP and Cyberport.

HKSTP offers a range of start-up support programmes covering different stages, including ideation, incubation, acceleration and global expansion.

According to its latest annual report, 570 start-ups graduated from its support programme in 2024-25, and it spent more than HK$415 million on incubation and tenant support during the period.

Cyberport had more than 200 start-ups graduate from its entrepreneurship schemes in 2025-26, including an incubation programme offering grants of up to HK$500,000 and rental subsidies of up to HK$200,000, as well as the Creative Micro Fund, which helps early-stage start-ups move towards incubation.

The Home and Youth Affairs Bureau has also launched a funding scheme for young entrepreneurs to start their businesses in Hong Kong, Macau and the nine Guangdong cities under Beijing’s Greater Bay Area blueprint.

Shui said funding for early-stage start-ups remained insufficient as local investors preferred “easier and more certain” options, and investment activity tended to be cautious amid a turbulent economic environment.

“Tech start-ups have a higher chance of failure, but when they succeed, they can bring high returns,” he said, urging the government to step up support for early-stage founders.

A start-up usually goes through multiple rounds of financing, including the pre-seed stage, when founders develop an idea and work towards a minimum viable product (MVP); the seed stage, when they refine the MVP for market fit; and the series A to C stages, when they scale the business, before exiting through an initial public offering or an acquisition.

According to a recent Our Hong Kong Foundation report, only 10 per cent of founders in the city received support from venture capital or angel investors, 30 per cent got funding from the government, and 85 per cent had to tap personal savings.

But the report highlighted a stark imbalance in the government’s funding allocation.

As of 2024, funding was concentrated heavily at the pre-seed stage, at HK$49.5 billion, and in late-stage investment beyond series C, at HK$62 billion, leaving those in between – often described as the “valley of death” – largely underserved, with only HK$3.4 billion in capital support.

Apart from a lack of funding and support, Hong Kong founders have complained on online forums about high office rents, talent costs and the city’s small market size, with some pointing to places such as Bangkok and Shenzhen as better choices.

Headwinds

Alberto Moel, a professor of practice in finance at the University of Hong Kong, said it would be harder for young entrepreneurs such as Wong and Mochizuki to grow businesses built from their own ideas in the city, as the government and universities dominated the local start-up ecosystem.

“We are in a stage in Hong Kong where university research projects are the ones driving the pool of innovation,” he said.

“If your idea is outside that pool, then you are basically up against the usual headwinds in venture capital that have been around for a long time, namely that it is difficult to get capital and difficult to put together a team.”

Moel added that Hong Kong’s risk-averse culture was also reflected in the investment behaviour of venture capitalists, resulting in limited capital for very early stage start-ups or those taking on more risk.

In contrast, funding for such companies in the US was much broader because the culture there was more inclined to “try things and see what happens”, while there was much more capital in the country, he said.

Hong Kong’s young entrepreneurs would stand a better chance of success if they looked at opportunities arising from university research projects, Moel said.

“If the policy is not focused on [independent ideas], you are more likely to fail, and it is going to discourage you,” he said.

“I would recommend young entrepreneurs look at the existing platforms and work within them because you will find much better chances and opportunities to monetise [ideas] into a company.”

The government should do more to publicise and create opportunities for building businesses from research projects by linking tech-minded businesspeople with innovative ideas, he added.

Derek Chim, HKSTP’s head of start-up ecosystem and development, agreed that access to early-stage capital remained important in helping innovative ventures scale up, and said the park had teamed up with the private sector to catalyse start-up growth.

“While different investors naturally have different risk appetites and return expectations, we are seeing growing interest in deep-tech and innovation-driven companies that require longer development horizons,” he said.

The Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau said the government attached importance to encouraging and cultivating a thriving I&T ecosystem for start-ups, and acknowledged that its sustainability relied heavily on private sector participation.

It said the government would launch an HK$10 billion Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund this year to channel more social capital into “emerging and future industries of strategic importance”, benefiting companies at different stages of development.

Despite the growing range of start-up funding options in Hong Kong, Mochizuki and Wong agreed the city’s cautious culture still made it hard for young entrepreneurs to strike out on their own.

“In Hong Kong, the culture drives most people down a very traditional path – primary school, high school, graduating from college, working in a full-time job – and it is very hard to pivot if you want to change your profession based on your interests,” Wong said.

“Everything is laid out for you, and this sense of security is embedded into young Hong Kong people growing up.”

item.title: [SCMP] What China’s expanded funding for HIV/Aids in Africa means as US cuts health aid
item.description:
China is expanding its role in the fight against HIV/Aids in Africa by funding new projects and backing local medicine manufacturing as part of its signature health initiative, the Health Silk Road.

Beijing’s larger presence comes as traditional Western aid wanes following the closure of the US Agency for International Development and sweeping cuts to the World Health Organization and the President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar).

Pepfar was a major bilateral American initiative providing life-saving antiretroviral treatment and healthcare support for millions of people in developing countries.
item.content:encoded:
China is expanding its role in the fight against HIV/Aids in Africa by funding new projects and backing local medicine manufacturing as part of its signature health initiative, the Health Silk Road.

Beijing’s larger presence comes as traditional Western aid wanes following the closure of the US Agency for International Development and sweeping cuts to the World Health Organization and the President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar).

Pepfar was a major bilateral American initiative providing life-saving antiretroviral treatment and healthcare support for millions of people in developing countries.

Instead, Washington has signed bilateral health agreements with some African countries, though a few such as Zambia and Zimbabwe declined to sign the deals over worries about data sovereignty and sensitive health information sharing.

Following a recent trip to China, UNAids executive director Winnie Byanyima revealed that China’s Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund was backing HIV prevention projects in Lesotho, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe.

South Africa, which has about eight million people living with HIV, received a US$3.49 million Chinese grant last year to fund prevention programmes targeting more than 50,000 young people and harm-reduction services for people who inject drugs.

In Uganda, Chinese funding supports the Triple Elimination Project to end mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B.

Byanyima said the China International Development Cooperation Agency (CIDCA) had invited UNAids to submit further project funding proposals for regions facing distinct HIV challenges.

“Grateful for China’s strong commitment to multilateralism and understanding that global epidemics must be fought together,” Byanyima said in July after the trip.

The funding ties into Beijing’s broader health diplomacy under the Health Silk Road initiative, which has previously seen China fund programmes addressing Ebola and malaria across the continent.

According to the Chinese Loans to Africa Database at Boston University’s Global Development Policy Centre, China committed US$1.3 billion in health financing to Africa between 2000 and 2024.

Beijing also funded and built the US$80 million Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) headquarters and reference laboratories in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, as a gift for Africa to help fight diseases.
