The Chinese government’s approach towards corruption is essentially one of zero tolerance. That is why cases of this kind are exposed from time to time.

We do not live in a vacuum, and the PLA is likewise not immune from the wider environment. It is regrettable that such matters can occur within the military.

However, the exposure of corruption and the decision to bring those responsible to justice can also be understood in another way: they demonstrate that we are trying to cleanse the organisation.

As a result, the PLA could become more effective. Developments have also demonstrated that it has not necessarily been weakened by these cases. As I mentioned earlier, we have seen Chinese missile launches in different locations, as well as the effective use of Chinese weapons systems by the Pakistan Air Force, among other examples.

I therefore believe that these anti-corruption efforts are healthy for the PLA.

Some assessments have linked the PLA’s 2027 centenary goal to Taiwan. How credible is this view, and has the risk of conflict in the Taiwan Strait declined since Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump met in May?

I think the Chinese government still sincerely hopes for peaceful reunification.

This has been demonstrated not only in remarks made by the Chinese leadership, but also, for example, during the visit of the chairwoman of [Taiwan’s main opposition party] the Kuomintang to Beijing. The visit involved not only warm handshakes, but also 10 preferential measures. These measures were, of course, intended for the benefit of the Taiwanese people, and they must have been carefully prepared. This means that they were not simply ideas developed overnight.

People always mention the “stick” element of mainland China without discussing the “carrot” element of its policy towards the Taiwanese people.

The reality is that we want normal cross-strait exchanges. However, the Taiwanese authorities are afraid of such exchanges. It is they who have stopped this kind of cross-strait interaction, including even academic exchanges.

Regarding the discussion of 2027, it is worth noting that, over the past 10 years or so, many American generals and admirals have made conflicting predictions. Has any one of them ultimately been proved correct?

I think this is entirely irresponsible. There is also disagreement at the highest levels of the US government regarding the 2027 claim about Taiwan. For example, the remarks of US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on the situation in the Taiwan Strait are almost the opposite of those of his predecessor Lloyd Austin at the Shangri-La Dialogue.

I believe that China still hopes for peaceful reunification, which is why it has not established a specific timeline. Because China still has hope, it will not provide such a timeline. The absence of a timeline leaves all these people continually guessing, though.

We have not renounced scenarios in which force may have to be used. These circumstances are clearly set out in Chinese law. Nevertheless, I believe that peaceful reunification remains the objective.

Editor’s note: Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

What is your assessment of US arms sales to Taiwan after the Xi-Trump meeting in May?

I believe that the United States’ arms sales to Taiwan will be more and more difficult in the future, right from now.

If the United States continues to sell arms to Taiwan, China could take three types of action.

First, China could also choose not to honour certain commitments it has made to the United States, including commercial agreements, if it believes that the United States has violated the one-China principle. This could involve products such as Boeing, beef and soybeans. None of these products is indispensable to China.

Second, China could adopt a broader range of countermeasures.

Finally, China could conduct increasingly frequent and sophisticated military exercises around the island to wear down the other side’s nerves.

Eventually, I believe the time will come sooner than the United States expects when it will have to ask itself the ultimate question: what are the actual benefits of selling arms to Taiwan, even if those sales are lucrative, when they create more risks than benefits?

Xi and Trump agreed during their meeting in May to pursue a bilateral relationship of constructive strategic stability. How stable, or fragile, is that relationship?

This concept is significant because this is the first time that China and the United States have agreed upon such a concept. It essentially refers to a form of equilibrium of strength between the United States and China.

I would say that this is more significant for China. Many Chinese people may believe that the United States has bullied China and looked down upon China.

As to whether this stability can be sustained, I believe that the word “constructive” means a great deal. It reflects good wishes for the future, but the question is how the relationship can become constructive rather than destructive.

Given the Taiwan issue, there is no guarantee that this objective can always be maintained. The United States maintains a policy of strategic ambiguity over the Taiwan issue. It is not guaranteed that it would become directly or fully involved in a conflict.

Moreover, the China-US relationship is fundamentally a competitive relationship, although this does not rule out areas of cooperation. The question is which aspect is predominant, and the answer is competition.

There will certainly be many challenges to this form of stability. The Americans may emphasise fairness and equality while China talks about mutual respect. Basically, they are talking about the same thing. But stability most certainly rules out the potential for conflict in the South China Sea and Taiwan.

Regarding Taiwan, do you think the Trump administration – or at least Trump himself – is moving away from the United States’ long-standing policy?

First, he said American soldiers should not fight a war 9,500 miles away. Second, he said that he had not made a decision regarding arms sales to Taiwan.

I think he is inclined to make such a decision, but he may find it very difficult. He didn’t say much on the Taiwan issue in Beijing, but there could be another three opportunities for the two leaders to meet. What would he have to say on the Taiwan issue and the arms sales during those meetings, and how might Beijing react? He has to consider all these matters.

Perhaps this indicates a possible adjustment, although this is only my own speculation. Trump’s proposed arms sale would be the largest in history.

This may mean that the United States intends to sell a larger quantity of weapons on fewer occasions. In terms of frequency, it could make each package larger while reducing the number of individual sales.

If you look at the record, arms sales have become increasingly difficult. Therefore, each time the United States decides to proceed, it may sell a large volume. China would then protest only once, rather than making three separate protests against three different sales.

Militarily speaking, the strength of the Chinese mainland is simply overwhelming in comparison with that of Taiwan. Therefore, it does not really matter what Taiwan buys. Nevertheless, the Taiwanese authorities feel that they have to purchase this insurance no matter how expensive it is.

Does the US effort to rebuild its shipbuilding and defence-industrial base signal a deeper industrial competition with China? How could this affect the long-term military balance and both sides’ ability to sustain a conflict?

From a military perspective, the United States is no longer as capable as it once was of projecting power globally.

Its growing focus on the western hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific reflects the fact that it no longer has sufficient resources to maintain an equally strong presence everywhere.

The US’ shipbuilding industry lags far behind China’s. This impact on its navy is already seen. Some estimates suggest that China’s shipbuilding capacity is over 230 times larger. I understand why Washington wants to rebuild its capacity, including through cooperation with Japan and South Korea, but I doubt this can be achieved quickly.

The picture varies by sector. The United States remains dominant in areas such as AI, but the gap is said to be a matter of months; its broader industrial and manufacturing capacity has clearly weakened.

This raises two questions: has the United States declined, and can it recover?

I describe Donald Trump as “Trump the Declinist”. His promise to “make America great again” implies that America has declined. In his own words, it is “carnage” that helped him to win his first presidency because many voters clearly accepted that argument.

The United States has recovered from periods of perceived decline before, including after the Vietnam war. Some believe it will do so again.

However, I think the situation may be fundamentally different this time. Even during the Vietnam war, the United States still had the world’s strongest industrial base.

Today, that foundation has weakened, suggesting that something more fundamental may have changed.

China conducted a missile test from a nuclear-powered submarine this month and subsequently disclosed information about it. What is your assessment of the test and US reactions?

I think people are somewhat curious about Chinese launches, in part because China actually didn’t have a lot of launches in the past.

A launch of this kind clearly carries strategic implications, although different countries may interpret it differently.

From a military and technical perspective, missile testing is necessary. Even after deployment, periodic tests remain necessary to verify that the system continues to function effectively and that the relevant operational capabilities are being maintained.

However, regarding what US officials reportedly said about China providing only a few hours’ notice before the launch, falling short of the practice of other nuclear powers, I don’t think there is any international standard specifying how far in advance such notifications should be given.

I believe an institutionalised mutual notification mechanism would be desirable, but it is unlikely while the United States continues with the Golden Dome project [a proposed missile defence system integrating land-, sea- and space-based sensors and interceptors].

Golden Dome represents an arms race at the highest level and would [threaten] China-US and Russia-US strategic stability. Although such a concept is broader than military affairs, it is primarily about military stability. During the Cold War, US-Soviet strategic stability was based on an equilibrium between their nuclear arsenals.

However, in my personal view, China-US strategic stability will never be based on numerical nuclear parity. I do not believe China would seek more than 5,000 nuclear warheads to match the American nuclear stockpile.

I have always argued that China should possess enough to ensure that the United States would never consider using nuclear weapons against it first.

If China’s objective is to deter the United States from using nuclear weapons against it, how many warheads would China need?

Even according to the Pentagon’s highest estimate – that China may possess 1,500 [nuclear] warheads by 2035 – the number would still remain far below that of the United States, assuming the estimate is accurate.

My argument is that China should possess enough nuclear weapons to deter any nuclear adventurism by the United States. The required number would depend on two factors: how the US nuclear arsenal develops and how China would need to respond to those developments.

In the worst-case scenario of a conflict across the Taiwan Strait, China would not want to be subjected to nuclear blackmail.

The second concerns the broader global strategic level, where the objective is to maintain strategic stability. This was also mentioned in [China’s] 15th five-year plan. We should preserve global nuclear stability. However, the question is how such stability could be maintained if China possessed only a few hundred nuclear weapons.

People should not be excessively concerned about China’s nuclear weapons because China’s no-first-use policy is one of its longest-standing defence policies.

How will AI capabilities affect the long-term military balance between China and the United States?

American dominance in AI is not a sure thing.

Even where one side may possess an advantage in certain areas, China may be stronger in the large-scale application of AI. This therefore makes the overall situation more complicated.

I think both countries are working very hard on the military application of AI.

The character of warfare has already changed, and military forces must become adaptable. If you observed the military parade last year, you would have seen that the PLA has not merely been watching these developments. It has already taken steps to respond to the emerging challenges.

A challenge is that we are not fully aware of how rapidly artificial intelligence can develop or in which particular fields it will advance most quickly.

During wartime, not only people but also artificial intelligence may learn and develop at the fastest pace. We have seen how rapidly AI has changed the battlefield in Ukraine and in the American war against Iran. This shows us how quickly the entire battlefield is being transformed.

I definitely believe that rules limiting AI’s role, such as in military decision-making, should be established. But sadly, as we saw in many cases, sometimes rules are only made after an incident. During the Cold War, there were quite a few false alarms of nuclear attack. Hopefully we shall never have false alarms triggered by AI.

The US military has continued to strengthen its posture along the first island chain. At the same time, the PLA has increasingly conducted operations beyond the chain. In your view, does the first island chain still carry the same strategic significance that it did during the Cold War?

Regarding the first island chain, I do not believe that it matters as much to the PLA as it once did, because the PLA is much stronger today and the overall US military presence at bases in these countries is not particularly large.

Second, I have serious doubts about whether these US allies could provide effective assistance to the United States in an actual conflict. I think all these countries would seek to hedge against such a possibility.

Japan might be an exception, in the sense that it is legally obliged to provide military bases to the United States. However, whether Japan would go further and fight shoulder to shoulder with the United States is not guaranteed, unless it believed that it faced an existential threat.

That is why, when [Japanese Prime Minister Sanae] Takaichi described such a scenario as an existential threat, she was strongly criticised within Japan itself. There is therefore no guarantee that what she described would actually happen in such a scenario.

There has been stronger military cooperation between Japan and the Philippines recently. How does this development challenge China’s strategic interests?

For military planners, any change in the surrounding security environment is naturally a concern because it adds new factors to their calculations. These are trends that China must watch, but I do not see them as game changers.

In the South China Sea, Japan’s role remains largely symbolic. Despite its assistance to the Philippines, there has not been a Japanese naval presence. I would describe it mainly as a political gesture with limited military implications.

In the Taiwan Strait, we should first remember that even US involvement is not guaranteed. The stronger China becomes, the more reluctant other countries will be to intervene. Japan’s role would therefore be secondary, apart from providing bases under its legal obligations.

Japan would have concerns even about providing bases because it would have to consider its own security. Japan could not simply say, “We are only providing bases and are not involved.”

If US aircraft took off from Japanese bases to take part in combat in the Taiwan Strait, China would regard Japan as involved. Japanese leaders would probably make such a decision only at the last moment.

I believe the Philippines is also aware of the risks. It wants to make use of the United States, but not to the extent that it becomes a target itself. That is why it has imposed conditions on US access to its bases, including limitations on their use for attacks during wartime.

Against the backdrop of strained China-Japan relations, could military encounters between the two increase the risks of a military incident?

Chinese and Japanese naval vessels seldom encounter one another. So, the risk is low. But Chinese and American naval vessels often encounter one another. China, the US and Japan are all members of the Code for Unplanned Encounters at Sea, or Cues, and they also have an air and maritime communication mechanism. These arrangements provide technical rules intended to prevent accidents, although they are not legally binding.

All these rules are technical rules, but politics always exists behind them.

There has therefore long been a tension between safety and security. Technical rules address safety, but security involves broader implications, on which the two sides may never agree.

Returning to this particular case, it would of course be safer if the Chinese and American navies could deconflict at sea. However, even if they maintain a so-called safe distance, the question remains: what constitutes a safe distance?

Unfortunately, there is no regulation or agreement that precisely defines a safe distance.

Safe conduct therefore ultimately relies on three abstract concepts: good airmanship, good seamanship and voluntary judgment – and that judgment is inevitably influenced by politics.

The rules were made because both sides have the bottom line, that is, none of us wants an accident. So, this is contradictory.

item.title: [SCMP] Will new batteries give China’s EVs the jolt they need to charge past their rivals?
item.description:
On a cloudy evening in late April, a tech event hosted at Beijing’s National Convention Centre by Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) drew nearly 1,000 people eager for a glimpse of next-generation electric vehicle (EV) batteries that could reshape the global automotive landscape.

Gao Huan, chief technology officer for the auto business at CATL, the world’s largest producer of EV batteries, exuded confidence while promoting the new Shenxing product series.

According to the company, its new, third-generation battery can charge from 10 to 98 per cent in under six and a half minutes. BYD’s second-generation Blade battery, by contrast, takes nine minutes to charge from 10 to 97 per cent.
item.content:encoded:
On a cloudy evening in late April, a tech event hosted at Beijing’s National Convention Centre by Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) drew nearly 1,000 people eager for a glimpse of next-generation electric vehicle (EV) batteries that could reshape the global automotive landscape.

Gao Huan, chief technology officer for the auto business at CATL, the world’s largest producer of EV batteries, exuded confidence while promoting the new Shenxing product series.

According to the company, its new, third-generation battery can charge from 10 to 98 per cent in under six and a half minutes. BYD’s second-generation Blade battery, by contrast, takes nine minutes to charge from 10 to 97 per cent.

With formations of electric current and heating effects projected on a giant screen, Gao sought to reassure his audience about how CATL designs and arranges cells to keep its battery packs safe and efficient.

Though more convenient, fast charging generates heat that can accelerate degradation in lithium-ion batteries, shortening their lifespan.

Gao explained how CATL’s technology isolated individual cells to prevent heat from spreading, saying the Shenxing series used independent sealed exhaust channels, allowing heat and electricity to exit the battery pack through separate paths.

“To accomplish product reliability, we have developed industry-leading testing methods and created a world-leading testing and verification centre,” Gao said. “In manufacturing, we make sure every single battery cell is made under extreme conditions in line with a stringent quality control system, with 7,000 quality checkpoints deployed along [each] product line.”

The battery pack, which accounts for about one-fourth of an electric car’s cost according to industry averages, is among the most important components of an EV and plays a decisive role in the global automotive industry’s shift to electrification, as technological advances are key to easing concerns over production costs, range and vehicle safety.

Higher-performance and lower-priced batteries will further drive electrification of the global automotive industry

Davis Zhang, Suzhou Hazardtex

CATL’s views on the sector carry particular weight.

The company, based in Ningde, in southeastern China’s Fujian province, led the global EV battery market with a 40.2 per cent share in the first five months of 2026, according to South Korea-based SNE Research.

Total global EV battery usage climbed 16.3 per cent from a year earlier to 469.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh), per SNE data. One GWh is enough to power about 20,000 EVs with a range of 500km (311 miles).

The Shenxing batteries’ greatly shortened charging time “materially alleviates consumer range and charging anxiety”, Morgan Stanley said in a research note a week after the CATL tech event. “On the flipside, debates about the safety and durability of ultra-fast charging continue.”

Over the past decade, improvements in manufacturing and rising sales volumes have helped drive down EV battery production costs, bringing some electric cars closer to cost parity with their petrol-powered counterparts.

Attention is now turning to technologies such as solid-state batteries, sodium-ion batteries, faster charging systems, and battery pack designs that enhance thermal management, as more car owners switch from petrol vehicles to electric cars.

In mainland China, the world’s largest automotive and EV market, pure electric and plug-in hybrid cars accounted for 57.4 per cent of the country’s new vehicle deliveries in the first half of 2026, according to the China Passenger Car Association.

The cost of EV batteries was as high as US$1,474 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in 2010. By 2025, global lithium-ion battery pack prices had fallen to about US$108 per kWh, according to BloombergNEF’s annual price survey.

A price of US$100 per kWh is seen by industry officials and analysts as a threshold for making unsubsidised EVs cost-competitive with their oil-guzzling peers.

China’s manufacturing heft has given its battery makers a cost advantage, with average prices in the country falling 13 per cent year on year to US$84 per kWh in 2025, BloombergNEF added, forecasting an average global battery pack price of US$62 by 2030.

Chinese EV battery makers also continued to dominate the global market as seven companies – including CATL, BYD and Gotion High-Tech – were among the world’s top 10 players, according to SNE Research.

Between January and May, the Chinese companies commanded a 72.6 per cent share of the global EV battery market, SNE data showed.

“Higher-performance and lower-priced batteries will further drive electrification of the global automotive industry,” said Davis Zhang, a senior executive at Suzhou Hazardtex, a supplier of specialised batteries. “Apparently, potential technological breakthroughs in solid-state battery could become a game-changer.”

Compared with existing liquid-based batteries, solid-state variants promise higher energy storage, longer driving ranges and improved safety, with a lower risk of overheating or fire. Beijing has been backing efforts to commercialise all-solid-state batteries, which, unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, do not rely on flammable liquid electrolytes.

In late June, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said China would intensify its research and development into key next-generation battery materials, including solid-state electrolytes, to support the growth of its EV sector.

Several companies have already begun those efforts. Chinese battery maker WeLion’s semi-solid-state batteries, for example, power some of the premium EVs assembled by Shanghai-based Nio.

And in March, the state-owned Chery Automobile, based in central China’s Anhui province, unveiled an all-solid-state battery capable of powering a vehicle for more than 1,500km of driving distance on a single charge.

Chinese battery makers and their supply chain vendors are also striving to extend the lifespan of lithium-ion batteries.

Ganfeng Lithium, the world’s largest producer of lithium metal, aimed to raise the lifetime capacity of its energy-storage battery to 18,000 charges by the end of the year, which would allow it to last as long as solar panels, the company’s president, Wang Xiaoshen, told the South China Morning Post in May.

Gotion High-Tech, the world’s fifth-largest EV battery maker by delivery volume, also launched a new product in May that it said could be fully recharged over 15,000 times.

A solar panel is typically estimated to be able to work 25 years or more, while lithium-ion batteries could last up to 10 years, according to analysts.

In China, there is no industry that is not competitive. That’s why China’s products could evolve so rapidly

Wang Xiaoshen, Ganfeng Lithium

Both Ganfeng and Gotion said they had managed to produce batteries with a capacity of more than 580 ampere-hours (Ah) and were planning to boost it to over 600 Ah.

An Ah is a unit of measurement to reflect the electrical charge a battery can hold and deliver over time.

Such advancements in battery technologies, as well as the reduction of costs, partly resulted from the fierce competition within the sector in China, according to Ganfeng’s Wang.

“In China, there is no industry that is not competitive,” Wang said. “That’s why China’s products could evolve so rapidly.”

Even if battery firms from other countries were able to claim achievements in cutting-edge technologies, China’s prowess in manufacturing and supply chains would support the country in retaining its competitive advantage when it came to mass production, said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings.

Chinese battery makers are also moving downstream to enhance profitability and deepen their ties with EV assemblers in fine-tuning thermal designs and battery management.

“If competition boils down to cell chemistry, production scale and price per kWh, margins will inevitably compress,” Gavekal Technologies analyst AJ Cortese wrote in a research report released in May. “But if a supplier’s cell format, pack architecture, thermal design or battery-management logic becomes embedded in a carmaker’s platform, the battery supplier gains more durable leverage.”

This structural integration, described as a cell-to-chassis model, targets building battery cells directly into a vehicle’s load-bearing structure, which eventually helps carmakers reduce weight, save space and increase energy density with hundreds of redundant components removed, according to the report.

In late 2024, CATL unveiled its Panshi intelligent chassis – encompassing the battery, motor, power electronics, suspension, braking and steering – and encouraged EV builders to adopt the technology. The company said the chassis would improve crash safety, extend the car’s range, provide a platform for intelligent driving and shorten vehicle development cycles.

In March, CATL – which counts Tesla, BMW and Volkswagen among its clients – reported a net profit of 72.2 billion yuan (US$10.7 billion) for 2025, up 42 per cent from 2024.

The figure was only 8 per cent lower than the combined profits of China’s top four listed carmakers – BYD, Chery, Geely Auto and SAIC – which reported net income of 78.6 billion yuan in 2025. CATL earned 2 per cent more profit than the 70.59 billion yuan made by the country’s 11 listed carmakers, including smaller and loss-making players.

On July 24, CATL reported a record 43.28 billion yuan in net profit for the first half of 2026, up 42 per cent from the year before.

Robin Zeng Yuqun, founder and chairman of CATL, said at the April tech event in Beijing that concerted efforts were being made by EV builders and battery producers to pursue technological advancement to promote electric cars around the world.

“As Chinese-developed technologies rev up the go-global drive, we cannot rely solely on speed and volume,” he said. “We must bank on high-quality innovation and proven capabilities. We hope that what goes global is not just the Chinese products, but also the credibility of Chinese brands.”

item.title: [SCMP] Ready player 3: India offers Asean a US-China alternative
item.description:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.
item.content:encoded:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.

“That’s the main reason why we decided to sign up on short notice,” she said of the Indusfood expo, held in Greater Noida at the start of this year.

“With India having a bigger population than China … and a lot of them are vegetarian, we thought they’d be more open to those types of food ingredients.”

Sheentaro’s products were previously showcased at the China-Asean Expo in Nanning and Cordero said the reception was so positive that “when this opportunity in India came about, we said ‘let’s try it again’”.

Southeast Asian nations are increasingly looking to India as an alternative market, arms supplier and technology partner as China and the US vie for regional influence.

India is more than happy to oblige, observers say – though it also knows its limits. It cannot out-trade China, nor can it supplant America’s security umbrella. What is offers instead is room to manoeuvre, free of the demand to choose sides.

That message travelled to Manila last month, where India’s foreign minister, S. Jaishankar, used Asean-led meetings to press the case for deeper cooperation, calling it the only way to “de-risk and diversify”.

He spoke of energy security and food security, and how precarious both had become. Neither these nor public health could be taken for granted in this new “era of volatility and disruption”, Jaishankar said, identifying maritime trade as a further source of anxiety.

A more stable and secure future was in reach, he said, but only by working together: an animating theme of India’s Act East Policy, launched 12 years ago to forge stronger economic, strategic, and cultural ties with Southeast Asia and the broader region.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi were also in the Philippine capital last month for talks with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on the South China Sea, supply chains and security – a reminder of how much great-power rivalry still shapes regional diplomacy.

The economic dimension of India’s engagement push was on full display earlier in July, when Delhi hosted talks on upgrading the Asean-India Trade in Goods Agreement, a decade-old free-trade pact that officials say no longer reflects current realities.

Two-way trade came in at US$128 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to India’s Commerce and Industry Ministry – respectable, but only a fraction of the US$1 trillion and change that China did with the bloc.

Analysts say India’s strategy appears to be centred around pairing diplomacy with trade, defence exports and maritime cooperation, offering Southeast Asia a third option beyond the US-China binary.

It is best described as “a search for mutual wins”, according to Arvind Raj, a geopolitical analyst and associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ Centre for Multilateralism Studies in Singapore.

A more multipolar neighbourhood would give Southeast Asian nations more choices and more room to hedge, he said – as India, in turn, secured a larger foothold in a region that it had long courted from the margins.

Summitry to substance

For years, India’s Asean diplomacy has been heavy on the ceremony, but light on the delivery.

“Asean sits at the centre of India’s Act East Policy on paper, but for most of the past decade the relationship ran on summitry rather than substance,” said Oorja Tapan, a doctoral researcher of international politics at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi.

Analysts say the clearest evidence of how that dynamic is beginning to change can be seen in the region’s expanding arsenals.

During a three-day state visit last month, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi sealed a deal for Jakarta to buy BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles – jointly developed by India and Russia – making Indonesia the third Southeast Asian buyer after Vietnam and the Philippines.

A separate deal for Jakarta to acquire India’s Astra air-to-air missiles was also signed.

Pooja Bhatt, an associate professor of international relations at India’s O.P. Jindal Global University, calls such defence cooperation “not only part of increasing trade with Asean but also a form of strategic signalling” – proof that Delhi can deliver hardware, not just handshakes.

India wanted to become Southeast Asia’s “resident partner”, Tapan said, offering “capability without a formal alliance demand attached” and without asking the region to choose sides.

Pairing defence exports with renewed free-trade negotiations showed that Delhi wanted to be seen as “a dependable partner offering security cooperation, technology-sharing and balanced regional influence”, said Shristi Pukhrem, a visiting fellow at the India Foundation think tank and director of its Act East Centre.

Foreign policy researcher Joanne Lin concurred that weapons sales alone would not be enough to anchor the relationship.

India’s relevance depended on it delivering across “trade, maritime security, connectivity, tech and supply chains”, said Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and visiting scholar at the MIT Centre for International Studies.

“This is why India is trying to address concerns over trade imbalance, rules of origin and possible re-routing of Chinese goods through Asean, while Asean looks forward to market access with fewer barriers.”

Beyond US-China?

Ultimately, India’s pitch boils down to optionality.

Delhi is not seeking “supremacy in Asean”, according to Abhishek Sharma of the Observer Research Foundation think tank in the Indian capital, but rather is trying to advance its own trade interests while pushing for a stronger, more secure – and more multipolar – Indo-Pacific region.

This framing allowed the South Asian nation to cast itself as an independent pole, distinct from both Beijing and Washington and without the associated baggage, said Sharma, a junior fellow with the foundation’s strategic studies programme.

Lin agreed that India functioned as an additional option for Asean rather than a direct replacement for either the US or China.

India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner

Joanne Lin, foreign policy researcher

“They are looking for partners that can widen their strategic space without forcing them into rigid alignments,” she said of Southeast Asian nations. “India’s strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and Global South positioning resonate with Asean’s own instinct to diversify partnerships and preserve room for manoeuvre.”

In Tapan’s telling, India “lowers the cost of hedging” for the region, due to it being “aligned enough with the West to be useful, [but] non-aligned enough that buying Indian missiles doesn’t read in Beijing as joining a containment bloc”.

Still, Lin was careful not to overstate Delhi’s diplomatic standing within the region.

India “is not yet in the same league as China or the US” in terms of Southeast Asia’s “perceptions of influence”, she said.

“China remains deeply embedded economically, while the US remains central to security calculations. India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner, useful, non-coercive and increasingly visible, but still needing stronger economic delivery.”

‘Some way to go’

India still had “some way to go” to match the scale of Chinese capital, trade volume and state-driven speed, said Bhatt, the international-relations professor.

China’s trade with Asean was about eight times higher than India’s last year – a gulf that does not look likely to close any time soon.

But Delhi’s diplomacy need not be based on countering China alone.

India and Asean spoke “a common language of non-alignment” and shared “a common belief in the Global South”, Bhatt said.

Soft-power advantages bolster India’s appeal, according to Pukhrem, pointing to Delhi-funded restoration work at heritage sites such as Cambodia’s Angkor Wat and Vietnam’s My Son temples as evidence of outreach that “builds soft power rooted in shared civilisational ties rather than transactional influence”.

Tapan agreed that it was not a case of “India vs China’s clout, but India raising the price of Chinese dominance”.

The recent BrahMos sales had demonstrated regional appetite for Indian weapons systems, she said, further pointing to demand for naval hardware, generic pharmaceuticals and digital public infrastructure “that no Chinese product can substitute”.

Tapan also identified India’s growing appeal as a “China plus one” destination for companies looking to diversify supply chains.

“None of this beats a trillion dollars of trade. But Asean’s operating logic is hedging,” she said. “The realistic question is whether India can be indispensable in the places where China is either unwelcome or absent.”

Lin cautioned against India defining its Asean engagement purely in oppositional terms.

“Asean does not want to be treated as a theatre for India-China rivalry,” she said, adding that Delhi could make the most impact by helping the bloc diversify supply chains, build maritime capacity and strengthen digital and health cooperation.

“India’s broader influence will depend on whether it can also deliver in areas that matter to Asean’s economic and development priorities,” Lin added.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Discouraged’ at university, maths star Wang Hong spurs Chinese education debate
item.description:
Many young students in China have been inspired by the achievement of Wang Hong, the first Chinese woman to receive the Fields Medal – the world’s most prestigious prize in mathematics.

But it is the 35-year-old’s candid remarks about feeling “discouraged” in her early years at an elite Chinese university that appear to have struck the deepest chord.

Those comments have set off a broader debate about the country’s education system and whether it provides the support students need to develop confidence and pursue original ideas.
item.content:encoded:
Many young students in China have been inspired by the achievement of Wang Hong, the first Chinese woman to receive the Fields Medal – the world’s most prestigious prize in mathematics.

But it is the 35-year-old’s candid remarks about feeling “discouraged” in her early years at an elite Chinese university that appear to have struck the deepest chord.

Those comments have set off a broader debate about the country’s education system and whether it provides the support students need to develop confidence and pursue original ideas.

Wang and her compatriot Deng Yu, 37, were among four mathematicians awarded the Fields Medal on July 23. It was also the first time two Chinese mathematicians had won the prize in the same year.

In interviews since then, Wang has spoken about how she lost confidence as a young undergraduate at Peking University but regained it when she continued her studies in France.

According to a profile of Wang in Guangxi Daily, she saw mathematics as an “inner sanctuary for the mind” when she was at secondary school.

But this changed when she started studying at Peking University at the age of 16.

“When I went to college, suddenly mathematics [became] difficult,” she said in an interview posted by the Simons Foundation, a US-based organisation supporting research in mathematics and basic sciences.

“It took effort and discipline to actually learn it, and it took me many years. I felt a little discouraged.”

In another interview with her alma mater Ecole Polytechnique, Wang said studying in France was a turning point for her.

“That was the first time I realised I didn’t have to figure out everything by myself, and someone is there willing to help me,” she said, recalling a reading course with French mathematician Yvan Martel that gave her the support she needed.

That helped her to become “more patient and less nervous”, Wang said, adding that she eventually learned to work through most mathematical problems independently.

Wang, who was born in the southern Guangxi Zhuang region, started her mathematical training at Peking University, graduating in 2011.

She continued her studies in France and completed a PhD at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2019. She is now a professor at New York University’s Courant Institute as well as at the Institut des Hautes Etudes Scientifiques in France.

Wang’s remarks appear to have resonated among young people in China, with “discouraged” becoming a buzzword on social media.

Many commenters say they have had a similar experience – plagued by self-doubt despite years of hard work as they navigated an education system where success is often only measured through academic achievement and visible outcomes.

In one post on social media, a doctoral student said she was relieved and grateful to hear Wang’s story. “Thank you, Wang Hong. You’ve made me realise that I have the right to feel discouraged,” the student wrote.

She said throughout university she had received little positive feedback and had few memories of discussing academic questions with her supervisors.

“The system placed almost exclusive emphasis on measurable outputs and I gradually internalised that standard,” she wrote. “The joy I once found in acquiring new knowledge and thinking through ideas was no longer recognised as meaningful feedback.”

This was not because her supervisors did not care – she said they helped students with publications, career opportunities and professional networks but simply did not have time for academic mentoring.

In China, academics are often required to balance their research output targets – which are linked to promotion and evaluation – with teaching and other responsibilities. It leaves little time for the mentoring and exchanges that are essential to academic development.

These struggles are part of a long-standing debate over China’s approach to education. While the country produces many high-achieving students, there are questions over whether its academic system provides enough space and support for students with potential.

One commenter on social media said Wang was fortunate to have eventually found a learning environment that suited her development.

“But how many ‘slow-blooming’ talents are discouraged before they ever have the chance to flourish?” the person wrote. “Perhaps the question we should ask is not whether individuals have worked hard enough, but whether we rely on an overly narrow standard to measure talent.”

China’s top decision-makers have for years called for changes to what is seen as an inflexible academic system with biased evaluation criteria and an overreliance on papers, titles, degrees and awards. Critics say the system has hindered the country’s efforts to innovate.

Song Chunwei, a professor at Peking University’s School of Mathematical Sciences who taught Wang when she was an undergraduate, said young people in the higher education system faced the pressure of “climbing step by step” through a series of evaluations, many of which were not directly related to their academic research.

Young researchers often faced intense pressure to pass these evaluations because failing could threaten their academic positions, Song told state-run newspaper The Beijing News.

He said that pressure could push them towards “short-term and easily measurable” work that might not be beneficial to their long-term academic development.

“When [students or academics] are under excessive pressure, even if they work hard, it is difficult to reach their ideal state. It is like being driven by a whip, rather than acting out of their own will,” Song said.

Hu Xijin, the outspoken former editor of nationalist tabloid Global Times, also weighed in on the debate, writing on social media that Wang’s story should not be viewed as a simple contrast between Chinese and overseas education.

He said there were two competing views – that Wang only fully realised her potential after leaving China, and that she had done this because of a strong educational foundation from Peking University.

According to Hu, the fact that both Wang and Deng had achieved their career breakthroughs overseas after undergraduate studies in China could be a source of “regret” for many people in the country.

Deng also began his undergraduate studies at Peking University before transferring to MIT, where he completed his mathematics degree. He earned a PhD at Princeton University and is now a mathematics professor at the University of Chicago.

“People would hope that Chinese universities and institutions such as Peking University would one day be able to directly nurture Fields Medallists and Nobel Prize-level scientists of their own,” Hu wrote.

“Many also believe that China is now closer than ever to producing recipients of the world’s highest scientific honours domestically.”

He added that the discussion could have a positive outcome by highlighting the value of “opening up” and the role of international academic and professional experiences in young researchers’ development.

item.title: [SCMP] 3 South Asian actors challenge Hong Kong cinema’s casting rules
item.description:
At its best, Hong Kong cinema has always been about more than the box office. It’s about a city showing the world what it is – tough, funny, romantic, contradictory and alive.

What Hong Kong cinema is not, however, is inclusive. It never has been.

Three young men working on the margins of the industry are quietly trying to change that and, in the process, prove that the city is more colourful than its films have been letting on. They might be taking a long shot, but fortune favours the bold in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
At its best, Hong Kong cinema has always been about more than the box office. It’s about a city showing the world what it is – tough, funny, romantic, contradictory and alive.

What Hong Kong cinema is not, however, is inclusive. It never has been.

Three young men working on the margins of the industry are quietly trying to change that and, in the process, prove that the city is more colourful than its films have been letting on. They might be taking a long shot, but fortune favours the bold in Hong Kong.

“I don’t want to just be famous. I want to be able to get inside a new industry with the right heart,” says Bipin Karma. At 29 years old, the performer, born and raised in Hong Kong, knows that he is in this “for the long term”.

Karan Cholia, a 25-year-old Punjabi, nods in agreement. Hong Kong born and bred, he speaks Cantonese like a native and one day wants to play a superhero.

“In Hong Kong, they’re only making police movies and romance. I would love to play a superhero who would represent Hong Kong differently.”

The other actor at the table is Inderjeet Singh, 30, who was also born and raised in the city.

“I just want to have a say in the local industry [and prove] that the outsider can also be an actor,” he says. “You don’t have to be Chinese to give your best.”

The three men share a single ambition: to build acting careers in the Hong Kong film industry, which has thus far proven a hard nut to crack for those of South Asian heritage. Gill Mohindepaul Singh – known affectionately as Q Bobo – is the closest thing their community has had to a film role model.

The TVB actor speaks fluent Cantonese and is recognised on the street by Hongkongers who have watched him for decades in films such as Rob-B-Hood (2006), Marriage With a Liar (2010) and The White Storm 2 (2019). While all three look up to Q Bobo, they are aware that the door he stepped through may never open fully.

Ethnic minorities make up roughly 8 per cent of Hong Kong’s population, according to Race Relations Unit Demographics data. Yet, their presence on local screens remains “negligible”, as casting director Kate Sullivan puts it.

“Not enough local films are writing and producing work with diverse characters,” she says. Even when local productions do turn to Sullivan for non-Chinese talent, they ask for Western faces.

“The talent is there – ambitious, hard-working, doing crazy hours for tragic pay – and doing it for the love of it. But they need good representation. They need to know where to showcase their craft beyond the Hong Kong and mainland China market,” says Sullivan. Thus, her advice for minority actors is to lean into what makes them unique.

“Own your culture, where you are from; embrace it and find a way to showcase it and the many roles you can play,” she says. “Create and write your own work and collaborate with the right filmmakers. And don’t undersell yourself.”

Karma has done just that, having written and acted in his own projects.

“The film I got discovered from was a film I was writing,” he recalls, of the 15-minute The Bench (2018), co-written with director Mo Lai Yan-chi, which led to a pivotal role in Hand Rolled Cigarette (2020).

“The Bench was seen by a [independent film distribution and production company] Golden Scene member, who recommended me to the director of Hand Rolled Cigarette. I’m an accidental actor; I had no initial drive to be an actor or famous. I just wanted to hide behind the camera and create cool stories.”

Thanks to his parkour background, Karma had been given his first screen break at 15, in filmmaker Adam Wong Sau-ping’s 2013 breakdancing film, The Way We Dance.

His upcoming short film, Bitter Apples, sees him play a villain in English for the first time. The film sheds light on artistic freedom and power, and reminded him of the strength of Hong Kong’s English-speaking and diverse filmmaking community.

But more than a decade on from his silver-screen baptism, Karma is backing away from the social media demands and anxiety of the casting carousel. Instead, he teaches, writes, directs and acts only in projects that genuinely interest him. Now and then, Karma disconnects from the business by attending silent-meditation retreats.

The other two are constantly in hustle mode.

“In the field [of acting], you have to memorise the script,” says Cholia. “For my higher education, I deliberately chose studying history – it made my memorisation skills better.”

Cholia speaks Cantonese to friends and Punjabi to family, and consumes a mix of Bollywood and TVB shows. He landed his first significant role, the lead in the 2021 romantic comedy My Indian Boyfriend, after the director found him on Instagram.

However, the film received mixed reviews and Chinese audiences found certain cultural conventions bewildering.

“When I was going for the premiere, one audience member asked me, ‘Is it really normal for you guys to say ‘I love you’ on the first meeting?’ I couldn’t think of anything so I just said, ‘Yeah, but in India,’” recalls Cholia.

“In most [Bollywood] movies I watched, it’s like this; the hero falls in love with the leading lady in Act One, almost immediately. But in Hong Kong, you say ‘I like you’, instead of ‘I love you’. That was one of the problems in the movie.”

More recently, he has appeared in the television series Homeland Guardian, playing a police officer, a role that delighted his parents. It required him to memorise complex Cantonese dialogue, prompting him to spend every minute in the make-up chair going over the lines.

“The script was all in Chinese. I can read Chinese, but not clearly. So I found a friend who helped me with the translation, and I wrote every Pinyin on the script. When I didn’t know how to read a word, I’d ask the make-up artist and they’d practise with me,” says Cholia.

It didn’t get easier on set. “The director was not reacting, not saying ‘Good take’ or anything. You get pressured. Whatever scene you’re doing, it is the constant fear that you’re going to ruin it. But, I got the hang of it.”

The structural challenges weigh heavily on Cholia, who works as a tutor to pay the bills while searching for his big break.

“The main challenge is the face card, man. If there’s a Chinese person over a brown person, obviously they’ll prefer the Chinese actor, because the audience can relate. But you see Squid Game? That guy from Pakistan – people understood his background and where he came from,” says Cholia, referring to Player 199, portrayed by Indian actor Anupam Tripathi, in the hit Netflix series. “If they give us more roles, people can have a better understanding about us.”

Singh appears to be the most settled of the trio when it comes to his identity. “I’m more of a Hongkonger than anything else at this point, because this is what the city provides and gives you.”

His filmography is the most eclectic. He shot his first commercial at 11, after an open casting call at his school. But his career began in earnest at 18, working as an extra alongside cinema royalty Chow Yun-fat, Andy Lau Tak-wah and Jacky Cheung Hok-yau in From Vegas to Macau III (2016).

Since then, Singh has appeared in Hollywood miniseries The Expats, a local film and, most significantly, this year’s Let’s Have a Cup of Doodh Patti Chai, a feature about ethnic minorities in Hong Kong that was among the officially selected titles at the Guwahati Asian Film Festival, in India. But his favourite on-set experience was working with Anthony Wong Chau-sang on The Sunny Side of the Street (2022).

“Observing how [Wong] was delivering the lines, the way he was guiding the whole set, making sure that everyone around him was on the same page – that was really fun,” recalls Singh. “Then, going to the Golden Horse Awards in Taiwan and seeing him win. And seeing my co-actor [Sahal Zaman] – who played my son – win [a nomination for] the newcomer award. Even though that’s my dream, seeing that happen, it was …,” he says, his voice trailing off.

“I’m aware of my limited opportunities,” says Singh, who runs an electronics trading business to make ends meet. “The main viewership [in Hong Kong] is Chinese, so they will only cast Chinese leads. But it can happen. It will happen. Don’t expect a lot, but don’t give up.”

Historically, minority actors in Hong Kong cinema have been relegated to either the villain or the comical sidekick roles. Then, there are the more problematic stereotypes, akin to racial caricatures.

“If you watch old Chinese movies, there was always one Indian guy, with his voice dubbed into some typical racist accent. The movies promoted that. That’s why they continue it,” says Cholia, who declines projects that disrespect his community. He says he once turned down a script that opened with his character addressing himself by a racist slur, with no narrative justification offered.

Similarly, Karma says he would turn down a role if it depicted Nepali people in a gratuitously negative light.

Singh’s worst casting experience was not race-related but involved an advertisement for which he was not forewarned that he would be expected to play a patient near death. “I walked off,” he says. “And then I had to [suggest] replacement actors on the spot from my own friends.”

Why do all three would-be film stars persevere?

“For me, I enjoy the process,” says Cholia. “When there’s work, you want it to finish fast, but when there’s no work, you want to do it again. I want more chances to get dream roles.”

For Singh, it’s “the magic of making movies” that keeps him going. “It’s fun, it’s challenging,” he says. “Working with different people, you get to learn so many things. Someone, somewhere, has seen you. One fine day in the future, my [as yet unconceived] kids can see it. I want to leave a mark.”

Karma is embracing the journey, rather than the destination: “Nothing is permanent. Instead of always trying to land a job, I want to find love in the process of it.”

The challenges persist, however, and are likely to increase as Hong Kong’s film output dwindles. Peak production was in 1993, with the release of 234 feature films, according to the Hong Kong Film Development Council. Three decades later, that number had plummeted to just 43 films released in 2023.

“Hong Kong wants a more vibrant cinema scene,” insists Karma. “It wants to regain its name for being a place that produces great cinema, like back in the day with Stanley Kwan, Wong Kar-wai, all of them.

“The new wave of filmmakers should look at their own people who are of different colours, so you can make your film as Hong Kong is, instead of what it pretends to be. It is multicultural; it is not one note.”

item.title: [SCMP] The numbers game: why the US is losing ground to China in the first island chain
item.description:
As the People’s Liberation Army marks its 99th anniversary on August 1, one year from the deadline for its centenary goals, its evolution highlights the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the second part of a series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Beijing is pushing the envelope on its near-seas island arc.

Beijing has urged the People’s Liberation Army to transform into a “world-class military” by the mid-21st century, intent on piercing US-led chokepoints along an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines.

Known as the first island chain, they underpin a US-aligned security architecture that Chinese strategists see as both a constraint on the PLA’s freedom to manoeuvre in a conflict and the likeliest entry route for US and allied forces in a regional crisis.
item.content:encoded:
As the People’s Liberation Army marks its 99th anniversary on August 1, one year from the deadline for its centenary goals, its evolution highlights the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the second part of a series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Beijing is pushing the envelope on its near-seas island arc.

Beijing has urged the People’s Liberation Army to transform into a “world-class military” by the mid-21st century, intent on piercing US-led chokepoints along an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines.

Known as the first island chain, they underpin a US-aligned security architecture that Chinese strategists see as both a constraint on the PLA’s freedom to manoeuvre in a conflict and the likeliest entry route for US and allied forces in a regional crisis.

Long associated with Cold War-era strategy, the first island chain has become a principal arena of military competition between China and the United States, with the Pentagon’s latest China Military Power Report identifying it as central to Beijing’s regional strategy.

A year ahead of its 2027 centenary goal, the PLA has shown progress in areas that could challenge the US defence line – specifically its dual-carrier operations, large-scale arms production and improved nuclear deterrence beyond the island chain.

Meanwhile, the US and its allies have also ramped up their input, including the expansion of American base access in the Philippines and increasingly sophisticated defence drills involving Washington’s regional partners.

More than geography

Stretching from Japan’s home islands and the Ryukyu archipelago through Taiwan to the Philippines and Borneo, the first island chain forms the maritime boundary between mainland China’s near seas and the open Pacific Ocean.

It encompasses narrow waterways and air corridors, including the Miyako Strait, the Bashi Channel and the Luzon Strait – the few routes through which the PLA can reach the wider Pacific.

During the Cold War, the first island chain formed part of a broader US strategy to deter Soviet and Chinese expansion in the Pacific.

Today, it links a network of forward-deployed forces of American and allied forces that have become more closely integrated in recent years.

Japan has accelerated defence spending and strengthened its military posture along its southwestern islands with new anti-ship and air-defence capabilities, while the US has expanded rotational access to military facilities in the Philippines, including several sites facing Taiwan.

Trilateral cooperation involving Washington, Tokyo and Manila has likewise evolved from largely symbolic exercises into sophisticated naval, air and amphibious training, transforming what was once a collection of bilateral alliances into a more integrated regional security architecture.

According to Oriana Skylar Mastro, director of the Indo-Pacific Policy Lab at Stanford University’s Freeman Spogli Institute, expanded basing and overflight access represents a consequential shift.

K. Tristan Tang, a non-resident fellow at the National Bureau of Asian Research, a US think tank, echoed the sentiment, noting that large-scale joint military exercises like Balikatan and Resolute Dragon “increasingly rehearse multidomain sensing, command and control, coastal defence, integrated fires and the defence of key maritime terrain”.

Chinese strategists increasingly view the island chains as “barriers, springboards and benchmarks”, said Andrew Erickson, a professor of strategy at the US Naval War College’s China Maritime Studies Institute.

This perspective also stemmed from the PLA’s transformation, Erickson added, from a force focused mainly on coastal defence into one seeking to operate across and eventually beyond the first island chain.

That shift in thinking extends beyond military terminology.

Chinese discourse had begun framing the objective in explicitly offensive terms, with Beijing “increasingly talking about ‘breaking through the first island chain’”, said Zhao Tong, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

In Zhao’s assessment, the PLA now believes the military balance along the chain is gradually shifting in its favour and that it could steadily erode long-standing US military dominance to establish itself “as a power willing and able to advance its perceived core interests” through its expanding capabilities.

In that vein, Mastro observed that Chinese thinking about the first island chain went beyond pure defence.

“Part of the reason China wants freedom of manoeuvre in the first island chain is to defend against attack, but also to defend against responses to its own aggression,” she said.

“It’s offensive. It’s defensive. It’s about power projection. It’s about great-power competition.”

Going further, Tang argued that the first island chain had “become more, not less, strategically important over the past decade”.

As the PLA’s power-projection capabilities grew, he said, “the chain’s value as a defensive barrier has therefore increased for all sides, even as it has become a central operational arena where control of key straits and air and maritime corridors could be decisive in wartime”.

Beijing’s push

In recent years, the PLA has undergone significant military changes that could help it better respond to the first island chain, ranging from naval expansion and doctrine to joint operations and deterrence.

Zhao cited the PLA’s naval expansion as the single most important driver of that transformation, alongside China’s possession of the world’s largest arsenal of theatre-range missiles, enabling Beijing to threaten strategic targets across the region.

Looking ahead, he said Beijing also appeared to be eyeing “a substantial expansion of its nuclear-powered submarine fleet”.

By combining stealth, endurance and long-range strike capability, the force could challenge one of America’s most enduring military advantages, Zhao added.

Once focused largely on coastal defence, the PLA Navy has evolved into the world’s largest naval force by hull count, conducting increasingly sustained operations east of Taiwan and Japan in waters that until recently lay largely beyond its routine reach.

For Beijing, these deployments reflect a deliberate effort to build a navy capable of protecting its expanding overseas interests while operating in an ever more contested environment.

According to Mastro, the scale of Beijing’s operations has already gone a long way towards eroding Washington’s traditional advantages in the northern waters of the chain, namely the East China Sea and Taiwan Strait.

“China has many more bases. They have the mass,” she said, noting that Beijing could also produce ships, missiles and military equipment far faster than the US.

“The United States is losing that numbers game, and we have for quite some time.”

Yet, further south, Mastro sees the balance as less favourable for Beijing.

China could increasingly complicate US operations across the wider first island chain, but projecting and sustaining military power over greater distances remained far more demanding than denying access close to the Chinese mainland, she said.

“Keeping the United States out of Asia is much easier than projecting power across those distances,” Mastro added.

According to Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in the PLA, the calculation is much simpler. Zhou said the first island chain’s importance was slipping as China’s military capabilities expanded, even as Washington continued to reinforce its forward presence.

From coastal defence to power projection

Analysts have noted an important shift in Beijing’s strategic purposes in the region, from keeping adversaries away with anti-access and area denial (A2/AD) strategy to operating farther from home and remaining there.

The strategy is underscored by Beijing’s pursuit of carrier strike groups, amphibious assault ships and replenishment vessels, as well as a growing overseas logistics network.

In 2024, the Liaoning and Shandong aircraft carriers conducted the PLA Navy’s first dual-carrier operations, while transits through the Miyako Strait into the Philippine Sea have become more routine.

Those deployments allow the PLA to rehearse the difficult requirements of sustained blue-water warfare, from coordinating multiple carrier strike groups to integrating escorts, carrier aviation and logistics over extended distances.

The launch of the Fujian, China’s third and most advanced aircraft carrier, is expected to substantially expand the PLA Navy’s carrier aviation capabilities, while the KJ-600 airborne early-warning aircraft promises to extend fleet air defence well beyond the reach of shore-based radar.

Tang regarded the Fujian and the maturation of China’s carrier strike groups as the most consequential development to watch.

“China’s earlier ski-jump carriers faced limitations in sortie generation and carrier-based fixed-wing airborne early warning,” he said.

“The Fujian’s electromagnetic catapults and KJ-600 aircraft can extend the fleet’s sensor coverage and improve the efficiency of sustained air operations in the Philippine Sea.”

As those capabilities matured, Tang added, forces positioned along the first island chain might have to prepare for pressure “coming simultaneously from the Chinese mainland to the west and carrier forces operating to the east”.

Learning to fight as a joint force

A more fundamental change has been under way in joint combat. Instead of treating the navy, air force, rocket force and support elements as largely separate services, the PLA now trains and organises to fight as an integrated joint force.

The effort is instrumental to denying US and allied forces the ability to operate effectively around the first island chain.

Central to that approach is the concept of “system destruction warfare”: prioritising the disabling of an adversary’s sensors, communications, command networks and decision-making processes rather than destroying individual platforms one by one.

The philosophy is reflected across the PLA’s force structure.

Long-range ballistic and cruise missiles are intended to hold forward-deployed forces at risk, bomber patrols through the Miyako Strait and around Japan have become frequent, and Beijing continues to expand its reconnaissance, surveillance and command networks across multiple domains.

In addition, as US allies strengthen cooperation along the first island chain, Beijing has sought closer military coordination with its strategic partner Russia through expanded joint bomber patrols and naval exercises around Japan and across the western Pacific.

Mastro described the arrangement as an “alliance grey zone”, saying Russia could, for example, close portions of its far-eastern airspace or provide logistical support to help China sustain operations during a prolonged crisis.

As Zhao sees it, the value of defence coordination for Beijing lies less in Russia’s capability than in the signal of “strategic coordination, shared objectives and mutual resolve in countering US military influence”.

Mastro said Chinese strategists had told her privately that closer coordination with Moscow was intended to send a signal to Washington and Tokyo about the potential costs of deepening US-Japan defence cooperation.

Beijing has simultaneously strengthened its strategic deterrence to show it could complicate US defence considerations beyond the first island chain.

In 2024, China publicly launched an intercontinental ballistic missile into the Pacific for the first time in decades.

And last month, it tested a submarine-launched ballistic missile in international waters, signalling the operational readiness of its sea-based nuclear deterrent.

According to Tang, these capabilities reinforce deterrence in complementary ways – carrier strike groups extend China’s conventional operational reach beyond the first island chain, while the submarine-launched ballistic missile strengthens the credibility and survivability of its nuclear second-strike capability.

His research suggests the Central Military Commission, which commands the armed forces, concluded by late 2024 that the PLA had largely achieved its objectives for “near-seas comprehensive operations”, with training shifting to “far-seas mobile operations”.

That said, having such capabilities is different from successfully employing them in combat.

Zhao pointed to a question that could ultimately prove decisive: which side will make more effective use of emerging technologies such as drones, autonomous vessels and AI-enabled weapons?

China “appears to enjoy certain advantages stemming from its industrial base and capacity to manufacture and field systems at scale”, he said.

But the US and its allies “may retain important advantages in innovation, operational adaptability and a more agile defence ecosystem”.

The PLA still had “comparatively limited operational experience” testing its new capabilities in large-scale joint operations, Zhao added.

“The jury is still out on which side will ultimately gain the more decisive military leverage along the first island chain.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 1,000-year-old tea heritage is being rediscovered and rehabilitated
item.description:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.

“I was born and raised in Hong Kong and it took a British instructor, Jane Pettigrew, mentioning tea gardens in Lantau for me to first hear about [Hong Kong’s tea heritage],” she says.

Ngong Ping Tea Garden, the plantation in question, on Lantau Island, was founded in 1948 by Brook Bernacchi, a British lawyer and politician who arrived in Hong Kong as a marine with the World War II liberation forces in 1945. He built a life on the plateau near the Po Lin Monastery. His Lotus Brand was marketed as “the only Hong Kong tea”.

By the early 1980s, unable to compete with mass production, the tea plantation area was downsized. After cycling through different hands and functions – a recreational space, a restaurant – the site was eventually abandoned in 2014, its remnants still sitting beneath a pine tree, on a trail south of the Big Buddha – a colonial relic.

Li went looking for it anyway. In March 2023, she and a small group of enthusiasts harvested what they could from the site’s overgrown tea bushes and processed them into a small batch of red and green teas. It didn’t amount to much, but it proved one thing: tea was still growing in Hong Kong, decades after Lotus Brand had folded and the city had moved on.

Li was determined to take local tea cultivation seriously, but she needed more than a ruin. Four months later, her search took her to the upper slopes of Tai Mo Shan, to Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden.

Established in 1956 by the Kadoorie brothers as an agricultural aid station for struggling farmers, the 148-hectare sanctuary is widely recognised for its “nature as a classroom” model, welcoming visitors to see its resident animals, wander the terraced gardens and breathe air that doesn’t taste like exhaust fumes. Less known is the fact that Kadoorie has been quietly growing tea on its property since the early 2000s.

Kadoorie’s plantation wasn’t always hidden in plain sight: the farm first brought tea plants over from Ngong Ping in the 70s and 80s, strictly for exhibition. In 2004, the decision to actually grow tea was made, born of a pragmatic desire to fully use the available land. At 400 metres above sea level, the mountainside terrace is a difficult site, plagued by strong winds, thin soil and no reliable water source. Vegetables would struggle in these conditions, the team at Kadoorie assessed. But the same terrain was ideal for tea.

“It was about picking the right plant for the right place,” says Yip Tsz-lam, Kadoorie’s regenerative agriculture manager, who has worked at the farm since 2003. “Of course, we also wanted to continue Hong Kong’s centuries-old tea culture.”

Single-lane and steep, the road up to the terraces is a series of hairpin turns. It takes about 10 minutes by car, before the incline levels out. On our visit, Tai Mo Shan lives up to its colloquial name – “Big Mist Mountain” – its slopes wrapped in clouds so dense the tea bushes in the distance vanish into white.

It’s the kind of climate tea plants dream about. China’s great tea-growing regions, such as Fujian and Yunnan provinces, thrive in similar environments. Mist diffuses the sunlight, slowing photosynthesis to give the leaves time to accumulate amino acids, the compounds that become sweetness and complexity in the cup.

On these terraces are three cultivars, all sourced from Fujian: Ming-fa, Wong-chi-heung and Purple Bud Buddha’s Hand. Many people assume green and red teas come from different plants, when, in fact, they all belong to the same species; the difference is in the processing. Likewise, herbal teas are not tea at all. Only leaves from Camellia sinensis qualify; the rest are tisanes (herbal infusions). What Kadoorie is growing is the real thing.

Of the 2,000 bushes planted in 2004, about half died in the first few years. “We lacked experience with the terrain,” says Yip. But the survivors spread into the gaps and the yield held steady.

Growing the tea, however, was just the start. Kadoorie’s first harvest, in 2008, caught the team off guard. “Our initial amateur attempts resulted in terrible-tasting tea,” Yip recalls.

Kadoorie needed help, and found it closer than they expected. A colleague at the farm’s apiary introduced his mentor, Wong Tung-pui. Si Gung (“Grandmaster”), as he was known, was a Hakka man from Huizhou, in Guangdong province, who came to Hong Kong in the 70s. In his youth, he managed a tea plantation on the mainland and had learned the Hakka tradition of pan-frying leaves by hand.

When Kadoorie approached him, Si Gung was no longer working in agriculture – he kept bees and grew plants for pleasure in the countryside – but he still had the knowledge. “We were lucky to find him,” Yip says. “At that time, finding anyone in Hong Kong who still knew how to manually fry and process tea was incredibly difficult; the broader tea industry, including in mainland China, had already shifted almost entirely to machine-processing.”

Si Gung passed on the pan-frying tradition of his people, a rare skill that has faded even within Hakka communities. Kadoorie adopted it by default. “It wasn’t a planned cultural preservation effort,” Yip says. “It was born out of sheer necessity.”

For the next 15 years, Kadoorie’s tea operation ticked along quietly, following the rhythm of the 24 terms in the solar calendar.
