Between the winter solstice and Ching Ming in early April, the plants were pruned and fertilised, then the leaves were harvested until the end of the rainy season, usually around the autumn equinox. A limited amount was sold at the farm shop. Kadoorie never thought to promote the tea; they saw no reason to draw attention to something that still felt unfinished.

Connecting with Li and her HKTPI co-founders, Chan Tsz-ting and Season Li Tin-on, gave Kadoorie the downstream partner it needed. Kadoorie would manage the tea-growing and HKTPI would take the leaves further than ever before, experimenting with oxidation levels, producing multiple styles from a single cultivar and bringing the results to the public through workshops. Without them, “a lot of the tea’s potential would be wasted”, Yip says.

Li developed a method she calls “guerrilla tea-making” to process the leaves. On harvest days, the initial withering took place on the farm, in the sunlight. By dusk, the leaves were packed and taken home. In her living room, with no climate-control equipment, she relied entirely on her senses: watching the leaves, feeling the humidity, adjusting each step. “My job is not to decide what the tea tastes like,” she says. “It’s to show what the land, the weather and the leaves are giving us.”

With just the Ming-fa cultivar, Li produced several teas with different characters, evoking Hong Kong’s history as a crossroads of tea cultures, where the toasted-rice notes of Hakka pan-fried green, the floral sweetness of British-style black tea, the intense fragrance of Chaozhou Phoenix Dancong and the roasted oolongs of Fujian had come together and been absorbed.

When Li gave a finished red-tea variant to Ip Wing-chi, founder of Lok Cha Tea House and a doyen of Hong Kong’s tea world, he likened it to Taiwan’s Oriental Beauty. Also known as Dongfang Meiren, Oriental Beauty is one of the most expensive oolong teas in the world – harvests can sell for thousands of dollars per kilogram – so this was no small compliment. But why would a red tea from Tai Mo Shan carry that same oolong note at all?

Plot 107, where the leaves were plucked, held the answer: the buds there were stunted, fibrous and difficult to process. “We investigated and found tea green leafhoppers,” says Li.

Barely visible, the leafhopper’s bite causes the plant to release a chemical defence with a honeyed fragrance: the signature of Oriental Beauty. In Taiwan’s Miaoli and Hsinchu regions, farmers deliberately cultivate these insects. A pest, under the right conditions, became a gift for the tea-makers.

Li had not expected to find leafhoppers thriving on Tai Mo Shan. Warmer temperatures, driven by climate change, scrambled harvest seasons, but it also made the insects more prolific.

“It’s a double-edged sword,” Li says. Leafhoppers trigger the sweet aroma, but they reduce yields to one-fifth of a standard harvest. For a farm already operating at micro scale, the numbers were punishing.

But the trade-off posed an important question: “Do we want volume or quality? Hong Kong has the means and should pursue quality. If we could only produce a plain, characterless tea, producing it here would be meaningless.”

Li does not claim perfection for the “Hong Kong Oriental Beauty”, but the experts have given their verdict. Dr Chen You-ren, former director of the Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station, and Dr Kim Young-suk, a Korean tea studies professor, were satisfied with the quality. It matters to Li that the validation comes from Asia’s tea-making heartlands: “It gave us confidence that Hong Kong tea can reach the international artisan stage.”

But Li had more in mind than just making good tea – she wanted to know its origins. HKTPI co-founder Chan, a tea historian, had dug through academic papers and Qing dynasty gazetteers in an attempt to map out where Hong Kong’s earliest tea gardens used to be.

His findings rewound the clock by centuries. Hong Kong Society Before the Colonial Era, a 1990 textbook by historian Siu Kwok-kin, described tea cultivation in the New Territories during the Ming dynasty (1368-1644). By 2019, Siu had revised his position, arguing for Song dynasty origins, and Chan found further evidence: Southern Song (1127-1279) records of tea-growing clans migrating to the New Territories and Northern Song (960-1127) tea-ware excavated at Sung Wong Toi, in Kowloon. Compare that to the start of British colonial rule, in 1841 – tea was never just a footnote in Hong Kong’s history.

During the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), the written record started to catch up. An account in the 17th century Guangdong Xinyu encyclopaedia described tea-growing on the cliffs of Bui Dou Saan – present-day Castle Peak – with “the scent of orchid and jasmine, sweet and fragrant”.

By the Jiaqing period (1796-1820), the Xin’an County Gazetteer, a pre-colonial record of the region, had listed four famous teas grown locally: Phoenix Tea, from Lantau’s Phoenix Mountain, harvested by indigenous villagers and prized for its cooling properties; Mung Saan Tea, from Castle Peak, steeped in cloud mist and said to rival its famous Sichuan province namesake; Daam Gon Tea, from Tsing Yi, known for aiding digestion; and Ching Ming Tea, from Tai Lam, a fermented, medicinal tea preserved with salt.

Chan’s research included a 1986 paper by Dr Patrick Hase, a historian specialising in the New Territories. It described Hakka families in Mau Tso Ngam, a village in the foothills of Fei Ngo Shan, who still grew tea, sustaining two centuries of continuous cultivation.

In December 2024, the co-founders went on a “treasure hunt” to Mau Tso Ngam, along the MacLehose Trail, timed to the flowering season of Camellia sinensis so its white blossoms would make surviving tea trees visible. What they found was not a ruin.

A handful of elders remained in Mau Tso Ngam, along with mature tea trees planted decades and centuries ago, by mothers, grandmothers and ancestors. Cheng Kwun-ming, the village head, walked the visitors through the trees, pointing: this one, his mother planted 50 years ago; that one, a woman in her 80s told them, had been there since her father-in-law was alive. He used to carry the leaves across Fei Ngo Shan to Hong Kong Island to sell. Stories unspooled, rooted in the soil, still growing.

One of the villagers still harvesting and processing the leaves is Cheng Hung-ying. Now in her 70s, “Sister Hung” has picked and pan-fried tea since her teens. In her 30s, she cleared a patch of bamboo forest on the slope behind Mau Tso Ngam and planted tea trees. “Her mother could only drink the village’s own tea,” Li says. “So, that’s why she started. It was an act of care.”

“Cheng [the village head] always asks me the same question,” Li recalls. “‘What do you taste?’ And I tell him about the aroma, the sweetness, the body. And he says, ‘No. It’s yan ching mei [the taste of connection and community].’”

Somewhere along the way, Li’s search for Hong Kong’s forgotten tea had become a search for herself. Last year, while consulting with Lam Man-ying, director of the Hong Kong Hakka Association, to gather context on Mau Tso Ngam, the conversation turned to her family background. As they mapped out her grandfather’s village, the pieces clicked: Li is of Hakka descent. She has, unknowingly, spent years chasing her own heritage.

Li keeps returning to Mau Tso Ngam. On another visit, Sister Hung shows her the Hakka pan-frying process from start to finish.

Moving through her tea trees with ease and familiarity, Sister Hung demonstrates how to pick the bud and the two youngest leaves, pinched clean with a flick of the wrist.

Back in the village, at an outdoor wok set-up weathered by years of use, she gets the fire going in just a few minutes, using wood she chopped herself, from behind the small row of houses, most of them now uninhabited. In the three hours it takes to pan-fry the leaves, one person tends the fire, the other keeps the leaves moving to stop them from burning. She uses no thermometer, no timer – only her hands and decades of instinct.

With the wok at around 300 degrees Celsius, Sister Hung works fast to saat ching (“kill the green”), using a Y-shaped wooden tool passed down from her father. Next, she rolls the leaves back and forth on a bamboo withering tray with her gloved palms – the same motion as kneading dough – until the cell walls break down and the juices coat the surface, so the flavour can build.

Finally, the leaves return to the wok at a lower heat. With her bare hands, she turns them, lifting and dropping, pressing and spreading, for the better part of two hours. If she loses the rhythm, the batch is ruined.

Sister Hung no longer lives in Mau Tso Ngam year-round, but she comes back to pan-fry tea and make alkaline rice dumplings, another Hakka tradition recognised as part of Hong Kong’s intangible cultural heritage. She is the last person in her family who knows how to do it.

“My children didn’t want to learn; they don’t even want to try the tea I pan-fry any more,” she says. “I come back every year anyway. It has become a ritual for me.”

Li, who trained in Taiwan, Japan and Britain, understands the science of oxidation, amino acids and catechins. But what Sister Hung knows is held in the body, passed down through years of watching and copying until the skill becomes instinct.

“My job is to understand her, to turn what she knows into something we can replicate, to carry forward the culture,” says Li.

When the village head learned that Li and her team worked with Kadoorie, he welcomed them without hesitation. In the 50s and 60s, the Kadoorie Agricultural Aid Association supported Hakka farmers across the New Territories; the trust already existed.

HKTPI is reviving that decades-old partnership for a new purpose. Mau Tso Ngam’s tea trees represent a living gene bank of cultivars that have adapted to Hong Kong’s terroir. If the ageing tea-makers can’t tend to them, the genetic knowledge will be lost.

Last November, HKTPI invited the villagers to Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden to plant saplings from Mau Tso Ngam’s heritage trees, bringing their cultivars into Kadoorie’s conservation infrastructure.

“We’re not reviving a lost craft,” Li says. “We’re a bridge. One end connects to the tea traditions Hakka ancestors cultivated; the other end connects to the present, the land, what’s still here.”

HKTPI and Kadoorie now co-host workshops where the public can harvest leaves from the terraces and try their hand at traditional pan-frying. At the Hong Kong International Tea Fair 2024, they poured cups of Tai Mo Shan tea for visitors who did not believe the city could produce anything worth drinking.

Some visitors asked what the point was. Even if the tea were good, what did a few kilograms from a mountainside matter? It’s true that Kadoorie’s harvests are too limited to sustain widespread commercial production. But Chan has greater ambitions than just retail growth: “Our dream is that one day, when foreign dignitaries visit the city, the tea they are served is ours.”

Inspired by her findings, Li is building another stage: the Hakka Tea Theatre, a clear expression of her role as a “translator”. Here, the tea served is Hakka pan-fried green, the food is Hakka yellow-wine chicken, the stories are from Mau Tso Ngam and the crafts are local. But the format is British afternoon tea.

The project mirrors her own trajectory, from running a British-style tearoom in Mong Kok, training overseas in various tea cultures, to serving tea at a consulate in London. She understands both lexicons – the formal precision of a Western tea service and the embodied knowledge of a Hakka village. At the Tea Theatre, the two meet. “I’m not asking people to choose between Chinese and Western,” she says. “I’m showing them that the tea doesn’t belong to either. It belongs to the land it came from.”

Chan thinks about the future in two timelines. In five years, HKTPI will have the resources to sustain the partnership with Kadoorie, safeguard tea-making traditions in Mau Tso Ngam, explore other forgotten tea plantations and stage more Hakka Tea Theatre experiments. In 10 years, a younger generation will join them, “to inherit the culture, the technique and the vision of this land”.

Li had learned, through a serendipitous journey, that this land belongs to her, too. She had started in a London classroom, followed the trail through an abandoned colonial plantation, up a misty mountain and into a tiny village that had never stopped making tea, and found herself inside the story she was chasing.

“Letting the next generation know that Hong Kong has this history is not just about tea,” Li says. “It’s the confidence of knowing that we are not rootless; we carry something we can be proud of.”

[Correction: An earlier version identified Cheng Sui-wing as the village head who welcomed the visitors to Mau Tso Ngam. It has been amended to Cheng Kwun-ming, who also serves as the village head for Mau Tso Ngam, alongside Cheng Sui-wing.]

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese luxury brands rise from challengers to market shapers as global houses lose lustre
item.description:
After months of declining gold prices, Li Yue recently spent nearly 28,000 yuan (US$4,148) on a 10-gram (0.35-ounce) pure gold necklace – more than double the prevailing market rate for the metal.

The piece in question: a gourd-shaped pendant from Laopu Gold, a Chinese heritage jewellery brand that has captured significant attention in recent years.

But for Li, a software engineer in Shanghai, the purchase had little to do with bullion value. She cared more about the necklace’s design – the gourd is a traditional symbol of fortune and prosperity – and the care with which it was crafted.
item.content:encoded:
After months of declining gold prices, Li Yue recently spent nearly 28,000 yuan (US$4,148) on a 10-gram (0.35-ounce) pure gold necklace – more than double the prevailing market rate for the metal.

The piece in question: a gourd-shaped pendant from Laopu Gold, a Chinese heritage jewellery brand that has captured significant attention in recent years.

But for Li, a software engineer in Shanghai, the purchase had little to do with bullion value. She cared more about the necklace’s design – the gourd is a traditional symbol of fortune and prosperity – and the care with which it was crafted.

“No one asks how much the fabric of their Louis Vuitton bag costs, right?” she said.

Li is precisely the kind of customer Laopu Gold is courting. Having cultivated a sophisticated customer base through its choice of retail locations and emphasis on craftsmanship and aesthetic expression, the brand has earned a place in the luxury echelon, becoming one of the bestselling labels in China’s high-end malls – even as overall luxury spending continued to decline, analysts said.

Like Laopu, a growing number of local brands are now appealing to premium consumers. As international luxury brands such as Cartier, Tiffany & Co, and Gucci close their doors on Huaihai Middle Road – one of Shanghai’s premier shopping thoroughfares – a wave of home-grown names has taken their place, from handbag label Songmont and shoe brand Pane to perfume house To Summer.

If top-tier Western luxury labels were status symbols that newly affluent Chinese consumers clamoured for in past decades, today’s shoppers were more discerning and rational – and they were increasingly turning to domestic brands that offered a “high-value sense of luxury”, according to Zhou Ting, a veteran researcher with decades of experience in the luxury goods industry.

The next decade will be [Chinese luxury brands’] golden era, with the entire segment growing into a market worth tens of trillions of yuan

Zhou Ting, Yaok Institute

Compared with global luxury houses, domestic brands had a superior grasp of Chinese consumers’ aesthetic sensibilities and contextual needs while offering a pricing framework that provided more compelling value, said Zhou, founder of the Shanghai-based Yaok Institute, which provides research and consulting services related to high-end goods.

“After the first wave of global expansion by European and American luxury houses, China is now emerging as the world’s second core incubator for luxury brands,” she said.

By 2035, Chinese luxury brands would match the China market share of their international counterparts in terms of sales, Zhou said.

The success of brands such as Laopu Gold and collectible toys creator Pop Mart extends beyond their financial performance. They had shown the viability of premium branding for Chinese labels, and provided a replicable framework for emerging domestic brands, she said.

Though no longer drawing the massive queues it saw during the recent surge in gold prices, Laopu Gold, with dozens of stores across China and one store in Singapore, “outperforms every other luxury brand in terms of sales revenue”, a source close to the firm told the South China Morning Post.

The company had 610,000 registered members as of the end of last year – more than 80 per cent of whom overlapped with those of major luxury brands such as Louis Vuitton and Cartier – and was now in talks with shopping malls in Japan and South Korea to open new stores, said the source, who declined to be named as they were not authorised to talk to the media.

Citing Frost & Sullivan data, the Hong Kong-listed company said in its 2025 financial report that it ranked second by revenue among global luxury brands in mainland China, and first in sales per store and per square metre within a single mall. Laopu issued a positive profit forecast for the first half of this year last week, estimating total revenue of about 20 billion yuan (US$2.96 billion), up about 60 to 65 per cent year on year.

“One major reason behind the brand’s rise is that it has created entirely new demand; before this, there was no gold-focused brand among top-tier luxury jewellery houses,” the source said.

“For established luxury players, gold is not a test of their technical mastery, but rather of cultural resonance and aesthetic sensibility.”

Global luxury leaders remain in the depths of a protracted downturn. Last week, Louis Vuitton parent LVMH reported a 3 per cent year-on-year decline in total revenue and a 4 per cent fall in profits for the first half of the year. The first-half results for Kering Group – manager of luxury brands Gucci, Balenciaga and Bottega Veneta, among others – showed revenue down 3 per cent and net income plunging 60 per cent from a year earlier.

China’s total retail sales of consumer goods grew just 1.3 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026, with the gold, silver and jewellery category contracting by 3.4 per cent in June alone, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed.

Meanwhile, China’s high-end consumption market stood at 1.56 trillion yuan in 2025 – a 5 per cent decline from the previous year, according to a Hurun Research Institute report released in January.

More than half of the 470 high-net-worth Chinese consumers surveyed by Hurun said they planned to cut expenses on daily luxury goods this year, underscoring a widespread move towards more value-conscious consumption.

While the slowdown of the overall economy has played a role, this came after a gradual shift in consumer mentality – from obsession with logos and brand heritage to greater emphasis on product quality, craftsmanship, innovation and the overall brand experience, said Zhou, the Shanghai researcher.

It is within this evolving environment that Icicle, a premier Chinese fashion brand using natural materials with a focus on comfort and durability, has stood out.

When it first emerged in the late 1990s, luxury consumption in China was closely tied to status and external recognition. But today, consumers were increasingly looking for products that reflected their personal taste, lifestyle and values, which had contributed to the brand’s double-digit compound annual growth in China in recent years, it said in a statement to the SCMP.

“There has been a broader shift away from conspicuous consumption towards what might be called ‘quiet luxury’ – quality that speaks for itself, rather than through logos or status signalling,” it said, adding that this played directly to the brand’s strengths.

With more than 200 stores globally, including five in Europe, the brand is pushing for further international expansion through a partnership with Kering, which in April acquired a minority stake in ICCF, the brand’s owner.

As international luxury houses become demystified for mainstream consumers and stripped of social distinction for high-net-worth shoppers, local high-end brands are now capturing market share and redefining luxury.

Despite a strong recovery in overseas tourism, 65 per cent of Chinese luxury spending occurred within mainland China last year, while domestic brands captured more share by appealing to cultural connections and local preferences, according to a Bain & Co report in January.

“Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers,” it said. “They are transforming the China luxury landscape with their distinctive fusion of global appeal and authentic Chinese identity and redefining what luxury means for modern Chinese consumers.”

Buying local luxury is not a compromise – it’s a statement of cultural identity and pride in Chinese heritage

Li Yue, Shanghai

And this was by no means a short-term phenomenon as consumers tightened their belts amid the current economic downturn, but a “long-term, irreversible shift” supported by multiple factors, Zhou said.

Those factors included a growing cultural affinity for home-grown brands, the maturation of China’s domestic supply chain, and the democratisation of information, she added.

“Chinese luxury brands are at the starting point of rapid growth. The next decade will be their golden era, with the entire segment growing into a market worth tens of trillions of yuan,” Zhou said.

On quality and service, Chinese brands were on par with – or even ahead of – top-tier luxury houses, thanks to China’s unrivalled supply chain and manufacturing expertise, she said. The real gap lay in brand legacy and global reputation, which required years of history and international exposure to cultivate.

Li, the Laopu Gold customer, said she would continue chasing traditional luxury brands while at the same time embracing new ones from local companies.

“To me, buying local luxury is not a compromise – it’s a statement of cultural identity and pride in Chinese heritage,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Investment with Chinese characteristics: how Beijing’s money is reshaping tech ventures
item.description:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.
item.content:encoded:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.

Rather than operating via a single entity, this public capital flows through a layered matrix of national funds, local investment vehicles, state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privately managed funds. It is a system that converts top-down policy priorities into private-market bets, with an alternative perspective on what can be considered a return on investment.

Last year, state-affiliated investors supplied more than 90 per cent of the committed capital tracked in China’s private-equity market, a surge from just under 79 per cent in 2021, according to domestic data provider Zerone.

This mandate comes directly from the top. At a high-level national science and technology gathering in Beijing on July 8, President Xi Jinping urged financial capital firms to “invest early, invest small, invest for the long term and invest in hard technology”.

How this capital is deployed could determine whether China will succeed in its ambitions to become a self-reliant tech superpower – or suffocate its economy under the weight of state-engineered overcapacity.

How the money moves

“2018 was roughly the turning point for us,” said Shen Qinhua, founding partner of Puhua Capital, a Hangzhou-based investment firm with about 40 billion yuan (US$5.91 billion) under management. Puhua aimed to raise between 7 billion and 8 billion yuan in 2026, with state-affiliated investors expected to account for about 90 per cent of the total, he said.

According to Shen, it was around eight years ago that traditional private-business owners in eastern Zhejiang province started to pull back their investments in Puhua, as they realised that venture funds’ long holding periods had failed to match their liquidity expectations.

China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage

– Zhou Kaibing, Hangzhou Venture Capital Association

Around the same time, dollar funds began retreating amid escalating US-China tensions. More recently, restrictions on investment in sensitive technologies from both sides have deepened the financial divide, while Beijing’s aggressive push into strategic technologies has drawn a diverse array of state investors.

This state support arrives in vastly different forms and at distinct stages of a company’s life cycle.

For CXMT, which is headed for a blockbuster public market debut in Shanghai next week, a combination of national, provincial and municipal investors supplied the massive capital, credit support and project construction resources required to build a capital-intensive memory chipmaker from scratch. Industrial and private investors came later.

It is one of the clearest examples of the “Hefei model”, under which the provincial capital of central China’s Anhui uses state investment vehicles to back strategic industries, absorb early risk and anchor companies locally before bringing in market capital.

By contrast, state funds entered Unitree Robotics much later in the game. That financing came after the robot maker had already proven its technological and commercial viability, timing that aligned with Beijing’s elevation of robotics to a strategic priority.

Unicorn artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek, initially funded entirely by private wealth, only recently drew backing from the national AI fund after emerging as a powerful symbol of China’s challenge to US tech supremacy.

Hong Kong-listed Zhipu, whose market cap at the market close on Friday was HK$585.95 billion (US$74.72 billion), attracted a cluster of local government funds when it neared its initial public offering in January, as cities vied for a stake to secure a share in the booming AI sector – or remain economically relevant.

One main delivery mechanism for state capital is the fund-of-funds model.

Puhua Capital, for instance, has twice been selected to manage sub-funds backed by the National SME Development Fund, which is financed by central and local fiscal capital alongside smaller state and institutional investors.

In this set-up, the national fund typically provides a 30 per cent anchor commitment. Puhua would raise another 30 per cent to 40 per cent from provincial, municipal or district-level state vehicles, before securing the remaining balance and deciding where to base the fund.

Puhua would retain its day-to-day investment autonomy, but operate under strict oversight. An appointed observer, separate from the investment committee, could join deal discussions from an early stage and veto proposed investments.

Furthermore, at least 70 per cent of the capital must be deployed into “522” companies – businesses with no more than 200 million yuan in annual sales, 200 million yuan in assets and 500 employees. Performance metrics and related-party transactions would be regularly audited.

“The requirements are higher,” Shen said, “but so is the support for policy direction and industrial coordination.”

In this way, a fund-of-funds brings in broader outside capital while steering it to policy priorities. Meanwhile, the National Venture Capital Guidance Fund, launched late last year, operates further upstream, channelling central fiscal money through regional funds into hundreds of professionally managed sub-funds focused strictly on early-stage technologies.

Some point towards specific industries. For example, the “Big Fund” – China’s flagship semiconductor investor – concentrates capital into this fiercely competitive arena, taking equity stakes directly and backing specialist funds across the chip supply chain.

Others can be deployed through local platforms that take stakes or finance construction, as in Hefei, as well as via investments and acquisitions by state-owned companies.

Who bears the risk?

Capital is pouring into strategic industries through funds with longer lifespans as exit routes expand. Platforms like Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market and the Hong Kong stock exchange now allow these companies to go public sooner, enabling broader retail investors to share in the potential gains.

“A loop is gradually taking shape, directing more capital towards hard tech companies,” said Mi Lei, founder of CAS Star, a venture-capital firm spun out of an institute under the state-run Chinese Academy of Sciences. The firm’s early bets on China’s photonics sector have begun to see tangible returns amid the AI boom.

However, state investors and private funds do not always share the same scorecard. While a market fund is judged mostly on financial returns, local governments must also account for the number of factories built, jobs created and taxes generated – competing goals that can weaken financial discipline and fuel intercity rivalries.

This local tournament has made China’s industrial policy unusually entrepreneurial – and competitive. Beijing signals the strategic direction, while cities fiercely contest fund structures, industrial estates, credit support and real-world applications.

In the nascent stages of an industry, this rivalry can foster healthy development, or what Shen described as “a hundred flowers blooming”. But it can also lead to severe overcrowding, driven by local governments’ fear of missing out on the next big macroeconomic wave.

The solar panel and electric vehicle (EV) sectors offer stark cautionary tales for today’s policy darlings, such as AI, semiconductors and embodied intelligence.

Expanding production capacity can benefit a single city seeking to boost its local economy, but when dozens of cities replicate the strategy simultaneously, the result is crippling overcapacity and collapsing profit margins on a nationwide basis.

“China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage,” said Zhou Kaibing, chairman of the Hangzhou Venture Capital Association. He noted that some companies with little initial appetite for scaling up began to aggressively add capacity after winning government support.

The structural risks of this approach were highlighted by state broadcaster CCTV in April through the downfall of Neta, a once-prominent EV brand owned by Hozon Auto.

Local governments in Tongxiang in Zhejiang province, Yichun in central Jiangxi province, and Nanning in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region all took equity stakes in Hozon, providing factories, land, subsidies and financing to secure production bases within their regions – even as the carmaker remained deeply unprofitable.

As its products lost ground in a brutally competitive domestic market, the company fell into court-supervised restructuring in 2025. The failure has put billions of yuan in state-backed equity, subsidies and fixed industrial assets at risk.

This raises an uncomfortable question for policy architects: are these losses an acceptable cost of doing business in a nascent industry, or do they represent a fundamental failure of discipline in public investment?

Zhou argued that to mitigate these risks, governments should avoid trying to act as talent scouts themselves. Instead, they should delegate capital management to professional fund managers, who are better equipped to pick market winners and diversify risk.

The state investment system excels at moving money, but it is still learning how – and where – to take risks, he said.

Course correction

Beijing, however, is very much aware of these structural vulnerabilities.

At the same science and technology gathering in Beijing, Xi issued a pointed warning, saying that regions must adapt policy to local conditions rather than blindly chase hot sectors or engage in wasteful, copycat development and “involution-style” competition.

The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure. You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return

– Mi Lei, CAS Star

Policymakers are now attempting a delicate balancing act: mobilising unprecedented capital for technology while imposing rigorous discipline on how it is deployed.

In recent years, this policy response has been rolled out in stages. The State Council’s 2024 policy document, which introduced 17 guidelines on promoting high-quality venture capital, served as the sector’s broadest overhaul since 2016.

It encouraged “patient capital” with a more long-term outlook, shifting the evaluation metrics from a deal-by-deal basis to that of a fund’s full life cycle, while protecting managers from liability for honest failures and broadening exit strategies beyond initial public offerings.

By 2025, new rules shifted the focus directly onto government fund management. This guidance curbed overlapping funds and duplicate local investments, demanded more professional management and called for a greater tolerance for legitimate, due-diligence-backed investment losses.

This year, the State Council’s guidance for investment approval extended the course correction to the factories, industrial estates and public liabilities that often accompany state-backed investments. It also tightened its oversight of fixed-asset projects, enabling it to halt disorderly capacity expansion while introducing lifetime responsibility for officials whose unlawful investment decisions cause serious economic consequences.

“The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure,” said CAS Star’s Mi. “You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return.”

The ultimate test for the equity investment model with Chinese characteristics is whether its bureaucracy can not only learn to accept the inevitable losers that are inherent to venture capital, but also retain the discipline required to cut their losses after failed bets.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s Bali financial hub ‘a matter of survival’: economic tsar
item.description:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.
item.content:encoded:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.

Indonesia, safely removed from the Iran war’s turmoil, was the obvious choice, he said.

“They said ‘We’d like to move our assets, we’d love very much to stay away from here and live in Bali, because it’s so peaceful in Bali’,” he recalled. “The Middle East conflict is not going to end next month or next year, I don’t believe that.”

Speaking to This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Nusa Dua Forum in Bali on July 17, the 78-year-old chairman of Indonesia’s National Economic Council was a study in moustachioed calm – a far cry from the crisis of confidence that has roiled Southeast Asia’s largest economy this year.

For us … it’s a matter of survival

Luhut Pandjaitan, National Economic Council chairman

Investors, spooked by scepticism over Prabowo’s populist policies and rattled further by a global energy crisis that sent fuel prices soaring, have pulled billions out of Indonesia in recent months.

Acknowledging the market rout and concerns over money laundering, Luhut pledged greater transparency and to stamp out corruption.

“Without this, it’s very hard to gain trust and credibility,” he said, going on to describe the financial hub in existential terms. “For us … it’s a matter of survival.”

On Tuesday, Indonesia’s parliament passed legislation paving the way for the new financial centre just 20 days after talks on it had first begun.

Its precise location and the full range of associated incentives are still under wraps, but Luhut says the legislative speed should come as no surprise – he first floated the idea two years ago.

The centre could be up and running as soon as next month, he said, hinting that Prabowo might time an official announcement to coincide with the country’s independence day on August 17.

Instead of Indonesia’s civil code, the centre will operate under international commercial law, according to Luhut, who drew a parallel with Hong Kong.

“It’s like one country, two systems,” he said. “Which is not the ideal … But the purpose is to improve the credibility and trust of Indonesia.”

Sceptical of the notion that only Singapore, Hong Kong or the United Arab Emirates could host such hubs, Luhut said he had consulted a range of investors – from American hedge fund manager Ray Dalio to the Porsche family – and found them in agreement.

“They said they love the aura of Bali,” he quipped.

Separately, at the forum – co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara – Indonesia’s former coordinating minister of maritime and investment repeated his pitch to a room filled with officials, investors and family office principals.

“We’re going to be very transparent. We’re going to be more efficient, there’s going to be less corruption,” he declared. “I’m pretty confident about that.”

Unshaken optimism

Luhut’s optimism does not end at the new international financial centre. He is convinced Indonesia’s digitalisation push and its young, skilled workforce can deliver Prabowo’s target of lifting economic growth from 5 to 8 per cent by 2029.

“I think 8 per cent – with digital infrastructure support, artificial intelligence and also with the family offices – I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he said, brushing off economists’ scepticism.

Technological progress over the past few years had been nothing short of “beautiful”, Luhut said, outlining how data collected from eight government ministries and major institutions now fed into an AI-supported system to drive efficiency gains.

“Indonesia will be different within two years,” he vowed, referring to a local “brain and talent factory” he founded where students are selected based on IQ scores and put through a curated curriculum.

Addressing the prevailing gloom surrounding coverage of Indonesia’s economy and policies, Luhut blamed a failure of messaging and argued that there was an information disconnect between the government and the public.

Earlier this year, global index provider MSCI warned it could downgrade Indonesia from emerging to frontier market status amid concerns over transparency and stock market manipulation. A May deadline it set to see signs of progress has since been pushed back to November.

A brighter spot came earlier this month, when S&P reaffirmed Jakarta’s sovereign credit rating, forecasting that recent financial strains would ease thanks to higher commodity prices and spending cuts.

The government projects its budget shortfall to widen to 2.85 per cent of gross domestic product this year, just shy of the 3 per cent statutory ceiling. Prabowo’s flagship free meals programme – a cornerstone of his populist economic agenda – has drawn much of the flak for exacting a heavy toll on state finances since its launch in January 2025.

On Tuesday, the programme’s budget was slashed again – now reduced by more than 100 trillion rupiah (US$5.6 billion) from its original allocation – and the agency chief charged with overseeing it resigned a day later, citing health reasons.

Luhut defended the scheme as essential to inclusive growth and insisted the administration had committed to making it more “targeted” by focusing on remote areas.

“You have to adjust, because every province faces a different situation,” he said.

Indonesia’s troubleshooter

Luhut’s current role is just the latest chapter in a political and business career spanning four decades.

A former four-star army general, he first entered politics as Indonesia started its transition to democracy in the late 1990s, before stepping away several years later to build a business empire in energy, minerals and coal.

He returned in 2014 after helping finance Joko Widodo’s successful presidential campaign that year, becoming his chief of staff – a newly created position – and trusted troubleshooter, later spearheading both Indonesia’s downstreaming strategy and its pandemic response.

Also Widodo’s point man on China, Luhut called Jakarta-Beijing relations “very good”, revealing plans for an impending meeting between Prabowo and around 20 Chinese firms invested in Indonesia.

In May, Chinese businesses had raised concerns about Jakarta’s rising levies and stricter enforcement, with several Indonesian ministers pushing back, insisting the country must prioritise sovereignty over its natural resources.

To avoid misunderstandings, Luhut said Prabowo’s relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping had to become “much closer”.

“I said to the president, the biggest investor in this country is still China, whether you like it or not,” he said, noting that Beijing was “very willing” to share its technology and research capabilities.

Prabowo’s stricter demands of tycoons – including a plan to funnel proceeds from palm oil exports and other key resources through sovereign wealth fund Danantara to curb under-invoicing – has further unnerved investors, but Luhut shrugs off the unease.

“This country, with a 300 million population, it’s not easy to govern,” he said. “But we explain to them that the best time to invest in Indonesia is today.”

During the 2024 presidential election, when Luhut backed Prabowo’s campaign, he declined any ministerial post, opting instead to remain an adviser, according to state news agency Antara.

Asked about Widodo’s surprise return to the political stage this year – touring the country to support his son Kaesang Pangarep’s Solidarity Party – Luhut was philosophical,

“Jokowi is still active because, of course, he has to survive,” he said, referring to the former president by his popular nickname. “Otherwise, if you retire fully, it’s easy to get very old.”

Luhut described urging both presidents to maintain a harmonious relationship for the country’s sake, which Widodo did in 2019 when he made former electoral rival Prabowo his defence minister.

“He was my deputy, and now he’s my boss,” Luhut said of the current president. “If it’s just the two of us, we talk in a very relaxed way. But I still respect him, because this is an institution. And we have to respect that.”

For a man widely seen as one of Indonesia’s most influential unelected figures, Luhut professes being content with his position just beneath the summit of power.

“I’m happy with what I am. That’s my destiny,” he said. “Everything under this sky, whatever it is, I try to contribute as much as I can because I love this country.”

Fittingly, he closed his pitch to investors at the Nusa Dua summit not with numbers, but a feeling. “You’ll never get bored in Bali,” Luhut said. “Whenever I land in Bali I can feel friendliness, harmony and hope.”

item.title: [SCMP] The best guest shifts in Hong Kong and Macau amid Asia’s 50 Best Bars 2026
item.description:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24
item.content:encoded:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24

Green Room x Three x Co

Ranked the No 15 best bar in Asia last year, Kuala Lumpur’s Three X Co is heading all the way up to the 49th floor of Upper House to take over Green Room for one night only. Represented this time by bar manager Rachel Hor and senior bartender Chris Ang, Three X Co focuses on contemporary cocktails such as those from its IndiVDuality menu. The Quiet Quinn riffs on the martini with a Tanqueray 10 base, a chrysanthemum infusion and Yzaguirre Dry Reserva Spanish vermouth, topped with orange bitters and grapefruit zest.

Where: Green Room, 49/F, Upper House Hong Kong, Admiralty

When: 6.30pm-9.30pm

The Local Pour – Dara x Flair Up

Dara, celebrated for its modern Filipino dishes and vibrant neighbourhood atmosphere, is teaming up with “flairtender” Washam Limbu for a special collaboration titled The Local Pour.

Limbu is the co-founder of Flair Up and frequently participates in the Young Chef, Young Waiter, Young Mixologist (YYY) competitions. He took home the 2026 YYY Story Teller Global title and was named the Young Mixologist of the Year in 2025, when he was also crowned champion in the 2025 Ichiko Cocktail Competition Hong Kong event.

Guests can expect high-energy performance, artisanal craft cocktails and a commitment to locally produced ingredients.

Where: Dara, Shop 3, Soho 189, 189 Queen’s Road West, Sai Ying Pun

When: 7pm until sold out

Saturday, July 25

The Road Less Travelled – Wing Lei Bar x Nomad Lab x Barc x Kiki Lounge

Even though Wynn Palace and Wing Lei Bar start their festivities earlier in the week, one of our favourites on the itinerary has to be this one – gathering bars from Mongolia, Nepal and the Isle of Man.

All three bars are represented by their co-founders. Nomad Lab’s Awaraa Awarzed is coming in from Ulaanbaatar as the self-proclaimed “first cocktail lab in Mongolia”, while Barc’s Abhishek Tuladhar is arriving from Nepal. The latter won the 2025 Michter’s Art of Hospitality award from Asia’s 50 Best Bars last year. Rounding out the takeover is Drew Fleming from Kiki Lounge in Isle of Man, the winner of the Spirits Business Awards Bar of the Year in 2024.

Where: Wing Lei Bar, West Esplanade, G/F, Wynn Palace, Avenida da Nave Desportiva, Coloane-Taipa, Macau

When: 5pm-8pm

25:00 x Thaipioka

Bartenders Hope Narawut and Supawit Thinpitayanurat, also known as Miguel, are arriving from Bangkok to take over 25:00 Twenty Fifth Hour, representing Thaipioka, which focuses on equal parts cocktails and music. Back home, Thaipioka offers fruit-centric cocktails like the Kyoho Balsamic Negroni, adding vinegar, shiso bitters and kyoho grapes to the traditional profile, or the Orange Thai Milk Tea, which soups up the citrus drink with rum, coffee, caramel and fresh orange.

Where: 13/F, Luk Yu Building, 24-26 Stanley Street, Central

When: 9pm-1am

Sunday, July 26 (early)

C108 celebrates its second anniversary with Sora Bar

C108’s second anniversary on Old Bailey Street is coming hot on the heels of its updated menu earlier in the month. Taking centre stage for Sunday’s anniversary party is a guest shift by Jonas Vittur, director of bars at Rosewood Phnom Penh’s rooftop bar, Sora, and its head bartender Phirun Lek.

Last year, the sky bar was ranked No 65 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars list and won the Ketel One Sustainable Bar Award. C108 is also working with Good Stuff to have four DJs play music all night long.

Where: 15 Old Bailey Street, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

The Old Man x AABBCC

Start your Sunday night at the top of the alphabet as AABBCC arrives from New Delhi to take over The Old Man on Aberdeen Street. The “retro-futuristic archive” bar sends co-founders Jairaj Singh Solanki and Aditi Singh, who are bringing cocktails such as a twist on the Godfather with dandelion, a Bellini using cacao butter, a caprese salad rendered in alcohol form, and a drink called the Mushroomisu.

Solanki’s former concept, Lair, also based in New Delhi, was ranked the 8th best bar in Asia last year.

Where: The Old Man, LG/F, 37 Aberdeen Street, Soho, Central

When: 6pm until sold out

Sunday, July 26 (late)

Dio x Bar Woody

There’s so much happening on Sunday and Monday that it’ll be easy to catch an early shift and a late shift on either night. Bar Woody has made a name for itself in Chengdu by anchoring its concept on the complexity of wood and herbs, with its signature cocktails such as the Cedar, the Benzoin and Sandalwood. Now there is a chance to try those earthy sips at Dio on Sunday, when Bar Woody’s Keith Lo and Austin Guo serve their wood-forward creations supported by Mizunara, featuring The Hachi Shochu and Wakshio 424 Gin.

Where: Dio, 8 Aberdeen Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

The Diplomat x Offtrack

Singapore’s Offtrack, last year’s No 23 best bar in Asia and known for its high-energy music and equally excellent focus on cocktails and food, arrives in Hong Kong to take over The Diplomat for one night only. At home, Offtrack’s co-founder Aslam Zainal and his team serve straightforward, inventive drinks like the Cora Middleton, combining raspberry, white almond, rum, lime, hibiscus and egg white. It makes perfect sense for Zainal to stage a guest stint at one of Hong Kong’s best bars for martinis, Irish coffees and burgers.

Where: The Diplomat, LG/F, H Code, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

Monday, July 27 (early)

Quinary x Native x Milli x Chanel Adams

Hong Kong’s first home of molecular mixology, Quinary, is starting the party early on Monday with a triple-header featuring Singapore’s Native and Milli, alongside a special guest. Native is represented by co-founder Vijay Mudaliar and mixologist Amillie Chan, who are showcasing their unique approach to obscure and foraged ingredients, while Danny is bringing a menu of playful cocktails from Milli, a rooftop bar atop Singapore’s National Gallery. Rounding out the line-up is Chanel Adams, who most recently worked at the Mandarin Oriental Bangkok, and at Please Don’t Tell in Hong Kong before that.

Where: Quinary, 56-58 Hollywood Road, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

Tell Camellia x Gong-Gan

Gong-Gan, famed for its zero-waste philosophy, arrives from Seoul to take over tea-inspired cocktail joint Tell Camellia. Ranked No 74 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars this year, Gong-Gan is represented by co-founders Evan Noh and Willy Park. Their signature cocktails include the Si-Jang, featuring the premium Korean spirit Igangju alongside bourbon, lemon juice, roasted rice and banana beer.

Where: Tell Camellia, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm onwards

Monday, July 27 (late)

Kinsman x Bar Truce x Bar Notes

Wong Kar-wai-inspired Kinsman brings together Indonesia and South Korea in a double header featuring Bar Truce from Jakarta and Seoul’s Bar Notes. The former is grounded in Japanese mixology tradition with a twist, serving cocktails like the Ogura Dream as a clarified twist on the Alexander. Meanwhile, Bar Notes puts its focus on storytelling – its owner Ricky is also a freelance writer – serving concoctions like the Ssanghwa, inspired by the portmanteau “halmae-nial” – a combination of “halmae”, meaning granny, and “millennial”, referring to millennials enjoying foods normally associated with the elderly – containing rum, cream, egg and the eponymous bitter tea.

Where: Kinsman, 65 Peel Street, Central

When: Bar Truce: 8pm-10pm; Bar Notes: 10pm-12am

Socio x Modernhaus

One of Jakarta’s best – Modernhaus – arrives to take over Socio, Hong Kong’s main venue focused on upcycling community ingredients. Modernhaus was named the No 12 best bar in Asia last year and focuses on conceptual, minimalist cocktails. At home, they serve drinks like the Turmeric, which involves a turmeric gin, coconut chai milk, cream, salted tamarind and lemonade soda, and the Apple, which spotlights smoked manalagi apple brandy, koji, umami bitters and apple miso.

Where: Socio, 17 Staunton Street, Central

When: 8.30pm onwards

Tuesday, July 28

Campari x Wynn Palace Asia’s 50 Best Bars after-party

Tuesday is the day we’ve all been waiting for. After our region’s most excellent bars get their flowers, Wynn Palace is joining hands with Campari to host an all-out after-party in Macau. Responsible for the vibes are some of the region’s best. Look out for veterans of the list to host this get-together: Singapore’s Cat Bite Club (No 86, 2026); The Cocktail Club (No 12, 2024) and Carrots (No 34, 2025), both from Jakarta; Opium from Bangkok (No 43, 2025); and Bengaluru’s Soka (No 28, 2025).

Where: Palace Reserve Club, Wynn Palace, Avenida Da Nave Desportiva, Cotai, Macau

When: Post-ceremony till late

Wednesday, July 29

Argo Mega Friends Takeover

Argo plays host to an exceptional night of mixology as Argo Mega Friends returns with three new regional names. This collaboration brings together teams from three of Asia’s top-ranked bars. Bangkok’s Bar Us is represented by co-founders Aum Veerach and Taln Sudarat; Dry Wave Cocktail Studio sends founder Supawit “Palm” Muttarattana and bartender Ammie Suparada; and Taipei duo William Wu and Cloris Huang of The Public House round out the line-up.

Expect a vibrant atmosphere where these master mixologists serve up inventive, culinary-forward cocktails, such as Bar Us’ famous Jackfruit & Sticky Rice.

Where: Argo, Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong, 8 Finance Street, Central

When: 6pm-9.30pm

Terrible Baby x Moebius Milano

Moebius Milano, ranked No 7 on the World’s 50 Best Bars last year, is housed inside a Milanese textile warehouse where Michelin-starred gastronomy, live jazz and avant-garde mixology collide.

For one night only, Moebius’ owner Lorenzo Querci and bartender Andrea Giraldo are taking over Eaton HK’s Terrible Baby. On the menu are cocktails like the Cocco & Salvia Negroni, which contains Bulldog gin and Del Professore Vermouth Rosso, as well as the aperitif Raspberry Lavorato Secco, which contains Campari and Rabarbaro Zucca.

Where: Terrible Baby, 4/F, Eaton Hong Kong, 380 Nathan Road, Kowloon

When: 7pm till sold out

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing and Manila should avoid South China Sea ‘miscalculation’: top diplomats
item.description:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Philippine counterpart in Manila on Wednesday, with both sides highlighting the need for “reducing the risk of miscalculation” and maintaining stability in the South China Sea.

The meeting on the sidelines of the Asean foreign ministers’ gathering marked the first formal talks between the top diplomats since Maria Theresa Lazaro assumed office in July last year.

It also came days after fresh tensions in the disputed waters, with Chinese coastguard and Philippine Navy vessels clashing on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, the first serious maritime encounter in months between the rival claimants.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Philippine counterpart in Manila on Wednesday, with both sides highlighting the need for “reducing the risk of miscalculation” and maintaining stability in the South China Sea.

The meeting on the sidelines of the Asean foreign ministers’ gathering marked the first formal talks between the top diplomats since Maria Theresa Lazaro assumed office in July last year.

It also came days after fresh tensions in the disputed waters, with Chinese coastguard and Philippine Navy vessels clashing on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, the first serious maritime encounter in months between the rival claimants.

The Philippine foreign ministry described Wednesday’s meeting between Wang and Lazaro as “candid, comprehensive and constructive”.

“The two sides underscored the importance of maintaining peace, security, and stability in the region, reducing the risk of miscalculation, and sustaining dialogue on matters of mutual concern,” it said in a read-out.

The talks covered a wide range of topics, including maritime disputes, security, law enforcement, trade and investment cooperation as well as tourism and regional issues, according to the ministry.

It said Lazaro reiterated Manila’s protest against “violent actions” by China Coast Guard personnel near the Second Thomas Shoal, known as Renai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines.

She also reaffirmed the Philippines’ position on the maritime dispute and raised concerns over Chinese actions that “have infringed on the maritime rights and entitlements, including incidents affecting the safety of Filipino personnel and fishermen”.

Beijing has accused the Philippines of instigating Monday’s incident by sending small rubber boats to approach its coastguard vessel, while Manila says one of its navy personnel was struck on the head with a wooden baton.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr summoned the Chinese ambassador on Tuesday, condemning the incident as a matter of national security.

Hours earlier, the Philippine envoy in Beijing had been summoned by the Chinese foreign ministry, which accused Manila of provocation.

The Wang-Lazaro meeting also came days after a diplomatic row over a Chinese state media video mocking the 10th anniversary of a South China Sea arbitral ruling favouring Manila.

The video, published by China Daily on July 10, showed a monkey dressed in traditional Philippine attire being manipulated by figures representing the United States and Japan before being blasted by water cannon, something China has been alleged to have deployed against Philippine vessels in contested waters.

Manila strongly condemned the depiction as racist propaganda and lodged a formal diplomatic protest.

Beijing distanced itself from the video, saying it did not represent an official position, while asserting its territorial claims.

Lazaro raised the issue with Wang, according to her ministry.

“Disagreements over legal and political issues do not justify resorting to disturbing imagery,” she was quoted as saying.

She also described the video as “deeply offensive, distressing, and unacceptable”.

“The Philippines emphasised the need to exercise restraint, avoid actions that increase tensions, and resolve disputes peacefully in accordance with international law, particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award,” the read-out said.

Lazaro also reiterated Manila’s one-China policy, it added.

Additionally, both sides underscored the importance of “maintaining open channels of communication, enhancing mutual understanding, and strengthening confidence-building measures”.

According to the read-out, both foreign ministers highlighted progress on the South China Sea Code of Conduct and reaffirmed their commitment to wrapping up related negotiations this year.

The Philippines is this year’s rotating chair of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Manila is hosting regional ministers this week for discussions on regional flashpoints ranging from the South China Sea to Myanmar and the economic impact of the Middle East conflict.

In separate meetings on Monday with Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn of Cambodia and Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan, Wang emphasised that maritime disputes should not derail ties and called for joint efforts to exclude perceived external meddling.

During his talks with Kao, Wang described the South China Sea as a shared home for regional countries while hailing Beijing as “the most important anchor of stability in the region”.

“Certain forces within the Philippine military and maritime law enforcement ranks have deliberately provoked incidents in the South China Sea to serve the interests of external forces, undermining the process of improving China-Philippines relations as well as peace and stability in the South China Sea,” Wang told Kao.

On July 12, the Philippines marked the anniversary of the 2016 arbitral ruling with a joint statement alongside the US, Japan and 11 other nations. Beijing denounced the declaration as “a distortion of facts and an act of vilification against China”.

The Wang-Lazaro meeting would be significant, Asean spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial of the Philippine foreign ministry had said on Monday, noting it would cover not only bilateral relations but also regional issues.

“We believe that this engagement is very important because not only will it address … the bilateral relations between the Philippines and China, but it will also have something to do with … the impact of what’s happening globally to the region, to Asean,” he said, according to the Manila Bulletin.

Imperial added that negotiations on the South China Sea code of conduct, ongoing for nearly 17 years, would “always be part of the discussions” during both bilateral and Asean meetings.

In 2023, Asean and China agreed to speed up talks with the goal of concluding the agreement within three years, but progress has been slow as both sides still dispute the legal basis of Beijing’s claims in the strategic waterway.

Despite expanding trade and Chinese investment in the Philippines, the South China Sea dispute remains central to their relations, which have fluctuated between tension and engagement since Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr took office four years ago.

Encounters between Chinese coastguard vessels and Philippine ships have become more frequent, particularly around Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal, over which Beijing asserts “indisputable sovereignty” alongside much of the South China Sea.

While China sees Asean as a critical arena to push back against what it considers “external interference” led by the US and Japan, the Philippines has hardened its stance in recent months, accusing the Chinese of aggressive manoeuvres.

Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, sanctioned by Beijing last month over “erroneous remarks”, has asserted that the Philippines is justified in avoiding defence engagements with China.

Manila has strengthened military ties with the US, Japan and their allies over the years, while maintaining bilateral channels with Beijing to manage disputes and avoid escalation.

Both sides have also kept communication channels open, despite frequent clashes and maritime incidents.

During a working-level dialogue in Manila on June 30, Liu Jinsong, director general of the Chinese foreign ministry’s Asian affairs department, urged the Philippines to “honour its commitments and match words with deeds”, while expressing “serious concerns” over what Beijing saw as negative moves.

Philippine officials at the meeting, led by Marshall Louis Alferez of the foreign ministry, reaffirmed a commitment to dialogue and the one-China principle, while expressing a readiness to manage disputes constructively and avoid unintended incidents.

Philippine read-outs described the talks as building on earlier bilateral sessions this year in Cebu, Beijing and Quanzhou, where officials discussed South China Sea issues, provisional arrangements to reduce incidents during resupply missions and potential practical cooperation.

item.title: [SCMP] Wang Yi and Marco Rubio at Asean discuss Xi’s planned US visit, South China Sea clash
item.description:
The Chinese president’s planned trip to the US and the Beijing-Manila South China Sea dispute led the agenda when the top Chinese and American diplomats met in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in the Philippine capital, Manila, for 90 minutes of talks on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ meeting, which ends on Thursday.

According to a readout published by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Wang described the meeting as “pragmatic, positive and constructive”, and urged both sides to pursue “strategic stability” and “peaceful coexistence”.
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese president’s planned trip to the US and the Beijing-Manila South China Sea dispute led the agenda when the top Chinese and American diplomats met in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in the Philippine capital, Manila, for 90 minutes of talks on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ meeting, which ends on Thursday.

According to a readout published by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Wang described the meeting as “pragmatic, positive and constructive”, and urged both sides to pursue “strategic stability” and “peaceful coexistence”.

Without explicitly mentioning the issue, Wang said he had conveyed China’s position on the “recent series of negative words and actions by the US” and called on Washington to respect China’s core interests.

“Our responsibility now is to follow the path set by the two heads of state, eliminate interference and overcome obstacles, and ensure that the consensus reached by the leaders is translated into consensus and action across the entire government and all sectors,” Wang was quoted as saying.

Rubio also said there were still differences between the two countries but that their job was to manage them.

He added that there were areas of potential cooperation, and they discussed President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the US, according to Reuters.

“The work we need to do now [for] September is to identify what those areas are, so that we can lay the groundwork for a very positive visit … we talked a lot about that,” Rubio said.

He described Monday’s clash between Beijing and Manila over Second Thomas Shoal as very negative and benefiting no one.

When asked about the progress of arms sales to Taiwan – a sensitive subject at the China-US summit in May – Rubio said they were still under internal review because Washington had to take its own stockpile and availability into consideration.

“There is a huge effort on our part to restart a definite defence industrial base and restart its ability to produce,” he said.

Washington is reviewing a US$14 billion weapons package to the island and has not yet formally submitted the proposed sale to Congress, with the delay attributed to production capacity and ammunition reserves.

After his trip to Beijing in May, US President Donald Trump said that holding off on the package could be a “negotiating chip”.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary.

Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

On the subject of America’s conflict with Iran, Rubio described China as in some ways cooperative with the US.

“One thing in particular is that they have been pretty clear that they don’t support any tolling or restrictions on global shipping through international waterways,” he said of China.

Before Rubio’s trip to Manila, the US State Department said the visit was meant to advance “a clear US priority: a free and open Indo-Pacific that delivers safety, security and prosperity for the region and for the American people”.

The diplomatic engagement comes as a rekindled US-Iran war puts Southeast Asian economies under intense economic and energy strain, and follows Washington’s allegations of Chinese electoral interference in the 2020 presidential election.

In a prime-time speech last week, Trump accused China of meddling in US elections, alleging it obtained 220 million American voter records beginning in the 2020 election cycle for “the largest compromise of election data in history”.

Beijing firmly rejected the accusation on Friday.

On Wednesday, Rubio said the allegations of election interference were not discussed in his meeting with Wang.

He also said the state of China-Japan ties was “troubling”, and that deep cooperation between Washington and Tokyo would continue.

Wang and Rubio last spoke in early July in what both sides described as a “positive and constructive” phone call. It was the first reported cabinet-level communication since Trump’s state visit in May.

The dialogue is a critical follow-up to the summit in which both countries pledged to establish a “new vision of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, with Beijing committed to buying more planes, agricultural produce and energy products.

The rival powers are in a fragile trade truce reached by Xi and Trump in October last year and are trying to manage risks and stabilise ties to avert a total decoupling.

But their underlying tensions and rivalry – such as on critical supply chains and advanced technology – remain unchanged.

China has increasingly said it calls for managed competition rather than confrontation, while avoiding major concessions on issues over trade or Taiwan.

Meanwhile, on Friday, the US did not renew a national emergency declaration over Hong Kong and lifted sanctions on nine government officials from Hong Kong and mainland China.

The move was welcomed in Beijing, which described Washington’s decision as “an important step in fulfilling the consensus reached in bilateral talks”.

On Tuesday, Trump signalled that Washington would confront Beijing over the alleged interference but played down the prospect of retaliation.

“We’re going to talk to them about it,” Trump said, adding that the alleged interference “took place a long time ago” and that China might be “a little bit different today than it was then”.

“They do things to us and we do things to them,” he said. “I’ll be honest, we do things to them too. It’s not a one-way street, but we’ll be talking to them.”

Both sides have indicated that Xi’s planned visit remains on track.

On Sunday, before heading to Manila, Rubio said Xi’s trip was still expected to happen in September.

And on Monday, China’s foreign ministry said that both sides had kept in contact on the arrangements for the heads of states’ interactions later this year.

“We anticipate that the trip is happening in September. They’ve continued to send over their teams to prepare for it, and I’ve heard nothing otherwise,” Rubio said.

item.title: [SCMP] The mystery of one man’s fortress in Longgang
item.description:
On the northeastern fringes of Shenzhen, standing among the low-rise tile houses of Longgang district, is a monolith that refuses to explain itself.

Erected during the late 1970s and 80s, the seven-storey building towers over the market town, a monument to something known only to its long-gone creator. Vegetation grows wild on the roof. Iron fencing and rusty cages crown its top. At night, it stands unlit; by day, its bare concrete facade looms over the narrow surrounding streets with the air of a wartime watchtower, attracting young explorers who ride Shenzhen’s Metro Line 3 to Shuanglong station, crossing the city just to see “Longgang’s Weird Building” for themselves.

A glance at the near-windowless exterior provides only hints of the man behind the Weird Building: Wen Yaoguang, a Longgang native who appears to have made his fortune in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
On the northeastern fringes of Shenzhen, standing among the low-rise tile houses of Longgang district, is a monolith that refuses to explain itself.

Erected during the late 1970s and 80s, the seven-storey building towers over the market town, a monument to something known only to its long-gone creator. Vegetation grows wild on the roof. Iron fencing and rusty cages crown its top. At night, it stands unlit; by day, its bare concrete facade looms over the narrow surrounding streets with the air of a wartime watchtower, attracting young explorers who ride Shenzhen’s Metro Line 3 to Shuanglong station, crossing the city just to see “Longgang’s Weird Building” for themselves.

A glance at the near-windowless exterior provides only hints of the man behind the Weird Building: Wen Yaoguang, a Longgang native who appears to have made his fortune in Hong Kong.

What is known of Wen’s life has been pieced together through oral accounts from neighbours, local lore passed between households and recounted to inquisitive visitors. As filmmaker Zhang Shengjia discovered while conducting research for his 2025 documentary, The Haunted Folk Fortress, Wen was, seemingly, an ordinary man driven by an extraordinary vision.

It is thought that Wen was born in Longgang and, sometime before World War II, crossed into Hong Kong, where he found work as a seafarer and later took over some farmland. He lived in Hong Kong through the Japanese occupation (1941-1945). During the city’s economic boom in the 60s, he is said to have received a sizeable land-requisition payout. After 1978, when mainland China began to open up under Deng Xiaoping, Wen returned to Longgang with his fortune and began to build.

Although it has never formally been opened to the public, the curious have found their way inside the Weird Building over the years. Their online accounts and footage – available through a virtual-reality tour – offer further understanding of its interior.

Longgang’s Weird Building is remarkably compact, with a footprint of roughly 36 square metres. Pass through the front entrance grilles and you are met with steep stairways leading both down to a dark, now-flooded basement and up to a small living area and kitchen.

Wen devised alternating-tread stairs as a space-saving solution; left and right feet land on separate, staggered steps, halving the width of each staircase. Throughout the property, staircases are adapted to their particular location; some veer off at unlikely angles, while others do not resemble conventional staircases at all.

Despite the building appearing to have few windows, much of the interior is well-lit and the upper floors offer panoramic views. What looks from the outside like solid concrete is, on one facade, in fact sheets of stainless steel punched with holes measuring roughly 5mm across.

Cast-in-place concrete furnishings are embedded into the structure of the third floor and most of the fourth floor is given over to bathtubs and water tanks, the purpose of which is unknown.

There may be as many as 20 bathtubs and eight toilets in the building, estimates Feng Guochan, executive chief architect at the Shenzhen General Institute of Architectural Design and Research, who had been allowed access by the local government to survey the building. Precise counts are difficult given the non-linear floor plans, says Feng.

The rooftop terrace, with its pavilion, is believed to have once served as a garden.

Rather than bricks or prefabricated blocks, Wen chose to pour everything – walls, floors, curved concrete benches arranged around tables – in situ.

“Choosing this approach is quite a challenge,” says Feng. Cast-in-place concrete requires a lot of formwork and carries the risk of blowouts, where wet material bursts through moulds. “And it’s very slow.”

That may explain why the building took more than a decade to complete but the permanence of concrete is perhaps the point, as the furniture is the building, fused with the structure. “When primitive people lived inside caves, they organised their lives according to the contours of the cave,” says Feng. “Instead of this being imposed by nature, [here] it occurs through one’s own thinking.”

In many ways, Longgang’s Weird Building echoes the qualities of Chinese vernacular defensive architecture, examples of which include the Kaiping diaolou of Guangdong province (fortress-like residences bearing elements of Western architectural traditions built by Chinese who returned from overseas in the 20s and 30s) and the Hakka paolou (fortified watchtowers erected on the peripheries of walled villages in Shenzhen).

Structures built by returnees “often reflect what the owner experienced abroad”, Zhang tells me. “As [this] owner was once a seafarer, the interior of the Weird Building not only reflects this experience at sea – with cabin-like spatial layouts – but continues the functional traditions of diaolou. It has massive water tanks, plots for raising chickens and growing vegetables – all built for self-sufficiency in a crisis.”

While the rest of China was opening up, Wen seemed to want to seal himself off, “like he was preparing for the end of the world”, says Feng.

In Zhang’s documentary, one local resident recalls Wen sitting under a banyan tree on a street corner, contemplating how his building could be modified: “I believe he is much like those of us who enjoy creative work – he is an artist and architect, and he possessed enough passion to persevere with the construction.”

Wen was probably also inspired by feng shui, says Zhang: “It’s rumoured that a feng shui master advised him to keep building to ward off bad luck, and there was definitely some consideration to feng shui principles indoors, too.”

Whatever the inspiration, the idiosyncratic construction has spatial complexity. Floors of differing heights flow into one another and bring to mind Austrian architect Adolf Loos’ Raumplan concept, which conceives of a building as an intertwined three-dimensional puzzle.
