“Hong Kong can serve as a bridgehead, as a brilliant pearl,” Chen said. “In this way, we can break the current Western monopoly on these high-end services and value addition.

“Hong Kong’s [role] in China becoming a marine superpower, what is its function? It must be this high-value-added shipping service.”

item.title: [SCMP] Bachelet-led panel urges Latin America not to choose sides in US-China rivalry
item.description:
Latin American countries should resist pressure to choose between the United States and China and use their vast reserves of lithium, copper and other strategic resources to strengthen their negotiating power, according to a high-level commission co-chaired by former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet and former Colombian president Ivan Duque.

But the commission acknowledges that the region’s room for manoeuvre is sharply constrained in security, technology and critical infrastructure, areas in which Washington remains dominant and has sought to curb Beijing’s growing influence.

The report, released on Tuesday by the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, argues that countries can work with different partners on different issues – maintaining security relationships with Washington while diversifying trade and investment towards China and other economies.
item.content:encoded:
Latin American countries should resist pressure to choose between the United States and China and use their vast reserves of lithium, copper and other strategic resources to strengthen their negotiating power, according to a high-level commission co-chaired by former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet and former Colombian president Ivan Duque.

But the commission acknowledges that the region’s room for manoeuvre is sharply constrained in security, technology and critical infrastructure, areas in which Washington remains dominant and has sought to curb Beijing’s growing influence.

The report, released on Tuesday by the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, argues that countries can work with different partners on different issues – maintaining security relationships with Washington while diversifying trade and investment towards China and other economies.

Presenting the report in Santiago, Duque said Latin America needed “a geopolitical vision of our own, not dictated to us”, arguing that countries should not become trapped in fixed alignments or automatically take sides between rival powers.

Governments should instead retain the flexibility to align with different partners according to their strategic priorities, shared principles and opportunities for trade and investment, he said.

Bachelet said the region had gained leverage because intensifying competition among global powers had increased the value of its resources.

“The world has changed, and the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean have many things that the world needs,” she said.

The commission identifies Latin America’s natural resources as a potentially powerful negotiating tool.

The region holds an estimated 46 per cent of the world’s lithium reserves, 35 per cent of its copper, 28 per cent of its graphite and 23 per cent of its rare earths, according to the report.

It is also the world’s leading net food-exporting region, hosts nearly half of the planet’s terrestrial biodiversity and possesses about one-third of its freshwater resources.

China becomes a new option in Latin American negotiations

Qian Liu, a Chinese business executive who served on the commission, said Beijing’s increasing economic presence provided Latin American governments with another option as they negotiated with major powers.

“The rise of China is providing the world with a different option and opportunity, and competition is good,” said Liu, founder and chief executive of Wusawa.

China has become South America’s largest trading partner, she noted, while Chinese and other Asian companies have shown strong interest in expanding their operations in the region.

But possessing large mineral reserves was not the same as capturing their economic value, Liu warned. Much of the region’s mineral production was still exported in raw or lightly refined form.

She urged governments to negotiate access to critical minerals as part of broader investment packages incorporating infrastructure, local processing, workforce development and technology transfer.

Regional coordination could also help countries move from being price takers towards becoming strategic partners with greater influence over the rules governing critical-mineral markets, she said.

The report similarly warned that the region’s resources would not automatically translate into economic development or greater global influence.

It called on governments to move beyond the extraction and export of raw materials by requiring foreign investment to support local processing, technology transfer, supplier networks and more advanced manufacturing.

China has already established a strong investment presence in the “lithium triangle” of Argentina, Bolivia and Chile, as well as in the copper industries of several countries, the report said.

US and China compete over strategic infrastructure in Latin America

Beijing is also a major source of infrastructure financing. More than 20 Latin American and Caribbean countries have signed memorandums of understanding to participate in China’s Belt and Road Initiative, while seven had joined the Beijing-backed Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank as of March.

At the same time, the US has intensified efforts to prevent Chinese companies from gaining control of strategic infrastructure and assets in the western hemisphere.

The commission said decisions involving energy, critical minerals, digital infrastructure and other strategic sectors were increasingly subject to outside pressure as national security considerations became intertwined with economic relations.

ECLAC executive secretary Jose Manuel Salazar-Xirinachs acknowledged that some governments remained apprehensive about addressing geopolitical questions viewed as “delicate and even risky”.

But declining to confront those questions was itself a choice, he argued.

“Paralysis and inertia are not neutral; they are decisions taken by virtue of inaction,” Salazar-Xirinachs said, calling for deliberate and coordinated action supported by a long-term vision.

“It is possible to be prudent and strategic at the same time. Indeed, that is exactly what we have to be at this time.”

The report draws an important distinction between the region’s economic and security relationships.

China is now the largest trading partner for much of South America and ranks among the three largest sources of imports for almost every Latin American and Caribbean country, it said.

Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, however, remain much more closely tied to the US through trade, investment and remittances.

In security, Washington remains “by far the dominant external player”, supported by an extensive network of military training, joint exercises, intelligence-sharing and cooperation against organised crime.

China has nevertheless expanded its defence diplomacy in the region. Since 2020, the number of Latin American and Caribbean military personnel attending Chinese military colleges has been more than five times the number enrolled in US institutions, the report said, citing previous research.

Stronger pressure to align with US on security, tech and infrastructure expected

Despite Beijing’s growing engagement, the commission concluded that Latin American governments would face considerably stronger pressure to align with Washington on security, advanced technology and critical infrastructure than on trade.

That assessment comes amid the Trump administration’s renewed assertion of US primacy in the western hemisphere and warnings that Washington will oppose Chinese control of ports, telecommunications networks and other strategic facilities in the region.

Rather than pursuing the same alignment across every aspect of foreign policy, the commission recommends “variable-geometry” partnerships: coalitions with different countries based on the issue being addressed.

A government could, for example, cooperate closely with Washington on security while maintaining extensive trade and investment ties with China and working with the European Union or emerging economies on climate policy, digital governance or development financing.

The commission said Latin American governments needed to develop greater “geopolitical muscle” – analytical capabilities within government, business and academia to identify their dependence on foreign powers, anticipate pressure and protect critical economic vulnerabilities.

It also called for stronger regional coordination, but stopped short of proposing another broad Latin American organisation.

Political divisions make comprehensive regional consensus unrealistic, it said. Governments should instead form smaller coalitions around specific areas where they share interests, such as critical minerals, energy, food security, digital standards, infrastructure and the fight against transnational organised crime.

Duque said the commission’s recommendations were intended as a practical road map rather than a geopolitical doctrine and did not require unanimity among the region’s ideologically divided governments.

Fears over global fragmentation, erosion of multilateralism

The commission was co-chaired by Bachelet, a centre-left former president of Chile, and Duque, a conservative former president of Colombia. Its 13 members included political leaders, economists, business executives and foreign-policy specialists from Latin America, China, the US, Europe, India and Africa.

The ideological contrast between its co-chairs underscored the commission’s broad political spectrum. Both said members nevertheless reached broad agreement.

Bachelet is currently a candidate to succeed Antonio Guterres as UN secretary general. She was nominated in February by the governments of Chile, Brazil and Mexico.

She said the erosion of multilateralism and the growing fragmentation of global governance were of particular concern to her.

The report therefore provides a window into her approach to the increasing divide between Washington and Beijing and the role that Latin America and other developing regions could play in an increasingly fragmented international system.

The commission described the world as moving away from a US-dominated order towards an asymmetric form of multipolar competition centred on the US-China rivalry.

China’s share of global gross domestic product, measured by purchasing power parity, rose from 4 per cent in 1990 to 19 per cent in 2024, while the G7’s combined share fell from 45 per cent to 30 per cent, the report said.

Bachelet also highlighted the commission’s conclusion that US soft power had declined in recent years while China’s had increased, reflecting a broader redistribution of economic, technological and political influence.

Nevertheless, the commission warned Latin American governments against replacing dependence on one great power with dependence on another.

The region’s goal, it said, should be to preserve flexibility, reduce vulnerabilities and extract greater development benefits from the growing international demand for its resources.

“Global powers are already acting,” the report said. “The United States, China and the European Union are deploying comprehensive strategies to secure access to the region’s resources.”

The central question was whether Latin American countries would respond collectively and strategically or continue to negotiate with major powers individually and reactively, the commission said.

Without a deliberate strategy of its own, the report warned, the region would not remain neutral. It would instead be shaped by the priorities and actions of more powerful countries.

“Our geopolitical future does not depend on what is set by a small number of countries,” Duque said.

Instead, he argued, it would depend on whether Latin America could identify its strengths and opportunities and establish its own role in the world.

item.title: [SCMP] VIP, APP, PPT: Are English abbreviations harming China’s cultural confidence?
item.description:
A Chinese speaker today might describe their day at work as first making a “PPT” (a PowerPoint presentation) and then having to “PS tu” (Photoshop an image). After clocking off, they might “chang K” (sing karaoke) with friends before taking the “C wei” (centre spot) in a group photo.

These novel phrases spring from the widespread habit of adopting English abbreviations directly into daily speech, usually pronounced letter by letter.

While this is the organic result of cultural exchange, the phenomenon has sparked concern in some quarters that the Chinese language is losing its “cultural confidence”, with one expert stressing the importance of preserving the language’s “capacity for self-renewal”.
item.content:encoded:
A Chinese speaker today might describe their day at work as first making a “PPT” (a PowerPoint presentation) and then having to “PS tu” (Photoshop an image). After clocking off, they might “chang K” (sing karaoke) with friends before taking the “C wei” (centre spot) in a group photo.

These novel phrases spring from the widespread habit of adopting English abbreviations directly into daily speech, usually pronounced letter by letter.

While this is the organic result of cultural exchange, the phenomenon has sparked concern in some quarters that the Chinese language is losing its “cultural confidence”, with one expert stressing the importance of preserving the language’s “capacity for self-renewal”.

In an interview published in the overseas edition of People’s Daily last Monday, Fang Jing, a member of the Shanxi Science Writers Association, said China was dealing with thousands of letter-based terms entering daily usage.

A key concern raised by the People’s Daily interviewer was whether the growing use of English abbreviations could limit the Chinese language’s own expressive capacity.

As new technologies entered the public’s everyday lexicon, they tended to circulate in two parallel forms – an English word and a formal Chinese name – without ever settling into common, easily understood Chinese equivalents, Fang said.

In March, People’s Daily launched a campaign inviting suggestions for a new Chinese name for artificial intelligence (AI).

In the article announcing the campaign, the Communist Party mouthpiece acknowledged that while AI already has a formal Chinese name – the literal translation of “artificial intelligence” – the English abbreviation had become more widely used because it was more concise.

It argued that AI deserved a catchier Chinese moniker to sit alongside its formal name rather than just a two-letter word with “not a trace of Chinese”.

The article also questioned whether the widespread use of “AI” aligned with the country’s law, which designates Chinese and standardised Chinese characters as the “national common language”.

In the interview, Fang argued that efforts to promote Chinese terms were closely linked to the “standardisation and continuity” of China’s “national common language”.

“Speeding up the creation of standard Chinese equivalents for letter-based terms and improving mechanisms for translating foreign expressions are matters that influence not only the expressive power of Chinese and convenience of communication, but also cultural confidence,” Fang said.

The concept of “cultural confidence” has official backing from the highest levels. In 2016, President Xi Jinping described the essential “Four Confidences” – confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The formulation was later added to the Communist Party’s constitution.

“With unwavering cultural confidence, a profound sense of mission and a spirit of relentless endeavour, we must unite our efforts to create a new culture for our times,” Xi said in 2023.

The debate over English influence long predates these buzzwords, however – it is not even exclusively Chinese.

For instance, the Academie Francaise has been battling against English loanwords in French for decades, coining its own versions of new words such as “esports”.

Concerns over the impact of Western languages on Chinese were already being discussed in literary circles in the 1970s and the 1980s.

Fang told the People’s Daily that at that time, prominent poet and translator Yu Kwang-chung criticised the indiscriminate imitation of foreign sentence patterns that could weaken Chinese modes of expression. Fang added that Yu also said that carefully adopted foreign influences could enrich the language.

Such debates have continued. State media and commentators have repeatedly criticised what they see as excessive use of English borrowings, calling for efforts to protect the “purity” of Chinese and reduce reliance on loanwords.

Meanwhile, they have also taken pride in the growing global circulation of Chinese-origin words, from internet slang to terms reflecting contemporary Chinese society, as a sign of the country’s expanding cultural influence.

“Shaolin”, “yin-yang”, “ni hao” (hello), and “dama”, a slang term for a middle-aged woman, were among the Chinese words most recognised in the English-speaking world, according to a report released by the China International Publishing Group in 2018.

In recent years, newer expressions have also appeared in international media. These include “996”, which refers to working from 9am to 9pm, six days a week; “tangping”, or “lying flat”, meaning dropping out of the rat race; and “neijuan”, or “involution”, describing excessive competition.

Fang said the growing use of letter-based terms was not a sign that Chinese had become less capable of absorbing foreign words. Rather, the way foreign terms entered Chinese had undergone a “structural change”.

Earlier borrowings were often stand-alone words that would be transliterated into Chinese and then written with Chinese characters, such as “kafei” (coffee), “shafa” (sofa) and “heike” (hacker).

Many newer terms, however, arrive as abbreviations – such as AI, GDP and CPU – which are made up of letters that carry little meaning on their own and are therefore harder to translate into concise Chinese equivalents.

A 2006 report by China’s Ministry of Education and State Language Commission found that 10 English abbreviations – including NBA, GDP, IT, MP3, DVD and CEO – had already entered the 5,000 most frequently used terms in the Chinese media.

She added that convenience and speed had also helped such words spread. Short forms such as “CT” and “APP” are easier to use in speech and writing than their longer Chinese equivalents – which are seven and four characters long, respectively – thus “squeezing out space” for Chinese versions.

Meanwhile, technological concepts now spread globally within days or weeks, allowing English words to become familiar before translated terms gain wider acceptance.

The priority should be to speed up the creation of Chinese names for emerging concepts and establish widely accepted equivalents quickly, Fang said.

“Protecting the Chinese language’s capacity for self-renewal is a shared responsibility of language professionals and all users of the language,” Fang said.

“Language carries the ways of thinking, values and historical memories accumulated by a nation over generations, serving as a vital foundation for the continuation and development of its culture.”

item.title: [SCMP] Massive Attack’s Singapore ban tests legal limits of artistic freedom
item.description:
The banning of British band Massive Attack from Singapore for pro-Palestine acts during their concert has split opinion in the city state, with some lamenting what they see as laws that are too strict and others urging foreigners to comply with local rules.

At their gig on Wednesday, the two-man band held up a Palestinian flag and shouted “Free Palestine” along with members of the audience.

Under the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act, it is illegal to display non-Singaporean flags in the city state. Holding a protest without a permit is also prohibited under the Public Order Act.
item.content:encoded:
The banning of British band Massive Attack from Singapore for pro-Palestine acts during their concert has split opinion in the city state, with some lamenting what they see as laws that are too strict and others urging foreigners to comply with local rules.

At their gig on Wednesday, the two-man band held up a Palestinian flag and shouted “Free Palestine” along with members of the audience.

Under the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act, it is illegal to display non-Singaporean flags in the city state. Holding a protest without a permit is also prohibited under the Public Order Act.

On Friday, police and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) said in a joint statement that the force investigated Robert Del Naja and Grant Marshall for supporting a political cause and unfurling a foreign flag during the concert. Police administered stern warnings and banned both members from re-entering Singapore.

The IMDA is also investigating a possible breach of licence conditions, including one stipulating there should be no display of flags in support of any causes.

“Notwithstanding the event organiser’s prior acknowledgement of the licence conditions, during the performance, two band members held a foreign flag on stage, and one of them also shouted ‘Free Palestine’,” the authorities said.

The IMDA will not grant any future application by the band to perform in Singapore.

On Sunday night, the Massive Attack members said on social media that they were “surprised and disappointed” to be detained by police, isolated and separately questioned, as well as subjected to hotel room searches and temporary passport confiscation.

“Before we set foot on the stage and again at the end of the show, large sections of the auditorium organically led chants of ‘Free Palestine’ – presumably aware but undeterred that this spontaneous expression alone could violate their government’s censorship laws,” they said.

The band members argued they did not imagine that “merely holding up the flag of a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries (Palestine) would violate any law” and called the experience “surreal”.

“On reflection, we are proud to have made this impromptu expression with our fans in Singapore who clearly felt a moral imperative to show solidarity with the people of Palestine in their ongoing reality of illegal occupation, apartheid and genocide, and we salute their courage in doing so,” they said.

This Week in Asia has contacted concert promoter Lushington Entertainments, an affiliate of publicly held Hotel Properties Limited, for comment.

‘Return gesture’

Concertgoers bemoaned the ban, noting that the atmosphere was orderly and the band’s flag waving was in response to the audience’s “Free Palestine” chants. The concert also touched on other themes such as AI, surveillance, corruption, war and the exploitation of workers, they said.

“[It was] a situation taken completely out of context, because the action of waving the flag wasn’t initiated by the members of the band, it was a return of their gesture to show solidarity with the audience and it felt right,” brand consultant Daniel Koh said.

While he agreed that artists should adhere to the legal systems of the country they performed in, Koh said there were always varying degrees and levels of legalities. “Trying to segregate politics from art and vice versa is a slippery slope,” he said. “I don’t see this as a ‘threat’ to domestic peace and social order but there will be naysayers.”

Another concertgoer, Janice Fong, recalled the band told the audience that they were unable to show some content on the accompanying screens – proving an intention to abide by Singaporean laws.

“I worry that this entire episode may make IMDA more cautious when assessing future performances and artistic works. If that happens, what initially seemed like progress for artistic expression in Singapore could ultimately result in two steps backwards for the range of content that audiences are allowed to experience,” said Fong, who works in finance.

Crystal Lim-Lange, chief executive of Forest Wolf leadership consultancy, questioned whether Singapore was too quick to apply rules without considering the context.

“The balance between respecting the law, preserving public order and allowing artistic expression isn’t always straightforward, and blanket enforcement may not always produce the best outcome,” Lim-Lange said in a social media post.

She did not condone laws being ignored or artists having free rein, she said, “but if Singapore wants to be seen as a global arts hub, these are the kinds of conversations we need to be mature enough to have”.

Slippery slope

The problem would be where to draw the line, though, criminal lawyers said.

Sunil Sudheesan, head of criminal law at Quahe Woo & Palmer, called the authorities’ treatment of the band “normal protocol” for foreigners who broke local laws, and it was common for culprits to be banned.

Singapore was definitely not anti-Palestine since it had donated extensively to humanitarian aid, he said. “If the band waved the Israeli flag, that same treatment would have ensued.”

Should leniency be exercised for artistic expression, this could open the floodgates to other laws being broken, he added.

Many of Cory Wong’s foreign clients had been deported or denied re-entry into Singapore after their case was over, the director at Invictus Law Corporation who specialises in criminal law said.

“The issue is not whether Singapore is for or against any involved parties, but it would be undesirable for Singapore to be used as a collateral or proxy staging ground by foreign actors,” he said.

Last August, American comedian Sammy Obeid accused Singaporean authorities of trying to censor his stand-up show, which often criticised Israel’s actions in Gaza, after his scheduled performance was cancelled.

Officials, however, said the permit was rejected because the application was lodged too late and ordered a correction order under Singapore’s fake news law. When Obeid did not comply, the government issued targeted directions to Meta Platforms and X, requiring them to put out correction notices to Singapore users who accessed, or would access, the posts.

In 2019, Swedish black metal band Watain was banned from performing in Singapore, with the authorities revoking its licence just two hours before showtime. They cited security concerns and the band’s history of “denigrating religions and promoting violence”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s military is laser-focused on ‘disruptive’ technologies
item.description:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just a year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the fourth part of a series, Amber Wang looks at the PLA’s pursuit of emerging technologies.

In an influential book published nearly three decades ago, a PLA military strategist argued that China should not try to match the US weapon for weapon but instead develop asymmetric advantages against its stronger rival.

Qiao Liang drew lessons from America’s victory in the Gulf War in the book, Unrestricted Warfare. He noted that warfare was entering an informationised era and that China was clearly lagging behind the United States.
item.content:encoded:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just a year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the fourth part of a series, Amber Wang looks at the PLA’s pursuit of emerging technologies.

In an influential book published nearly three decades ago, a PLA military strategist argued that China should not try to match the US weapon for weapon but instead develop asymmetric advantages against its stronger rival.

Qiao Liang drew lessons from America’s victory in the Gulf War in the book, Unrestricted Warfare. He noted that warfare was entering an informationised era and that China was clearly lagging behind the United States.

Qiao – who co-authored the book with Wang Xiangsui – also said finance, cyberspace and psychological operations would be important in future wars.

“We don’t necessarily need to have what the US has,” Qiao wrote, back in 1999. “We need to have what it doesn’t.”

In the years since then, the book has drawn significant attention in Western military circles and has been studied at the US Military Academy in West Point, New York as part of broader discussions on Chinese strategic thinking.

It also continues to resonate among military strategists in China, as the People’s Liberation Army pursues emerging and “disruptive” technologies as part of its modernisation efforts – from artificial intelligence and quantum tech to hypersonic weapons and directed-energy systems.

Decades later, Qiao said the theory in his book still held.

He told the SCMP that militaries around the world were “increasingly moving towards building weapons for the wars they expect to fight, rather than fighting wars with the weapons they possess”.

The PLA leadership has said it aims to build a “world-class military” by the end of 2049. It is expected to disclose some of its modernisation goals in August next year when the military marks its centenary.

According to analysts, China is not just trying to close the gap with America on military capabilities but also to compete on shaping the next era of warfare through disruptive technologies – and to use them to boost deterrence.

After decades of learning from the US, China is now seen by some to be blazing its own path and even taking the lead in areas such as sixth-generation fighter jets, hypersonic and laser weapons.

Future battlefield

When a mysterious tailless aircraft was spotted in skies over the southwestern city of Chengdu in 2024, it turned heads – all over the world.

Shaped like a ginkgo leaf, it did not look like previous generations of Chinese stealth fighter jets. And it prompted speculation that China might have gained an upper hand in developing a next-generation fighter.

The timing of its appearance was also highly symbolic, with the flight taking place on December 26 – the birthday of Mao Zedong, founding father of communist China.

In Mao’s time, China had limited home-grown defence capabilities and relied heavily on Soviet technology.

The fighter jet over Chengdu, along with another tailless prototype revealed two years earlier, represented more than a new design – it signalled China’s entry into the global race for sixth-generation air power.

America’s programme, known as Next Generation Air Dominance, or NGAD, is developing the Boeing F-47 stealth fighter. Other countries, including Russia, Japan, Italy and Britain, are also developing next-generation combat aircraft.

It has been a long and difficult path for China to reach this point. It took nearly three decades to move on from the first domestically designed fighter jet from the 1960s, the J-8, to the next-generation J-10 in the 1990s.

“For many years, we simply struggled to make breakthroughs,” military analyst Fu Qianshao said.

China eventually entered the fifth-generation fighter jet era with the J-20 and J-35, but they entered service later than their US counterparts.

But the emergence of a sixth-generation aircraft could be a turning point.

“This is a landmark event,” according to Fu.

“In the past, it was always the US and Russia leading the trend while others followed in a race to catch up. But now, a total reversal has taken place.”

It is not just about catching up – it also offers insight into the PLA’s vision for future warfare. According to analysts, that vision is built around “intelligentisation” – or the integration of emerging technologies with mechanisation and informationisation.

“Future aircraft will not be judged only by their speed, manoeuvrability or situational awareness. They will combine the roles of fighter and commander, with human pilots directing multiple unmanned aerial platforms as part of integrated joint operations,” Fu said.

“Similarly, tanks are evolving beyond traditional armoured platforms. Through informationisation and intelligentisation, they are becoming integrated combat systems capable of operating with unmanned platforms,” he said.

“Each tank could become a node for sensing, data exchange and intelligent decision-making.”

President Xi Jinping has pushed for faster development of “new combat capabilities”, while an overhaul of the PLA saw the creation of the Strategic Support Force in 2015 to oversee space, cyber and electronic warfare. It was split into three arms in 2024 – aerospace, cyberspace and information support.

China’s military technology has made progress at a rapid pace – from the advanced electromagnetic catapults on the Fujian aircraft carrier to its unmanned aerial and underwater systems, and AI-powered drone swarms.

Fu said the future would be more about integrated operations, with less direct human involvement.

“We are heading towards an integrated, cross-domain warfighting system – combining aerial drones, surface vessels and underwater uncrewed platforms – with humans taking a back seat in command and control.”

This is all underpinned by a broader technological foundation of advanced materials, advanced manufacturing, AI and high-performance computing.

“The foundation lies in technology: power plants, radar, avionics, flight control and materials,” Fu said, pointing to the development of fighter jets as an example. “Metamaterials represent the development of a complete, systemic technology.”

These advances are supported by the PLA, research institutes, universities and civilian tech companies through China’s military-civil fusion strategy.

As the US and its allies also integrate emerging technologies into their military systems, China’s strengths lie in policy mobilisation, manufacturing scale and engineering, according to Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.

“China may be better positioned in scaling technologies and integrating industrial capabilities, while the United States may retain advantages in frontier innovation and the ability to coordinate global technology ecosystems,” he said, adding that China still had work to do in areas like advanced semiconductors.

Disruptive tech

In military terms, disruptive technologies refer to capabilities that go beyond improving existing weapons and have the potential to alter how wars are fought – by changing operational concepts, creating new vulnerabilities, or providing an advantage if they are successfully integrated.

Chinese military mouthpiece PLA Daily has frequently identified emerging technologies with disruptive potential such as AI, quantum, hypersonic weapons, directed-energy systems and biotech.

Malcolm Davis, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said these areas – and how they came together – were “significant” for future warfare, as were autonomous systems, robotics and nanotechnology.

“As to who wins this race, it’s really uncertain. Clearly it’s a race between China and the United States,” he said, adding that China was making steady progress and was probably ahead in areas like hypersonics while facing fewer constraints in ethically challenging fields such as biotech.

China’s priority on advanced systems like electronic warfare, unmanned systems and precision-guided munitions was seen in its military parade last year, according to the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

“Such weaponry enhances China’s ability to impair US forces from conducting complex military operations in much of the Asia-Pacific,” the Washington-based think tank said in an article in October.

In January, China’s military said it was using quantum technology to gather high-value intelligence from public cyberspace. More than 10 quantum cyber warfare tools are “under development” – many of them being “tested in frontline missions”, according to official newspaper Science and Technology Daily.

The PLA Information Support Force is also reportedly working with the National University of Defence Technology’s supercomputing lab to advance a “quantum + supercomputing” project.

China has invested heavily in quantum communication and computing. In 2016, it launched Micius – the world’s first quantum communication satellite – and has since developed a large-scale space-ground quantum communication network.

Davis said quantum was a key military technology in terms of computing power, potentially with links to AI, cryptography and communications.

“It allows large problems to be solved rapidly, very secure communications and unbreakable cryptography of those communications,” he said.

But Wu Riqiang, a missile expert and professor with Tsinghua University, said while the technology could eventually be disruptive on the battlefield, its practical military impact was still uncertain.

Hypersonic weapons are meanwhile being developed as part of the PLA’s “assassin’s mace” capabilities to exploit US military vulnerabilities.

Travelling at speeds exceeding Mach 5, hypersonic weapons are difficult to intercept because of their speed and ability to manoeuvre during flight. China is widely regarded as the leading developer of these weapons.

A PLA strategist, who requested anonymity, said hypersonic weapons were designed for potential conflict with the US, but also for deterrence.

“With these capabilities, the US will have to think twice before making a move,” he said.

Of all the emerging technologies, artificial intelligence is seen as one of the most immediate drivers of military transformation.

AI is already starting to influence military operations through faster decision-making, autonomous systems, battlefield data processing and intelligence analysis, as seen in recent US strikes on Iran where AI-enabled systems helped target and support battlefield decision-making.

China’s military has reportedly tested AI-enabled drone swarm warfare, claiming that a single soldier could control a swarm of more than 200 drones.

And in 2024, AI firm DeepSeek launched large language models that drew global attention and highlighted China’s progress on artificial intelligence.

Meanwhile, China has been closely watching the Russia-Ukraine war and the conflicts in the Middle East, where drones – and counter-drone capabilities – have played a key role.

Fu said China’s directed-energy weapons designed to counter drone swarms could give it an advantage in the future.

“Countering drone swarms with directed-energy weapons such as laser weapons is the future of air defence,” he said. “Our toolkit is expanding fast, and China is making rapid progress in this area.”

Several high-energy laser weapons and high-power microwave systems were showcased during China’s military parade in Beijing last year as part of the PLA’s emerging anti-drone capabilities.

Chinese researchers are also focused on biotechnology, including concepts involving biological-computer interfaces and human-machine integration – though military applications remain at an early stage.

A Pentagon report on China’s military last year said there was a push to develop biotech including through major military-civil fusion projects in fields such as biology and brain science.

“We do not know which specific applications will eventually become viable, or what capabilities they will ultimately deliver, but clearly both countries are pouring great resources into them,” Wu said.

Analysts noted that the impact of emerging technologies should not be overstated and that they would also bring new risks.

“I believe the importance of disruptive technologies is real, but claims that possessing a particular technology alone can fundamentally determine the outcome of a war are often exaggerated,” said Sun from Tsinghua.

“Emerging technologies are unlikely to replace traditional military capabilities. Instead, they will be integrated with existing assets such as missiles, ships, aircraft, manpower and industrial capacity.”

Davis also pointed to the risks. “Losing control of technologies is a key one, and one that – at least in liberal democracies – is acting as a constraint in areas such as AI and autonomous systems,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] After Ref Cam lights up World Cup, what’s next for Lenovo’s AI tech in football?
item.description:
Having created one of the runaway television hits of this summer’s Fifa World Cup, Lenovo is plotting to up the AI ante for the women’s version next year in Brazil.

In addition to building digital twins for all 1,248 players to enhance semi-automated offside technology for the 2026 finals, labelled “the first AI World Cup”, and rolling out an analytical tool aimed at “democratising football”, the tech giants were responsible for Ref Cam, which made its major tournament debut in North America.

Ken Wong, executive vice-president of Lenovo, said the company was “exploring with Fifa what else we can bring” for future tournaments, as well as looking at how they can bring the technology “into the football mainstream”.
item.content:encoded:
Having created one of the runaway television hits of this summer’s Fifa World Cup, Lenovo is plotting to up the AI ante for the women’s version next year in Brazil.

In addition to building digital twins for all 1,248 players to enhance semi-automated offside technology for the 2026 finals, labelled “the first AI World Cup”, and rolling out an analytical tool aimed at “democratising football”, the tech giants were responsible for Ref Cam, which made its major tournament debut in North America.

Ken Wong, executive vice-president of Lenovo, said the company was “exploring with Fifa what else we can bring” for future tournaments, as well as looking at how they can bring the technology “into the football mainstream”.

“These technologies are only available for Fifa right now, but we want to replicate them so they’re available for everyone,” added Wong, who also serves as president of Lenovo’s solutions and services group.

In the six-to-nine months before the World Cup, Lenovo was tasked with considerably reducing a 40-second wait time for broadcast-quality Ref Cam images.

“There’s a juicy story behind it,” said Wong, talking exclusively to the South China Morning Post in Atlanta.

“Fifa wanted the footage to be processed and available for broadcast within five seconds. Even we could not resolve it in the first place.”

Fifa’s technology partner since 2024, Lenovo entered the collaboration intent on “being aggressive, but with appropriate risk taking”, according to Art Hu, the company’s senior vice-president and chief information officer.

Extraordinarily popular with the World Cup’s global audience of around 6 billion, Ref Cam captured several memorable moments, providing up-close views of challenges and goals, and allowing viewers to see Lionel Messi telling referee Joao Pedro Pinheiro, during Argentina’s quarter-final victory over Switzerland, to “speak to me properly, don’t disrespect me”.

It also recorded Jude Bellingham telling Ismael Elfath, the official for England’s semi-final loss to the South Americans, he had made some “shocking decisions”.

“But all the best,” added Bellingham, giving those watching on television a voyeuristic glimpse into the raw emotions of a man who had just seen his dreams shattered.

“The cameras had to be really small, because the referee is going to wear it for more than 1½ hours,” Wong said. “There are vibrations, rough clashes with players and, sometimes, he’s hit by the ball.

“It also needs a long battery life. A lot of hardware technology is not applicable, we used a lot of AI and software technology because they carry no weight.”

Also the technology provider for Formula One since 2022, Lenovo had experience of delivering moving images from drivers’ on-board cameras.

But Wong confessed he felt “a lot of pressure” in the lead-up to the opening World Cup fixture between Mexico, the co-hosts, and South Africa.

“The technology was proven, but we’d never used it for football,” he said.

“Because I’m so involved, it has almost become business as usual for me, but when this first hit the ground and I saw the feedback from Fifa, from friends and from social media, I thought, ‘Wow, this is really impressive’.”

Regardless of their wish to alert the planet to their artificial intelligence capabilities, Lenovo also had something in common with the referees who wore their cameras: the desire to not generate the legion of headlines that would have followed a high-profile error.

The Beijing-founded, Chinese multinational generated the avatars of players that were used for the semi-automated offside system; and were again forced to provide still-screen images of close calls within five seconds.

“This is a lot of pressure,” Wong acknowledged. “That’s why I sleep two hours a day.

“But we’re not building everything customised for Fifa [from scratch], because we already have our tech stack and offering. We have 32 factories and are pumping out six devices every second.

“To make technology and, especially AI, work, it is critical to have a marriage between the technologist and domain expert, which is Fifa.”

Lenovo and football’s global governing body collaborated to deliver Fifa AI Pro, a platform that assessed more than 2,000 different metrics to provide an analytics tool and tactical simulator for team strategists, and which was made freely available to the 48 teams that competed in the USA, Canada and Mexico.

“It’s like a ChatGPT for Fifa,” said Wong, who rejected the idea that partnering with the global governing body and under-fire president Gianni Infantino risked reputational damage.

“Our job is to provide the technology, it’s up to Fifa to decide how they use it,” he added.

“We used technology to establish the knowledge base, then gave each team the ability to create their own AI agent to dig out the insight they wanted.

“The output could be text, images or video. This is the beauty of the democratisation of the Fifa proprietary data points and insights, and availability of AI to all 48 teams.”

Last year’s Club World Cup, Lenovo’s first major Fifa tie-in, acted as a successful “stress test” for the international bonanza. Soon after, the company repeated their “zero-error computer solution alliance” from the Beijing 2008 Olympics when they flawlessly governed technology for the cross-border 2025 National Games.

“It was the first edition hosted outside mainland China and there was zero margin for error,” Wong said. “The results were quite impressive and there was a lot of excitement around the country and the city.”

Wong reflected similarly contentedly on a World Cup where 48 teams contested 104 matches across three countries, but he conceded that, with another global tournament fewer than 12 months away, he could “never switch off”.

“There’s a lot of work to do for next year,” Wong said. “We’re also having lots of discussions about how we can make [our AI technology] available to the mainstream.

“Pressure exists, but … we proved to the world and to our customer partner that if our technology works for the most complex event and biggest global audience, it’ll work for everyone.”

item.title: [SCMP] Who are the officers filling the big shoes left behind in PLA anti-corruption drive?
item.description:
The sweeping anti-corruption drive in China’s military appears to have cleared the way for a new batch of officers to quietly assume de facto leadership of key People’s Liberation Army bodies.

According to a South China Morning Post analysis of official insignia and protocol seating from state media coverage of recent meetings, dozens of fresh commanders have stepped into the roles of their ousted predecessors, positioning them to lead the world’s largest standing army.

Many have assumed major portfolios previously held by full generals, having recently been promoted from within their respective departments. Several others attained the rank of lieutenant general less than a year ago, according to the SCMP tally, even though they are roughly the age their full general predecessors were when assuming the same leadership roles.
item.content:encoded:
The sweeping anti-corruption drive in China’s military appears to have cleared the way for a new batch of officers to quietly assume de facto leadership of key People’s Liberation Army bodies.

According to a South China Morning Post analysis of official insignia and protocol seating from state media coverage of recent meetings, dozens of fresh commanders have stepped into the roles of their ousted predecessors, positioning them to lead the world’s largest standing army.

Many have assumed major portfolios previously held by full generals, having recently been promoted from within their respective departments. Several others attained the rank of lieutenant general less than a year ago, according to the SCMP tally, even though they are roughly the age their full general predecessors were when assuming the same leadership roles.

“Many of them have had a relatively short tenure as lieutenant generals, but they are fulfilling the duties of full generals,” noted a Chinese political expert who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.

“These lieutenant generals will face challenges – they haven’t served as senior military leaders long enough. Compared to more senior full generals, they need time to adapt to a higher perspective and establish leadership within their departments,” the expert added.

A defining moment

These internal shifts come at a pivotal moment for China’s military and political trajectory.

The PLA celebrated its 99th anniversary on Saturday, entering the final countdown to its centenary modernisation goal.

Meanwhile, the Communist Party is expected to hold its 21st national congress in the autumn of next year, when Beijing will choose a new leadership line-up for both the party and the Central Military Commission (CMC).

The CMC is the PLA’s highest commanding body, chaired by President Xi Jinping.

The current CMC began its five-year term with seven members following the 2022 national congress. But the anti-corruption drive within the PLA has left it with only two – Xi and vice-chairman Zhang Shengmin.

Convention dictates that CMC members must hold the rank of full general and have previously led a major military department, theatre command or service branch. However, the recent wave of dismissals means Beijing may need to reach deeper down the ranks to build its next high command.

Since 2023, a total of 26 full generals have been placed under investigation, while another 12 have disappeared from public view. All previously held key positions in the PLA.

The latest major upheaval came in January, when authorities announced that CMC vice-chairman Zhang Youxia and fellow member Liu Zhenli were under investigation.

Their downfall brought the number of active full generals visible to the public down to four, before promotions in July brought the total back up to six.

New faces have been steadily filling gaps in the chain of command over recent months, according to official announcements as well as video footage from various meetings, including last Friday’s official reception to mark 99 years of the PLA on August 1.

State media footage showed the new officers seated in the front rows usually reserved for senior military leaders. They were also the highest-ranking officers displaying their department’s specific insignia, indicating that they were in charge of those military bodies.

Officers with air force backgrounds appeared to have made the most gains. According to the SCMP tally, nine of the 20 key positions reassigned during the reshuffle went to air force officers. In five of those roles, the predecessors had come from other military branches.

The expert noted that while the anti-corruption campaign had inflicted a heavy toll on the PLA Ground Force, Rocket Force and Navy – the power bases of several disgraced heavyweights – the air force had emerged relatively unscathed.

The rise of air force generals could further weaken the army’s long-standing dominance within the PLA, the analyst said, referring to a decades-old tradition widely viewed as outdated and ill-suited for the joint combat requirements of modern warfare.

Changes within CMC bodies

Zhang Shuguang, who was promoted from lieutenant general to full general in July, has since been named secretary of the CMC’s discipline inspection commission. This role traditionally carries a seat on the CMC and was previously held by Zhang Shengmin, who was promoted to vice-chairman last October.

After the fall of several top generals from the CMC last year, Air Force Lieutenant General Chen Demin and Vice-Admiral Xiong Zhaoyuan appear to have taken charge of the commission’s Political Work Department, which manages ideological matters and personnel changes within the PLA. The pair have represented the department at major recent events.

The department’s former director, CMC member and former admiral Miao Hua, was placed under investigation in November 2024.

Chen and Xiong were promoted to their ranks by last November at the latest. Xiong is a veteran of the second artillery corps – the predecessor to the PLA Rocket Force, which oversees China’s strategic nuclear arsenal – and previously served as secretary general of its Political Work Department. Notably, Zhang Shengmin is also a former director of that same department.

Among others in the emerging leadership is Zhu Chuansheng, who now heads the CMC’s Joint Staff Department, once led by disgraced former CMC member Liu. Zhu was promoted to lieutenant general in March 2025 and previously served as the department’s deputy chief of staff.

Vice-Admiral Zhang Like, former deputy head of the CMC’s National Defence Mobilisation Department, was promoted to lead the department no later than last October.

The most senior lieutenant general in the line-up is Dong Li, head of the CMC’s Joint Operations Command Centre, who has served at that rank for more than five years. Dong’s predecessor, Wang Xiubin, was expelled from the party last October.

Head of forces

Clear leadership has also emerged across the PLA’s main service branches.

Wang Gang, promoted to full general alongside Zhang Shuguang in July, was also confirmed as commander of the PLA Air Force. Full general is the highest active rank in the PLA.

Wang’s co-leader as acting political commissar appears to be Shi Honggan, who was promoted to lieutenant general around December. His last publicly announced role was secretary of the air force’s discipline inspection commission.

The air force’s original commander has been removed from the national legislature, and its original political commissar has not been seen in public since last year, with no replacements formally announced.

Under the PLA’s dual-command structure, the commander focuses on military tactics and combat operations while the political commissar is in charge of political supervision, troop morale and ideology.

Cai Zhijun appears to be the new leader of the PLA Ground Force, according to the latest clues. He was promoted to lieutenant general no later than July last year, and his previously disclosed position was army chief of staff. The ground force’s original commander was removed from the national legislature before it convened earlier this year.

In another shift, Zhang Zheng – a former captain of China’s first aircraft carrier, the Liaoning – is now responsible for the navy’s military affairs. He was promoted to vice-admiral no later than September 2025, having previously served as navy chief of staff.

The navy’s original commander, Hu Zhongming, has also not been publicly seen since late last year and missed the high-profile commissioning in November of the Fujian, China’s most advanced carrier.

The navy’s political affairs are being led by Hu Yuhai, who appears to have been promoted to vice-admiral no later than last December. His previously disclosed position was deputy political commissar of the navy. He has also worked within the military’s anti-corruption infrastructure.

Lieutenant General Lei Kai has emerged as the apparent commander of the rocket force, where he previously served as chief of staff. Notably, Lei is also from the air force, where he was a top-rated pilot.

Lieutenant General Zhou Jingjiong now oversees political affairs for the rocket force, where his previously disclosed role was director of the political work department.

Earlier in his career, Zhou directed the political work department of the rocket force’s Base 56 – a unit where Zhang Shengmin also previously served as political commissar.

Lei and Zhou were promoted to lieutenant general no later than last December.

Theatre commands: picture unclear

While key leadership shifts across the CMC and rocket force are coming into focus, uncertainty still surrounds the leadership of the PLA’s five theatre commands – which are responsible for combat missions.

Only Han Shengyan and Yang Zhibin – both promoted to full general last December – have been confirmed as theatre commanders. Both are long-serving air force officers.

Han leads the Central Theatre Command and served as chief commander of the Victory Day military parade in Beijing last September. Headquartered in Beijing, this command is tasked with protecting the capital while providing operational support to the other theatre commands.

Yang is head of the Eastern Theatre Command, which is responsible for operations and deployments relating to Taiwan.

item.title: [SCMP] Is China’s climate returning to that of Tang dynasty golden age? Experts warn of a trap
item.description:
In China’s arid northwest, state media have been celebrating an increase in much-needed rainfall.

The Ningxia Hui autonomous region usually averages about 300mm (about 12 inches) of rain per year, but the annual total has risen in recent years by around 12mm.

The rain belt was moving northwards, shifting the 400mm precipitation line – the vital boundary that separates China’s arid grazing lands from its humid, agricultural heartland, the Ningxia Broadcasting News Centre reported last month.
item.content:encoded:
In China’s arid northwest, state media have been celebrating an increase in much-needed rainfall.

The Ningxia Hui autonomous region usually averages about 300mm (about 12 inches) of rain per year, but the annual total has risen in recent years by around 12mm.

The rain belt was moving northwards, shifting the 400mm precipitation line – the vital boundary that separates China’s arid grazing lands from its humid, agricultural heartland, the Ningxia Broadcasting News Centre reported last month.

This “heavenly fortune” would bring “climate dividends”, the report said, promising that “loess soil will turn green and farming area will expand”.

During the Tang dynasty “warm period”, it said, temperatures in northern China were 1 to 2 degrees Celsius (1.8 Fahrenheit) higher than now, and the area that is Ningxia today used to serve as the granary north of the Great Wall.

“The warming and greening of northwest China is not accidental but the restart of a millennia-long climate cycle,” the broadcaster reported on social media on July 21.

“As the rain belt moves northwards, the north is experiencing a warm and humid climate comparable to the prosperous Tang dynasty (618AD to 907AD). Ningxia is the most vivid example of this benefit.”

But it also warned that climate change was a “gentle double-edged sword”, bringing new challenges such as flash floods, higher evaporation rates and new crop pests.

On July 26, intense rainstorms battered the city of Guyuan in Ningxia, driving the official warning level from the lowest to the highest in just six hours. Peak rainfall reached nearly 100mm, forcing the emergency evacuation of scores of residents.

Climate scientists warn that romanticised narratives ignore the volatile reality of modern climate change.

While they agree Ningxia has seen an increase in rainfall and a warming-wetting trend, they caution that framing it as a “return to a golden age” is scientifically misleading and potentially dangerous for long-term policy and economic planning.

“I would be very cautious about describing this as a simple ‘return to a golden age’,” said Benjamin Horton, dean of the school of energy and environment at City University of Hong Kong.

More rainfall would not guarantee long-term water security, he warned, noting that rising temperatures increased evaporation rates, potentially offsetting rainfall gains while drought risks persisted.

Climate extremes may also worsen, with heavy downpours accelerating erosion, triggering flash floods and damaging infrastructure.

Ecological disruptions could follow, with invasive species, pests and pathogens surviving more easily under rapid greening and warmer winters.

Horton noted that while a supportive climate might have played a role in the flourishing of the Tang dynasty, that was only part of the story.

“While some evidence suggests parts of China were warmer and wetter during periods of the Tang era, its prosperity depended on political stability, trade, technology and governance, not climate alone.”

On a global scale, Horton said, “climate change creates a small number of winners and many losers”, pointing to widespread extreme heat, flooding, drought, sea-level rise, wildfires and food and water insecurity.

“Even Ningxia is not insulated from these wider impacts through supply chains, migration, markets and increasing climate volatility,” he added.

“The scientific takeaway is therefore not that climate change is beneficial but that some regions may experience temporary or localised advantages within an overall global trend that remains overwhelmingly disruptive.”

According to Yu Shiyong, a professor at Jiangsu Normal University’s school of geography, geomatics and planning, while “warming and wetting” trends have historical precedents, they are not uniform climate shifts.

“It was inaccurate to generalise that China’s arid regions became humid during past warm periods,” Yu said, citing research that showed varied responses to past warming.

His recent paleoclimate research found that some 8,000 to 6,000 years ago, growing season temperatures in the Hulun Lake basin in Inner Mongolia – northern China’s largest lake region – were about 1 degree Celsius higher and water levels 2.75 metres (9 feet) higher than today.

Yu urged caution on interpreting the trend.

“The warming and increased rainfall in arid and semi-arid regions of China are more likely manifestations of enhanced water cycle, redistribution of rainfall and increased extremes caused by global warming,” he said.

“Whether this represents a steady transition from arid to humid climate requires long-term observational data for verification.”

The northward shift of the multi-year average rain belt did not guarantee consistent rain every year, nor would rain fall when it was best for crop growth, Yu said, echoing Horton’s point about higher evaporation rates under warmer conditions.

He also highlighted the risk of maladaptation: a social and economic trap in which policymakers and farmers make irreversible, large investments based on a temporary climate window.

“The narrative of ‘heavenly fortune’ could influence land use and investment decisions including expanding marginal farmland and planting more water-intensive crops, increased density of orchards and tree plantations, scaling up cities and industries, and reducing drought preparedness,” he said.

“Decades later, if rain belts shift southwards, evaporation continues to increase or glacial water supply declines, these high-cost agricultural and urban infrastructure would remain locked in.

Yu also cautioned about “hidden degradation”, a phenomenon involving “greening on the surface while the deeper soil dries out”.

“When consecutive droughts occur, excessively high vegetation density could increase the risk of large-scale withering, pests and fires.”

Further, Yu said, global warming was driven mainly by human-induced greenhouse gas emissions at an unprecedented rate and that the risks today with modern cities, populations, agriculture, reservoirs and groundwater extraction were not comparable to those of ancient China.

“This ‘heavenly fortune’ is a real yet time-limited and potentially reversible climatic window,” he said. “It should not be seen as a permanent, unchanging natural condition.”

“It may offer opportunities for local adaptations, but it is not a simple repetition of the Tang dynasty’s climate, much less a natural benefit that can be realised indefinitely.”

Looking ahead, Yu said the evaluation of “wetting and warming” should shift its focus from simple metrics of total rainfall and greening to a comprehensive assessment of effective water balance, soil and groundwater reserves, streamflow stability, extreme events and ecological resilience.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong has bounced back since the bleak days of the pandemic
item.description:
Absence, it is said, makes the heart grow fonder. This week marks the fourth anniversary of my departure from Hong Kong, a city I came to love during 28 years as a resident. It was not easy to leave. Hong Kong had become my home. But it was, for me and for many others back then, the right time to make the move.

My reasons were complex, although the wearying pandemic restrictions and dramatic legal and political reforms played their part. The city had changed so much.

Returning to my native England, though, was a leap in the dark. Us British expats used to say the UK was a nice place for a holiday but we wouldn’t want to live there.
item.content:encoded:
Absence, it is said, makes the heart grow fonder. This week marks the fourth anniversary of my departure from Hong Kong, a city I came to love during 28 years as a resident. It was not easy to leave. Hong Kong had become my home. But it was, for me and for many others back then, the right time to make the move.

My reasons were complex, although the wearying pandemic restrictions and dramatic legal and political reforms played their part. The city had changed so much.

Returning to my native England, though, was a leap in the dark. Us British expats used to say the UK was a nice place for a holiday but we wouldn’t want to live there.

In the four years since my departure, Hong Kong has bounced back from the bleak pandemic years. The city I left is a distant memory.

The airport, when I left, on August 3, 2022, was deserted and a mask was clamped to my face. The requirement to wear masks in public would not be lifted for months. Travel restrictions had left Hong Kong isolated from the rest of the world.

Now, the tourists have returned, along with talent and investment. Hong Kong is aiming to become a hub of hubs, a centre for pretty much everything from finance to culture, legal services and sport.

There is a breathless schedule of conferences, exhibitions, concerts and sporting contests, as the city establishes itself as a host of “mega-events”. I would have enjoyed attending this week’s football festival.

As the push for status and connectivity continues, Hong Kong is formulating its first five-year plan to align with national strategy and sees itself as key to the rise of the Greater Bay Area.

There has been a good deal of talking-up Hong Kong, in answer to the government’s call to “tell good stories” about the city. But there is no denying it has come a long way since the pandemic. Like many former residents looking on from afar, I have been delighted to see its progress.

My time in Hong Kong spanned a momentous and often turbulent period in the city’s history and I was privileged to cover it for the South China Morning Post.

The pomp and ceremony of the handover from Britain to China in 1997 was followed by landmark constitutional court cases, as the city struggled to get to grips with the novel “one country, two systems” concept.

It was an exciting time. The newly enacted Basic Law provided comprehensive protection for human rights and people were quick to try to assert them, seeking favourable judgments from the city’s independent judiciary.

Politics was dominated by the Basic Law’s requirement that there be gradual and orderly progress towards the “ultimate goal” of universal suffrage, a destination that still seems a long way away.

The months of often-violent anti-government protests in 2019 proved to be a watershed. Beijing’s response, in the form of a sweeping national security law in 2020, along with a new system ensuring only “patriots” would govern, marked the beginning of a new reality for Hong Kong.

As I said in my first column on returning to the UK, I have many wonderful memories of the city but they mostly belong to a different era. Britain beckoned in 2022, just as it did for the thousands of Hong Kong residents who moved there under a new visa scheme for holders of British National (Overseas) passports. But the UK was never going to be a panacea.

A headline in The Times the week before I arrived read: “Britain slides into crisis.” There have been many more crises since then.

I returned to a country led by Boris Johnson. He was quickly replaced by Liz Truss. But she only lasted 45 days. Then it was Rishi Sunak’s turn. Keir Starmer took over at the helm in 2024 after winning a landslide in the general election. Now, he has been ousted and succeeded by Andy Burnham. This dizzying merry-go-round does not help long-term planning, but is a reflection of the British people’s frustration with their politicians and deep-rooted desire for change.

Burnham has made a promising start, putting a little money back into people’s pockets. The popularity of his Labour Party has risen.

The honeymoon period will not last long. Britain has a multitude of seemingly insoluble problems. A slumbering economy, cost of living crisis and struggling public services will not evaporate just because there is a new prime minister.

But for all of the depictions of Britain as “broken”, my experience on returning after so long away has been a positive one. I love the tranquillity of my home in the English countryside and, after so many years in rented Hong Kong flats, it is a joy to have a house and a garden. The cost of living is high – but not as high as for an expat lifestyle in Hong Kong. My interactions with the National Health Service have, so far, been smooth. And – touch wood – crime has not been a problem. But the taxes are punishing and they are likely to rise.

I enjoy the freedom to say whatever I like about the British government and the ability to regularly vote in elections, choosing from a wide range of candidates. I just wish Count Binface was standing in my constituency!

This is just my experience. Others will have different stories to tell. There has been much debate in recent years about whether Hong Kong or Britain is the better place to live. My answer, an obvious one, remains the same as four years ago. One is not superior to the other. They both have much to offer. Preferences depend on personal circumstances.

Just because you leave Hong Kong, it does not mean you stop caring. As the city continues to integrate with mainland China, it should not lose sight of the distinctions which were intended to make it special.

These include a high degree of autonomy, protection of human rights and independent courts trusted to deliver judgments in accordance with the law. Controversial court cases should be welcomed.

The sun might have set on a period in Hong Kong’s history which I lived through and loved. But I continue to wish the city well and hope it will embrace diversity, compassion and tolerance amid the drive to grow and prosper.

item.title: [SCMP] Cambodia and Thailand must define the border to achieve lasting peace
item.description:
Cambodia has adopted a comprehensive approach to resolving its border dispute with Thailand, yet substantive progress will only occur once the two sides agree on where the border actually is.

The Cambodia-Thailand border dispute is complex: the result of a tangle of colonial-era treaties, competing maps, contested temples, unsettled demarcation and recurring nationalism. The rise of ultranationalist groups on both sides has made reconciliation harder still. Armed clashes, partly driven by domestic political developments, erupted in July and December 2025, showing how quickly the dispute can turn violent and how costly that violence can be for both economies.

From Phnom Penh’s perspective, the immediate priority is pressing Thailand to withdraw its troops while rejecting attempts to redraw borders through force, coercion or fait accompli. Cambodia’s approach rests on three tracks: bilateral mechanisms, international legal processes and third-party mediation. For any of these to deliver results, however, both sides must first settle demarcation itself.
item.content:encoded:
Cambodia has adopted a comprehensive approach to resolving its border dispute with Thailand, yet substantive progress will only occur once the two sides agree on where the border actually is.

The Cambodia-Thailand border dispute is complex: the result of a tangle of colonial-era treaties, competing maps, contested temples, unsettled demarcation and recurring nationalism. The rise of ultranationalist groups on both sides has made reconciliation harder still. Armed clashes, partly driven by domestic political developments, erupted in July and December 2025, showing how quickly the dispute can turn violent and how costly that violence can be for both economies.

From Phnom Penh’s perspective, the immediate priority is pressing Thailand to withdraw its troops while rejecting attempts to redraw borders through force, coercion or fait accompli. Cambodia’s approach rests on three tracks: bilateral mechanisms, international legal processes and third-party mediation. For any of these to deliver results, however, both sides must first settle demarcation itself.

1. Bilateral negotiation. The first track runs through existing mechanisms. These include the Joint Boundary Commission (JBC), established in 2000 under a memorandum of understanding on land boundary survey and demarcation. The JBC is the main technical body for survey, mapping and demarcation, working alongside the General Border Committee on security and military matters and the Regional Border Committee on local incidents.

In April, Prime Minister Hun Manet stated that “even if only 1 per cent” of diplomatic opportunity remained, Cambodia was “committed to fully exhausting all peaceful mechanisms rather than resorting to prolonged conflict”. Existing mechanisms are often slow-moving and constrained by domestic political pressures, yet they remain indispensable for confidence-building, preventive diplomacy and the pursuit of practical technical solutions.

2. International law. The second track concerns international legal processes. Cambodia’s approach to border demarcation centres on the 1904 and 1907 Franco-Siamese instruments and the maps drawn from them. In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that the Preah Vihear Temple lay within Cambodian territory; in 2013, it clarified that Cambodia had sovereignty over the whole promontory. These rulings continue to shape Phnom Penh’s strategic thinking, reinforcing its belief that international adjudication – though time-consuming – can provide legal solutions where bilateral talks are blocked by nationalism, political shifts or competing historical narratives.

Last year’s renewed border tensions hardened this logic. In May 2025, a Cambodian soldier was killed and disputes escalated around several contested areas. The following month, Cambodia brought a case before the ICJ concerning the Mom Bei area and the Ta Moan Thom, Ta Moan Touch and Ta Krabey temples. Thailand rejected the court’s jurisdiction, arguing that submission would undermine its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

A parallel legal track has opened at sea. After Thailand terminated an MOU on overlapping maritime claims in the Gulf of Thailand this May, Phnom Penh invoked compulsory conciliation under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and Bangkok agreed to participate in the process. Conciliation under Unclos is designed to produce recommendations rather than binding rulings, but it still serves an important purpose by internationalising the issue, creating structure, reducing the risk of unilateral action and subjecting both parties to greater diplomatic scrutiny.

3. Third-party mediation. The third track is mediation. Cambodia has sought support from Asean, China, the United States and others during periods of armed conflict. As last year’s chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, Malaysia played a crucial role in facilitating ceasefire efforts, with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s mediation helping to create diplomatic space when direct contact between Phnom Penh and Bangkok had broken down. Beijing and Washington lent the process strategic weight, with US President Donald Trump actively involved, in particular.

The July 2025 ceasefire showed the effectiveness of coordinated diplomacy. It was followed by the Kuala Lumpur peace accord that October, which, among other things, saw the two sides agree to de-escalation and confidence-building. But these agreements failed to prevent a second round of armed conflict largely due to the lack of credible monitoring, verification and enforcement. Fighting resumed in December on a much larger scale, with the conflict lasting 21 days and displacing more than half a million people.

China’s subsequent engagement was decisive. Both Cambodia and Thailand accepted China’s role as a mediator and the China-led trilateral meeting in Yunnan that December, also known as the Fuxian Consensus, helped restore the ceasefire through quiet diplomacy and high-level strategic engagement. Beijing also offered to provide a platform for both sides to engage in more comprehensive and effective communication and trust-building, including through track-two diplomacy, while providing parallel humanitarian aid to communities affected by the conflict and supporting demining efforts along the border.

What next?

Cambodia’s approach combines bilateral and multilateral frameworks while placing primary emphasis on bilateral settlement mechanisms. Phnom Penh has sent multiple diplomatic notes calling for a special JBC session and the deployment of joint survey teams to resume fieldwork. Bangkok has requested repeated postponements, however, citing internal procedures, elections, the appointment of a new prime minister, cabinet formation and the need to approve a new JBC leadership structure. Thailand has also shown little enthusiasm for Cambodia’s decision to initiate compulsory conciliation.

Moving forward, political will, good faith, reliable hotline communication and confidence-building measures are essential to creating a solid foundation for bilateral negotiations.
