There are some positive signs of a revival in bilateral negotiations, which makes establishing stable and effective channels of communication between the two capitals all the more urgent. Cooperation against online scams should be further strengthened, while people-to-people exchanges and economic ties ought to be restored and gradually normalised.

But cooperation on scams and tourism cannot substitute for progress on the border issue. Until the JBC resumes substantive boundary surveys – and the disputed temples and maritime zones move from contention to formal demarcation – the current ceasefire, like the ones before it, will remain tenuous and fragile rather than permanent.

Dr Chheang Vannarith is a Visiting Senior Fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

item.title: [SCMP] China’s Politburo pledges policy support, spending to counteract sluggish growth
item.description:
Beijing has pledged to step up macro policy support and enhance the resilience of capital markets for the remainder of the year, sending signals to stablise growth amid a recent slowdown in economic activity and rising volatility in global markets.

After a meeting of the Communist Party’s 21-member Politburo – a major decision-making body led by President Xi Jinping – that ended on Thursday, the party’s upper echelon vowed to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending and speed up the transition from old to new growth drivers.

“[We need to] fully leverage the effectiveness of existing policies and roll out practical and effective incremental measures in a timely manner,” the Politburo said, according to a statement published by state news agency Xinhua.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing has pledged to step up macro policy support and enhance the resilience of capital markets for the remainder of the year, sending signals to stablise growth amid a recent slowdown in economic activity and rising volatility in global markets.

After a meeting of the Communist Party’s 21-member Politburo – a major decision-making body led by President Xi Jinping – that ended on Thursday, the party’s upper echelon vowed to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending and speed up the transition from old to new growth drivers.

“[We need to] fully leverage the effectiveness of existing policies and roll out practical and effective incremental measures in a timely manner,” the Politburo said, according to a statement published by state news agency Xinhua.

Amid growing concerns from Western politicians over China’s widening trade surplus, the leadership also urged the country to “expand the scope for mutually beneficial international economic and trade cooperation” and “promote more balanced trade development.”

The Politburo also said the fifth plenary session of the party’s powerful Central Committee would be held in October. This session carries particular importance, as it comes a year before the party’s next national congress, when a major leadership reshuffle is expected and Xi could be elected to a fourth term as general secretary.

Analysts said the meeting sent a more supportive signal to stabilise growth as the country’s economy faced “challenges and difficulties,” but stopped short of suggesting a large-scale stimulus package, instead pointing to more targeted measures.

The emphasis is on measures that are practical and effective – in other words, policies that deliver tangible results

Ding Shuang, Standard Chartered

“The focus remains on making better use of existing policies, while keeping additional measures in reserve,” said Ding Shuang, chief economist for Greater China and North Asia at Standard Chartered.

“It’s not simply a matter of spending more money,” Ding added. “The emphasis is on measures that are practical and effective – in other words, policies that deliver tangible results.”

The meeting was held in the wake of second-quarter figures that showed a slowdown in gross domestic product despite strong trade numbers, a dichotomy indicating a widening gap between surging exports and sluggish activity at home.

The elevated trade surplus has also fuelled pushback from the West, with politicians in the European Union and the United States threatening or taking action against China’s industrial overcapacity – a claim Beijing denies.

Su Yue, principal economist for China at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the explicit reference to “trade balance” in the readout suggested Beijing was becoming more sensitive to international concerns over China’s trade surplus and sought to create greater room for external cooperation.

“Although this alone is unlikely to fundamentally ease trade tensions, it points to a more pragmatic tone that could provide a modestly more stable backdrop for US-China economic relations,” she added. “EU-China trade relations will remain under strain due to structural issues.”

Working teams from Beijing and Brussels have held more than 20 meetings in the past month, following an initial round of trade talks in Brussels between Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and his European counterpart Maros Sefcovic, commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong said on Thursday.

“China is ready … to explore practical, workable solutions to each side’s concerns in trade and economics,” He said.

Top policymakers have also been wary of heightened volatility in global capital markets, with hi-tech stocks facing a broad sell-off on concerns that an artificial intelligence-driven rally may have outpaced fundamentals.

Against this backdrop, the Politburo underscored the importance of deepening reforms to capital market investment and financing, while “enhancing the resilience and confidence of capital markets.”

Ding pointed to recent intervention by the “national team” – state-backed institutions that support domestic markets – and said stabilising the capital market can help improve household balance sheets and support domestic consumption.

China’s gross domestic product growth slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter – the softest quarterly expansion since late 2022, down from 5 per cent in the first quarter. Growth for the first half stood at 4.7 per cent, remaining within the “4.5 to 5 per cent” target range set for the year.

The Politburo reiterated the importance of “effectively expanding domestic demand” and unlocking the potential of the services sector, and said Beijing would make comprehensive use of monetary policy tools and “adjust them as appropriate”, while improving co-ordination between fiscal and financial policies to boost domestic demand.

It also stressed the need to strengthen social welfare, protect the rights of flexible and gig workers, and ensure agricultural production.

Su Jian, an economics professor at Peking University, said the readout placed greater emphasis on boosting domestic demand, expanding service consumption and promoting trade in services.

“Strengthening social welfare can help reduce income inequality and ease consumers’ concerns about the future, thereby supporting consumption,” he said.

Meanwhile, analysts also pointed to infrastructure investment as an effective tool for boosting domestic demand and stabilising growth in the second half of the year, as the readout underscored the need to advance the construction of the “six networks” – a broad infrastructure initiative covering water, power, computing, next-generation telecommunications, underground utilities and logistics networks.

China’s contracting fixed-asset investment, coupled with a higher incidence of natural disasters this year, leaves policymakers ample room to ramp up infrastructure spending, Ding said.

Amid a rise in extreme weather events this year, the readout stressed the need to “resolutely prevent major accidents”, strengthen risk identification and mitigation, and step up flood control, emergency response and disaster relief efforts.

Other priorities outlined in the readout included continuing efforts to tackle “involution-style” competition, stabilising the property market and pressing ahead with the government’s debt-restructuring plan.

Separately, Xi held a symposium on Friday with representatives of the country’s non-communist political parties to hear their views on the current economic situation and priorities for the second half of the year, the People’s Daily reported on Thursday.

Xi said that China’s economy had “pressed ahead under pressure” and “showed strong resilience and vitality” in the first half of the year, while acknowledging “some difficulties and challenges”, as reported by the Communist Party’s official press organ.

The president emphasised the need to strengthen the effectiveness of macro policy in the second half of the year, prioritising the tapping of potential domestic demand, deepening the integration of technological and industrial innovation, improving people’s livelihoods and continuing to defuse risks in key sectors.

Additional reporting by Xiaofei Xu

item.title: [SCMP] The Philippines, sovereignty and the Pax Silica Industrial Hub – how US’ Helberg sees it
item.description:
The struggle between the US and China over who will lead in artificial intelligence is one of the defining competitions of our time. In the third part of our exclusive interview with a key player defining Washington’s policy on AI, Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs, gives a commitment to the Philippines on the Pax Silica Initiative.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used his State of the Nation address in Manila on Monday to staunchly defend a proposed US-backed artificial intelligence hub, promising it would create “quality jobs” and inject new life into the economy.

The venture is the flagship project in a US-led coalition seeking to build China-free AI supply chains spanning critical minerals, semiconductors and logistics.
item.content:encoded:
The struggle between the US and China over who will lead in artificial intelligence is one of the defining competitions of our time. In the third part of our exclusive interview with a key player defining Washington’s policy on AI, Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs, gives a commitment to the Philippines on the Pax Silica Initiative.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr used his State of the Nation address in Manila on Monday to staunchly defend a proposed US-backed artificial intelligence hub, promising it would create “quality jobs” and inject new life into the economy.

The venture is the flagship project in a US-led coalition seeking to build China-free AI supply chains spanning critical minerals, semiconductors and logistics.

“A product of the 23-member strong and US-led Pax Silica Initiative, the Pax Silica Industrial Hub will create an ecosystem that will have AI at its core,” Marcos said.

“It will bring quality jobs to our people, accelerate our industrial competitiveness, and revitalise our economy.”

The promise is to establish an advanced manufacturing and logistics centre in the global AI and technology value chain.

But critics warn that the project could erode Philippine sovereignty, displace farming communities, and cause environmental harm.

In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post earlier this month, one of the US government architects of the Pax Silica Initiative rejected suggestions that US interests within the zone would have special treatment.

“We will ensure that the zones will uphold the sovereignty of the host country,” said Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs.

Helberg said the US administration was “still in the process of negotiating the shape of these long-term agreements” but the concerns of the Philippines and the investors would be met.

The new economic zone would provide “international investors with the kind of policy and regulatory certainty that they need in order to allocate large pools of capital to do a significant industrial buildout”.

The hub, he added, would also help “American companies secure strategic inputs that they need for their supply chains”.

We will ensure that the zones will uphold the sovereignty of the host country

Jacob Helberg, US undersecretary of state for economic affairs

Manila, a close US ally, joined the Pax Silica Initiative in April as repeated confrontations with Beijing in the disputed South China Sea worsened already-frayed relations between the two Asian nations.

The initiative is the framework for the proposed 1,619-hectare (4,000-acre) industrial hub in New Clark City, 100km (60 miles) north of Manila, the anchor project of the Luzon Economic Corridor – a trilateral connectivity project led by the United States, Japan and the Philippines.

The hub plans reflect deepening economic cooperation between Manila and Washington as they seek to reduce their dependence on Beijing for critical supply chains, including in rare earths, an area that Beijing dominates and is increasingly willing to leverage.

In May, Philippine officials said American officials had requested that the zone be placed under US jurisdiction, but they “did not agree to that”.

Helberg’s assurances were welcomed by Philippine ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez, who said they affirmed that the “proposed economic security zone will uphold Philippine sovereignty as its host country”.

“This is fully consistent with the Philippine government’s position that all development initiatives within the country operate under the Philippine Constitution, Philippine laws, and Philippine jurisdiction.”

Retired American diplomat Edgard Kagan said he took Helberg “at his word” on sovereignty, adding that Washington fully understood the importance of “full respect” for Philippine jurisdiction.

“There is neither interest in nor precedent for the United States seeking sovereignty in an economic zone,” said Kagan, the US ambassador to Malaysia from December 2023 to February this year.

The economic zone also featured last week during US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ forum.

“From the South China Sea to Pax Silica and the Luzon Economic Corridor, the US-Philippine Alliance makes both our countries stronger, safer and more prosperous,” Rubio said after his meeting with Marcos in Manila.

As part of its commitment, Washington would deliver US$100 million in new foreign assistance for the Luzon corridor to upgrade infrastructure and advance logistics and energy projects, the State Department said.

“Secretary Rubio and President Marcos also discussed opportunities related to the Philippines’ membership in Pax Silica and hosting the initiative’s first Economic Security Zone in Clark,” the department said.

Romualdez said both sides were “committed to developing a framework under Pax Silica that advances mutually beneficial economic objectives”.

“The focus of both governments is to establish an investment environment that is competitive, transparent and predictable, enabling high-value industries to flourish and bilateral trade relations to thrive better than ever before,” he added.

Wendy Cutler, a senior vice-president at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the plan suggested that the Donald Trump administration was “serious about experimenting with different and innovative approaches to build secure supply chains particularly when it comes to AI”.

“Unlike free trade agreements, this zone covers only a limited geographical area, does not include tariff-free reciprocal access, and seems to be limited in scope in terms of lifting restrictions and regulations,” she added.

Zack Cooper, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said the details about the project were “still coming together” and he expected there would be “robust support from US policymakers to ensure that the Philippines benefits from this arrangement”.

“I think the critical thing here is that the US government has been consistent from [Joe] Biden to Trump in trying to invest in the Philippines to help demonstrate the value of the alliance in both Manila and Washington,” he said.

Despite assurances of a win-win partnership, the proposal has drawn criticism from opposition parties, environmental groups and farmer organisations.

“The dynastic government is just ripping us off. They brought in Pax Silica. They are seizing more than 4,000 hectares from farmers in Central Luzon,” labour rights leader Leody De Guzman was quoted as saying by Philippine news outlet Inquirer.net on Monday.

Activist groups say the project will displace farming communities, reduce agricultural land, and strain local water resources.

Supporters of the project, including the Philippine ambassador to the US, who is also Marcos’ second cousin, argue that it has the “potential to create hundreds of thousands of jobs over time while reinforcing the country’s long-term industrial competitiveness”.

“The AI-native industrial acceleration hub represents an important opportunity to strengthen the Philippines’ position in the global value chain for semiconductors, critical minerals processing, advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence-enabled industries,” Romualdez said.

Neither side asks the harder question: not whether Pax Silica is desirable, but what is traded for it

Jewellord Nem Singh, Stimson Centre

The Philippines, the world’s second-largest nickel producer and biggest exporter of raw nickel ore, sends the bulk of its output to China and Chinese-owned processing facilities in neighbouring Indonesia.

The government hopes that the project will help the country move beyond exporting raw ore to China at low prices by developing domestic processing capacity, creating more value at home and supplying the US market.

However, in a Substack post on Monday, Jewellord Nem Singh, a non-resident fellow at the Stimson Centre, said one big issue was still to be addressed.

“Neither side asks the harder question: not whether Pax Silica is desirable, but what is traded for it,” Singh wrote.

“Used well, it could anchor the productive base the state has yet to build for its industrial goals. Used badly, as critics point out, it could simply become an export platform, for allied rather than Chinese buyers.”

item.title: [SCMP] How China’s US$900 million port deal in Angola shows its dominance over US interests
item.description:
On the South Atlantic coastline, Angola stands out as rare ground on which the United States has been willing to vie with China for influence in Africa.

It was the only country on the continent visited by former US president Joe Biden, albeit in the twilight of his term in December 2024.

During the trip – the first by a sitting US president – Biden made the case for investment in the strategic Lobito Atlantic Railway.
item.content:encoded:
On the South Atlantic coastline, Angola stands out as rare ground on which the United States has been willing to vie with China for influence in Africa.

It was the only country on the continent visited by former US president Joe Biden, albeit in the twilight of his term in December 2024.

During the trip – the first by a sitting US president – Biden made the case for investment in the strategic Lobito Atlantic Railway.

The administration of Biden’s successor, Donald Trump, also threw its weight behind the Lobito rail project.

The railway links Angola’s Port of Lobito to neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, providing the US with what it considers its own access route to critical mineral supplies from both countries.

So far, the US has invested US$553 million in the project through its International Development Finance Corporation, the agency mainly charged with countering China’s economic influence around the world.

Yet, despite Washington’s renewed focus on securing critical minerals via the Lobito route, Beijing is extending its infrastructure dominance, leaving the US to play catch-up.

On July 20, Huatong Angola, the local subsidiary of China’s Huatong Group, signed a US$900 million deal with state-owned Barra do Dande Development Society, S.A. (SDBD) to develop new port facilities in Barra do Dande, about 600km (373 miles) north of the Lobito port.

The port is part of the Barra do Dande Integrated Development Free Zone, an export-led venture designed to provide both a manufacturing, export and logistics hub just north of the capital, Luanda. This will be done by transforming remote terrain on the edge of the Atlantic Ocean.

It is the kind of heavy engineering project that Chinese companies execute frequently across Africa at low cost, a feat their Western counterparts cannot match.

Chinese companies have used this factor to their advantage on the continent, and there is unlikely to be any US response to this latest project in Angola, according to Eric Olander, an analyst and editor at the China Global South Project, a US-based research non-profit.

“The US doesn’t have the kind of construction companies that can operate at the lower end of the cost structure the way that Chinese firms have been so successful over the years,” Olander said. “The [US] administration’s Africa policy is largely focused on security and securing access to raw materials; that’s it.”

The investment protocols signed by Huatong Angola, its financial partner, Berkshire Waterhouse Infrastructure, and the SDBD – representing the host government – comprise two agreements.

The first covers the 25-year concession of the port terminal costing US$450 million, while the second, also for the same amount, covers the provision of port infrastructure.

The first phase of construction is scheduled to be completed in two years and will feature a completed terminal that can enable exports from the free-trade zone.

Two more phases will be completed by 2030, leaving a port that can handle 80,000-tonne vessels, employ 21,000 people and generate US$10 billion annually, according to Roque Saraiva, president of the SDBD’s board of directors.

“The investment is provided entirely by the private sector,” Saraiva said, stressing the project’s viability and investor confidence.

The concession to manage the ports will last for 25 years. It adds to China’s growing maritime footprint in Angola.

In 2022, two Chinese state-owned companies, Citic Construction and Shandong Port Group were the winners in an international public tender to run the container and general cargo terminals of Angola’s Lobito port for 20 years. The port is the terminus of the Lobito Railway in which the US invested.

Then in January, China Energy Engineering Corporation completed a major revamp of the Cabinda port, further north of Barra do Dande. The aim was to enable the port to receive container ships and other large roll-on-roll-off vessels meant for Angola and neighbouring countries.

While the deal builds on groundwork laid under the Biden administration, its significance has sharpened under President Donald Trump

Alex Vines, European Council on Foreign Relations

Biden’s 2024 trip was partly to mend fences given that the US had opposed the Angolan ruling party’s rise to power and for decades after the country became independent, backed a rebel movement that sought to topple the People’s Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA) government.

Diplomatic relations were established in 1993, almost 20 years after Angola’s independence.

The Biden administration framed the Angolan investment as part of efforts to move the US towards an energy transition. For this, critical minerals were needed for battery technology and EVs.

“While the deal builds on groundwork laid under the Biden administration, its significance has sharpened under President Donald Trump,” said Alex Vines, director of the Africa Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

“It reflects a move away from climate-focused diplomacy towards a harder geoeconomic approach centred on critical mineral supply chains, regional trade integration and great power competition.”

Among officials in Washington, there was even talk of winning Angola over from China to the side of the US. But the consideration seemed to ignore the depth of relations Beijing had developed with Luanda, observers noted.

Though China briefly backed the MPLA before switching to a rival group during Angola’s liberation war against Portugal, it repaired relations after the ruling party came to power and established diplomatic relations by 1983.

Both nations forged closer relations under former president Eduardo dos Santos and China financed major infrastructure projects, some in exchange for Angola’s oil.

The close relations continued under President Joao Lourenco, who succeeded dos Santos in 2017. During a 2024 visit to China, Lourenco steered the conversation with China towards mining, agriculture and projects that would help to build an industrial base and diversify the country away from oil dependence.

The two countries also upgraded their relations to “a comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership” – one of the highest levels.

In contrast to China, the US had restricted its African interests to security and getting access to critical supplies, Olander of the China Global South Project said.

“Sure, they don’t like the Chinese and would prefer they not succeed in a place like Angola, but they’re not going to do anything to respond to this announcement.”

item.title: [SCMP] Discover India’s ‘last village’: a hub of Balti culture on the Pakistan border
item.description:
An inky darkness blankets the road as I step out of the car. I blink to get my bearings, the silhouettes of trees slowly forming beneath a startling canopy of stars.

“Sorry to make you walk in the dark, but this is a shortcut,” says Rashidullah Khan, our companion and guide for the evening. He leads the way up through the trees, our phone torches illuminating pebbled, muddy slopes.

After 10 minutes, we reach a narrow lane flanked by stone walls punctuated with wooden doors. A sculpture of a large bird perches above one doorway, an unassuming entrance to what a sign identifies as the Yabgo Palace Turtuk. Inside the central courtyard of the wooden building, intricately carved upper balconies appear in the candlelight, plush bolster cushions and low tables clustered below: the setting for dinner with Turtuk’s king.
item.content:encoded:
An inky darkness blankets the road as I step out of the car. I blink to get my bearings, the silhouettes of trees slowly forming beneath a startling canopy of stars.

“Sorry to make you walk in the dark, but this is a shortcut,” says Rashidullah Khan, our companion and guide for the evening. He leads the way up through the trees, our phone torches illuminating pebbled, muddy slopes.

After 10 minutes, we reach a narrow lane flanked by stone walls punctuated with wooden doors. A sculpture of a large bird perches above one doorway, an unassuming entrance to what a sign identifies as the Yabgo Palace Turtuk. Inside the central courtyard of the wooden building, intricately carved upper balconies appear in the candlelight, plush bolster cushions and low tables clustered below: the setting for dinner with Turtuk’s king.

I am in the “last village” of northern India, a few kilometres from the Pakistan border. Living in a corner of the Ladakh desert – India’s northernmost region, known for its stark and arresting landscape – the villagers of Turtuk, Thang, Tyakshi and Chalunka consider themselves part of Baltistan, but flipped nationality overnight, after the 1971 Indo-Pakistani war. Families were split as the now Indian villages were separated from the larger Balti population on the other side of the border.

Until 2010, this sensitive area was closed to outsiders. Now, through tourism, residents are gently asserting their Balti identity, eager to share their heritage with the wider world.

Turtuk is deliciously lush, rich with apple and apricot orchards and green buckwheat fields, cut through by the icy blue Shyok River. At around 3,000 metres (9,843 feet), it sits at a relatively low elevation within Ladakh, but during the first few days anywhere in the area, the altitude makes activity strenuous.

My journey begins in Leh (around 3,500 metres/11,483 feet), Ladakh’s capital, where the air is palpably thin and, initially, a heavy head and breathlessness are common after even gentle walking. To prevent altitude sickness, visitors must acclimatise here for a couple of days before travelling onwards. Non-residents require a permit to travel beyond Leh – Inner Line Permits for Indians and Protected Area Permits for foreigners – which can be applied for in advance, or obtained through Leh travel agents, the process taking between 24 and 48 hours.

I spend my first day resting, hydrating and gazing at the purple mountains from the window of my room at The Pal Hotel. A brief stroll to Leh market reveals that the crowds weaving around and through the souvenir shops and cafes serving cakes and steaming momos – Tibetan dumplings filled with meat or vegetables – are larger than usual, in anticipation of the visiting Dalai Lama’s public address the following day.

Leh is more than a pit stop in which to, literally, catch your breath. It’s an introduction to the region’s history and culture, the Buddhist leanings visible in fluttering prayer flags and a landscape dotted with monasteries. The world’s highest peace pagoda, the white-domed Shanti Stupa, spans two circular levels filled with reliefs depicting the life of the Buddha and offers panoramic views of Leh and the surrounding mountains.

Twenty kilometres (12 miles) away, the stupas, paintings and statues of the 15th century Thiksey Monastery, one of the largest in the area, amount to a treasure trove of Buddhist art. Some visitors circle and prostrate themselves before a 15-metre-high (49-feet-high) Maitreya Buddha, a bodhisattva believed to be a future Buddha; others sit in quiet contemplation.

Juxtaposed against these peaceful symbols are stark reminders of conflict. Ladakh remains heavily militarised, having been the site of clashes between India and Pakistan or China. Leh’s Hall of Fame museum and memorial has displays on the 1999 Kargil war; Ladakhi culture; soldiers’ personal memorabilia; and the challenges of high-altitude warfare, as well as life in general.

From Leh, the drive to Turtuk winds through constantly changing landscapes – rugged peaks marbled with purple, gold and rust stripes; sandy deserts; the lush, boulder-strewn river plains sliced through by the Shyok; and the dizzying Khardung La pass, at around 5,400 metres (17,717 feet), before finally descending into the Shyok Valley.

“The Himalayan region of Baltistan, famously known as Gilgit-Baltistan, was on the Silk Route,” says Turtuk’s king, Yabgo Mohammad Khan Kacho, at dinner. “Some of the world’s highest peaks – Karakoram one and two [K1 and K2] – and prominent glaciers like Baltoro and Siachen are here [on the Pakistani side of the border].” Pakistani Baltistan is often known as “Little Tibet” due to its alpine scenery.

His title is unofficial but Kacho is a direct descendant of the Yabgo dynasty, Baltistan’s rulers for 2,000 years.

Wearing an elegant cream shuqa – a traditional men’s woollen overcoat – embroidered with flowers, and an ivory and gold turban, his soft yet clear voice floats gently through the courtyard, as he recounts Baltistan’s tumultuous history with invaders, including Genghis Khan (in the 13th century) and Alexander the Great (in the 4th century; although historians doubt either made it this far). We talk over a traditional Balti meal: buckwheat crepes with tangy yogurt and spinach dip; baleh, a buckwheat noodle, thyme and vegetable soup; and meat dumplings with a punchy chilli oil.

“We still eat many of our traditional dishes,” says Kacho, although his son says he prefers a less carbohydrate-heavy, more protein-rich diet, to better suit his gym regimen.

The 14th century wooden palace doubles as Kacho’s residence and a museum. Weapons, maps and artefacts showcase Balti history while Buddhist and Islamic art reflect the region’s mixed heritage.

Like most of his “subjects”, Kacho was separated from family in 1971.

“My sisters and cousins are in Pakistan. My riyasat [princely state] is there,” he says.

This division becomes tangible in nearby Thang, where Indian visitors (Thang is off-limits to non-Indians) can view the Line of Control between their country and Pakistan. Guide Rukiya Bano directs my gaze through binoculars, pointing out which mountains and bunkers are Indian and which are Pakistani. Her finger points to fields across the river: “That is Pakistan.” It is just 2km (1.2 miles) away yet feels much more distant for the residents of these four villages, as getting a visa to visit relatives is challenging.

Thang is home to botanist Mohammed Ali Bari, known as Goba Ali, whose colourful house overflows into a flourishing garden. Ali was five years old when he was separated from his parents.

“During the 1971 war, many feared the consequences if our village was captured. So, the women and most children went to hide a little further away. My grandfather, brother and I stayed,” says Ali, offering me grapes and dried apricots. When the war was over, the border was redrawn in haste, and those in hiding on that fateful December night were stranded on the wrong side of the new divide.

Ali speaks gratefully of the Indian Army for having raised him and his brother, a childhood with no formal education and a tent in a soldiers’ camp for a home. “They would dress me in red and take me to a spot where my parents could see me through binoculars from across the border and know that I was all right.”

In 2014, he was granted permission to visit his family in Pakistan, reuniting with them for 10 months. Photos from that trip hang in a small museum in his home and include one of Ali resting his head on his mother’s shoulder, household items and work tools in the background representing Balti culture. This separation from their larger community has made it difficult for many of the villagers to piece together their heritage. It took Rashidullah Khan seven years and several conversations with family in Pakistan to replicate the design of a traditional palace in his 12-room boutique hotel, Virsa Baltistan, in Turtuk.

“Virsa is the dream of a boy who grew up in this war-torn area, with very little money. This was intended to be more than a hotel, but a representation of Balti culture and identity,” says Khan.

The structure, with intricately carved windows and balconies, was created by 200 local woodcarvers, blacksmiths and stonemasons using riverbed mud, timber and hand-carved wood. Guest experiences include visits to traditional weavers, potters and metalworkers, and a five-course Balti tasting menu prepared by local women.

Under apricot trees, Zainab didi (“older sister”, a term used to address elder women in India) makes buckwheat crepes on a griddle while Khan plates each course: kisirnarang-thur, crepes cut into thin strips and a dollop of tangy yogurt dip placed on a leaf; praku, a thumb-pinched pasta cloaked in walnut sauce; and phading, a dessert of boiled apricots, apricot kernels and basil leaves shaped into a sticky caramelised square.

“These ladies think that my plating and portions are stingy,” laughs Khan. “I explain a tasting menu to them, but they believe food should be served generously and eaten with the hands to enjoy it.”

Finding hospitality professionals in this remote area is challenging and Khan has trained former mechanics and clerks, valuing their willingness to learn and cultural knowledge over industry experience.

“Involving the community is an integral part of Virsa,” he says.

Evenings bring music and dance to the hotel’s orchard – drummers and woodwind players accompany performers re-enacting Balti legends with swirling swords and athletic leaps.

Music plays an integral role in another Balti tradition: polo.

This free-spirited, rougher version of the game is accompanied by live instruments, the horses trained to musical cues.

Unfortunately, no game is scheduled for when I’m visiting, but while passing a pitch – sandy, uneven ground, with fading lines demarcating the goals – it’s easy to imagine how boisterous it gets when two teams of six players jostle on such a narrow strip, the first to score 10 goals being the winners. The prize is meat, sometimes a goat or sheep. Although a trophy is a recent addition, celebratory “goat parties” are still popular.

The four villages have eight teams, competing in tournaments for a few weeks starting at Navroze (the Persian New Year, in late March, which also signals the arrival of spring) and later, in July or August.

“We also hope to take the game beyond Turtuk, and represent Baltistan in national tournaments,” says Nassir Hussain, a player on Khan’s Virsa team.

Ordinarily, visitors en route to the border have stopped in Turtuk only to eat lunch at its riverside cafes. But with more guest houses, homestays and camping facilities now available, villagers are encouraging tourists to stay for longer, to fully experience what the area has to offer.

A steep but short hike to the Turtuk Monastery is rewarded with sweeping views over mountains, river, fields and a cascading cemetery.

Within the village, a 140-year-old home has been converted into the Balti Heritage Museum, with a display of utensils and traditional clothes: well-worn, rugged, functional-looking items made from animal skin and fur, for warmth; loose trousers of coarse cloth; fur-lined coats and tunics in cream, beige and rust hues. Among the fancier robes are shuqa in cream accented with bright embroidered flowers.

The house was built using traditional construction techniques – interlocked wooden and stone structures that serve as pillars, reinforced timber lacings and a half-timbering method – to protect against earthquakes and provide insulation in the extreme cold of winter. The pillars and doorframes are intricately carved with Buddhist and Bon (an ancient spiritual tradition that predates Buddhism and Islam in the region) motifs: left-facing swastikas, or yungdrung; florals; and knots of eternal loops, weaving back into each other.

Nearby is a centuries-old nangchung, meaning “cold house”, one of eight in the area. These bunkers were built in such a way that cool mountain air could circulate through gaps between the stones. Before electricity and fridges arrived in Turtuk, these served as communal stores for perishable food.

Elsewhere, the Bunker of Memories recalls the region’s history as a war zone. Used by the Ashoor family (the nearby Balti Heritage Museum is their ancestral home) during the Kargil war, the sturdy underground stone shelter displays military detritus, several pieces repurposed as utilitarian objects: jerrycans as water carriers and thaps – traditional stoves; ammunition boxes as safes; and rocket shells as butter churners.

It’s a sobering space, and a reminder of the resilience shown by Baltis in challenging conditions.

Later, while sipping on apricot juice with nutty kernels bobbing on top at The Balti Kitchen restaurant, Abdul Rashid Khan, Rashidullah’s father, recalls the dust and rubble during the 1999 war. “It was scary, and several people retreated from the village. I chose to stay home. When it was over, the calm and silence were disorienting,” says the jovial, soft-spoken man, who now runs a speciality store selling jams, nuts, dried apricots, oils and other local products.

“Before 1971, there was a smaller population, and few schools. Now there are more schools and girls are educated.”

A balancing of gender roles is also evident in the visibility of women in tourist businesses, noticeably at a cafe managed by the Women’s Empowerment and Welfare Association and at The Balti Kitchen, which is run by Khan’s sister and set on an open wooden platform amid organic flower and vegetable gardens. The menu lists specialities such as tsapon, home-baked bread toasted in white butter, onion and spices; squu, a potato, barley, pea and Himalayan herb stew; and kambo kushu, apple-flavoured cookies topped with mulberries and chocolate syrup.

Outside tourism, there is an ambition among the villagers to showcase their identity beyond Turtuk, whether through representing Baltistan in national polo tournaments or taking part in Khan’s plans to launch a Balti design label with local artisans. This aspiration represents preservation and renewal for a community whose identity has been defined by borders, and is now eager to move beyond those restrictions.

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese executive filmed taking cash on Colombia metro, South America’s biggest project
item.description:
Colombian prosecutors are investigating allegations that executives of a Chinese state-owned contractor building the Bogota metro demanded cash from a local subcontractor in exchange for releasing payments owed for work on the project, according to an investigation published over the weekend by Semana, the country’s leading news magazine.

The consortium building the line has denied any wrongdoing, saying the money seen changing hands was a retention payment agreed upon between the two firms in a contractual dispute over the quality of the subcontractor’s work.

The allegations centre on a 26-minute video showing the legal representative of a Colombian subcontractor handing over 60 million pesos (US$19,000) in cash to a commercial manager of China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) at the firm’s former offices in Bogota’s Teusaquillo district on April 18.
item.content:encoded:
Colombian prosecutors are investigating allegations that executives of a Chinese state-owned contractor building the Bogota metro demanded cash from a local subcontractor in exchange for releasing payments owed for work on the project, according to an investigation published over the weekend by Semana, the country’s leading news magazine.

The consortium building the line has denied any wrongdoing, saying the money seen changing hands was a retention payment agreed upon between the two firms in a contractual dispute over the quality of the subcontractor’s work.

The allegations centre on a 26-minute video showing the legal representative of a Colombian subcontractor handing over 60 million pesos (US$19,000) in cash to a commercial manager of China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) at the firm’s former offices in Bogota’s Teusaquillo district on April 18.

In the footage, the Colombian contractor pulls a dark bag from his suitcase and passes it to the Chinese executive, identified in the criminal complaint only as Yang, telling him in English that each package contained 5 million pesos (US$1,600).

The executive then spends roughly 10 minutes counting the banknotes before writing what appears to be a receipt in a notebook.

According to the complaint cited by the magazine, the payment was demanded as a condition for CHEC to approve invoices worth from 1 billion to 1.2 billion pesos (US$320,000 to US$380,000) that the subcontractor, Union Temporal Metrobuild, said it was owed for work carried out in March.

The subcontractor told prosecutors it agreed to pay because it had more than 350 workers on its payroll, along with obligations to suppliers, banks and other creditors arising from the financing of the work.

South America’s biggest building site

The 24km elevated line was awarded in 2019 to a consortium led by CHEC, with a 15 per cent stake held by Xian Rail Transportation Group, under a concession worth some US$4 billion at the time of signing.

It is the largest infrastructure project currently under construction in South America, with more than 15,000 workers on site and the works just past 80 per cent complete at the end of June.

The system’s 30 driverless trains are being built in Changchun by Chinese state-owned rolling stock manufacturer CRRC, and 15 have arrived in Colombia. Trial runs are due to begin in September 2027, with commercial operation planned for 2028.

Bogota debated building a metro for more than half a century before the first line was contracted, and the project has been fought over throughout its construction.

Outgoing president Gustavo Petro pressed for years to convert part of the line into an underground route, raising the idea with the consortium during a 2023 visit to Beijing, while mayor Carlos Fernando Galan was elected that same year on a promise to keep the elevated design.

The report was published days before president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella, a right-wing lawyer backed by US President Donald Trump, takes office on August 7.

De la Espriella has instructed his incoming cabinet to deepen ties with Washington and to approach the relationship with China “with pragmatism”, after Colombia joined the Belt and Road Initiative under Petro in 2025.

‘If you do not do it this way, he does not sign’

Semana reported that the April 18 handover followed a meeting on April 8, which the subcontractor also recorded in audio.

At that meeting, according to the complaint, Yang said that CHEC’s general manager of projects, identified as Wang Chuang, would only sign off on the March payment cycle if the subcontractor delivered 60 million pesos in cash to the company’s offices.

Metrobuild told prosecutors it had signed at least four contracts with CHEC since 2024, worth a combined 32 billion pesos (US$10.2 million), to build foundations, columns and other substructures for the metro viaduct.

The firm said delays in payment approvals began in March 2026, with Wang’s signature the only one missing.

The subcontractor argued that the 2026 contract contained no mechanism for the discounts CHEC cited, and that the Chinese company already held more than 1.2 billion pesos in quality-guarantee retentions deducted from every payment.

It added that no further demands were made after the cash was delivered, but that CHEC still held back more than 2.5 billion pesos (US$800,000) in invoices awaiting a signature.

Julian Quintana, the lawyer representing the subcontractor, told Semana the conduct could amount to extortion and collusion, a crime under Colombian law involving officials who extract payments by abusing their position.

He asked prosecutors to seize the devices used to record both meetings to preserve the chain of custody.

A sanctioned parent company

CHEC is a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), one of the world’s largest construction groups and a major contractor under the Belt and Road Initiative.

The World Bank barred CCCC and all its subsidiaries from bidding on bank-financed road and bridge projects until 2017 over fraudulent practices in a Philippine road programme, as successor to a firm sanctioned in 2009.

In 2020, the US Commerce Department placed CCCC units on its Entity List over their role in building artificial islands in the South China Sea.

The parent company’s corporate structure has already caused problems in Bogota. In 2024, two consortiums were disqualified from the tender for the metro’s second line after the city and its multilateral lenders found a conflict of interest, since CCCC both controlled CHEC and held a stake in Portugal’s Mota-Engil, a member of a rival bidding group.

That tender was later declared void after no offers were submitted, and was relaunched this year. The contract is expected to be awarded under the new government in early 2027.

Consortium says payment was agreed

Consulted by the Colombian magazine before publication, the Metro Linea 1 consortium said through its public relations office that it would open an internal investigation if it received detailed information, but did not provide a formal statement by the time the magazine went to press.

In a statement issued after the report was published, the consortium denied that any illegal demand had been made and gave a different account of the cash handover.

According to Metro Linea 1, the subcontractor had submitted an invoice for 960 million pesos that CHEC’s unit disputed over the quality of the work, but the company decided to pay it anyway to avoid further delays in workers’ salaries.

The 60 million pesos seen in the video was a “provisional retention” agreed between the two firms while Metrobuild corrected technical defects, the consortium said, delivered to the finance area of CHEC’s unit four days after the invoice was paid and backed by a signed receipt.

The statement said the video had been “covertly recorded” by Metrobuild representatives, and that its release generated “confusion in public opinion”.

The consortium said it had opened a priority internal investigation under its compliance programme, repeated that it held a policy of zero tolerance towards bribery and corruption, and pledged to act if any breach of internal procedures was established.

The Empresa Metro de Bogota, the public company that oversees the project, said it “categorically rejects any conduct that could constitute acts of corruption” and filed its own criminal complaint with the attorney general’s office.

The company identified Wang as the manager of the girder-launching process for the subcontractor and asked prosecutors to establish whether “criminally relevant” conduct took place.

In its complaint, the public company stressed that the executive had no “labour, contractual or functional relationship” with it, and that the events “occurred in the sphere of private dealings” between CHEC, its unit and third parties in the project’s subcontracting chain.

It added that it had notified the multilateral banks backing the project, that the money involved was private and did not compromise the works, and that it had paid the concessionaire on schedule, meaning Metro Linea 1 was obliged to pay its own subcontractors on time.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota did not immediately respond to a request by the South China Morning Post for comment.

The case has also drawn demands in Bogota’s city council.

Councilman Juan David Quintero, of the Nuevo Liberalismo party, called on the city and mayor Galan to ask CHEC to immediately suspend the executive named in the complaint, saying that not even a suspicion of corruption could be tolerated in what he called the most important project in the city’s history.

Andres Barrios, of the opposition Centro Democratico, filed a motion for a formal oversight debate to examine whether the project’s supervision mechanisms had failed.

item.title: [SCMP] Will Philippines’ push for seabed rights derail South China Sea code talks?
item.description:
The Philippines’ latest push for seabed rights in the South China Sea could complicate its efforts as this year’s Asean chair to build regional consensus, analysts say, adding another layer of complexity to already slow-moving talks on a code of conduct for the disputed waterway.

On July 28, Manila delivered an official presentation of its partial submission on its extended continental shelf in waters the Philippines considered its territory to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said on Wednesday.

In a statement, Rogelio Villanueva Jnr, DFA assistant secretary and spokesman for maritime affairs, said the submission “was a demonstration of the Philippines’ steadfast commitment to the United Nations Charter” and the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines’ latest push for seabed rights in the South China Sea could complicate its efforts as this year’s Asean chair to build regional consensus, analysts say, adding another layer of complexity to already slow-moving talks on a code of conduct for the disputed waterway.

On July 28, Manila delivered an official presentation of its partial submission on its extended continental shelf in waters the Philippines considered its territory to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said on Wednesday.

In a statement, Rogelio Villanueva Jnr, DFA assistant secretary and spokesman for maritime affairs, said the submission “was a demonstration of the Philippines’ steadfast commitment to the United Nations Charter” and the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

Article 76 of the convention provides the basis for coastal states such as the Philippines to establish the outer limits of their continental shelf, including the seabed and subsoil of submarine areas extending beyond 200 nautical miles (370km) but not more than 350 nautical miles from their baselines.

Such submissions concern seabed and subsoil rights rather than sovereignty over disputed islands or waters, and the UN commission’s role is to assess the scientific and technical basis of a claim before making recommendations.

“The presentation further underscored that the submission was part of the country’s responsibility to secure a peaceful South China Sea through the rule of law in order to sustain the livelihoods of Filipinos, foster trade, protect marine biodiversity, and unite coastal and littoral States,” the DFA said in its statement.

Overlapping claims

Questions remain over how the UN commission will handle the submission in contested South China Sea waters, where the Philippines’ assertion and overlapping ones by Southeast Asian neighbours sit alongside China’s sweeping claim over nearly the entire waterway under its 10-dash line.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal in a case brought by the Philippines found no legal basis for China’s historic-rights claims in the disputed sea. Beijing has dismissed the ruling as “illegal, null and void”, arguing the tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction.

In response to Manila’s UN presentation, Beijing accused the Philippines of “flagrantly infringing” on Chinese sovereignty and undermining regional peace.

It also said Manila was using the submission “as a pretext to hype up” the 10-year-old arbitral award.

Analysts caution that the Philippines’ UN presentation remains an early step in a long process.

“The recent presentation before the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf represents an important procedural milestone, but it is not yet a final recognition of the Philippine claim,” said Gary Ador Dionisio, dean of the De La Salle – College of Saint Benilde’s School of Diplomacy and Governance.

“The scientific and technical evaluation process remains ongoing and may take several years, particularly in areas where overlapping claims have been formally raised.”

The Philippines’ claim will undergo several steps under the commission’s rules of procedure, including a scientific and technical examination to assess whether it meets Article 76, a formality check and publication for three months to allow other states to provide comments.

Darwin Angeles, a lecturer at the University of the Philippines’ College of Law, said fulfilling these steps was the crucial part, noting that a subcommittee would be formed to prepare recommendations on the claim based on scientific and technical evaluation and the comments of other states.

In 2024, Malaysia and Vietnam lodged their own protests against the Philippines’ submission.

Kuala Lumpur sent its own diplomatic note rejecting Manila’s claim, saying the Philippines’ identification of its extended continental margin was projected from the baselines of Sabah and “clearly disregards Malaysia’s indisputable sovereignty over the state of Sabah”.

Manila has a long-standing dormant claim over Sabah, a dispute rooted in historical ties to the Sultanate of Sulu in the southern Philippines.

Vietnam filed its own extended continental shelf claim a month after the Philippines’ move but said it was willing to discuss mutually beneficial solutions with Manila.

Given Malaysia and Vietnam’s claims, the UN commission “may consider this a dispute under Unclos and therefore, it may just make a decision on the non-contentious portions in accordance with Rule 46 of the Rules of the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf”, Angeles said.

“The disputing states may raise their respective claims for adjudication by the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.”

Code complication

Analysts say the Philippine submission would not derail talks on a South China Sea code of conduct – a long-delayed Asean-China framework meant to set rules for behaviour in the disputed waterway and reduce the risk of confrontations – but could make it harder for the bloc to agree on a common position.

“Malaysia and Vietnam are expected to continue protecting their respective legal positions, particularly where overlapping claims exist,” Dionisio said.

“Such diplomatic protests are normal and should not be interpreted as a breakdown of Asean solidarity. Instead, they underscore the importance of sustained dialogue and legal diplomacy.”

Joanne Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, told This Week in Asia that while the Philippines’ submission “should not directly derail” code of conduct negotiations, “it highlights the difficulty of forging a common Asean position when member states hold overlapping maritime claims and differing legal interests”.

Lin said this could complicate consensus on other sensitive code-related issues, particularly its geographical scope, and place a greater burden on the Philippines as Asean chair to separate its national position from its regional role “and act as an honest broker”.

“Ultimately, the main obstacles to concluding the COC [code of conduct] remain the long-standing disagreements between Asean and China over its substance, legal character and implementation rather than the Philippine submission itself,” she said.

Dionisio stressed the Philippines’ “dual responsibility” as Asean chair was to “firmly uphold its sovereign rights while maintaining its credibility as an honest broker capable of advancing regional consensus”.

He said: “The appropriate path forward is continued bilateral and trilateral consultations, technical engagement among claimant states, and adherence to Unclos mechanisms without prejudicing future maritime boundary negotiations.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore jails man who had secret sexual ‘relationship’ with niece, 13
item.description:
In getting into a sexual relationship with his 13-year-old niece, a man sexually exploited her, raped her during staycations and “punished” her with sex acts when he grew jealous about a schoolmate she was dating.

The 38-year-old Singaporean man, who cannot be named to protect the victim’s identity, was sentenced to 21 years’ jail and 16 strokes of the cane on Monday.

He pleaded guilty to six charges that included statutory rape and sexual assault. Another 17 charges were considered in sentencing.
item.content:encoded:
In getting into a sexual relationship with his 13-year-old niece, a man sexually exploited her, raped her during staycations and “punished” her with sex acts when he grew jealous about a schoolmate she was dating.

The 38-year-old Singaporean man, who cannot be named to protect the victim’s identity, was sentenced to 21 years’ jail and 16 strokes of the cane on Monday.

He pleaded guilty to six charges that included statutory rape and sexual assault. Another 17 charges were considered in sentencing.

The court heard that the man was close to his brother, the victim’s father.

At the time of the offences, the offender was in a relationship with a woman whom he later married in May 2024. However, they did not live together.

He lived with his grandmother until she died before getting his own home.

Pair grew closer after her 13th birthday

When the victim was below the age of 13, her interactions with her uncle were limited to family gatherings and outings on special occasions.

In September 2022, the man took the victim out to celebrate her 13th birthday and she rode on his motorbike.

She said she enjoyed it and wanted to do it again, so he took her out for supper several days later.

While out, the girl saw her ex-boyfriend and told her uncle that he had touched her sexually and that she did not take issue with it.

From that day onwards, the pair grew closer and the girl would visit her uncle after school.

On one occasion, he molested her and asked if that was what her ex-boyfriend did. Although the girl was shocked, she did not object or react.

From October 2022, the pair considered themselves a couple, exchanging romantic messages daily, kissing and engaging in sex acts.

On a family trip to Malaysia around November 2022, the man molested the girl while they were alone in his room.

During the girl’s school holidays in the same month, the girl got permission from her parents to sleep over at her uncle’s place.

His grandmother had died by that time and they were alone at home.

After drinking alcohol, they engaged in sex acts and the man tried to rape her but could not. He did it the next morning on her agreement.

After this, the pair had sex about four times a week at the man’s home.

He also went out to eat and shop with the victim, but avoided behaving intimately when their family members were around.

In 2023, the victim received permission from her parents to go on a staycation with her uncle. He took along alcohol and toys, and they had sex at a hotel.

They continued seeing each other in 2024, with the teenager visiting her uncle after school. The man joked about committing incest with her.

Teen starts dating schoolmate

In January 2024, the teenager got to know a schoolmate named only as “A1” in court documents. They grew closer and got into a romantic relationship, and she began reducing her visits to her uncle.

The man noticed a change in her behaviour and found out about her relationship with A1, which dismayed him.

Jealous, he urged her to end her relationship with the boy and continued to engage in sexual activity with her.

In May 2024, when she was 14, he engaged in sex acts with the victim as a form of punishment for her interactions with A1.

He told his niece that she had made a mistake and needed to repay him. If she did not comply with the sex acts, she would need to break up with A1.

The teenager did not want to end her relationship with A1, so she gave in to her uncle’s demands.

The man continued to exploit her despite his niece experiencing pain sexually.

They had another staycation at a hotel in June 2024 where they had sex.

In August 2024, the man went through his niece’s phone while she was asleep and discovered that she had a TikTok account linked only to A1.

Enraged, he scolded his niece for not putting in as much effort into their relationship. They then engaged in sex acts after he offered to pretend that he had not seen her TikTok account.

While taking her home later, he told her to break up with A1, which made her cry.

He diverted to a shopping centre to try and calm her down, but shouted at her on the way out of frustration.

He said he did not want her and A1 to end up at the same polytechnic and told her that he would continue to control her life while she was at university.

The victim got out of the vehicle at her uncle’s prompting and went to a nearby toilet where she cried. He kept texting her, saying she seemed to love A1 more than him.

In early August 2024, after she told her uncle that she would not break up with A1, he threatened to leak her nude photographs and videos, which he had taken without her consent.

He threatened at least five times to publish them on a pornographic website, to send them to her friend, and to circulate them on Telegram.

He also said that he was prepared to go to jail, but did not disseminate the materials ultimately.

The teenager finally agreed to cut contact with A1 to pacify her uncle. He demanded that she publicise her break-up on social media, but did not force it eventually.

When she told A1 what had happened, he said that her uncle’s behaviour was “out of line”.

The victim tried to end her relationship with her uncle at least eight times, but he guilt-tripped her each time. He would also tell her that he was depressed and wanted to end his life.

Victim informs teacher

Tired of her uncle’s manipulative behaviour, the victim informed her teacher on Aug 6, 2024 about her relationship with him.

The matter was escalated to the Child Protection Services under the Ministry of Social and Family Development, which filed a police report.

The day the victim reported the matter to her teacher, her uncle had gone to her school to wait for her.

He sensed something amiss and saw his niece being escorted into a vehicle around 6pm. He deduced that his inappropriate relationship with her had come to light.

He was arrested the next day.

Deputy Public Prosecutors Chin Jincheng and Joelle Loy sought 19-and-a-half to 21 years’ jail and at least 16 strokes of the cane for the man.

Chin said that the man had kept up a facade of being nothing but a caring uncle to the victim, but blatantly violated her parents’ trust.

He also said that the man robbed his niece of her innocence by taking her virginity when she was 13 and “habituated her to all kinds of illicit sexual activity with him”.

Chin added that the man had abused his position of authority over the victim and abused his brother’s trust in him to gain access to the teenager.

He also manipulated the victim emotionally by refusing to let her end this “perverse relationship”.

“Towards the tail-end of the relationship, he was cruel to the victim and she caved into his demands out of fear,” Chin said.

Defence lawyer Ramesh Tiwary sought 16 years’ jail and 16 strokes of the cane instead.

He urged the court to take into account his client’s remorse in addition to his guilty plea.

He pointed out that his client had admitted to everything he had done and apologised to the victim’s parents.

“The fact that this remorse is true is reflected in a letter signed by the parents and the girl,” Tiwary said. “The best evidence in this case of genuine remorse … is that the victim’s family feel that he has shown remorse.”

He added that his client apologised in person to his brother, and that his sister-in-law was not ready to meet him at that time but did so later.

Tiwary said that the most important mitigating factor in cases such as these is perhaps the fact that the offender does not make the victim of a sexual offence testify in front of strangers and relive the trauma.

At this, Justice Andre Maniam questioned if this was already accommodated for in the 30 per cent sentencing discount for the early plea of guilt.

Tiwary acknowledged this. Justice Maniam did not give any extra credit for the remorse.

For each charge of statutory rape, the man could have been jailed for up to 20 years and fined or caned.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore battles speed of youth radicalisation as concerns mount
item.description:
Recent arrests in Singapore of young people who succumbed to extremist ideologies and planned attacks, including school stabbings, have sent a chill across the city state, with authorities noting that the speed of radicalisation has doubled.

Over three months this year, three teenagers have been detained, sparking public discussion on school security and whether more can be done to protect students or encourage critical thinking.

Last Monday, the Internal Security Department (ISD) said three youths, aged 14, 15 and 19, who were each detained between April and June, were radicalised by groups including Islamic State (Isis), Hamas and far-right extremist ideologies.
item.content:encoded:
Recent arrests in Singapore of young people who succumbed to extremist ideologies and planned attacks, including school stabbings, have sent a chill across the city state, with authorities noting that the speed of radicalisation has doubled.

Over three months this year, three teenagers have been detained, sparking public discussion on school security and whether more can be done to protect students or encourage critical thinking.

Last Monday, the Internal Security Department (ISD) said three youths, aged 14, 15 and 19, who were each detained between April and June, were radicalised by groups including Islamic State (Isis), Hamas and far-right extremist ideologies.

The 19-year-old, Tan Jun Jie, planned knife attacks against Singapore Armed Forces personnel at Sembawang Air Base and LGBTQ students at his school. The 14-year-old was arrested a month before his planned stabbing attack at his secondary school during the June school holidays.

On whether security measures at schools would be stepped up, Senior Minister K Shanmugam, who is also coordinating minister for national security, said last Monday: “You can’t turn every school into a garrison or a cantonment, then it won’t feel like a school.”

Education Minister Desmond Lee said on the same day that schools had multiple layers of vigilance, training and contingency planning in place, along with measures such as security staff, closed-circuit cameras, and selective bag checks when necessary.

“But schools are places where people learn. They spark the joy of learning. They are places where people must feel comfortable learning,” Lee said.

Under Singapore’s Internal Security Act, the ISD can detain individuals deemed a threat to national security without trial.

In recent years these detainees have increasingly come from Singapore’s youth aged 20 and below, with the ISD telling This Week in Asia that social media and online platforms have accelerated the time between an individual’s first encounter with extremist elements and their subscription to such ideologies.

In the last 10 years, 23 young people aged between 14 and 20 have been dealt with under the ISA, compared with one before 2015, according to the ISD and then senior minister Teo Chee Hean in 2024.

In forum letters in Singapore’s newspaper The Straits Times last week, members of the public debated whether schools should offer more religious knowledge and critical thinking modules to counter radicalisation.

Lee noted last Monday that schools had Character and Citizenship Education to help students discern and reject harmful online content, including extremist ideologies, and the ministry would look at how to further strengthen it.

The education ministry also worked with the ISD to run counter-radicalisation outreach activities for school staff and student welfare officers, enabling them to spot warning signs in their students early, Lee added.

Down the rabbit hole

The ISD said algorithms on social media and video-sharing platforms recommended more extremist material to individuals once they viewed such content, resulting in a “rabbit-hole” syndrome. Online communities also became echo chambers.

“Over the past decade, the time taken for self-radicalisation for ISA cases has essentially halved – from an average of 24 months before 2015, to an average of 12 months between 2021 and 2025,” the ISD said.

The department noted that young people, as digital natives, were more susceptible to exposure and engagement with extremist materials online. It cited the case of a 15-year-old pro-Isis girl who was issued a restriction order in February 2025 after she was radicalised in weeks.

When asked if the Israel-Gaza conflict was a trigger for more young people to become radicalised, the ISD said the conflict was an emotive issue, with Singaporeans deeply concerned about the dire humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and rightly so.

“However, Singapore draws the line at the importation, support and promotion of extremist narratives which leverage on the conflict to promote hatred and violence,” it said.

Shashi Jayakumar, executive director of SJK Geostrategic Advisory, noted that some critical faculties might not have fully formed in young people, making them more susceptible to online echo chambers.

“In this process, one meets like-minded people who seem to be validating one’s own predilections. The same process in many cases is conducive to the formation (in one’s perception) of an ‘out group’ – the enemy,” Jayakumar said.

“The lack of critical faculties means in many cases an inability to see opposing points of view, or to accept counter-narratives.”

Jayakumar noted that in some of these cases, what might be needed was not simply “deradicalisation” but counselling or psychological interventions to “disengage” the individual from a negative or violent pathway.

He said “mentoring” had been cited as part of counselling efforts in Singapore recently.

“This is precisely what has been tried elsewhere, including in the West, and has been shown to hold some promise,” Jayakumar said.

Salim Mohamed Nasir, a member of the Religious Rehabilitation Group which mentors radicalised youth, told This Week in Asia that Singapore’s response could not simply be to block or restrict young people’s access to information since they should be encouraged to care about global issues and humanitarian suffering.

“The more important task is to help them engage with these issues thoughtfully, critically and compassionately. We want them to ask questions, seek different perspectives, verify information, and understand that caring deeply about injustice should never be manipulated into believing that hatred or violence is the only answer,” Salim said.

“By strengthening critical thinking, digital literacy, emotional resilience and trusted relationships with parents, teachers and mentors, we can better equip young people to reject extremist narratives before they take root and to channel their convictions into peaceful, constructive and lawful action.”

Salim said the most effective safeguard was building stronger relationships so that students felt they belonged and had trusted adults who cared about them, since this would make them less likely to become isolated or vulnerable to extremist influences.

Schools could continue to strengthen professional learning for educators in areas including digital radicalisation, online influence, media literacy and conducting respectful conversations on sensitive issues, he added.

“When young people feel connected to their schools, supported by their families, guided by their communities and confident that they can ask difficult questions without fear or judgment, they are far less likely to be drawn towards violent extremist narratives,” Salim said.

Singapore is not the only country in the region grappling with its young people becoming radicalised by extremist ideology.

In the Philippines, two boys, aged 14 and 15, opened fire on their schoolmates in June, killing three and wounding 20. Investigators and cybersecurity experts said during a Senate hearing on July 1 that their attack might have been linked to a global online extremist network that recruited and radicalised vulnerable children through popular video games.

In February, Malaysian police arrested six people aged 16 to 21 during coordinated counterterrorism raids across the country. Three of the suspects were under 18. The group was charged with pledging allegiance to Isis, distributing extremist propaganda, and planning local attacks.

item.title: [SCMP] A military base, a displaced people and Trump’s China fears: Burnham’s Chagos test
item.description:
Bertrice Pompe was born in Diego Garcia, situated in the Indian Ocean halfway between Tanzania and Indonesia, in 1971, making her one of the last Chagossians to enter the world on an island that her family would soon be forced to leave.

“Some families, like brothers, sisters, were separated,” she said. “Some went to the Seychelles, some to Mauritius … close family, brothers, sister, mother, father, separated … and they never saw each other again.”

Before Mauritian independence in 1968, the British government detached the Chagos Islands from the Mauritius administrative boundaries to create the British Indian Ocean Territory.
item.content:encoded:
Bertrice Pompe was born in Diego Garcia, situated in the Indian Ocean halfway between Tanzania and Indonesia, in 1971, making her one of the last Chagossians to enter the world on an island that her family would soon be forced to leave.

“Some families, like brothers, sisters, were separated,” she said. “Some went to the Seychelles, some to Mauritius … close family, brothers, sister, mother, father, separated … and they never saw each other again.”

Before Mauritian independence in 1968, the British government detached the Chagos Islands from the Mauritius administrative boundaries to create the British Indian Ocean Territory.

The entire population of the largest island in the Chagos Archipelago was removed in the late 1960s and early 1970s to make way for one of the most strategically important US-British military bases in the world.

“We were always identified as different,” Pompe said, about growing up in the Seychelles.

Now based in London, she has become a prominent voice in the Chagossian fight for the right to return. She also opposes the 2025 agreement to transfer sovereignty to Mauritius and allow Britain to retain a 99-year lease on Diego Garcia for billions of dollars.

“There is nothing in that deal for us,” Pompe told the South China Morning Post, adding: “I will not be allowed to go back to Diego Garcia. What’s in there for me?”

It is a question that cuts through decades of geopolitical bargaining. For more than a century, Chagos has been shaped by the strategic interests of larger powers – from Britain and the US to Mauritius, and now by the rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

As a crucial military hub, Diego Garcia supports US operations across the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific. However, the arrangement was challenged and the International Court of Justice backed Mauritius’ claim that Britain’s administration of the islands was unlawful.

Last year, then-British prime minister Keir Starmer defended the agreement to transfer sovereignty to Mauritius and instead lease Diego Garcia as necessary to protect the future of the military base.

Without it, Britain “would not be able to prevent China or any other nation setting up their own bases on the outer islands or carrying out joint exercises near our base”, he argued.

But Starmer soon found himself at odds with Washington. After initially calling the deal the “best” achievable arrangement, US President Donald Trump reversed course, urging London to scrap it as an “act of great stupidity”.

Handing sovereignty to Mauritius could open the door to greater Chinese influence in the Indian Ocean because of its close ties with Beijing, Trump warned.

Since then, the White House has floated the alternative possibility of the US buying the islands outright, saying discussions with Britain are under way.

That leaves Andy Burnham – Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade – with a difficult inheritance: an unresolved agreement negotiated under his predecessor and one of the first domestic and foreign policy tests of his premiership.

While Starmer held back on settling the future of the Chagos Islands after Trump publicly opposed the deal, Burnham – who maintained cordial ties with China as mayor of Greater Manchester – is signalling that he may move ahead with the arrangement.

The test for Burnham will be less about the substance of the Chagos policy itself and more about how he manages disagreements with the US president, according to analysts. Not everyone believes he will be able to insulate Britain from Washington’s pressure.
