Nilanthi Samaranayake, a security analyst focusing on the Indian Ocean, said that while Burnham appeared set to adopt a similar view on Chagos as Starmer, from a US perspective the more important difference might lie in style rather than substance.

“What’s different is that he may handle issue differences with Trump, like Greenland and Iran, more deftly than Starmer,” she said.

Samaranayake also noted that the idea of US-Mauritius bilateral discussions was not without precedent. Pravind Jugnauth, during his term as Mauritian prime minister, had previously suggested providing the US with a 99-year lease on Diego Garcia.

Still, it was India rather than China that was most likely to shape the space for any such arrangement, Samaranayake argued.

“India has significant weight in Mauritius’ national security calculus. Even during the best of times in the US-India relationship, India may not want the US to be a resident Indian Ocean country,” she said.

Grenville Cross, a senior counsel and former director of public prosecutions in Hong Kong, was among those questioning Burnham’s ability to withstand pressure from the Trump White House.

Writing in China Daily, Cross observed that it would be “fascinating to see how [Burnham] responds once Trump applies the thumbscrews, as he did with his predecessors”.

“The Trump administration has shown it wants to determine Britain’s domestic and foreign policies, and it has walked all over Starmer,” he added.

For Dominique Soopin, president of the self-declared transitional government of the Chagossian people, the biggest question is not who ultimately controls Chagos, but whether the people who were removed are finally allowed a voice in deciding their future.

In a letter to Burnham, Soopin called on the British government to formally recognise Chagossians as a distinct community before any final decision was made over the islands’ future.

“Before long-term political outcomes are determined, the Chagossian people should be formally recognised as a distinct community, enabling them to participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their future,” she wrote.

Chagos is ‘not for sale’

For Soopin, the dispute is not a chess game between global powers. It is about a people whose homeland has been treated as a strategic asset for generations.

“Powerful countries just see Chagos as strategic. I don’t see strategic,” she said in a separate interview with the SCMP.

“I see the human life. I see the human value, the connection, the nature, the stories that people left because people decided for them by ignoring them, because they were not considered as human.”

As Washington weighs the strategic importance of the islands, Soopin has a message for any government deciding the archipelago’s future without Chagossians: “Chagos is not for sale. It is a homeland that needs to be repaired with its people.”

That argument has gained unexpected political weight in Britain. A YouGov poll released days before Burnham’s arrival at No 10 showed that 72 per cent of adults believed Chagossians should have a vote on whether the islands’ sovereignty was transferred to Mauritius.

Only six per cent opposed the idea, according to the survey, commissioned by campaign group the Great British Political Action Committee. Chief executive Claire Bullivant described the result as “one of the clearest messages you will ever see from the British public”.

Frustration has also taken a more dramatic form. In February, a small group of British-Chagossian campaigners landed on a remote island north of Diego Garcia and have refused to leave.

Misley Mandarin, a member of the group, has said the campaigners want the islands to remain under British sovereignty. An effort to remove them stalled when a court granted a temporary protection order. A final ruling is expected in September.

Their presence challenges one of the central realities of the Chagos dispute – that the islands remain a tightly controlled British military territory where ordinary Chagossians are not allowed to freely return or settle.

Middle path

The puzzle for Burnham to solve is whether any realistic middle path still exists – one that protects the Diego Garcia base, manages the relationship with Washington and finally gives the people who were removed a meaningful voice in their own future.

Some analysts argue such a path is still possible. According to Nitya Labh of Chatham House, Chagossian resettlement and the continued operation of the military base are compatible, with British-US-Mauritius maritime cooperation helping to ensure its uninterrupted functioning.

However, diplomats had long assumed Mauritius represented Chagossian interests, Labh warned. “This assumption is dangerous,” she said, arguing that it overlooked the racial and socio-economic dynamics that had repeatedly marginalised Chagossians.

Labh also suggested that both governments might delay the final sovereignty transfer to reduce political scrutiny and allow regional tensions to ease.

With the US continuing to use Diego Garcia for regional operations and logistics, its “position in the ongoing conflict further complicates any considerations of a sovereignty transfer”, she said.

For now, Pompe has made clear that she does not yet trust either Burnham or Trump.

“Until [Burnham] or Trump come to speak with us … put us on the table, see us, include us in the negotiation, not just tell us afterwards what they’re doing … we don’t trust no one,” she said.

“I didn’t vote for anyone … who voted for him? The trust will come after, but if he doesn’t do that, why would we trust him?”

item.title: [SCMP] How America’s 250-year China dream became its greatest strategic challenge
item.description:
One morning in February 1784, a converted privateer called the Empress of China sailed out of New York harbour. It was bound for a country almost no one aboard had ever seen – China, then ruled by the Qing dynasty.

Six months later, it dropped anchor at Canton, the only port where the Qing government allowed Western maritime trade.

At the time, the Declaration of Independence was less than a decade old, and the Treaty of Paris recognising American independence had been signed less than a year before.
item.content:encoded:
One morning in February 1784, a converted privateer called the Empress of China sailed out of New York harbour. It was bound for a country almost no one aboard had ever seen – China, then ruled by the Qing dynasty.

Six months later, it dropped anchor at Canton, the only port where the Qing government allowed Western maritime trade.

At the time, the Declaration of Independence was less than a decade old, and the Treaty of Paris recognising American independence had been signed less than a year before.

The newborn republic had no navy and little standing in the world. What it did have was a dream of China.

Two and a half centuries later, the country that once drew American merchants across the Pacific has become Washington’s principal competitor. The United States and China, now the world’s two largest economies, are locked in a struggle over trade, technology, security and the shape of the global order.

For historians, that first voyage marked the beginning of a relationship in which America repeatedly reinvented what China represented – from coveted market to admired civilisation, from missionary project to strategic rival. Each reinvention said as much about America as it did about China.

Even during his visit to Beijing in May, US President Donald Trump invoked the Empress of China during the state banquet hosted by President Xi Jinping, recalling the first American merchant ship to reach Chinese shores.

The market

It is easy to forget how important the idea of China was to the founding of America, according to Xu Guoqi, the David H.Y. Chang Professor of Chinese History at the University of Hong Kong (HKU).

The tea that was dumped into Boston harbour in 1773, the act of defiance that helped ignite the revolution, was Chinese tea.

“The dream of independence for future Americans came, to a certain extent, from their dream of the China market,” said Xu.

Tea, which Americans called “green gold”, was effectively a hard currency, he said.

“Everybody seemed obsessed with Chinese tea after the British brought it to the West.”

That fascination predated the US itself, Xu added. “Europeans had dreamed of finding a route to China since the days of Marco Polo, a quest that famously sent Christopher Columbus across the Atlantic in 1492,” Xu said.

“That is the irony of the shared history between China and America – it was interconnected from the very beginning.”

When the Empress of China sailed to Canton in 1784, it embodied a belief that access to the Chinese market could help to secure America’s future.

That belief endured for more than two centuries.

In the 19th century, it took the form of the China trade and, later, the Open Door Policy – Washington’s call for equal commercial access to China rather than allowing foreign powers to divide it into exclusive spheres of influence. It was an era when a weakened Qing empire, battered by the opium wars and unequal treaties, was being forced open by imperial powers.

A century later, the same aspiration reappeared in the language of reform and engagement.

By the time China joined the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001, many in Washington and on Wall Street believed opening up the Chinese economy would not only create one of the world’s largest export markets but also reinforce the assumptions of the American-led global economic system.

These hopes were captured in then-US president Bill Clinton’s 2000 remarks supporting China’s WTO accession.

“Economically, this agreement is the equivalent of a one-way street. It requires China to open its markets – with a fifth of the world’s population, potentially the biggest markets in the world – to both our products and services in unprecedented new ways,” he said.

But rather than converging towards the American economic model, China developed a state-led system that Washington increasingly viewed as a strategic challenge instead of an opportunity.

The first Trump administration launched a trade war in 2018. The second expanded it in 2025, signalling a new consensus that China itself had become the challenge.

A mutual misunderstanding

If Americans first imagined China as a market, they also imagined it as one of the world’s great civilisations. But the China they admired was often one they barely understood.

“Americans now easily forget that the United States was a very small country back then, when everything was just being founded,” said Wang Yuanchong, an associate professor of history at the University of Delaware.

“At the start China was strong and America was small, and only slowly did that situation reverse,” Wang said.

When the Empress of China arrived, Wang said, its crew carried a “sea letter”, a kind of all-purpose passport, addressed to no one in particular and merely listing every title its bearers could think of.

“That actually proves they knew nothing,” he said.

“They were completely in the dark about China’s administrative system, its society, its history and culture. They simply came.”

Qing officials, for their part, knew little about the new republic. They saw foreign visitors through the old imperial lens of tribute and trade.

Two centuries later, the ignorance is not mutual, Wang said.

Ordinary Chinese, he said, could name several American presidents, while many Americans “can’t name a single Chinese leader”.

As Americans imagined China, historians suggest that they were also constructing an image of themselves.

Unlike the European empires carving up Qing China, the young republic preferred to see itself as a more progressive kind of power.

One reason was America’s comparatively restrained presence in China during the 19th century.

Unlike other Western powers like Britain and France, the US seized no colonies on Chinese soil and championed the Open Door Policy, which called for equal commercial access rather than exclusive spheres of influence.

In 1868, the Qing court invited the departing US minister to China, Anson Burlingame, to represent China on a mission to the West. Burlingame acted as a mediator between China and Western countries and won the trust of Chinese officials.

The Burlingame Treaty that followed recognised that the two peoples could travel between the countries as equals and study in each other’s country.

Later, the US returned part of the Boxer Rebellion indemnity to fund Chinese schools and scholarships for study in America, benefiting the predecessor of Tsinghua University.

But historians warn that this picture of a kinder America leaves out a lot.

Xu at HKU argues that America’s difference reflected a genuine sense of exceptionalism. Having recently broken from the British monarchy, the US saw itself as fundamentally different from Europe’s imperial powers.

“The US looked down on the old European countries,” Xu said. “They thought they were corrupt.”

Wang of the University of Delaware said that throughout the 19th century, “America’s main focus in China was commerce.”

It had no garrison in China as Britain did, and until it took the Philippines from Spain in 1898, it had little real armed force in the western Pacific, according to Wang.

“It was just a country that came to share the spoils,” Wang said. “The ones out front were mostly Britain, France, Russia and Germany.”

Gordon H. Chang, Olive H. Palmer Professor in Humanities at Stanford University, similarly cautioned against romanticising America’s role.

“It’s a myth that America did the Boxer indemnity for China’s purposes,” he said, adding that former president Theodore Roosevelt’s calculation “was to advance American influence in China”.

The idea of an innocent America also sits uneasily alongside the experience of Chinese migrants within the US itself.

Thousands of Chinese labourers helped to build the transcontinental railroad, completed in 1869. Thousands more worked in mining, agriculture and small businesses, Chang said.

But their contribution was soon buried by the politics of exclusion.

“The fact that it was forgotten or neglected or covered up is part of that history of discrimination,” Chang said.

The mission to change China

If commerce was America’s first Chinese dream, transformation became its most enduring ambition.

“The sense that the United States should shape, mould or change China is quite deep,” Chang said – first turning China into a Christian country through missionaries, then a capitalist one, and now a non-communist one.

The ambition, he said, was always trailed by frustration, because “China continues to be what it is, regardless of what the United States wants.”

Wang dated the start later.

For most of the 19th century, he said, Washington stayed mostly silent on China’s political system. The belief that America should design and drive change in China did not truly take hold, Wang argued, until “after the second world war, in the Cold War years”.

Richard Nixon’s 1972 visit to China is often remembered as a realist turn, a strategic opening designed to balance the Soviet Union. But the normalisation of diplomatic relations in 1979, Deng Xiaoping’s visit to the US and China’s reform and opening-up soon encouraged a view in Washington: that engagement itself could transform China.

After the Cold War, supporters of engagement argued that trade, investment and China’s integration into global institutions would not only expand commerce but gradually encourage political liberalisation.

China’s entry into the WTO became the clearest expression of that belief.

In Beijing, however, many top leaders drew the opposite conclusion.

The strategy that Americans described as engagement was often interpreted as an effort to reshape China’s political system. That suspicion was reinforced by the Cold War concept of “peaceful evolution”, the idea that communist governments could eventually be transformed through the gradual spread of Western political values rather than military force.

It is a doubt rooted deep in the minds of generations of Chinese leaders, who have repeatedly warned that the same could happen in China – even though both the Biden and Trump administrations have assured Beijing they do not seek regime change.

Chang remained cautious about these assurances.

“If Donald Trump could snap his fingers, of course he would like to have a change in China,” he said.

“We’re going back to the past,” he said. “But the past is the 1950s, not the 1990s. The period from 1990 to around 2015 was the unusual period, and I don’t think we’re going back to it.”

The reversal of power

If America’s ambition was to shape China, history had another surprise in store: the balance of power itself would not remain fixed.

When the two countries first encountered one another in the late 18th century, China was the older, richer and more established civilisation. The US was a fragile new republic looking for its place in the world.

That balance began to shift around the turn of the 20th century.

As China reeled from the Boxer crisis and the occupation of Beijing, the US – its civil war long settled – was enjoying the prosperity of the Gilded Age and emerging as a Pacific power.

“The US is a late-developing country, founded just as the industrial revolution was beginning, so it caught the express train from the start,” Wang said.

“China’s misfortune is that its whole 19th century was a descent, while America rose the whole way – two completely opposite trajectories.”

Today, many Chinese see history as turning once again.

In January 2021, just days after the riot at the US Capitol, Xi advanced the argument that “the East is rising and the West is declining”, signalling China’s growing confidence in its development model and international standing.

The theory has since been discussed throughout official and popular Chinese discourse.

That reversal also changed how Washington viewed the world, Wang argued.

Before the two world wars, and especially before the second, Wang said, the US never had a fixed global rival. Treating first the Soviet Union and then China as its primary adversary, he said, was a strategic logic that emerged only after the US became a global power.

Fixing another country as a “main enemy” to be managed over the long term had not been a constant in more than two centuries of Sino-American contact, he said.

Hope, fear and the road ahead

If the US repeatedly reinvented China, China also reinvented the US.

Before the end of the first world war, Chinese intellectuals held up then-US president Woodrow Wilson as a symbol of idealism, hoping his principle of national self-determination would help China recover its rights.

The Paris Peace Conference’s decision to give Japan control of Germany’s former privileges in the Chinese province of Shandong shattered that hope.

After 1919, Xu said, “the Chinese became radical, became desperate, and turned to a third civilisation: Russia”.

Looking back across 250 years of contact, Chang at Stanford sees a recurring pattern.

Rather than moving steadily from friendship to rivalry, he argues, the relationship has repeatedly swung between excessive optimism and excessive fear.

Both, he suggests, have obscured a more complicated reality.

Wang believes that reality depends on maintaining contact, even as political tensions deepen.

“Without exchange, there is nothing,” he said. “Wasn’t ping-pong diplomacy exactly this?”

None of the historians who spoke to the South China Morning Post expected the warmth of an earlier age to return easily.

Chang put it bluntly: “The idea that China and the United States should become great friends has never been the case, and I don’t think it ever will be.”

But for Rana Mitter, S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, the point was that the relationship had never stood still, and never stopped mattering.

“China and the US have been rivals, enemies, partners and collaborators during the past two centuries, in particular the last century,” Mitter said.

“It’s worth remembering that history changes over time but the two countries remain important to each other.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Xinjiang offers Hong Kong a bridge to Central Asia — and what the risks are
item.description:
Hong Kong businesses can leverage Xinjiang’s connectivity with Central Asia to expand into new markets while the city’s financial, trade and professional services can help businesses in the region enter Southeast Asia, according to political analysts.

But an economist and a textile industry veteran have warned of potential risks for Hong Kong businesses building ties with Xinjiang in northwestern China.

Western countries have imposed sanctions on officials and entities tied to the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region over alleged suppression of ethnic minority members – accusations Beijing has repeatedly denied.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong businesses can leverage Xinjiang’s connectivity with Central Asia to expand into new markets while the city’s financial, trade and professional services can help businesses in the region enter Southeast Asia, according to political analysts.

But an economist and a textile industry veteran have warned of potential risks for Hong Kong businesses building ties with Xinjiang in northwestern China.

Western countries have imposed sanctions on officials and entities tied to the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region over alleged suppression of ethnic minority members – accusations Beijing has repeatedly denied.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu led his largest delegation to date to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in May and June, aiming to explore new markets amid geopolitical uncertainties and help mainland Chinese companies go global.

Li Lifan, a research fellow at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, said Xinjiang could play a role in fostering collaboration between Hong Kong and Central Asia.

Li noted that Xinjiang had two major railway hubs in Alashankou and Khorgos at its border with Kazakhstan, a country through which most freight trains running between China and Europe passed.

“Xinjiang is essential to trade between Hong Kong and Central Asia,” he said, adding that the region had a strong appetite for advanced and innovative electronic products.

“For example, products can be designed in Hong Kong, manufactured in Xinjiang and exported to Central Asia.”

Li added that Hong Kong commercial associations could consider setting up offices in key Xinjiang border cities, such as Khorgos, to help foster connections for their counterparts in Central Asia.

Ethnic Kazakhs in prefectures close to Kazakhstan could help Hong Kong firms communicate with stakeholders, he suggested.

Additionally, Hong Kong could assist Central Asian and Xinjiang businesses in expanding into new markets as they currently relied on the port of Lianyungang in eastern Jiangsu province to export to Japan and South Korea, he said.

“Hong Kong serves as a good gateway for Xinjiang and Central Asia to venture into the Southeast Asian market,” Li said.

The analyst added that companies in Xinjiang and Central Asia could source capital from Hong Kong and use the city’s mediation and legal services in case of any trade disputes.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Hong Kong could serve as a springboard for Xinjiang businesses seeking new and friendly markets outside Western countries.

Lau noted that Xinjiang had one of the fastest-growing economies in China and served as a hub connecting the rest of the country with Central Asia and Europe under the Belt and Road Initiative, while Hong Kong was tasked with helping mainland businesses go global.

“Most importantly, both places should leverage their strategic positions to cooperate and facilitate development,” he said.

Hong Kong could take advantage of Xinjiang’s location and its cross-border infrastructure as it looked to build ties with Central Asia, Lau added.

Xinjiang has for years been a source of strain between Beijing and Washington.

Western countries have imposed sanctions on China over its alleged use of forced labour and detentions in the region, a claim that Beijing has strongly denied.

The Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act that came into force in 2022 blocks the import of all goods sourced wholly or partly from Xinjiang unless the companies involved can prove their supply chains are free of coercive practices.

Esquel Group, a Hong Kong-based textile and apparel company, and two of its mainland-based subsidiaries were blacklisted over their cotton sources.

A Hong Kong textile industry veteran, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the chances were slim for other Hong Kong companies to expand into the region due to costs and sanction-related concerns.

The insider said Esquel’s presence on the mainland was unique as it had expanded in Xinjiang since the 1990s and built its supply chain.

The representative said that the appetite for Xinjiang cotton was also low, except among mainland brands, as global apparel companies could avoid trouble by using cotton from Pakistan and India at competitive prices.

Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, said cotton and food products from Xinjiang had been heavily politicised, and companies would try to minimise their risks of being targeted.

Instead of sourcing materials from the region, the city could help re-export Xinjiang products to overseas markets where there was a demand and promote the area’s tourism, he said.

Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways last year launched direct passenger flights to Urumqi, the region’s capital.

The South China Morning Post recently visited Xinjiang on a media trip, where the local cotton industry sought to clear its name.

Zhao Xin, who owns 113 hectares (279 acres) of cotton fields in the city of Shihezi in Xinjiang, said in response to accusations of forced labour that many procedures had already been automated and mechanised.

He pointed to the general application of drip irrigation technology, which involves installing small hosepipes underneath a thin plastic sheet covering the soil to irrigate crops while preventing evaporation and retaining heat.

Zhao added that farmers relied on satellites to increase precision when sowing seeds and operating harvesting machines.

“It has significantly saved manpower and increased productivity,” he said.

“Forced labour does not exist. All modernised efforts have removed the need for manpower. How can we exploit them? It has been mechanised.”

A manager at a factory of Shihezi Baifeng Cotton Industry Company, which processes cotton into yarn, also said automation had cut employee headcount from 900 to 250, with workers focusing on monitoring and maintaining the machines.

The factory is located in the 180-hectare Shihezi Textile Industrial Park, which is home to 17 businesses less than two years after its opening.

With an occupancy rate of more than 60 per cent, the park also brings in waterless dyeing technology from Esquel.

Liu Zhen, general manager of Shihezi Jingyi Technology, a company formed by Esquel and a Xinjiang business, said the technology helped tackle a bottleneck in the industry, as textile dyeing caused pollution and water was scarce in the region.

“We hope to introduce green and sustainable technologies to promote positive development in the industry,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] A Vietnamese refugee returns to the Hong Kong island where echoes of a lost childhood remain
item.description:
“This is where my bed was.”

Katie Aung stands at the centre of Tai A Chau, an uninhabited island south of Lantau, with former marine police officer Les Bird, pointing to a spot on the ground.

“This is where I lived.” She turns slightly, and gestures again. “My bed faced this way. Head this end, feet down here. I lived right here for many years of my childhood.”
item.content:encoded:
“This is where my bed was.”

Katie Aung stands at the centre of Tai A Chau, an uninhabited island south of Lantau, with former marine police officer Les Bird, pointing to a spot on the ground.

“This is where I lived.” She turns slightly, and gestures again. “My bed faced this way. Head this end, feet down here. I lived right here for many years of my childhood.”

In the 1990s, it was to this 1.2 sq km speck of land in the South China Sea that Aung, a former Vietnamese refugee, was confined.

Tai A Chau today is almost entirely reclaimed by nature – a deserted outcrop. But its past as a detention centre remains etched into the landscape, lingering beneath the undergrowth: the concrete spine of a former camp cutting through the island, the foundations of village houses that once stood there – quiet, stubborn reminders of what once was. It is this past that Aung and Bird, who oversaw the search-and-rescue operations for tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees in Hong Kong across three decades, have come to recall.

After disembarking at the old jetty of Tai A Chau, Aung walks inland with Bird. Along the way, they spot an ornate, rocky fish pond, built by other refugees who had once inhabited the island. Aung recognises it immediately; she and the other children would gather around its edge, watching the colourful fish that darted through the water.

Upon entering the main clearing of the island, Aung slows and looks around. Framed by hills on both sides, the space opens up before her, its present at odds with what it once held. Here is where she makes sense of her old sleeping quarters.

“We both stood there in silence for some time,” Bird says, recalling the visit he made with Aung in February. “Katie was lost in her memories in a moment that must have been pretty poignant for her.”

In the late 70s through to the 90s, waves of refugees fled Vietnam’s post-war turmoil, risking their lives on rickety boats in the South China Sea. Many were rescued – or intercepted – by authorities. Under British colonial administration, Hong Kong established temporary detention centres on isolated islands and former military sites. One of them was Tai A Chau, where children and adults alike spent months, or even years, under tightly controlled conditions. For them, these camps became formative, often traumatic, spaces.

“In my mind, I still see the island as it was during that first week in 1989 [when the camp was opened],” says Bird. “We received about 3,000 desperate people. We had to provide shelter, food and fresh water – and there was nothing on the island. It was mayhem.”

What unfolded in those early days was improvised survival. “I remember fathers, dressed in rags, scavenging for materials – broken boats, tree branches, anything – to build shelter, and mothers, many with babies, trying to find ways to feed them. There were no sanitation facilities. No power. At night, the island was in complete darkness,” Bird says.

He recalls the threat of disease being inescapable. “We knew, in the heat of the day, it wouldn’t be long before something would spread.” Even now, the sensory memory lingers. “As Katie and I walked across the island, I could still see those scenes,” he says. “I could still smell the smoke from the fires people used for cooking – and that strong ointment of White Flower Oil everyone relied on, hoping to keep illness away.”

After a few years of operating as a ramshackle “tent city”, the government built an all-purpose holding centre on Tai A Chau, in 1991. Life on the island continued to be regimented and constrained.

Detainees were housed in shared halls, movement was restricted and repetition often replaced any sense of freedom. But within these walls, small acts of resilience – learning new languages, forming friendships and even building fish ponds – offered the faintest glimmers of normality.

Aung was just nine years old in 1989, when she left her parents and hometown of Da Nang to join her two aunts aboard a small dinghy. Boat No 761 carried 77 people on a perilous journey to Hong Kong that would last seven days and seven nights.

“We had to leave at night, then head to the mountains for a night or two,” she recalls. “We left during the Lantern Festival, so there was a lot of distraction; that way, the police didn’t catch us.”

Much of the journey remains blurred. “I don’t remember a lot of details,” Aung says. “The strange thing about memory is that the brain blocks most of the trauma.” What endures are fragments: the confined space of the boat and the physical reality of survival.

“All I remember is being in a tiny cabin, curled up – kind of like hugging your knees.”

Aung recalls men in green uniforms transferring them, one by one, from the sinking boat to a larger vessel, its deck crowded with others bound for Hong Kong’s Green Island, then used as a processing centre for new arrivals, as well as detainees awaiting release or relocation.

“I remember arriving late at night at the dock, and they sprayed me,” she says. “They asked me to turn 360 degrees so they could spray me with pesticide – to kill any germs or bacteria I might have carried. They basically treated me like an insect.”

As a child, Aung remembers life on Tai A Chau as something akin to imprisonment. “Guards opened the door, and then it shut, and they locked it,” she says, describing the camp being made up of large, hut-like structures. “You weren’t allowed to go outside. Everybody stayed in their bunk beds. I’ve never been to prison, but what I imagine it to be – this was it.”

For Aung, the years that followed were marked by constant movement. “I was at Whitehead [Ma On Shan] – that was the worst – and then they moved me to Tai A Chau.”

It was there, around 1992 or 1993 until 1996, that she spent the longest stretch, before being transferred through several more detention camps. Guards, she recalls, came from a range of backgrounds, and included Afghan and Indian personnel. Daily life was defined by a quiet, unrelenting monotony.

“As a child, I didn’t know what hopelessness was, but I knew what boredom was,” she says. “Every day was the same.”

But during those years, Aung picked up Cantonese through shows such as Enjoy Yourself Tonight – the camp was allowed one hour of television each evening – and began learning English at a school in the camp.

Her name appeared on deportation lists more than once. “Each time, somehow, I was left off.” Eventually, after her aunt – who had secured her own release – advocated on her behalf with the help of a lawyer, Aung was granted her freedom.

“At first, I thought they were calling me again for deportation. But this time, they told me I was free to go.”

She spent a final few months at a detention centre near Kai Tak, which she calls a “freedom camp”, while awaiting relocation to her next destination.

Later, during a period of looser restrictions, Aung was allowed to work outside the camp as a seamstress, in a factory producing hospital gowns bound for the United States, though she had to return each night.

In 1997, Aung left for the US, closing the chapter that had defined her early life and, in many ways, rewrote its trajectory. She arrived in Louisiana with little English, navigating high school through sheer determination before earning a place at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, where she studied chemistry before building a career as an analyst at a chemical company. But her story did not settle into a single path.

In time, she met her husband, started a family and quietly began building something of her own. Now, she is the force behind ventures such as Yummi Sushi in Dallas, Texas, where she is based – a successful entrepreneur whose journey speaks not just of survival, but of reinvention.

Last year, Aung came across Bird’s book, Along the Southern Boundary: A Marine Police Officer’s Frontline Account of the Vietnamese Boatpeople and their Arrival in Hong Kong (2022), an encounter that saw long-dormant memories resurface, drawing her back to Hong Kong. It began with a childhood friend from the Tai A Chau Detention Centre, who had tracked down Bird after researching the island and later organised a reunion for former residents.

“She found Les and asked if he could take us back,” Aung recalls. After initial contact in January, Bird reconnected with her ahead of her trip to Hong Kong in early February.

On the boat to Tai A Chau, Bird showed Aung a PowerPoint presentation featuring photographs from 1989, when the island had been turned into a refugee camp.

“She was fascinated by every image, studying them closely – searching for faces, for fragments of memory, for anything or anyone she might recognise,” he says. “When she did recognise something, she would tell me the story behind it. I found that fascinating. It became a kind of history lesson for me as well, shaped by Katie’s own experiences.”

Each photograph prompted further questions, the answers to which pieced together a clearer picture of the past.

“By the time we arrived at Tai A Chau,” Bird says, “I had a fairly good idea of where Katie would have lived on the island during her time there.”

Since the release of his book, Bird has been contacted by numerous former refugees eager to share their stories. One of them, Connie Sam, reached out after seeing a photograph of Vietnamese refugees on the deck of the people-smuggling freighter Huey Fong. Others have written to say, “That’s me in your book”, or, in one case, “That’s my mother looking directly at the camera – and that small child standing next to her is me.”

“Once something like that happens, I pack a bag and go wherever they are,” Bird says. “I’ve travelled to some pretty remote places, and the meetings are always emotional. I can’t plan or imagine what I’ll say. It’s surreal, having someone who appears to be a complete stranger hug you and refuse to let go of your hand, and then listen to their stories.”

In 2022, Bird gave a talk at the Vietnamese Heritage Museum in Orange County, California, where the impact of these connections was clear: “Everyone in the audience was a former refugee, many rescued from the South China Sea, who had spent time in the Hong Kong camps. My talk lasted 45 minutes; the Q&A continued for three hours. People stood up to tell their stories. For many, it was the first time they had found the courage to speak publicly about what they had endured. It impressed on me how difficult it is for people to talk about trauma – even when they have survived almost certain death and gone on to thrive.”

Like Aung, many former refugees went on to achieve remarkable things. David Tran, featured in Bird’s book, created hot-sauce producer Huy Fong Foods and the popular Sriracha brand. Oscar-winning actor Ke Huy Quan has spoken publicly about his own refugee journey.

The Tai A Chau’s detention centre closed in 1996 and its buildings were demolished. Although it now stands empty and eerie, the island stirred memories for Aung.

“I haven’t fully processed the trip yet,” she admits. “I’m a busy mum, businesswoman and wife, so I haven’t had the time.”

Still, the journey brought clarity. “I don’t see myself as a victim. I appreciate the time I spent in the camp. It trained me, in a way, for the road map I’m on today.”

item.title: [SCMP] In Vietnam, diamonds are not forever after smuggling ring bust
item.description:
Ho Chi Minh City’s bustling jewellery quarter has fallen unusually quiet. Customers are not browsing for engagement rings or necklaces any more – instead they are clutching old receipts and certificates, hoping to sell diamonds they no longer trust.

The discovery of what appears to be Vietnam’s biggest-ever diamond smuggling network has rippled through the industry. Investigators allege more than 30,000 stones worth over 1.5 trillion dong (US$57 million) were brought into the country over the past two years, hidden in luggage, shoes and clothing after being sourced in India and routed through Hong Kong.

In gem-certification labs, diamonds were stripped of their original Gemological Institute of America laser inscriptions before being re-engraved and issued with reports that overstated their quality, police said, allowing them to be sold at far higher prices. Authorities are still investigating how widely the stones spread through the market, while dozens of jewellery shops have temporarily closed.
item.content:encoded:
Ho Chi Minh City’s bustling jewellery quarter has fallen unusually quiet. Customers are not browsing for engagement rings or necklaces any more – instead they are clutching old receipts and certificates, hoping to sell diamonds they no longer trust.

The discovery of what appears to be Vietnam’s biggest-ever diamond smuggling network has rippled through the industry. Investigators allege more than 30,000 stones worth over 1.5 trillion dong (US$57 million) were brought into the country over the past two years, hidden in luggage, shoes and clothing after being sourced in India and routed through Hong Kong.

In gem-certification labs, diamonds were stripped of their original Gemological Institute of America laser inscriptions before being re-engraved and issued with reports that overstated their quality, police said, allowing them to be sold at far higher prices. Authorities are still investigating how widely the stones spread through the market, while dozens of jewellery shops have temporarily closed.

“I’m truly worried,” said Thanh Hang, an online clothing shop owner who bought her diamond ring in Ho Chi Minh City. The stone had been graded by PNJ Laboratory, one of the companies under investigation.

Hang had sought a refund at the retailer in question, but found the branch was shut. In Vietnam, it is common for jewellery stores to offer a buy-back programme as a sort of sales tool – it gives buyers confidence they will have an exit route at some point in the future, while encouraging them to return to the same jeweller when they want to upgrade or resell.

The response Hang received when she eventually got hold of the company was not encouraging. “We’ll settle the payment next year,” was the best they could do, she said.

What began as a criminal investigation is now reverberating through Vietnam’s diamond trade, prompting calls for tougher regulation of the industry after it ensnared two of the country’s most well-known jewellery brands.

Phu Nhuan Jewellery (PNJ), the country’s largest listed jeweller, has insisted that none of the tainted diamonds entered its retail network after police detained the former head of the company’s gem certification subsidiary.

PNJ said the allegations related to the former executive, not the company. Still, CEO Phan Quoc Cong acknowledged the developments had “become a crisis moment for the entire industry”.

The fallout has been swift: nearly half of PNJ’s market value has been wiped out, authorities have widened inspections of the jewellery market, and consumers are increasingly questioning whether the diamonds they bought are worth what they thought.

The manager of Tam Luxury Diamond, also in Ho Chi Minh City, where much of the country’s gem trading takes place, said some days he received up to 100 clients coming back wanting to trade in their precious stones. New customers, meanwhile, are in short supply.

A wave of arrests of prominent jewellery shop owners in mid-July triggered several well-known retailers, including Kim Ly Gold Shop, to suspend operations. A month-long trade ministry-led inspection of the broader gemstone and precious metals markets has been set for August, with a focus on product origin and labelling.

Another major chain, Saigon Jewellery (SJC), came under pressure after police detained a further four people over a related smuggling ring that allegedly supplied more than 3,400 lower quality diamonds worth about 500 billion dong to its retail network between 2022 and 2024. SJC has not said anything publicly and did not respond to a request for comment.

Regulations needed

The government needed to implement a “proper regulatory framework for the diamond market,” Huynh Trung Khanh, vice-chairman of the Vietnam Gold Traders Association, said. Despite its name, the body also deals with silver and other gemstones and its members include some of the industry’s biggest names, including PNJ and SJC.

“An independent gem certification authority is needed to strengthen oversight and bring greater transparency and accountability to the market,” Khanh said.

Until that happens, the rush of concerned customers making a beeline to retailers’ doors is unlikely to let up.

PNJ has limited daily payouts for buy-backs, saying the immediate priority is to preserve liquidity, maintain operations and protect the company’s long-term value. It also plans to hire international firms to assess its diamond inventory in a bid to bolster its credibility.

For many Vietnamese families, diamonds are more than just a luxury purchase; they are a store of wealth and prestige. The nation imported more than US$122 million of diamonds during the first half of 2026, most from India and then Belgium, customs data show.

That predilection is rooted partly in history.

Decades of war, inflation and Vietnam’s former centrally planned economy, where investment options were limited and confidence in financial assets was often weak, encouraged households to hold tangible assets, like gold, that could be easily stored and passed down through generations. The preference remains deeply embedded today, even as the economy has modernised.

“If people are smuggling diamonds, however large or small numbers, into Vietnam, the likelihood is they’re smuggling other stuff as well,” said Kenneth Scarratt, the vice-president of the World Jewellery Confederation. “Rubies, sapphires, emeralds … it’s probably time the customs and excise authorities in Vietnam looked a little inward and started to sort it out.”

A global surge in synthetic diamonds, of which China is the largest producer, is also complicating the picture. It is not clear whether synthetic diamonds are part of the problem in Vietnam but they have become so convincing that even experts can struggle to tell the two apart.

“There’s no way a normal jeweller can just look and separate” them simply by eye alone, Bangkok-based Scarratt said.

For now, the immediate challenge is restoring confidence. With customers more cautious, retailers would have to place a greater emphasis on authenticity, certification and product provenance, said Nguyen Thi Sony Tra My, a senior analyst at Maybank Investment Bank.

“Smaller and less-established jewellery shops could face greater challenges in maintaining customer trust and liquidity, particularly in the current environment,” she said.

Some Vietnamese are trying to eschew retailers altogether.

“I’ve been posting my diamond rings on Facebook groups with a 30 per cent discount,” Thanh Dat, a real estate broker who lives in Ho Chi Minh City, said. But with would-be buyers pressuring him to offer 60 per cent, “I may just keep them”.

item.title: [SCMP] Pain or gain? US moves to decouple its defence industry from China’s rare earths
item.description:
A recent US executive order requires major arms manufacturers to trace their multi-tier supply chains and actively phase out Chinese rare earths, aiming to end years of reliance on cheap minerals from China.

Far from a radical policy shift, industry observers view the directive as a long-overdue enforcement crackdown designed to inflict short-term contractor pain for long-term national security gain.

While contractors face immediate hurdles to requalify suppliers and find non-Chinese alternatives, US analysts said the market adjustments were manageable, though delivery timetables for future military hardware could slightly stretch.
item.content:encoded:
A recent US executive order requires major arms manufacturers to trace their multi-tier supply chains and actively phase out Chinese rare earths, aiming to end years of reliance on cheap minerals from China.

Far from a radical policy shift, industry observers view the directive as a long-overdue enforcement crackdown designed to inflict short-term contractor pain for long-term national security gain.

While contractors face immediate hurdles to requalify suppliers and find non-Chinese alternatives, US analysts said the market adjustments were manageable, though delivery timetables for future military hardware could slightly stretch.

They also warned that true strategic independence needed sustained, long-term capital investment in non-Chinese midstream processing.

Signed on July 20 by US President Donald Trump, the executive order significantly tightens the conditions under which the Department of Defence can issue waivers for defence-critical imports from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea.

US defence procurement rules strictly prohibit sourcing from adversary states certain “covered materials” – ranging from rare earth magnets to newly added inputs like gallium and germanium – with exemptions available under waiver conditions.

However, because China controls about 90 per cent of global processed rare earths and two-thirds of mining capacity, the Pentagon has routinely granted waivers to keep military production lines moving.

Beginning next year, such routine exemptions will end.

Contractors seeking waivers must submit formal mitigation plans proving “exhaustive efforts” to source compliant materials, detailing explicit steps to phase out non-compliant suppliers and setting strict implementation timelines.

The order also mandates comprehensive supply-chain mapping within 180 days, requiring companies to trace components “from raw materials to end products”.

A White House statement said: “Despite long-standing prohibitions on the use of sensitive materials sourced from geopolitical adversaries, supply-chain resilience and domestic production have been historically underprioritised.”

The latest directive tells defence contractors that the era of relatively easily available waivers and the Trump administration’s repeated retreats from enforcing policies in this area is over, according to Eugene Gholz, an associate professor of political science at the University of Notre Dame.

“The executive order is about finally enforcing laws that have been on the books for a while,” said Gholz, who formerly served as senior adviser to the US deputy assistant secretary of defence for manufacturing and industrial base policy.

“It is not a major policy shift … There is a bipartisan consensus in the United States in favour of limited decoupling from China on critical materials supply.”

Cory Combs, head of supply-chain research at advisory firm Trivium China, said the order raised the bar for waivers to force technical diversification and stimulate non-Chinese supply growth.

“To the extent it works, it is designed to be ‘short-term contractor pain for long-term national security gain’,” Combs said.

Yet, implementing full supply-chain visibility presents formidable practical challenges.

Courtney Weatherby, a fellow at the Stimson Centre’s energy, water and sustainability programme, highlighted two major bottlenecks: the administrative burden of tracing deep-tier supply chains and the practical difficulty of finding feasible non-Chinese alternatives.

Weatherby said a primary obstacle on the supply side lay in China’s midstream refining, where critical minerals from disparate sources are blended into mixed batches, making it hard to trace the origin of a single raw material.

“In the short term, the informational gaps may pose challenges to companies seeking to meet requested levels of traceability,” she added.

“In the long term, it could pose challenges in terms of pricing and deliverable timelines if waivers are not approved due to potentially higher costs and lower availability of limited alternative sources.”

The move marks Trump’s latest push to cut overreliance on foreign critical materials for those used in domestic defence supply chains, especially when the US is rushing to restock ammunition drained by its war with Iran and scale up output of strategic bombers and missiles.

It comes just one month after Beijing added 10 US firms – including rare earth specialists MP Materials and USA Rare Earth – to its export control list.

Since last year, China has dramatically tightened export controls on rare earths, while Washington has complained that it is still not receiving sufficient critical mineral exports from China despite the two sides’ trade truce struck in Busan last year.

According to Mineral Commodity Summaries issued by the US Department of the Interior and the US Geological Survey, China is one of the leading foreign suppliers for several “covered materials”, including tantalum, tungsten, gallium and germanium.

The US relies entirely on imports for materials like gallium and tantalum, while its net import reliance for tungsten exceeded 50 per cent of apparent consumption in 2025.

Heavy rare earths, such as dysprosium and terbium, are vital for manufacturing high-performance permanent magnets.

These components underpin critical US defence technology, from radar arrays and missile guidance units to advanced propulsion systems.

According to Combs, “The US’ first strategic imperative is to diversify military supply chains. Despite all the political focus, commercial supply diversification is in practice a secondary and much longer-term objective.”

Amid the hurdles, Gholz said market adjustments were manageable and would not compromise current military readiness.

The main hurdle for major defence primes is that they rarely buy critical minerals directly, forcing procurement teams to trace complex, lower-tier supply chains. But he viewed this administrative audit as “manageable” within months rather than years.

Government or defence demand for many critical materials was a small fraction of overall demand, Gholz added, noting that non-adversarial suppliers could meet military needs if Washington was prepared to absorb higher costs.

“This executive order has to do with sourcing for production of weapons in the future. It also is unlikely to impact readiness. It may cause some production timelines for the future to slip, but probably not much if at all.”

Meanwhile, Weatherby said that sourcing was only half the battle, and that Beijing’s stranglehold on processing and refining techniques would require a certain scale of investment to catch up.

She argued it was unclear whether the supply-chain tracing process “will lead to long-term gain without a strategic, multi-step approach to nurture robust alternative and diversified supply chains. That will take time and investment.”

Meanwhile, Combs anticipated that the new waiver restrictions would not drive new large-scale investments, saying the defence demand alone was inadequate to set up the mining and processing infrastructure for diversification.

“Though we do expect it’ll help transfer some value from contractors to select existing non-Chinese suppliers, which will be a boost to the latter’s financial health.”

item.title: [SCMP] PLA and coastguards stage South China Sea drills days after Philippine territorial bid
item.description:
The Chinese military held joint naval and air drills near Scarborough Shoal, a disputed reef in the South China Sea, on Saturday.

The training exercise came after Beijing hit out at the Philippines for an “illegal” attempt to extend its seabed rights off the coast of Palawan and map out its claims to the reef.

“This is a necessary action taken in light of the current situation in the South China Sea and in response to the acts of certain countries within the region that have undermined regional peace and stability,” the PLA Southern Theatre Command wrote in a social media post.
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese military held joint naval and air drills near Scarborough Shoal, a disputed reef in the South China Sea, on Saturday.

The training exercise came after Beijing hit out at the Philippines for an “illegal” attempt to extend its seabed rights off the coast of Palawan and map out its claims to the reef.

“This is a necessary action taken in light of the current situation in the South China Sea and in response to the acts of certain countries within the region that have undermined regional peace and stability,” the PLA Southern Theatre Command wrote in a social media post.

“The training exercise aims to test and enhance the forces’ real combat capabilities to safeguard China’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests.”

Scarborough Shoal, known as Huangyan Island in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines, is one of the main flashpoints in the long-running territorial dispute between the two countries.

Saturday’s drills were staged in and around the reef’s territorial sea and airspace, testing the PLA’s ability to coordinate air and sea operations and provide rapid reinforcements, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

It added that the exercise covered areas such as reconnaissance and warning, deterrent patrols, control of the air and sea, as well as joint strikes.

H-6K bombers armed with YJ-12 anti-ship missiles were deployed during the drill, video footage released by the PLA Southern Theatre Command showed.

The YJ-12 is an air-launched anti-ship missile that maintains supersonic speed throughout its flight and accelerates to Mach 4-5 during its terminal phase. It has an estimated range of 400-500 km (250-310 miles).

The missile’s heavy explosive payload could pose a significant threat to large surface combatants, “which could serve as a powerful deterrent against provocations by relevant parties”, the CCTV report quoted Chinese military commentator Zhang Junshe as saying.

China has repeatedly accused “external forces” – a reference to the United States and its allies – of interfering in the South China Sea disputes.

Since July, the US has stationed six coastguard vessels at Subic Bay in the Philippines and deployed the aircraft carrier USS George Washington to the South China Sea.

The exercise footage also shows Z-20J assault helicopters and Z-8C transport helicopters conducting take-off and landing operations on a Type 071 amphibious transport dock, alongside Wild Horse air-cushioned landing craft entering and exiting the ship’s well deck.

Type 054A and Type 056A guided-missile frigates were also seen taking part in the exercise.

The exercise demonstrated the PLA’s multidimensional amphibious warfare capability, combining vertical air assaults with heavily armed amphibious beach landings for potential contingencies, Zhang told CCTV.

“By deploying this elite naval and air force contingent on a combat readiness patrol, the Southern Theatre Command sought to send an unequivocal signal to the Philippines and external actors, underscoring China’s determination to defend its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests,” he said.

“This is a clear warning to relevant parties to cease their futile provocations and infringements.”

The China Coast Guard also held an exercise in the area, with focus on operations such as intercepting ships, boardings and inspections, and towing vessels away, according to spokesman Jiang Lue.

Saturday also marked the 99th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Liberation Army.

The official PLA Daily published an opinion piece that urged the force to “keep a close eye on changes in technology, warfare and adversaries, and intensify practical, combat-oriented military training”.

“[We should] strengthen the building and application of forces for new domains and new modes of warfare … to effectively safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests,” it added.

Also on Saturday, China released a set of rules for the nature reserve it established last year to assert its control over the reef.

The regulations ban unauthorised fishing, mining and the harvesting of corals or giant clams.

State news agency Xinhua said the island had a unique coral reef ecosystem and distinct geological formations, as well as significant populations of rare and endangered marine species.

Earlier this week, the Philippines formally presented a bid to the United Nations to extend its seabed rights off the island of Palawan beyond its 200-nautical-mile (370km) exclusive economic zone, arguing that the area in question was a natural extension of its continental shelf.

China’s sweeping territorial claims in the South China Sea overlap with those of several Southeast Asian countries, including the Philippines.

Manila’s submission to the UN referred to a 2016 ruling from an arbitration tribunal in The Hague that rejected China’s claims, but it insisted that its claim was “without prejudice” to sovereignty disputes or future boundary talks with neighbours.

China did not take part in the 2016 arbitral proceedings and rejects the ruling as “null and void”.

Last week, the Philippines also formally deposited its official nautical chart of Scarborough Shoal with the UN in an effort to “reinforce the legal certainty of its maritime entitlements”.

The Chinese foreign ministry responded by saying it would never accept Manila’s establishment of a “territorial sea baseline” on the shoal.

“The Philippines has frequently provoked and stirred up trouble near Huangyan Island, violating China’s sovereignty and maritime rights, escalating maritime tensions and undermining peace and stability in the South China Sea,” it said.

“China demands that the Philippines earnestly respect China’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights, and refrain from any infringing or provocative actions in the Huangyan Island area; otherwise, China will resolutely respond.”

In 2024, China released its own baselines for the territorial sea around Scarborough Shoal.

China’s mission to the UN also criticised the bid to extend Philippine seabed rights off the coast of Palawan, saying the move violated its sovereignty and urged the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf not to consider it.

Scarborough Shoal has been the scene of repeated confrontations between Chinese and Philippine ships in recent years, including a series of clashes last week that involved the use of water cannons by the Chinese coastguard.

Manila condemned the Chinese actions as “illegal, coercive and aggressive”.

The clashes happened days after a meeting between Foreign Ministers Wang Yi and Maria Theresa Lazaro, where they stressed the importance of “reducing the risk of miscalculation” and maintaining stability in the South China Sea.

Manila’s efforts to strengthen defence and security ties with Washington and Tokyo have also put Beijing on high alert.

The Philippines is considered a vital link in the “first island chain”, a series of archipelagos that form a barrier between mainland China and the open waters of the western Pacific.

item.title: [SCMP] As more South Koreans shun drinking, Seoul nightlife reinvents to stay relevant
item.description:
On a midsummer Thursday night, the entertainment district of Hongdae in Seoul is slowly coming alive.

Short for Hongik University, Hongdae neighbours several university campuses and typically attracts thousands of young people to its flashy streets.

Just a few blocks away from the main clubbing area, the atmosphere is quieter with hardly any patrons at a row of pubs and restaurants.
item.content:encoded:
On a midsummer Thursday night, the entertainment district of Hongdae in Seoul is slowly coming alive.

Short for Hongik University, Hongdae neighbours several university campuses and typically attracts thousands of young people to its flashy streets.

Just a few blocks away from the main clubbing area, the atmosphere is quieter with hardly any patrons at a row of pubs and restaurants.

“Hongdae is not what it used to be like,” said Chris Kim, a 27-year-old who works in the fashion industry.

“My friends and I used to go clubbing a lot and the places were always packed. There’d be fights all the time, and you’d constantly see police cars showing up.”

The pandemic was a turning point as Hongdae’s reputation as an entertainment hotspot took a hit, Kim said.

“In the past, the whole point of getting together was often to drink until you got drunk. But drinking isn’t the main reason for meeting up any more,” he said, referring to a discernible decline in young drinkers in Hongdae.

“It feels like the divide is really clear today.”

The national trend appears to attest to Kim’s observation. In the first quarter of this year, household spending on alcohol in the country fell nine per cent compared with the same period a year earlier, the largest drop since the Korean Statistical Information Service began tracking such data in 2019.

And in 2024, domestic alcohol shipments totalled 3.15 million kilolitres (83 million gallons), down from 3.8 million kilolitres in 2014.

According to the Tax Statistics Information Service, that represents a 17.3 per cent decrease of volume supplied domestically over a decade.

Young South Koreans are also consuming less alcohol. Among South Koreans in their twenties, 56 per cent either abstain from alcohol or drink less than once a month, according to data from the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.

This figure was 37.9 per cent in 2005, when data was first collected.

The number of pubs and bars in South Korea fell by almost 10 per cent to 28,178 in March, a decrease of 2,998 from last year, according to data from the Tax Statistics Information Service.

Changing social scene

For many years in South Korea, alcohol has been the social lubricant at events ranging from university gatherings to company dinners. As alcohol consumption falls, Seoul’s nightlife has transformed itself to reflect changing lifestyles.

A 20-minute taxi ride from Hongdae is Itaewon, another nightlife destination known for its diversity and international atmosphere.

Sitting on a kerb with her friend, 21-year-old university student Baek Ga-hee said that staying out late on a weekday was unusual for her.

“I think people just don’t do as much stuff in groups any more,” she said. “Everyone seems a bit more focused on spending time by themselves.”

Baek said the social activities of people her age changed during the pandemic due to restrictions on large gatherings.

“It became awkward and unnatural to hang out in big groups,” she said.

Myung Wook, an adjunct professor of barista and sommelier studies at Sejong Cyber University who has written on the country’s drinking culture, said the role of alcohol in South Korean society had changed over time.

“In the past, drinking together was a medium through which people communicated, exchanged ideas and got to know one another. But interpersonal relationships are no longer as essential as they once were,” Myung said.

“University students used to depend on one another much more, borrowing notes before exams or seeking advice, naturally leading people to buy each other meals or drinks in return. This culture is now perceived to be burdensome among younger generations.”

Nightclubs adapt

Entertainment venues in Seoul are adjusting to the evolving lifestyle trends and demands of customers.

In Itaewon’s main clubbing district, Soap Seoul has seen a noticeable decline in alcohol purchases among its nightly crowd of 300 to 400 guests, according to creative director Yann Cavaille.

“This has made it harder for us to afford to bring in foreign DJs and artists like we used to do,” he said. “It just means that we have to be marketing our events that much more.”

The creative director recalled a time when bringing in a well-known artist was enough to guarantee a crowd. As regular clubbing became less common among young South Koreans, clubs had to be more creative in their offerings to stay relevant in the highly competitive entertainment scene.

To lure some of the crowd back, Cavaille says he started the trend of incorporating 3D graphics in digital posters that would advertise club events on Instagram.

Soap Seoul was also one of the first clubs in Seoul to ban smoking on its premises to attract customers who would otherwise avoid nightlife venues.

“We need to put out enticing events every week, and this requires creating a lot of content on our side. We wanted to upgrade the experience and bring people that normally wouldn’t go clubbing,” he said.

Soap Seoul has diversified its business and opened a cafe in the nearby Haebangchon neighbourhood, organising large-scale pop-up events with marquee names like Samsung and Nike and building its brand through such partnerships and official merchandise.

Across the street from Soap Seoul, underground club Bolero has been drawing crowds with its curated events.

Owner Son Ki-jeong has transformed what was once a restaurant into a club after inviting friends to play music for customers. Today, Bolero hosts globally renowned DJs and local artists and organises parties based around musical genres.

The changeover has paid dividends – the club Bolero now hosts 500 to 700 visitors on average on weekends.

“If people used to go to clubs less for the music and more to meet new people, drink and enjoy a flashy night out, people today pay attention to the kind of music being played and choose venues with DJs who really understand that genre,” Son said.

Eschewing extravagance, Son has set up a modestly looking DJ booth, with faint neon lighting to illuminate the dance floor.

“The younger generation is investing their time and money into nightlife as a way to explore and express their own tastes rather than using it to get drunk or escape from everyday life,” he said.

“I see this as a positive and healthy change. Consumers are starting to understand what they genuinely enjoy and choose spaces that match their own interests and preferences.”

item.title: [SCMP] From Mao to now: why China’s Communist Party is intent on control over the military
item.description:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just one year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the third part of a series, Yuanyue Dang and William Zheng examine how Beijing leans on Mao-era doctrines and anti-corruption drives to guarantee absolute party control over the armed forces.

In December 1929, then Communist revolutionary Mao Zedong led a pivotal meeting in Gutian, Fujian province.

The Communist Party’s armed wing at the time was a coalition of rebel forces fighting the ruling Nationalists or Kuomintang (KMT). The “Gutian conference” defined the Chinese Workers’ and Peasants’ Red Army as “an armed body for carrying out the political tasks of the revolution” and set up party organisations throughout the military.
item.content:encoded:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just one year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the third part of a series, Yuanyue Dang and William Zheng examine how Beijing leans on Mao-era doctrines and anti-corruption drives to guarantee absolute party control over the armed forces.

In December 1929, then Communist revolutionary Mao Zedong led a pivotal meeting in Gutian, Fujian province.

The Communist Party’s armed wing at the time was a coalition of rebel forces fighting the ruling Nationalists or Kuomintang (KMT). The “Gutian conference” defined the Chinese Workers’ and Peasants’ Red Army as “an armed body for carrying out the political tasks of the revolution” and set up party organisations throughout the military.

The next two decades witnessed some of the defining moments leading up to the Communist victory of 1949, including the Long March, the consolidation of Mao’s leadership and the renaming of the armed forces as the People’s Liberation Army (PLA).

In 1938, as the party faced a turning point following the departure of co-founder and Mao’s revolutionary rival Zhang Guotao, Mao wrote: “Our principle is that the party commands the gun, and the gun must never be allowed to command the party.”

Nearly a century on, those principles still serve as the political bedrock of the party’s control over the military.

In 2014, President Xi Jinping convened a military political work conference in Gutian, in a clear tribute to Mao’s doctrines from more than 80 years before.

Urging the PLA to reflect on discipline and uphold its revolutionary tradition, Xi said: “Upholding the party’s absolute leadership over the military is the soul of building a strong army.”

These ideological doctrines drove the massive PLA overhaul launched the following year. Paired with the military’s most aggressive anti-corruption campaign in decades, the reforms swept through every level – from service branches and theatre commands to equipment procurement and top-level appointments.

They were also central to Beijing’s messaging during the latest anti-corruption drive targeting the Central Military Commission, the PLA’s top command body led by Xi. Five of the seven-member CMC, including former vice-chairmen Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, have been removed from office.

Only Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin, a vice-chairman who previously oversaw anti-corruption work in the military, now remain on the body whose current term began in 2022.

Zhang Youxia was the CMC’s first-ranked vice-chairman, China’s most senior military officer after Xi.

An editorial in the official PLA Daily shortly after Zhang’s downfall said he had “seriously trampled on and undermined the CMC chairman responsibility system” as well as “seriously fuelled political and corruption problems that affect the party’s absolute leadership over the military and endanger the foundations of the party’s rule”.

As the PLA gears up to mark its centenary next August, analysts say Beijing’s relentless focus on “the party’s absolute leadership over the military” highlights concerns that extend well beyond corruption.

Control of the military is foundational to the party’s power, they note. This mindset – shaped by the historical lessons from the collapse of the KMT in mainland China and later that of the Soviet Union, as well as the political turmoil of the Mao era – helps to explain Beijing’s resolute rejection of what it calls the “nationalisation of the military”.

Zhang Youxia was placed under investigation in January, alongside Liu Zhenli, fellow CMC member and chief of staff of its Joint Staff Department.

This came three months after CMC vice-chairman He Weidong and Miao Hua, former head of the commission’s Political Work Department, were expelled from the party and the military over allegations of corruption and serious discipline violations.

In October 2023, former defence minister Li Shangfu was removed from office and expelled from the party eight months later, also over corruption.

His predecessor, Wei Fenghe, was similarly investigated, expelled from the party and stripped of his rank in 2024. Both men received suspended death sentences in May.

Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University’s school of international service and a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Xi’s view was that corruption could affect the military’s political choices at critical moments.

“He believes that the military will only serve the party during moments of political crisis at home and in wars abroad if it has the right world view,” Torigian said.

“When a military leader is corrupt, that means materialism and consumerism have eroded the conviction and idealism Xi believes are necessary for the PLA to make the right decision.”

Lessons from the KMT

The Communist Party has long viewed discipline and organisational capacity as central to its 1949 victory over the KMT in the civil war. Peking University historian Wang Qisheng has similarly traced the KMT’s defeat in part to weak organisational structure.

In his 2003 book, Party Members, Party Power and Party Struggles: The Organisational Form of the Kuomintang, 1924–1949, Wang wrote that the KMT borrowed organisational techniques from the Soviet model in the 1920s, but never replicated its substance.

Unlike the Soviet system – where party authority was supreme over the state and military at every level – local KMT branches remained weak and marginal, lacking the authority to oversee or discipline officials. After the civil war broke out in 1927, real power shifted decisively towards the military, leaving KMT leader Chiang Kai-shek increasingly dependent on forces under his personal control, according to Wang’s book.

Elizabeth Perry, Henry Rosovsky Professor of Government at Harvard University, said that the Communist Party “is proud of its revolutionary heritage, in which the Red Army had a reputation for not stealing from the peasants”.

“It sometimes broke those rules, but for the most part the Red Army was a well-disciplined army, whose connection to the peasantry helped the Chinese Communist Party win the revolution,” she added.

“The difference in levels of corruption between the Kuomintang and the CCP, and between their militaries, is often cited as an important reason for the victory of the Chinese Communist Party.”

Unlike the KMT, the Communist Party brought the PLA under direct party control.

Party organisations exist at every level of the PLA. Political commissars and military commanders share leadership responsibilities, while the appointment, education and disciplinary supervision of officers are also handled by party bodies within the military.

A Beijing-based political scientist who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, said the arrangement was a result of the military’s somewhat unique status in China.

“After all, the PLA is largely a system on its own,” the academic said.

As an example, the academic noted that the party’s organisation department did not handle military personnel – a responsibility that fell to the CMC’s political work department.

The party’s top anti-corruption body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, does not directly investigate corruption in the military either. Such cases are handled by the CMC’s own discipline inspection commission.

Within this relatively closed system, the flow of information, personnel and resources becomes central to party control over the military.

“So the party’s rule over the military basically hinges on the party’s general secretary being the sole and final decision-maker on the CMC,” the political scientist said.

“That requires detailed and strict workflow design in the CMC’s daily work to ensure the chairman holds the ultimate decision-making power on key things like personnel, budget, major military actions and technology developments.”

The CMC “chairman responsibility system” sits at the top of this institutional structure.

China’s constitution – adopted in 1982 – stipulates that the state CMC operates under a chairman responsibility system. Xi further strengthened the system after taking the helm in 2012.

Following the 2014 Gutian meeting – which came in the wake of a corruption scandal involving a former top general – the CMC set up three mechanisms to ensure that critical issues and information were reported directly to the chairman.

The mechanisms covered requests and reports, supervision and inspection, and information services.
