Then came sweeping military reforms. The overhaul launched in 2015 dismantled the four general departments in favour of multiple functional departments directly subordinate to the CMC.

A new command structure was created, under which the CMC retains overall authority, the theatre commands oversee joint operations, and individual services focus on force development.

According to the anonymous analyst, the reforms elevated joint operations while curbing the agency of the former general departments and individual services over personnel, equipment, and resource allocation.

In 2017, the CMC chairman responsibility system was written into the party constitution. Follow-up regulations mandated that the military treat the system’s roll-out as its highest political requirement and core disciplinary standard.

According to Beijing, the CMC chairman oversees its overall work and makes final decisions on major military issues. The vice-chairmen and other members assist him and are responsible for implementation.

But the military’s daily operations still require extensive delegation.

“The most critical part of the system is where you draw the line,” the Beijing-based political scientist said.

“The CMC chairman’s office cannot make all the decisions … The CMC must have clear guidelines on what are classified as ‘major decisions’ to be decided at the top and what reports shall be sent to the chairman’s office.

“That is a very delicate balance. It seems the trend now is to over-report rather than under-report.”

The present arrangement gives CMC vice-chairmen, commissioners and the leaders of the services and other forces significant intermediary authority.

They can influence what information is reported, how the chairman’s orders are interpreted and which officers are placed on promotion lists. Personnel networks can also lead subordinate officers to direct their loyalty first towards the superiors who promoted them, according to the anonymous observer.

At the heart of history

Time and again, the PLA has proven to be a decisive factor at the party’s most critical historical turning points.

A stark instance was in 1971, when Mao’s deputy and designated successor Lin Biao died in a plane crash while fleeing China after an alleged coup attempt – his downfall triggering investigations into a slew of generals seen as close to him.

The arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976 and the martial law imposed to clamp down on the Tiananmen protests in 1989, meanwhile, are regarded by the party as examples of the military obeying the central leadership during political crises.

Torigian at American University said: “Xi believes that the party has only survived for so long because at moments of crisis, like the split with Zhang Guotao, the fall of the Gang of Four, and the Tiananmen crackdown, the PLA made the ‘right’ choice.”

China’s party-army system is sometimes compared with North Korea’s state policy of songun, or “military-first politics”.

After then-leader Kim Jong-il implemented songun in the 1990s, the Korean People’s Army (KPA) gained greater political status and priority in resource allocation, while becoming extensively involved in infrastructure, agriculture, trade and other economic activities.

Jongseok Woo, an associate professor of political science at the University of South Florida, argued in a 2014 paper that Kim adopted songun as a strategy for regime survival, shifting “the locus of political power” from the party to the military.

But Woo also wrote that Kim developed mechanisms to prevent the armed forces from dominating politics.

In a 2018 paper, Woo drew a distinction between the military’s elevated institutional status and its independent political influence. “The military has not been a politically influential organ from the state-building to the current Kim Jong-un era,” he wrote.

China’s official description of its own party-army system is more direct.

A document issued by the CMC in 2017 said: “The system of ultimate responsibility resting with the chairman of the Central Military Commission is a major system stipulated in the constitution and the party constitution, and is the fundamental system and fundamental form of realising the party’s absolute leadership over the military.”

Yet both systems reject a professional military that remains neutral during a political crisis.

In China, this rejected model is usually described as the “nationalisation of the military”. Beijing believes that such a model could undermine party rule.

The dissolution of the Soviet Union further reinforced this wariness.

In Beijing’s view, the Soviet Communist Party’s loosening grip on its armed forces led directly to the military’s failure to defend the party during the 1991 political crisis.

“Xi believes that the Soviet Union collapsed because the party lost control of the military,” Torigian said.

In September 2025, a PLA Daily commentary said the Soviet military had at the time “become estranged from the party and disobeyed its commands, and even colluded with the opposition”.

For Beijing, the collapse of the Soviet Union offers a clear lesson: the PLA must always uphold the principles established by strong leaders Mao and Xi at Gutian – the party must always lead the military.

item.title: [SCMP] US scientist Elsa Reichmanis defends global collaboration amid scrutiny of science exchange
item.description:
American materials scientist Elsa Reichmanis, whose pioneering work helped lay part of the foundation for modern semiconductor manufacturing, said scientific collaboration should transcend rivalry after receiving one of China’s highest honours for foreign experts, describing science as “a universal language” that benefits all of society.

Reichmanis, a professor of chemical engineering in Lehigh University’s department of chemical and biomolecular engineering and the director of its Institute for Functional Materials and Devices, was one of nine recipients of the China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award in early July.

The award recognises exceptional contributions to scientific exchanges and collaboration with Chinese researchers.
item.content:encoded:
American materials scientist Elsa Reichmanis, whose pioneering work helped lay part of the foundation for modern semiconductor manufacturing, said scientific collaboration should transcend rivalry after receiving one of China’s highest honours for foreign experts, describing science as “a universal language” that benefits all of society.

Reichmanis, a professor of chemical engineering in Lehigh University’s department of chemical and biomolecular engineering and the director of its Institute for Functional Materials and Devices, was one of nine recipients of the China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award in early July.

The award recognises exceptional contributions to scientific exchanges and collaboration with Chinese researchers.

Reichmanis is best known for her groundbreaking work on chemically amplified photoresists – light-sensitive materials used to etch microscopic circuits onto silicon wafers.

Her chemistry made it commercially viable to pack tens of millions of transistors – or more – onto a single silicon chip, laying the groundwork for the nanoscale semiconductor industry.

“I was shocked,” said the 72-year-old Reichmanis, an accomplished US chemistry and materials scientist, in an interview with the South China Morning Post.

China held the award ceremony on July 8 at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. Recipients came from eight countries: the US, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Russia, Australia, Belgium and Portugal, representing marine engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), photovoltaics and oncology, among other fields.

The award, established by the State Council – China’s cabinet – in 1994, honours those who collaborate with Chinese partners on significant scientific achievements, introduce advanced technologies, cultivate domestic scientific talent and promote international scientific exchange and cooperation.

This year’s award carries added significance as it comes at a fragile moment for US-China scientific exchange, which faces growing scrutiny amid intensifying technology competition and tightening research restrictions.

On the day of the award ceremony, the US National Science Foundation said in an open letter that it would bar its funded researchers from collaborating with restricted parties, particularly Chinese universities and technology firms, an escalation after years of mounting scrutiny of research ties with China.

Reichmanis said fundamental scientific research should remain distinct from technological competition.

In a sense, the development of technology can be independent from the science

Elsa Reichmanis

“Science is a universal language,” she said. “Scientific collaboration and communication, and having diversity of interactions … provides global society with a knowledge base that can benefit everyone.

“In a sense, the development of technology can be independent from the science”, she added, saying the discipline could be used to build pathways and understanding across borders to help further innovation globally.

Reichmanis’ own relationship with China developed gradually, beginning with early exchanges between the two countries’ chemical societies before expanding to collaborations with Chinese institutions.

A little over two decades ago, she began taking part in joint activities between the American Chemical Society (ACS) and the Chinese Chemical Society, helping organise academic exchanges and build ties with Chinese researchers.

Organisational exchanges gradually developed into a research partnership with Shanghai-based Donghua University. Since 2013, she has worked with the university’s State Key Laboratory of Advanced Fiber Materials to jointly train doctoral students, advance research collaboration and cultivate talent.

Reichmanis said decades working with China had given her a first-hand view of the country’s rise in research capabilities.

When she first visited Chinese laboratories in the early 2000s, state-of-the-art scientific instruments had begun to appear, she said, though some were still relatively underutilised.

But since then, she had observed sustained investment in research infrastructure, growing numbers of scientists and students, as well as steadily improving research quality.

As one of the executive editors of the ACS journal Chemistry of Materials, Reichmanis said she had seen a sharp increase in submissions from Chinese institutions.

“The number of manuscripts being accepted is increasing,” she said, calling it “a testament to the quality of the research that is being done”, adding that the research taking place in China was globally competitive.

Despite her long collaboration with Chinese institutions and early focus on chemically amplified photoresists, Reichmanis dismissed suggestions that she had helped China develop photoresist technology.

China has pushed to develop domestic photoresists to cut its reliance on foreign suppliers. It has made progress in entry-level materials, with a self-sufficiency rate of more than 20 per cent in older G-line and I-line photoresists used for power chips and LEDs, though the high-end market is still dominated by Japanese and US companies.

After Reichmanis received the science cooperation award, voices emerged online linking her pioneering work on chemically amplified photoresists to China’s drive to develop substitutes and localise chipmaking technology.

[Scientific] communication and networking … are going to continue. And it’s really at the essence of making the world a better place

Elsa Reichmanis

Reichmanis said that since her research in the field had been published openly in peer-reviewed journals decades ago, it now served as part of the broader scientific discoveries available worldwide.

“The research I do … is not application-specific. It’s in the realm of fundamental science,” she said, adding that “the research that I do now is very far removed from my early research”.

According to the Lehigh University website, Reichmanis’ work focuses on studying how to control materials at the sub-nanometre scale in “transistor devices, photovoltaics and high-capacity energy storage”.

An Australian emigrant who moved to the US, Reichmanis started her industry career at the AT&T Bell Laboratories, now known as Nokia Bell Labs, following a three-year postdoctoral fellowship at Syracuse University, where she earned her PhD in organic chemistry at age 22 in 1975.

At Bell Labs, Reichmanis and her team helped solve a critical bottleneck in modern semiconductor manufacturing by developing new “chemically amplified resists” for deep ultraviolet lithography, allowing chipmakers to print extremely small and precise circuit patterns that conventional optical photoresists could not achieve.

Her chemistry work made it commercially viable to pack tens of millions of transistors – or more – onto a single silicon chip, laying the groundwork for the nanoscale semiconductor industry.

Reichmanis credited the achievement to Bell Labs’ collaborative culture, emphasising that the breakthrough had been a team effort.

“I’m a very small piece of that really large effort,” she said, adding that advances in chipmaking had depended on contributions from chemists, physicists, engineers, materials scientists and equipment designers working together.

That collaborative philosophy at Bell Labs, she said, had shaped her entire career.

“Just about everything I’ve done in my career has been the result of very valuable collaborations.”

When asked about whether growing US-China tensions would threaten future scientific cooperation, Reichmanis remained optimistic.

“[Scientific] communication and networking … are going to continue,” she said, adding that technology would facilitate continued interactions with global support for multidisciplinary, fundamental research to underpin everything that scientists do.

“And it’s really at the essence of making the world a better place.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can China and Indonesia’s strong financial ties withstand ‘resource nationalism’?
item.description:
Back in 2009, when China’s economy was expanding at about twice today’s pace, a little-known private firm made a quiet bet on uncharted territory: Indonesia.

The company was on a quest: to secure nickel, a vital industrial metal used in stainless steel production and, increasingly, to power advanced batteries.

That bet proved lucrative. By leveraging Indonesia’s vast nickel reserves – the world’s largest – and securing greater control over upstream supplies, Tsingshan Group has grown into a leading global stainless steel producer. It joined the Forbes Global 500 in 2021, and in 2025 generated 432 billion yuan (US$63.8 billion) in revenue, with operations spanning from Zimbabwe to the United States.
item.content:encoded:
Back in 2009, when China’s economy was expanding at about twice today’s pace, a little-known private firm made a quiet bet on uncharted territory: Indonesia.

The company was on a quest: to secure nickel, a vital industrial metal used in stainless steel production and, increasingly, to power advanced batteries.

That bet proved lucrative. By leveraging Indonesia’s vast nickel reserves – the world’s largest – and securing greater control over upstream supplies, Tsingshan Group has grown into a leading global stainless steel producer. It joined the Forbes Global 500 in 2021, and in 2025 generated 432 billion yuan (US$63.8 billion) in revenue, with operations spanning from Zimbabwe to the United States.

The company, founded in Wenzhou in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, is one of a growing number of Chinese enterprises helping to forge deeper trade and industrial ties between the world’s second-largest economy and Southeast Asia’s largest.

What began as a push to secure raw minerals has evolved into a broader commercial relationship spanning resources, downstream metal processing, manufacturing and, most recently, financial services – though one increasingly shaped by Jakarta’s shifting domestic priorities.

“Indonesia provides the resources, while China contributes capital, technology and manufacturing expertise, creating an increasingly integrated economic ecosystem,” said Zhao Xijun, a finance professor at Renmin University of China in Beijing.

Chasing the battery boom

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has prioritised capturing greater added value from the nation’s mineral deposits since taking office in late 2024, said Hu Jie, executive director of the Southeast Asia Centre at the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

Among the most important is nickel: a critical input in electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing and lithium-ion batteries, leading Jakarta to court foreign capital in downstream processing, said Hu, who keeps close ties with Indonesian officials and provides advisory services to Chinese firms looking to invest in the country.

Faced with weak domestic demand and industrial oversupply at home, Chinese producers are driven to deepen their presence in Indonesia

Hu Jie, Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

This ambition has quickly translated into aggressive domestic targets. Indonesia has set a goal of deploying 2 million EVs and 12 million electric two-wheelers by 2030. According to data from its Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (MEMR), the nation currently has about 11 million active cars on its roads.

To meet this demand, Chinese car manufacturers are expanding local production facilities. In April, local media outlet Jakarta Globe reported that BYD’s factory in West Java – designed to deliver up to 150,000 EVs annually – was scheduled to begin operations and produce its first vehicles this year, with a total investment of 11.2 trillion Indonesian rupiah (US$616 million).

China’s industrial footprint in Indonesia has also shifted further downstream along the nickel supply chain, with technology-focused players taking centre stage. Earlier this month, Shenzhen-listed Azure Corporation unveiled plans for a US$290 million lithium battery manufacturing facility there. The project is expected to have an annual production capacity of 5 gigawatt-hours for a range of lithium batteries.

However, industry analysts stressed that attracting foreign investment formed part of a much larger Indonesian blueprint. The International Institute for Sustainable Development, a Canada-based think tank, wrote in a 2025 research report that “the ambition is not only to create a market for EVs – the country has the largest nickel reserves in the world and aims to become a leading producer of EV batteries.”

According to the Jakarta Globe, EV sales in the country surged 141 per cent year on year in 2025 to more than 100,000 units, hitting a record in December.

“Chinese manufacturers and Indonesia’s market are naturally aligned. Faced with weak domestic demand and industrial oversupply at home, Chinese producers are driven to deepen their presence in Indonesia,” said Hu from the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

And as Chinese businesses become more deeply embedded in Indonesia’s industrial ecosystem, a parallel financial architecture is also taking shape.

Alternative payment channels

In June this year, the People’s Bank of China designated Bank of China (Hong Kong)’s Jakarta branch as Indonesia’s official yuan clearing bank, while Bank Mandiri became a direct participant in the Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) – Beijing’s payment infrastructure often seen as an alternative to the Western-dominated Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, commonly known as Swift.

That same month, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the PBOC and Bank Indonesia, the Southeast Asian country’s central bank, also signed a trilateral memorandum to ease the use of the rupiah and offshore yuan in transactions between Indonesia and Hong Kong. This followed the PBOC and Bank Indonesia expanding a 2021 bilateral local-currency settlement framework last year to cover all balance-of-payments transactions.

This institutional push builds on the rapid growth seen in 2025, when bilateral local-currency settlement between the two countries more than doubled to US$13.19 billion from US$4.9 billion in 2024, according to Indonesia’s central bank, as cited by Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

“A mutually reinforcing ecosystem is gradually taking shape,” said Matteo Giovannini, a senior finance manager at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China.

“Resource cooperation supports industrial investment, which in turn creates greater demand for cross-border financial services, local currency settlement and trade financing.”

Deeper trade and investment ties, he added, would make the yuan “naturally more attractive” by lowering foreign-exchange costs and reducing reliance on third currencies.

Indonesia has also begun tapping China’s capital markets through its inaugural 7 billion yuan issuance of panda bonds – yuan-denominated debt securities sold in China’s domestic bond markets.

Giovannini, also a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation, said these recent developments underscored Indonesia’s growing role in Beijing’s push to internationalise its currency.

“Indonesia represents an important testing ground for the gradual expansion of the yuan’s use in [the Association of Southeast Asian Nations], particularly if local-currency settlement mechanisms continue to mature,” Giovannini said, though he acknowledged the US dollar would remain dominant for the foreseeable future.

This growing financial alignment, however, is unfolding against a shifting domestic backdrop in Indonesia, where operations on the ground are running up against political currents.

Tightening the screws?

What many Chinese scholars describe as a wave of “resource nationalism” has swept across Indonesia this year. The trajectory of domestic companies, especially Tsingshan Group, captures both sides of the story: a company that built its global dominance on the country’s nickel riches, only to face a more challenging policy landscape years later.

In its “Macroeconomic Policy Report on Indonesia” published in June, the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences said “policy overhauls targeting nickel mining, in particular, have dealt severe blows to foreign investors, with Chinese enterprises already bearing the brunt of the fallout.”

As part of this shift, Indonesian President Prabowo has adjusted domestic policies on nickel production. Reflecting a tightening regulatory grip, Indonesia’s MEMR has capped the national production quota for 2026 at 260 million to 270 million tonnes, implying a 30 per cent year-on-year decline.

Weda Bay Nickel in Indonesia – the world’s largest nickel mine – is a joint venture formed by Tsingshan Group, French miner Eramet and local firm Antam, with Tsingshan holding a majority share. In June, Eramet told Mining Weekly, a South African trade magazine, that production there had been suspended since late May and that the company had reduced its workforce and entered a maintenance phase.

“The mining output quota has been exhausted,” said Jerome Baudelet, chief executive of Eramet Indonesia.

Such operational halts reflected a calculated strategy, analysts said. “Jakarta hopes to wield its regulatory toolkit as an effective policy lever to underpin nickel prices. Global benchmark nickel did rally to a peak before pulling back, leaving it with gains of roughly 20 per cent from the late 2025 level,” said Xu Yu, analyst at Orient Futures.

“The country also raised relevant tax levies. The rationale behind this regulatory tweak is plain to see – elevated nickel prices would lift fiscal receipts and fuel broader economic expansion.”

Chinese enterprises must evolve to manage policy risks and adapt to the shifting strategic interests of the host country – this is a lesson every company going global must learn

Zhao Xijun, Renmin University of China

According to the Indonesian government, the nation’s budget deficit is expected to widen to 2.85 per cent of gross domestic product this year, surpassing both its prior forecast of 2.68 per cent and last year’s reading of 2.81 per cent.

At the same time, blowback from the Iran war is spilling over into the domestic economy while pressure from the United States is mounting. Faced with challenges at home and overseas, the Indonesian rupiah has sustained a steep depreciation.

Against this backdrop, the market’s earlier trailblazers could be weighing a pullback. In June, Reuters reported that Tsingshan Group was considering a major development in Madagascar, while Hong Kong-listed Lygend Resources – a Chinese operator offering services across the full nickel value chain – was mulling a project in Tanzania.

“President Subianto’s [Prabowo’s] policies – marked by resource nationalism and protectionism favouring domestic enterprises – have left some Chinese investors more cautious about committing capital today”, said Hu of the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.

At the same time, “Chinese capital remains pivotal to its economic development, a reality well acknowledged by their government officials,” Hu said.

The future of the partnership

Despite Jakarta’s push for self-reliance, the numbers reveal a stark truth. According to the Chinese embassy in Jakarta, China has remained Indonesia’s largest trading partner for 13 consecutive years and had been among its top three sources of foreign direct investment over the past decade.

Bridging that dependence with domestic ambition, analysts noted that recent policy tightening marked an attempt to leverage Indonesia’s natural resources to bolster the domestic economy, rather than simply laying the groundwork for others to reap the benefits.

“Chinese enterprises expanding into Indonesia are undergoing a profound shift: their strategy is evolving from merely ‘going global’ to deeply embedding themselves within local industrial ecosystems,” said the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences in its June report.

“In the near term, Indonesia will no longer offer a low-cost and low-threshold investment destination.”

Aaron Ang, non-executive director at Hong Kong-based cybersecurity firm Edvance, also flagged investment hurdles in Indonesia, including “a tangled regulatory landscape and skilled talent shortages”.

“Our strategy centres on collaborating with local commercial partners instead of competing against them. This approach will allow us to establish a lasting foothold there,” Ang said.

As Chinese firms recalibrate their local strategies amid mounting challenges, policymakers in Beijing and Jakarta are also stepping in to keep bilateral cooperation on track.

Responding to concerns about whether Chinese firms were becoming less welcome in Indonesia, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said on Tuesday that Jakarta had “on multiple occasions expressed readiness to deepen cooperation with China on industrial and supply chains, and welcome Chinese enterprises to invest in the country”.

“We believe that Indonesia will continue to protect the lawful rights and interests of Chinese companies and foster a sound environment for investment and operation there,” Lin added.

During the World AI Conference in Shanghai earlier this month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met Airlangga Hartarto, the Indonesian coordinating minister for economic affairs. The Southeast Asian nation became one of the founding members of the World AI Cooperation Organisation, a new China-led initiative promoting global artificial intelligence governance.

Wang said he hoped Indonesia would provide a fair and equitable business environment, while Airlangga stated that Indonesia had continued to welcome Chinese enterprises to invest.

“Over the long run, the key determinant of Chinese firms’ sustainable success in the country is to become a co-developer rather than remaining mere product exporters,” said the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences in its report on Indonesia.

But navigating Jakarta’s evolving domestic priorities is likely to remain a delicate balancing act. Zhao from Renmin University said China and Indonesia’s complementary strengths had fostered an increasingly integrated economic partnership but cautioned the relationship was not without friction.

“Chinese enterprises must evolve to manage policy risks and adapt to the shifting strategic interests of the host country – this is a lesson every company going global must learn,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Only in Hangzhou: Hang Lung’s new Westlake 66 complex blends hi-tech and history
item.description:
Hangzhou is a city of contradictions. It is home to West Lake, a Unesco World Heritage site that has inspired poets and painters for more than 1,000 years, since at least the Tang dynasty (AD618-907). It is also the birthplace of Alibaba (owner of the South China Morning Post) and a growing centre of artificial intelligence and robotics, thanks to Zhejiang University’s engineering pipeline and a local government that offers subsidies, low-cost rentals and a hands-off approach, creating an ecosystem that has made the city a natural home for companies such as DeepSeek and Unitree Robotics.

One of the seven ancient capitals of China – once praised by Marco Polo as the “city of heaven” – is now one of the country’s most dynamic tech hubs. Building something that honours Hangzhou’s multilayered identity is no small feat, but that is exactly the opportunity the creative minds behind Westlake 66, Hang Lung Properties’ newest mixed-use development, in the Wulin Central Business District, saw in the project.

“Hangzhou is one of the most incredible cities I’ve ever experienced,” says Jeffrey Kenoff, FAIA, design principal at Kohn Pedersen Fox (KPF) architectural firm. “It’s a city with centuries of history, yet being reinvented by Alibaba and its peers as a kind of ‘Silicon Valley of Asia’. Westlake 66 gave us a chance to rethink office, hospitality and retail for a new generation.”
item.content:encoded:
Hangzhou is a city of contradictions. It is home to West Lake, a Unesco World Heritage site that has inspired poets and painters for more than 1,000 years, since at least the Tang dynasty (AD618-907). It is also the birthplace of Alibaba (owner of the South China Morning Post) and a growing centre of artificial intelligence and robotics, thanks to Zhejiang University’s engineering pipeline and a local government that offers subsidies, low-cost rentals and a hands-off approach, creating an ecosystem that has made the city a natural home for companies such as DeepSeek and Unitree Robotics.

One of the seven ancient capitals of China – once praised by Marco Polo as the “city of heaven” – is now one of the country’s most dynamic tech hubs. Building something that honours Hangzhou’s multilayered identity is no small feat, but that is exactly the opportunity the creative minds behind Westlake 66, Hang Lung Properties’ newest mixed-use development, in the Wulin Central Business District, saw in the project.

“Hangzhou is one of the most incredible cities I’ve ever experienced,” says Jeffrey Kenoff, FAIA, design principal at Kohn Pedersen Fox (KPF) architectural firm. “It’s a city with centuries of history, yet being reinvented by Alibaba and its peers as a kind of ‘Silicon Valley of Asia’. Westlake 66 gave us a chance to rethink office, hospitality and retail for a new generation.”

All of this enthusiasm reflects a deeper shift that has reshaped Hangzhou, propelled by the “Six Little Dragons” – Game Science, DeepSeek, Unitree Robotics, Deep Robotics, BrainCo and Manycore Tech – setting up operations in the city. With a population of 12.62 million, according to a 2024 census, including a growing number of AI and tech workers, Hangzhou has a pressing need for spaces where people can connect, collaborate and unwind beyond the office. It calls for a different approach from the one that has shaped many American cities, and one that New York-based KPF was keen to explore.

“A lot of modern [American] cities developed in the 1980s and 90s were leaning towards more efficiency,” says Kenoff, describing them as “single‑use districts: all residential, all office, all shopping. People were driving on highways back and forth from destination A to destination B”.

In his view, that obsession with efficiency hollowed out a sense of community, something China is trying to rebuild by looking to “reinvent the way that people actually occupy public space”.

For KPF, that meant rejecting the generic glass-and-steel monument that “ticked all the boxes” – they wanted a building “that couldn’t exist anywhere else”. So, they turned to Hangzhou itself for guidance.

Hangzhou’s geography was the obvious place to start. Westlake 66 occupies a unique position midway between the Grand Canal and West Lake, creating a natural pathway between the two landmarks. “What dawned on us was to lean into that seclusion. Rather than thinking about ‘architecture as building’, it was really more about ‘architecture as landscape’,” Kenoff explains, adding that his team drew inspiration from Huang Gongwang’s famed 14th century shanshui painting, Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, translating its layered, terraced landscapes into the project’s stepped towers and sky park. Its design allows light to filter down to street level, while the site’s location informed a vision of the complex as a green valley rather than an isolated block.

Reverence for the city’s natural landscape carried over into the project’s sustainability ambitions. “It had to be conceived with nature at its centre,” says Kenoff, adding that the building received LEED Platinum, China Green Building Label 3-Star and WELL Platinum certifications. “But the goal was not just to build a ‘green’ building. We wanted to create a space that encourages sustainable behaviour as well.”

Surrounded by metro stations, the complex promotes mass transit and reduces car dependency. It uses low-carbon concrete bricks – a first for commercial developments in mainland China and Hong Kong – and solar panels installed on rooftops. Its five towers, each with its own distinct design and height, bend and open in different ways to maximise light and breeze, reducing energy consumption throughout.

All of the architectural pieces are linked through “The Oasis”, a 10,000-plus square metre “urban sanctuary” that connects the shopping mall, office towers and upcoming hotel within a panoramic corridor. “It’s an invitation to meander,” Kenoff says. “I love architecture that pulls people in.”

Another element binding Westlake 66 together is a 550-metre-long facade of modular metal panels, lined with warm-toned, glazed terracotta to wrap the project’s various components – a nod to local traditional material and craft while lending the complex a textured, “human-scale” presence that glass towers often lack. Kenoff explains that the “terracotta materiality respects culture; the cell modularisation humanises scale. It breaks down such big buildings and makes them more pleasurable to walk along. Its fluidity echoes the West Lake experience”.

It also extends the project’s longevity. Kenoff cites “the time between conception and completion” as the biggest challenge with such buildings. “By the time they are built, there are a million changes. What you think is a store becomes a restaurant, and that means the facade is constantly being asked: should it be transparent glass, solid or mechanical for venting?” He posits that “the cell solves this common problem”.

Respect for Hangzhou’s heritage didn’t stop at the facade; the city’s time as the capital of the Southern Song dynasty (1127-1279), when commerce, art and scholarship thrived, was a rich source of inspiration, and the same local terracotta tradition caught the attention of James Pierce, senior director at the Oval Partnership, the retail interior design consultant for Westlake 66. “It inspired both the materiality and colours we used. For the interior, the team chose a muted palette, with soft, rich textures that reference period ceramics, but also West Lake.”

As visitors move through the space, from north to south, he adds, colours shift subtly from warm to cold, while materials and forms transition between metals, stone and marble. In the south atrium, blue tones conceptually evoke the lake itself.

Just like KPF, Pierce’s team made heritage central to their design narrative, but their approach extends to the visitor experience itself, as the goal was to create a place where history was felt, not just observed.

“Historically, the area [Baijingfang] was known as the ‘place of 100 wells’, where people gathered, drew water and socialised,” Pierce explains. “So, that idea became the foundation of our design. We created well-like forms that cut through the floor plates, bringing light through the space and giving it a powerful sense of immersion.”

The Oval Partnership carried that same thinking through to the lower level, where a gallery with glass flooring allows visitors to literally walk over the past, a fitting solution for a project that incorporates Song and Yuan dynasty relics in a 2,700 square metre in-mall exhibition hall. Explains Pierce, “It’s thought of as a functional space where the mall can host events; there have been catwalk shows, educational programmes and community gatherings. It’s really intended as a hub within a hub.”

For all its tributes to Hangzhou’s former existence, the Oval Partnership also embraced modern technology.

“In our relics area, a huge video screen will play the site’s history like a movie sequence,” Pierce says.

Hang Lung is also thinking beyond the site itself; the company has taken a lease on the neighbouring building to give Westlake 66 a front door on Wulin Square, with interconnected bridging levels. In the future, the existing 105,900 square metre retail area is expected to grow by another 40 per cent.

In a city that balances ancient heritage with futuristic ambition, Westlake 66 is designed for today and whatever comes next. If Hangzhou’s past is any indication, the best chapters are still being written.

item.title: [SCMP] Chile’s Kast courts China day after US hits exports with forced labour tariff
item.description:
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast received China’s ambassador to Santiago, Niu Qingbao, at the La Moneda Palace on Friday morning, in an encounter that lasted more than an hour and marked the first meeting between the two men since the right-wing leader took office in March.

According to the presidency, Kast, Foreign Minister Francisco Perez Mackenna and Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Patricio Torres used the meeting to review their bilateral agenda, the minister’s coming trip to China and the preparations for the president’s participation in the Apec leaders’ meeting, to be held from November 18-19 in Shenzhen.

Kast sat down with the ambassador a day after the US Trade Representative (USTR) confirmed a 12.5 per cent tariff on Chilean imports, a measure the agency justified by what it called Chile’s failure to prohibit imports produced with forced labour.
item.content:encoded:
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast received China’s ambassador to Santiago, Niu Qingbao, at the La Moneda Palace on Friday morning, in an encounter that lasted more than an hour and marked the first meeting between the two men since the right-wing leader took office in March.

According to the presidency, Kast, Foreign Minister Francisco Perez Mackenna and Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Patricio Torres used the meeting to review their bilateral agenda, the minister’s coming trip to China and the preparations for the president’s participation in the Apec leaders’ meeting, to be held from November 18-19 in Shenzhen.

Kast sat down with the ambassador a day after the US Trade Representative (USTR) confirmed a 12.5 per cent tariff on Chilean imports, a measure the agency justified by what it called Chile’s failure to prohibit imports produced with forced labour.

The levy, which also covers 59 other trading partners, took effect on Friday and leaves out copper, the country’s largest export, while affecting the salmon, timber and food industries.

The USTR first proposed it on June 3, opening a window for the Chilean foreign ministry and the export associations to make their case.

Santiago said in a statement that it would keep talking to the Trump administration to improve access conditions, including the exclusion of products it considers essential to the country’s export basket.

The tariff has left Kast in much the same position he found himself in on his first day in office, caught between the two powers that dominate the Chilean economy.

Kast uses Trump’s strategy to gain power, flatter US

The president was elected in November with just over 58 per cent of the vote on a platform modelled closely on US President Donald Trump’s, promising a wall on the Bolivian border and a crackdown on crime he blamed on Venezuelan migrants.

He also promised a closer alignment with Washington, and flew to Miami days before his inauguration to attend the launch of Trump’s Shield of the Americas initiative.

That alignment was already in trouble by the time he reached La Moneda, the seat of the president of Chile, in March.

Weeks before the end of his term, the outgoing left-wing president Gabriel Boric had quietly authorised the start of proceedings on an undersea fibre-optic cable managed by China Mobile International linking Chile directly to Hong Kong, 19,873km (12,348 miles) long and with a 30-year concession.

Then Transport and Telecommunications Minister Juan Carlos Munoz signed the decree on January 27 and rescinded it two days later, citing typographical errors, after warnings from the American embassy.

Washington did not consider the matter closed, and in late February US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions against three Chilean officials accused of supporting activities that compromised critical telecommunications infrastructure.

The South China Morning Post confirmed at the time that Munoz, telecoms undersecretary Claudio Araya and Subtel head Guillermo Petersen were among those affected.

Boric later acknowledged that he had personally ordered the reversal after receiving explicit threats from Washington, including the possibility of Chile losing its place in the US Visa Waiver Programme, the only South American country in the scheme.

The dispute wrecked the handover between the two governments. Kast said he had not been properly briefed, dissolved the transition coordination task force after a 22-minute meeting with Boric, and announced an audit of ministerial communications.

Niu defended the cable in public at the time, calling it a mutually beneficial idea and dismissing American claims about strategic risk as not grounded in fact.

Chile exports 37 per cent of its goods to China, mainly copper, lithium, lemons and cherries, and imports a quarter of what it consumes from the Asian country, with bilateral trade reaching US$65.33 billion last year.

The United States remains the largest source of foreign direct investment, with a cumulative portfolio of US$12.5 billion against China’s US$4.6 billion, according to the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean.

Friday’s meeting closed a week dominated by foreign affairs, in which the government attended the presidential handover in Peru, hosted South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, restored consular relations with Venezuela and filed a claim at the United Nations over part of the extended continental shelf around the Juan Fernandez archipelago.

US tariff threat raises concerns in Santiago

The tariff imposed by Washington has also unsettled parts of the governing coalition, with Agriculture Minister Jaime Campos and Defence Minister Fernando Barros both criticising the American decision in public.

US ambassador to Chile, Brandon Judd, responded by warning that statements of that kind make trade negotiations harder, and the government moved to lower the temperature, insisting that the talks were being handled exclusively by the foreign ministry.

Speaking to CNN Chile on Thursday night, Senator Arturo Squella, president of the Republican Party that Kast founded, said the tariff had shown how little Chile had got in return for courting Washington.

“A huge effort has been put into having the best possible relations with the United States, only for them to pull some sort of forced labour claim out of a hat,” Squella told the broadcaster.

“At the end of the day you draw your conclusions and you say, look, there was no interest here in even recognising and respecting what has been signed with Chile,” he added, calling on the foreign ministry to argue the case as far as necessary “so that the word that is written down, when it comes to respect for free trade and everything that goes with it, counts for something again”.

Asked about Chinese interest in Chilean ports, Squella drew a distinction between ordinary trade and strategic assets, arguing that there are activities in which the country should be wary of capital or interested parties that do not answer to the national interest, and that Chile still lacks a protocol to deal with them.

His assessment of the two powers was blunt once that caveat was out of the way.

“If you ask me which one I would like to go deeper with, in terms of doctrine or of how a society should be run, obviously I see the United States as much closer,” Squella said.

“But I have no recollection of China creating difficulties or failing to respect the rules of the game.”

Squella said the episode had left him weighing what the relationship with Washington is worth in practice.

“It seems there is not much point in making so much effort to have a good relationship if in the end they arrive and out of nowhere impose tariffs on us that hit us at the waterline, in activities that are fundamental to us.”

item.title: [SCMP] Cambodian jobseekers fear debt trap over Thailand’s border reinforcement
item.description:
Vin Lors used to earn about US$20 a day working on construction sites in Bangkok, nearly twice what he now makes in Cambodia.

After the border conflict between Thailand and Cambodia broke out last July, the 37-year-old and his wife decided to return home to Siem Reap province, worried about their safety and concerned about workplace discrimination.

When he heard the government was helping returning migrant workers find jobs, Lors registered through his village chief.
item.content:encoded:
Vin Lors used to earn about US$20 a day working on construction sites in Bangkok, nearly twice what he now makes in Cambodia.

After the border conflict between Thailand and Cambodia broke out last July, the 37-year-old and his wife decided to return home to Siem Reap province, worried about their safety and concerned about workplace discrimination.

When he heard the government was helping returning migrant workers find jobs, Lors registered through his village chief.

“They registered my information and said they [the ministry officials] would contact me, but they never did,” he said.

Waiting was not an option for Lors, who had microloan debts to service. His predicament has become a familiar one in Cambodia’s west, where the border row with Thailand has hit jobs, remittances, trade and tourism.

Now, after Thailand announced it had completed a 1.3km stretch of reinforced border fence on July 22, Cambodians face a more practical question: what happens if those links do not return? Nearly 1 million Cambodian nationals have returned since last year’s conflict.

Trade between the two neighbours has taken a hit. In the first five months of this year, two-way trade fell by almost 40 per cent to US$1.15 billion, according to official Cambodian preliminary figures.

In the meantime, Cambodia has tapped alternative fuel and industrial supply sources, such as from China and Singapore, to help cushion the impact on its economy. However, questions are being raised about whether the workaround would cushion the economic impact on Cambodia’s western provinces, which are most exposed to Thailand.

In a paper on the conflict’s economic impact released in May, Harvard’s Asia Centre fellow Richard Yarrow and Cambodian economist Kenh Sovath concluded that Cambodia had absorbed the initial shock better than expected, helped by trade diversification and alternative supply routes.

Yarrow, who is also a visiting scholar at the University of Tokyo, separately told This Week in Asia that Cambodia had been hit “more mildly than expected at the national level”, but cautioned that this did not mean the western provinces along the Thai border had recovered.

“The immediate costs of adjusting are much higher in the western Cambodian provinces,” he added, noting that the provinces’ economies had long relied on Thai tourists, traders, agricultural processors and supply chains.

For instance, cassava and other crops that previously crossed the border to Thailand for processing were redirected to Vietnam or domestic processors, even as this increased logistics costs and greater spoilage risks for farmers already facing weak prices. The conflict has also interrupted a Thai tourism market that had been particularly important to Cambodia’s western border towns.

Cambodia’s economy has become less dependent on Thailand in recent years. Vietnam overtook Thailand as Cambodia’s second-largest source of imports by 2022, according to the May paper citing official data.

Thailand’s share of Cambodia’s imports fell from around 15 to 20 per cent during the 2010s to roughly 12 per cent by 2024, according to Yarrow and Kenh.

Much of the fuel previously sourced from Thailand had already arrived by sea through Sihanoukville, while importers have also turned to other suppliers, including Singapore. China has also replaced Thai suppliers of products such as plastics, iron and steel components, and some textile inputs.

But Thailand remains an important source for fuel, vehicle parts and agricultural processing and plays a key role in Cambodia’s western provincial economies.

The bilateral row has cut off a higher-paying labour market for hundreds of thousands of Cambodians, whose families depend on their remittances.

Some Cambodians continue to return to Thailand for work, risking arrest by local border patrols. The Thai government has also not offered any feasible solution for Cambodian workers with expired permits, according to labour activists.

Those who could reach Thailand were undocumented migrant workers, and this put them at risk of workplace abuse and exploitation, said Tharo Khun, a programme manager at the non-government organisation Centre for Alliance of Labour and Human Rights (CENTRAL).

Without adequate protection, these Cambodians face risks of human trafficking, debt bondage and labour exploitation, according to Khun.

Lors said he had not considered returning to Thailand, but finding stable work in Cambodia had proved difficult. After leaving Siem Reap, he and his wife moved between construction sites in Phnom Penh, Sihanoukville and Bavet City in search of employment. Contractors at two of his jobs had failed to pay them.

In May, the couple found construction jobs in Phnom Penh’s Tuol Tumpoung district, but Lors said their income was still far short of what they had earned in Bangkok. While he has reduced his outstanding debt from US$10,000 to US$1500, he still has to pay about US$80 a month for household needs.

“After paying the loan and sending some money to support my child back home, there’s nothing left for us,” he said. To feed the family, Lors sometimes buys food on credit and repays later.

Thueng Rithy, 49, faces even more dire circumstances. A former security guard in Bangkok, Rithy’s house in Banteay Meanchey was only 300 metres from the border. He called the Cambodian Labour Ministry’s hotline seeking work, but was turned down due to his age.

Rithy now lives in a displaced persons camp after his home was damaged and his village occupied by Thai forces. He owes US$3,000 to a microfinance institution, secured against land he can no longer access.

“I do not know yet how I will repay because my collateral land is occupied by the Thais,” Rithy said.

Khun said debt was the single biggest risk facing returning migrant workers and their families.

According to a survey released by CENTRAL in March, 71 per cent of Cambodians who had returned from Thailand reported being in debt, with an average household debt of US$5,000 to US$6,000 and 85 per cent of households unable to keep up with payments.

The government has responded to the influx of displaced workers by stepping up efforts through job placements, vocational training and financial relief.

Labour authorities have organised employment forums and directed workers to vacancies and training through a ministry hotline. For example, employment forums held in February and March this year saw 811 people getting jobs and another 413 registered for skills courses in the Battambang and Pursat provinces.

Last month, the ministry announced more than 8,000 vacancies across various sectors in three central lowland provinces aimed at returning workers from Thailand and local jobseekers.

The National Bank of Cambodia has also advised lenders to waive fees and penalties, defer interest and principal payments, and allow eligible displaced individuals and returning migrant workers to restructure their loans.

Despite the official support, Cambodia’s western provinces still face major challenges in helping displaced workers in a region that has attracted far less industrial investment than Phnom Penh and the southeast.

“If trade and wider relations do not recover, there’s a difficult adjustment process for the region over the next few years,” Yarrow said.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Anwar suffers another election loss to BN in Negeri Sembilan
item.description:
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim suffered a second election setback within weeks on Saturday after his Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition lost to rivals in the Negeri Sembilan polls.

Official results at midnight showed Barisan Nasional (BN) winning 18 seats, coupled with Perikatan Nasional’s (PN) seven for a supermajority of 25 over PH’s 11 in the 36-seat assembly.

The country’s second state election in under a month was a test of the stability of Anwar’s coalition government, as PH locked horns again with federal ally BN at the state level. The latter had partnered with the opposition PN in Negeri Sembilan.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim suffered a second election setback within weeks on Saturday after his Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition lost to rivals in the Negeri Sembilan polls.

Official results at midnight showed Barisan Nasional (BN) winning 18 seats, coupled with Perikatan Nasional’s (PN) seven for a supermajority of 25 over PH’s 11 in the 36-seat assembly.

The country’s second state election in under a month was a test of the stability of Anwar’s coalition government, as PH locked horns again with federal ally BN at the state level. The latter had partnered with the opposition PN in Negeri Sembilan.

The victory for BN-PN was another blow to PH, fresh off its drubbing in the Johor polls on July 11. It could also mean a snap general election called well ahead of the February 2028 deadline.

In the last state election in 2023, PH won 17 seats, BN secured 14 and PN won five, with PH and BN partnering to form the state government.

BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on Saturday night thanked voters for putting their trust in BN’s candidates and the coalition’s machinery, adding that the electoral understanding with PN would produce a stable state government.

The Election Commission said final voter turnout was 72.64 per cent, with 646,084 votes cast, including early, postal and normal voters. In the 2023 polls, final voter turnout was 68.35 per cent.

Some 860,000 people were registered to vote at 401 polling centres statewide, with 36 state assembly members to be elected from a field of 103 candidates in tight three-way races.

Parties contesting centred their campaigns on the economy, jobs and public service.

Electoral cooperation between BN and PN has also shaped the battle. While they contested separately, BN deputy president Mohamad Hasan said his machinery would help PN candidates in agreed constituencies under a seat understanding, similar to the strategy adopted in the Johor election.

The Johor showdown on July 11 saw BN sweeping 48 seats – up from 40 in 2022, while PH managed only eight and lost ground from its previous 12. BN’s two-thirds majority retained gives it absolute power to pass constitutional amendments and redraw electoral boundaries in Johor.

The Negeri Sembilan results also saw surprise losses by PH candidates including Transport Minister Anthony Loke and caretaker chief minister Aminuddin Harun.

Loke, also the Democratic Action Party’s (DAP) secretary general, lost his seat in Chennah to BN’s Siow Kong Choon by fewer than 500 votes. BN’s Mohd Faizal Ramli clinched Linggi with 8,427 votes to Aminuddin’s 5,881.

“This is the straw which breaks the camel’s back – in terms of the party secretary general losing their state assembly seat,” said Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia and senior fellow at Singapore Institute of International Affairs.

He said DAP would need to do some serious “soul searching”, including distancing itself from PH.

“By continuing to associate themselves with this government, they are asking for trouble and will continue this losing streak,” Oh said.

DAP, long branded as a Chinese-majority party, forms the largest bloc of PH’s coalition. It is mistrusted by Malays who perceive the party as a threat to the dominance of their ethnic group.

Sunway University political scientist Wong Chin Huat agreed that Loke’s defeat could trigger a call from within the party to distance itself from Anwar’s PH to retain its base. “It would be a tough decision either way.”

Local media said Loke was considering relinquishing his position as Negeri Sembilan DAP state chairman to take responsibility for the party’s poor performance, but would consult party leaders first.

On his national party role as secretary general, however, Loke said he would discuss with the party’s central executive committee.

Analysts earlier said that voter turnout, Malay sentiment and whether opposition PN could gain ground in 23 Malay-majority constituencies would determine if PH could still retain power in Negeri Sembilan.

“Voter turnout is very critical, especially in the Malay-majority constituency,” Azmi Hassan, senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, told This Week in Asia.

Azmi said BN could score support from Malay voters in constituencies where PN was not contesting.

“The cooperation between BN and PN could influence voting in Malay-majority constituencies, with PN supporters potentially backing BN candidates where PN is not contesting,” he said.

The snap state election was called after months of political and constitutional uncertainty, during which disputes involving the Negeri Sembilan palace coincided with the collapse of the PH-BN state administration after BN withdrew support for Aminuddin. The state legislative assembly was officially dissolved on June 5.

Voter Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid, 49, who cast his ballot in Paroi on Saturday morning, said he hoped the next state government would be highly competent and of unquestionable integrity.

The chief economist at Bank Muamalat Malaysia said Negeri Sembilan’s economic potential and future were untapped. “The state government can play an effective role as an enabler that facilitates a competitive and fair economy for businesses, investors and the man on the street.”

More than a verdict on the state administration, analysts say the election has become a test of whether voters approve of how Anwar’s unity government handles issues such as cost of living.

The outcome could shape PH’s political trajectory while testing the strength of the BN-PN informal cooperation, adding pressure on how all three blocs would set the stage for any future state contest and ultimately the next general election.

“Results and promises matter to voters, and no amount of sentiment will be enough to appease the electorate and sustain continued political dominance,” said Ahmad Mohsein Azman, a senior analyst at BowerGroupAsia.

The election tested whether voters were rewarding policy delivery, reform and welfare over traditional political narratives, he said, while the outcome would offer early indication of the direction of Malaysia’s political landscape ahead of the next general election.

On whether the BN-PN informal cooperation could be a durable electoral strategy, Ahmad Mohsein said a win for the bloc would “indicate a growing return to the norm of a BN-led Malay political hegemony, despite efforts from the opposition party Bersatu and even PH to fill in that role”.

Ahmad Mohsein said BN’s strong showing on Saturday could well carry the so-called blue wave – the coalition’s campaign colours – across the incoming general election given that PH was now fractured and in disarray, while the BN-PN cooperation riding on the Malay-Muslim unity narrative had yielded promising results.

“The circumstances we have today would make the blue wave more of a question of when, rather than if,” he said.

PH would have to work day and night to bring back its supporters and increase voter turnout in its favour, a factor which had significantly dampened its chances in both Johor and Negeri Sembilan, he added.

Additional reporting by Vincent Tan

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong restaurants score extra HK$500 million thanks to World Cup
item.description:
The World Cup brought in an extra HK$500 million (US$63.8 million) for Hong Kong’s catering sector this year, an industry leader has said, after restaurants and shopping centres hosted overnight viewings of the final with dim sum, snacks and milk tea.

Businesses were also urged on Monday to devise creative strategies and set competitive prices to maintain the momentum from the city’s World Cup fever.

The final between Spain and Argentina drew crowds of football fans, including children and the elderly, who flocked to shopping centres at 3am – packing every floor of Tuen Mun Town Plaza, Olympian City, MCP in Tseung Kwan O and Kai Tak Mall.
item.content:encoded:
The World Cup brought in an extra HK$500 million (US$63.8 million) for Hong Kong’s catering sector this year, an industry leader has said, after restaurants and shopping centres hosted overnight viewings of the final with dim sum, snacks and milk tea.

Businesses were also urged on Monday to devise creative strategies and set competitive prices to maintain the momentum from the city’s World Cup fever.

The final between Spain and Argentina drew crowds of football fans, including children and the elderly, who flocked to shopping centres at 3am – packing every floor of Tuen Mun Town Plaza, Olympian City, MCP in Tseung Kwan O and Kai Tak Mall.

Simon Wong Ka-wo, president of the Hong Kong Federation of Restaurants and Related Trades, estimated that the catering industry had pocketed an additional HK$500 million between June 30 and Monday, representing an uptick of about 6 per cent from its initial estimate in July.

In Tuen Mun Town Plaza, cheers erupted as Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal appeared on a 540-inch screen, building to a crescendo when Spain clinched victory 1-0 after extra time.

Stalls and restaurants sought to capitalise on the crowds, setting up booths nearby to offer bubble tea or delivering dim sum directly to the viewing area.

Supermarket chain ParknShop stayed open overnight, selling drinks and fruit, while some spectators ordered food deliveries to the venue.

Many vendors offered promotions such as “buy three, get one free” to attract customers. Taxis also lined up at the mall’s entrance, ready to pick up passengers after the match.

Nini Man, manager of Nap Tea’s Tuen Mun branch, said the World Cup pop-up stand had only started turning a profit in the last two matches after the spot opened for a trial run on July 3.

She said she was inspired by the strong turnout at the mall for the Brazil-Japan match earlier in the tournament. As more vendors joined, the screenings evolved into a plaza-wide event.

“It was worth continuing [during the World Cup],” she said.

Man added that the exposure had helped introduce the shop to nearby residents who had never visited before.

“We have become like old neighbourhood friends,” she said, referring to the rare opportunity to interact with customers face-to-face.

Terence Chan Tak-ming, general manager of the portfolio leasing department at Henderson Land, said MCP recorded double-digit growth in both foot traffic and sales turnover throughout the World Cup.

He noted that tenants offering sports, lifestyle retail goods, or food and drinks had performed particularly well, creating business opportunities outside traditional peak hours.

In addition to vendors offering snacks and drinks ranging from coffee to craft beer, MCP also arranged free shuttle buses to Central and Mong Kok to help fans travel directly to work on Monday morning after watching the final.

Catering sector leader Wong said that while the significant time difference between Hong Kong and North America had dampened the usual business boost over the match period, many fans still visited restaurants and shopping centres to watch the final.

Venues raking in extra business included traditional Chinese dim sum restaurants.

“Restaurants need new directions in operations to attract new clientele. For important matches in the future, now that large screens have been installed, restaurants can roll out different activities and discounts to attract customers,” Wong said.

Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui, who watched the final at Kai Tak Mall, said that even with mega-events, businesses need to think creatively about strategies to attract customers.

She highlighted the emerging trend of traditional dim sum restaurants live-streaming World Cup matches as a successful example.

“I used to think watching a match in a dim sum restaurant might seem out of place, but it is actually feasible,” Law said. “That is why everyone has to rack their brains and examine their own strengths to discover more business opportunities.”

She added that a proactive approach from these businesses would help boost the economy.

Economist Simon Lee Siu-po said he believed business among restaurants and retailers would return to baseline levels after the World Cup, given lukewarm nighttime spending sentiment.

He urged the catering industry to be transparent and creative to attract patrons, citing the example of Lin Heung Lau’s Sheung Wan branch.

The restaurant rolled out an HK$3,888 eight-person VIP package and a HK$368 set for singles for the final match, with tea and service charges included.

Lee said the operator addressed the two pain points of Chinese restaurants by setting out their prices clearly and catering to the needs of solo diners.

“Hong Kong has too many options. With a competitive price and quality food, patrons will be interested,” he said, adding that restaurants could offer smaller meal portions to attract those dining alone.

Among those drawn to the city’s shopping malls for the final match’s “vibrant” atmosphere was Tuen Mun resident Shannon Dias, 42, who came to support Spain.

“A lot of people are here for both teams. It feels like a stadium – it’s better to be here,” he said.

Although he had eaten before the match, Dias said services by vendors at the shopping centre were “pretty good”.

“They’re doing their best to set up shop, especially for an event like this,” he said. “It definitely helps boost the economy.”

Another fan, Kit Ching, attended with his family after seeing promotions on social media.

Despite the crowds, he said he enjoyed the atmosphere and spent about HK$50 on drinks and snacks from ParknShop before kick-off.

“It was good to have something to eat while watching,” he said.

But some Argentina supporters left disappointed after the final whistle.

McQueen Zeng, who watched the match with friends, said it was a “pity” Argentina could not defend their title.

“I applaud Spain, and I also applaud our Argentinian players because they kept making efforts and trying to score,” he said. “I’m grateful to them for that.”

Zeng added that he would continue to support the team and hoped to watch a future World Cup in person, noting that Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay would co-host the opening three centenary matches for the 2030 Fifa tournament.

Additional reporting by Jess Ma

item.title: [SCMP] Negeri Sembilan votes as Malaysia’s political allies lock horns again
item.description:
Voters in Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan headed to the polls on Saturday, the second election in the past month as political allies governing the country locked horns at state levels.

Candidates from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition are going head-to-head with those of federal partner Barisan Nasional (BN), which trounced its rival in last month’s Johor race.

Voter turnout is at 28.11 per cent as of 11am, according to the Election Commission.
item.content:encoded:
Voters in Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan headed to the polls on Saturday, the second election in the past month as political allies governing the country locked horns at state levels.

Candidates from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition are going head-to-head with those of federal partner Barisan Nasional (BN), which trounced its rival in last month’s Johor race.

Voter turnout is at 28.11 per cent as of 11am, according to the Election Commission.

The commission is targeting a voter turnout of between 72 and 75 per cent. In the 2023 polls, final voter turnout was at 68.35 per cent.

The target is higher this year as some 20,000 new voters are eligible to cast their ballots the first time – coupled with intense campaigning from contesting parties.

Negeri Sembilan has traditionally been a stronghold for PH, which won 17 seats in 2023 while BN secured 14, allowing the two coalitions to form the state government with a combined 31-seat majority.

The opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN) won the remaining five seats.

Nearly 890,000 voters are registered to cast their ballots at 401 polling centres statewide, with 36 state assembly members to be elected from a field of 103 candidates in tight three-way races.

Parties contesting have centred their campaigns on the economy, jobs and public service.

One voter, Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid, 49, who cast his ballot in Paroi in the morning said he hoped that whoever leads the next state government would be highly competent and possess unquestionable integrity.

The chief economist at Bank Muamalat Malaysia said Negeri Sembilan’s economic potential and future were untapped. “The state govt can play an effective role as an enabler that facilitates a competitive and fair economy for businesses, investors and the man on the street.”

Electoral cooperation between BN and PN has also shaped the battle. While they are contesting separately, BN deputy president Mohamad Hasan has said his machinery will help PN candidates in agreed constituencies under a seat understanding, similar to the strategy adopted in the Johor election.

The Negeri Sembilan polls will further test the strength of Anwar’s coalition government and whether PH can maintain momentum despite frustrations over rising costs of living and wider economic pressures.

The Johor showdown on July 11 saw BN sweeping 48 seats – up from 40 in 2022, while PH managed only eight and lost ground from its previous 12. BN’s two-thirds majority retained gives it absolute power to pass constitutional amendments and redraw electoral boundaries in Johor.

Analysts say voter turnout, Malay sentiment and whether opposition PN can gain ground in 23 Malay-majority constituencies will determine if PH can still retain power in Negeri Sembilan.

“Voter turnout is very critical, especially in the Malay-majority constituency,” Azmi Hassan, senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, told This Week in Asia.

Early voting was held on Tuesday, with total turnout reaching 91.06 per cent or 14,995 early voters, local media reports said.

In the 2023 state election, early voters accounted for 56.67 per cent, with 14,778 of 26,079 eligible individuals casting ballots.

Azmi said BN could score support from Malay voters in constituencies where PN was not contesting.

“The cooperation between BN and PN could influence voting in Malay-majority constituencies, with PN supporters potentially backing BN candidates where PN is not contesting,” he said.

A pre-election survey released on Thursday by IDE Research Centre, a Malaysian-based think tank and research hub, suggests turnout and late-deciding voters could prove decisive.

It found that 51.9 per cent of voters aged between 18 and 30 said they were certain to vote compared with 67.4 per cent of those aged 31 to 60, with voting motivation lower among Chinese and Indians than Malays.

Pollster Ilham Centre pointed to a tighter contest this time, projecting BN and PN to secure a majority if Malay votes were consolidated.

“PH continues to face a significant deficit in Malay support, while Chennah, Linggi, Nilai, Repah and Temiang remain highly competitive and too close to call,” it said in its pre-election assessment released on Friday.

High-profile candidates include Democratic Action Party Secretary General and Transport Minister Anthony Loke, defending his Chennah seat, and Negeri Sembilan caretaker chief minister Aminuddin Harun, who is contesting in Linggi instead of his long-held Sikamat constituency.

Mohamad Hasan, who is also foreign minister, is seeking another term in Ranrau, while Negeri Sembilan Umno chief Jalaluddin Alias will defend Pertang.

The snap election was called after months of political and constitutional uncertainty, during which disputes involving the Negeri Sembilan palace coincided with the collapse of the PH-BN state administration after BN withdrew support for Aminuddin. The state legislative assembly was officially dissolved on June 5.

The crisis has put political stability under the spotlight, with PH and BN now battling for a clearer mandate to govern the state.

Reform campaign

The polls have also seen the long-delayed release of the Royal Commission of Inquiry report on the country’s Islamic pilgrimage fund, injecting governance and corruption into the final stretch of the campaign.

Analysts say while the report was justified on public interest grounds, its timing created opportunities for PH to reinforce its reform and anti-corruption narrative.

Awang Azman Awang Pawi, an associate professor at Universiti Malaya, said the report represented a governance measure and its findings could help mobilise PH’s existing Malay supporters and put BN temporarily on the defensive.

“The issue could help PH among three groups: Malay-Muslim voters, undecided voters, and younger or professionally oriented Malay voters concerned about political appointments and institutional competence,” he said.

Asrul Hadi Abdullah Sani, associate vice-president at The Asia Group, said while PH remained a favourite, support among Malay voters appeared far from secure.

“Malay voter sentiment will be central because even a modest shift could determine several Malay-majority and mixed constituencies, particularly if Chinese and Indian turnout is lower,” he said.

According to Asrul, key contests could be in marginal Malay-majority and mixed constituencies.

“A strong BN win would suggest that Johor may have marked the beginning of a broader political recovery, particularly if it performs well among Malay voters and in mixed constituencies,” he said.

“A convincing PH victory would indicate that BN’s Johor success was driven more by local strength than by a wider national shift.”

Polling centres will close at 6pm, with the Election Commission expecting full results as early as 10pm.

item.title: [SCMP] Pakistan, Bangladesh face economic squeeze as US-Iran crisis widens
item.description:
Pakistan and Bangladesh are entering the latest phase of the US-Iran conflict with thinner cushions than many Asian economies, raising the risk that another oil shock could quickly spill into higher food, transport and electricity costs for millions of people, analysts have said.

Both economies rely heavily on imported fuel, leaving them particularly vulnerable to any prolonged spike in oil and diesel prices.

Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, said both economies could face significant inflationary pressure in the near term, noting that weak inventory buffers meant the impact on domestic prices would be “relatively quick”.
item.content:encoded:
Pakistan and Bangladesh are entering the latest phase of the US-Iran conflict with thinner cushions than many Asian economies, raising the risk that another oil shock could quickly spill into higher food, transport and electricity costs for millions of people, analysts have said.

Both economies rely heavily on imported fuel, leaving them particularly vulnerable to any prolonged spike in oil and diesel prices.

Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, said both economies could face significant inflationary pressure in the near term, noting that weak inventory buffers meant the impact on domestic prices would be “relatively quick”.

Oil markets already reflect these concerns, with prices on track for their biggest monthly gain since March by the end of July, including double-digit increases in crude and products such as diesel.

Benchmark Brent crude prices were up nearly 21 per cent to US$84.85 a barrel in Asian trading on Friday afternoon, from US$70.18 on July 1, while WTI was up by around the same margin to US$81.84 a barrel over the same period.

The risks are no longer confined to Gulf shipping lanes, after a drone strike on gas vessels in Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Damietta on Wednesday added to concerns about shipping risks around the Suez Canal, one of the remaining routes for Saudi oil.

For Pakistan and Bangladesh, two governments already constrained by debt and International Monetary Fund-backed reforms, another energy-price shock could mean renewed pressure on their currencies, subsidies and public finances.

The pressure could persist if the conflict, now in its fifth month, widens further, with US President Donald Trump weighing whether to escalate attacks after Iran targeted American military installations and assets in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain.

In a report published on Wednesday, Oxford Economics analysts said they were concerned about emerging markets such as Pakistan Egypt, Mozambique, Nigeria and Kenya facing a mix of political and geopolitical risk, as well as high debt-servicing costs.

“In each case, debt service costs have risen sharply since 2019,” said Gabriel Sterne, head of global emerging markets, and Evghenia Slepsova, senior emerging markets economist.

According to Oxford Economics, Mozambique, Pakistan, Kenya, Ghana and Tunisia – each with thin reserve buffers – would suffer the sharpest deterioration.
