“In a downside scenario in which the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues through 2027, sovereign stress will compound through inflation, currency weakness, and financing costs,” Slepsova said.

For Pakistan and Bangladesh, the challenge is magnified by IMF-backed reform programmes that require fiscal discipline, leaving governments with less room to absorb higher energy costs through subsidies or delayed price increases.

Bangladesh faces a different but related squeeze, with domestic inflation, energy shortages, a banking crisis and international trade hurdles already weighing on the economy.

“Typically, countries prioritise debt repayments to international institutions like the IMF, but I won’t be surprised if Bangladesh in particular may be required to renegotiate for additional forbearance,” Lim said.

The most severe risk would be a prolonged disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway between Iran and Oman through which about a fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow.

Neil Shearing, group chief economist at Capital Economics, warned in a report last month that oil markets could reach a tipping point if the strait remained closed for an extended period, with prices likely to hit US$120 per barrel or higher.

Traders are also watching supply disruptions elsewhere, including renewed interruptions to Kazakhstan-linked crude exports through the Black Sea.

The world economy was weathering the shock of the war in the Middle East with no signs yet of a global slowdown, but risks remained high, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said last month.

For smaller South Asian economies, however, the pressure is more immediate.

Gnanasekar Thiagarajan, founder of Commtrendz Research, said such economies were among the most vulnerable because they did not have oil reserves to shield themselves from the impact of higher energy prices.

Pakistan, which has emerged as a key mediator between the US and Iran, has as much at stake as other emerging nations in reaching a speedy resolution of the conflict, he added.

Security worries

That economic exposure has pushed Pakistan into a more delicate balancing act, as Islamabad presses for de-escalation while also strengthening security ties with Gulf states unnerved by the widening conflict.

The response reflects Pakistan’s dual role in the crisis: a country vulnerable to higher energy prices and regional spillover, but also one with long-standing military links that Gulf states are looking to leverage as they reassess their reliance on the US.

Earlier this week, Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah met his Pakistani counterpart Ishaq Dar in Islamabad. Both sides discussed stronger cooperation, including Kuwait’s ratification of a five-year defence pact.

The development comes less than a year after Saudi Arabia signed a landmark Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Islamabad in September last year, pointing to efforts to develop a broader security architecture across the Gulf region.

“Pakistan can offer military personnel, training, drones, air-defence support and protection for critical infrastructure at lower cost than another major Western deployment. Its long-standing relationship with Saudi Arabia also gives it credibility in the Gulf,” said Uday Chandra, a political-science professor at India’s Ashoka University.

“But Pakistan cannot replace the existing American security umbrella. It would also like to avoid getting embroiled in a war against Iran or aggravating sectarian tensions at home. Its role is, therefore, likely to be limited and transactional.”

Gulf states have long relied on the US for advanced air defence, intelligence-sharing and wider military deterrence.

Srinivasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Indic Researchers Forum, said a prolonged Middle East conflict would not be in Pakistan’s interest, irrespective of any security realignment.

It could expose Islamabad to competing pressures from Washington, Tehran, Beijing and Middle Eastern capitals.

“Domestic energy shortages and border risks [of a conflict] with Iran [can] only sharpen the squeeze,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘A living neighbour’: Singapore residents fight to save Maju forest as clearance looms
item.description:
Singaporean Jo Teoh has spent over three decades waking up to birdsong, the rustle of leaves as macaques jump through trees, and the lingering smell of damp earth.

Much of her time living in the western estate of Sunset Way revolves around the adjacent forest, where she and her family watch hornbills glide over the canopy.

“The neighbourhood lives with the forest,” said the media producer, 68. “It has shaped the character of our home and community.”
item.content:encoded:
Singaporean Jo Teoh has spent over three decades waking up to birdsong, the rustle of leaves as macaques jump through trees, and the lingering smell of damp earth.

Much of her time living in the western estate of Sunset Way revolves around the adjacent forest, where she and her family watch hornbills glide over the canopy.

“The neighbourhood lives with the forest,” said the media producer, 68. “It has shaped the character of our home and community.”

But the chirps and faint crickets may soon become a lived memory. On July 10, Singapore’s Housing Development Board (HDB) announced plans to clear about 15 of 23 hectares (56.8 acres) of Maju forest for public housing in the coming years.

Residents like Teoh have since called for greater transparency in the planning process. “Seeing a place so rich in life reduced to a coloured polygon on a planning map was devastating,” she said. “It felt like watching a living neighbour transformed into a development parcel.”

Educator Anna Ng chose to build a home at Clementi’s Sunset Way some two decades ago to allow her children to grow up alongside nature in a city state filled with skyscrapers. “When the kids were young they could just ride their bikes around the estate and even wander into the forest,” she said.

The project would affect more than biodiversity, she lamented. “[It will] inadvertently lead to changes in traffic, people, the quality of air and unquantifiable things like our psychological well-being.”

While noting that dialogue sessions were being held, Ng questioned if it was “heavy-handed” to hold talks only after announcing the redevelopment plans.

For outdoor lover Derrick Lo, the announcement signalled one fewer venue for his love of organising hiking trips across Singapore.

Lo, 59, said visits to Maju forest helped many tide through the Covid-19 pandemic when indoor spaces were banned. “Too many forests have already been sacrificed for housing,” he said. “Once these habitats are cleared, they cannot be brought back.”

About 20 per cent of Singapore, which is 745 sq km (288 square miles) in size, is covered by forests, but this figure has been falling over the years. According to local media, more than 90 per cent of its original primary rainforests, mangroves and freshwater swamps have been lost to development over the past two centuries.

A petition to stop the Maju plan has collected over 33,500 signatures as of Friday.

‘False binary’?

The Sunset Way redevelopment project aimed to provide more housing options for Singaporeans, including young families who wished to live near their parents, HDB said in its announcement, noting that demand for homes remained strong.

The greenfield site had largely been zoned for residential use since Singapore’s Master Plan 1980.

The latest move was made public after the conclusion of an environmental study assessing the development’s impact. The study, commissioned by the National Parks Board and published on July 10, recorded 286 flora species and 113 animal species, including endangered ones such as the sunda pangolin and the straw-headed bulbul.

To provide refuge for wildlife and facilitate fauna movement, an eight-hectare plot would be retained, HDB said, adding that various stakeholders such as nature groups were engaged throughout the planning process.

But to many, the plot is nowhere near enough. Environmental groups and activists have called for a pause on the clearance and suggested prioritising brownfield sites such as expiring golf courses and ageing industrial land for housing.

“The narrative framing of forest versus housing has a false binary,” said Julie Tang, a climate organiser at green group SG Climate Rally. “I think a lot of Singaporeans agree that a good and full life is one we get to live in harmony with the flora and fauna around us.”

Speaking to local media a week after the announcement, HDB chief town planner Chong Fook Loong said the first priority was brownfield sites, but those were few and far between in the Clementi area.

He said there was a “great need” for more housing supply, referring to a recent build-to-order launch in Clementi that was oversubscribed four times.

While prioritising brownfield sites would reduce pressure on natural ecosystems, earmarking such places could be challenging as they might not be suitable or readily available, said Tan-Soo Jie-Sheng, director of the Institute for Environment and Sustainability at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

“Some remain under lease, others continue to support important industrial or institutional functions, while some require substantial remediation and infrastructure upgrades before they can be redeveloped,” he said.

“Ultimately, the key question is not just whether other brownfield sites exist, but whether they can deliver comparable housing outcomes within similar cost and time constraints while achieving the same planning objectives like population rejuvenation.”

Hoping for a U-turn

HDB said plans were not yet finalised and invited the public to share their feedback following the announcement.

In response to queries, HDB said it had received 2,712 responses regarding the Sunset Way site as of Tuesday.

“All feedback received will be reviewed alongside the findings of the environmental study, as well as other planning considerations, before agencies finalise the detailed development plans for the site,” it said.

Several lawmakers have said they will raise the matter at the next parliament session, which starts next Tuesday.

Residents’ concerns had been relayed to HDB, said People’s Action Party MP Sim Ann on Friday, who added that she believed the views would be “considered thoroughly and seriously” and “help shape the eventual outcome”.

Another housing redevelopment project at Gillman Barracks, an art and lifestyle compound which formerly housed British Army regiments, has also incited environmental concerns. A petition campaigning against that project, which was announced simultaneously with Sunset Way, has received over 12,600 signatures as of Friday.

Tang said she remained “cautiously optimistic”, noting that the government had on rare occasions changed course after public pleas.

“The organic energy on the ground is really very strong,” she said. “It’s not manufactured, it’s a real response from the people of Singapore saying that we feel quite strongly that we shouldn’t go ahead.”

Following similar public outcry, Singapore in 2021 revised its plans to clear Dover Forest, retaining most of the greenery and developing about a third of its 33 hectares for housing.

Sociologist Tan Ern Ser noted that Singapore was increasingly becoming a post-materialist society which valued environmental protection and quality of life. “We now also have a more critical citizenry prepared to voice environmental concerns,” he said.

He believed the government would revise the plan as it recognised that redevelopment was “people-centric” and meant to enhance residents’ quality of life.

“The political leadership too prioritises environmental protection, and would initiate conducting environmental impact assessment as part of its redevelopment plans,” said Tan, who is also an adjunct principal research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies. “After all, the government’s tagline is that Singapore is a city in nature.”

While the Dover Forest project was an “important precedent”, Tan-Soo said the public response was more likely to influence the project’s implementation instead of halting it altogether.

He recalled the construction project for the Cross-Island train line, which included plans to build a tunnel under a nature reserve which was Singapore’s largest patch of primary rainforest. Environmental groups and activists proposed an alternative route that skirted the reserve and ran below private homes.

Singapore retained its original plan, saying it would result in a shorter travel time than the alternative and would be more environmentally friendly in the long run due to “lower energy consumption”.

Teoh and the residents of Sunset Way are determined to fight down to the wire.

“The tragedy is not simply that we may lose a forest,” said Teoh, who has since started a social media page to spark discussions on balancing development and nature.

“No amount of tree planting can recreate decades of ecological complexity within our lifetime. An everyday relationship between people and the living world built over generations may disappear with it.”

Additional reporting by Jean Iau

item.title: [SCMP] EU-China trade war: Beijing turns the screws as Brussels tests limits of restraint
item.description:
Last Thursday, the European Union added 14 Chinese companies to its latest round of sanctions, accusing them of providing support for Russia’s war against Ukraine – but few of the names were recognisable to anyone outside narrow trading and compliance circles.

Officials were taken aback less than 24 hours later, when Beijing – which had been notified of the ragtag group of traders and freight forwarders to be listed by the EU as far back as June – fired back ferociously. Unlike the long notice afforded to their own diplomats, China gave Brussels just a one-hour warning, according to people familiar with the exchange.

Europe’s own listings had been carefully calibrated, intentionally omitting major Chinese actors to ensure its own member states would support the package amid fears of retaliation. Beijing, on the other hand, went for the jugular.
item.content:encoded:
Last Thursday, the European Union added 14 Chinese companies to its latest round of sanctions, accusing them of providing support for Russia’s war against Ukraine – but few of the names were recognisable to anyone outside narrow trading and compliance circles.

Officials were taken aback less than 24 hours later, when Beijing – which had been notified of the ragtag group of traders and freight forwarders to be listed by the EU as far back as June – fired back ferociously. Unlike the long notice afforded to their own diplomats, China gave Brussels just a one-hour warning, according to people familiar with the exchange.

Europe’s own listings had been carefully calibrated, intentionally omitting major Chinese actors to ensure its own member states would support the package amid fears of retaliation. Beijing, on the other hand, went for the jugular.

Added to a list that effectively bars them from buying certain goods from China were 14 EU defence organisations, including the continent’s biggest defence company, Rheinmetall, and a prominent Polish university.

The firms named are also effectively cut off from receiving those same Chinese-origin materials via overseas suppliers, an extraterritorial reach that does not exist in the EU’s own measures, and which could send a chilling effect through their supply chains, Brussels officials fear.

“They have threatened for years but until now they barked a lot and didn’t bite. This time they didn’t bark much, but they bit,” one senior official said.

In Brussels, the view is that the retaliation has less to do with the Russian sanctions and more to do with their simmering trade war, and in particular, an October deadline the European Commission has set for progress in talks aimed at rebalancing bilateral commerce with China. If this fails, the bloc has vowed to take action.

More broadly, Beijing’s flex illustrates how differently the two sides are approaching the three-month negotiating window before October – and may also offer clues as to their respective stomach for a fight.

After successfully forcing the US to back down in a brief but fierce trade war last year by weaponising its rare earth dominance, Beijing is once again seen to be pursuing “escalation dominance” – a concept rooted in Cold War nuclear strategy, now increasingly used in economic statecraft.

The term refers to the ability to out-escalate an opponent at every step. EU officials see Chinese counterparts now trying to ratchet up the pressure in an effort to force Europe to back down – and strike fear into its 27 member states before they make tough decisions over what to do about what is commonly described as the “China shock 2.0” in the autumn.

“It signals the willingness to escalate and the belief that Beijing has escalation dominance, which is totally coherent with China’s current EU policy,” said Mathieu Duchatel, director of international studies at Institut Montaigne, a Parisian think tank.

Brussels, by contrast, is moving cautiously.

Officials view the three-month negotiating window as an opportunity to see whether Beijing is prepared to address long-standing concerns over market access and industrial overcapacity. They have been surprised that Beijing has made positive noises through more than 10 rounds of talks since a ministerial meeting last month.

But privately, it has been described as a proof of concept: if China fails to deliver meaningful concessions by October – as is expected – it will strengthen the case for a far more interventionist trade policy.

In the background, Europe is quietly continuing to build an industrial policy designed to wean itself off reliance on China, but it is keen to avoid major fireworks ahead of October – or at least launching any of its own. In meetings with business representatives, trade chief Maros Sefcovic has assured them the EU will play things carefully, according to people present.

“It makes sense to avoid putting oil on the fire,” said a second senior official. “We have given them an ultimatum for October – we will see what happens by then.”

Investigations into unfair trade in China’s chemicals sector that could lead to emergency tariffs and quotas have been paused, online media platform The Capitol Forum reported, lest they upset negotiations.

This would not be the first time measures have been scrapped or paused to protect dialogue formats. In April, the EU removed sanctions on two Chinese banks, which had been listed last year, after the commerce ministry committed to stop them using crypto transactions to ship goods covered by existing EU sanctions to Russia.

The decision was controversial: some wanted to keep the obscure financiers on the list, since it had clearly gotten Beijing’s attention and therefore presented rare leverage. Sources confirmed to the SCMP, however, that the removal happened after China threatened to cancel talks on the financial sector, which officials involved were determined to preserve.

“We are cooked,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, an economist specialising in China’s economy at Belgian think tank Bruegel.

“Officials are prioritising the dialogue track over immediate industrial defence for a sector that is already under severe import pressure.

“For me it is quite clear: Europe is signalling that the political cost of further friction with Beijing currently outweighs the cost of delayed protection for its chemical industry,” she said, referring to the safeguard probes.

China, on the other hand, faces “no equivalent internal constraint and is willing to escalate against high-visibility European names the moment secondary sanctions touch its entities”.

After last Friday’s gambit from Beijing, business associations’ phones rang off the hook, as companies listed wondered if they could still access Chinese minerals required to make military goods, while those further down the supply chain fretted over whether they could still sell products to those named.

As of Thursday, the European Commission was still awaiting an explanation from Beijing. There are fears that the move could hamper the bloc’s rearmament efforts, as well as its plans to provide military support for Ukraine.

Crucially, the move shows that Beijing is willing to exploit its economic chokepoints to cow its opponents, a trait that is the envy of some European bureaucrats.

Working-level talks will continue in August, even as most EU officials leave Belgium for their summer holidays, with the level of negotiations to pick up in September – even if expectations are managed in Europe as to how much ground China is ready to yield.

September will see a visit of the EU’s top trade enforcer Denis Redonnet to the Chinese capital, followed by Sefcovic’s own trip, planned for early October. The EU’s national leaders are then set to discuss the China shock again in October and December.

Back in Brussels, the October deadline is not seen as an end point for tensions with China, rather the beginning of a new stage – and a test for whether Europe’s dialogue-first approach survives contact with Beijing’s escalation.

item.title: [SCMP] Is China’s biotech boom at risk? Fear of policy backlash after death in gene-editing trial
item.description:
The death of a six-year-old girl after receiving an experimental gene-editing therapy has been described by scientists as a tragedy that highlights the need to improve trial safeguards.

But some in the biotechnology industry fear Chinese policymakers may curtail the regulatory flexibility that scientists have long enjoyed in initiating clinical trials – a key mechanism behind China’s competitive edge in frontier treatments.

“I hope this tragedy does not have a lasting negative impact on China’s investigator-initiated clinical-research system, but there is a real risk of a regulatory backlash,” said Wang Haoran, chief executive of Neoland Biosciences, based in Shandong province.
item.content:encoded:
The death of a six-year-old girl after receiving an experimental gene-editing therapy has been described by scientists as a tragedy that highlights the need to improve trial safeguards.

But some in the biotechnology industry fear Chinese policymakers may curtail the regulatory flexibility that scientists have long enjoyed in initiating clinical trials – a key mechanism behind China’s competitive edge in frontier treatments.

“I hope this tragedy does not have a lasting negative impact on China’s investigator-initiated clinical-research system, but there is a real risk of a regulatory backlash,” said Wang Haoran, chief executive of Neoland Biosciences, based in Shandong province.

“China has advanced rapidly in several frontier areas, partly because the mechanism has provided greater flexibility for carefully supervised early clinical exploration. That speed has increased the sense of urgency across the biotechnology industries in the United States and Europe.

“This case appears to reveal serious failures in risk assessment, transparency and institutional oversight. Stronger safeguards are clearly necessary, especially for first-in-human gene-editing treatments involving children.”

The girl, identified only as Mei, died days after receiving a bespoke therapy designed to correct a neurodevelopmental genetic mutation in March last year, according to a joint investigation by Retraction Watch and the journal Science published on July 23.

The revelations sent shock waves through global research and biomedical communities, with the report framing the tragedy as “a new stumble in China’s push to rival the United States as a biotech power”.

The trial was led by Qiu Zilong, a neuroscience researcher at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s brain centre, through an investigator-initiated trial (IIT), according to the report.

Under China’s IIT framework, researchers need clearance only from research hospitals rather than national regulators to test novel therapies on humans – an institutional set-up that has helped drive China’s biotech boom.

Unlike traditional clinical trials requiring rigorous approval from national authorities, IITs offer a nimble route for companies and institutions to determine whether experimental treatments are promising, according to industry outlet Endpoints News in an article published in December.

This mechanism had helped China’s biotech sector catch up with Western rivals, particularly by cementing China’s position as a competitive force in cell and gene therapy, the article said.

However, Wang criticised the culture among some Chinese researchers, particularly younger academics whom he said rushed to generate quick clinical data to secure grants, projects and promotions.

“In this case, many scientific and technical problems had not been solved, yet the principal investigator still pushed forward brashly,” Wang said.

“Cell and gene therapies are often easy to design, but the closer they get to clinical application, the harder they become. Academics often underestimate that difficulty.”

Mei suffered from Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the CHD3 gene, which can lead to developmental delays, speech impairment, intellectual disability and autistic traits. Her symptoms, however, were relatively mild.

In July 2023, Mei’s father contacted Qiu, saying the family was willing and able to cover the research and treatment costs. After months of preparation, the trial was conducted in March last year at the Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital.

Qiu’s team used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector – the most common delivery vehicle in gene therapy – to deliver a base editor into Mei’s cerebrospinal fluid, aiming to alter the disease-causing CHD3 gene in her brain.

Had it succeeded, Mei would have been the first person in the world to receive a brain-directed gene-editing therapy. Instead, she died days later of a severe immune reaction reportedly linked to the treatment.

The therapy carried high risks, mainly because of the massive viral dose required, according to several life scientists.

Because only a small fraction of these viruses reach their target cells and activate the base-editing machinery, correcting enough brain cells would demand hundreds of trillions of viral particles.

“Gene-editing therapies using AAV vectors are highly dose-dependent in terms of toxicity; and because Qiu’s therapy was injected directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, the toxicity profile may have been different,” said Cui Xiang, a senior scientist at the multinational biotech firm, Novartis.

The investigation revealed that all four monkeys receiving the therapy during preclinical testing developed moderate to severe liver damage regardless of dosage, yet the human trial was not suspended.

Cui noted that the hospital ethics committee had failed to adequately verify the safety of the technology or properly assess the treatment’s risk-benefit ratio.

The Novartis scientist pointed out that while an infant with a life-threatening metabolic disorder successfully received a personalised CRISPR gene therapy in the US in May last year, Mei’s condition was “far from life-threatening”.

This incident might “cause a long-lasting impact” on the reputation of China’s rapidly rising biotech industry, Cui said.

China’s efficiency and lower development costs have attracted international pharmaceutical giants seeking cheaper cutting-edge assets and clinical research capabilities.

But whether this incident would change how foreign investors and multinational drug makers viewed China’s biopharmaceutical sector remained to be seen and deserved close attention, Cui said.

If, in the aftermath, the Chinese government handles the case seriously and strengthens oversight through legislation – including imposing tougher penalties for violations – it may yet be able to rebuild investors’ confidence, according to Cui.

However, a bioethics expert cautioned that the full impact could only be evaluated once a comprehensive investigation was published.

“Currently, the relevant information comes mainly from the media, and an authoritative independent third-party investigation has not yet been published. If what is said in the Science report is true, this exposes many loopholes in ethics reviews, scientific regulation and institutional oversight,” said Zhai Xiaomei, executive director of the Centre for Bioethics at the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences.

“We should adhere to laws, regulations and objective facts when judging this case, and not be influenced by public opinion.

“We look forward to the national independent investigation publishing the truth as soon as possible so that further judgments can be made based on the facts.”
